Source: 7A #37
A previously healthy 32-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 1 hour after awakening with vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping. She has not had her first prenatal visit. Her pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 127/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows mild bleeding from a closed cervical os. The uterus is consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Endovaginal ultrasonography shows a gestational sac with an 8-week fetal pole and visible fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Determination of blood type and Rh factor B) Measurement of serum β-hCG concentration C) Intramuscular medroxyprogesterone therapy D) Oral progesterone therapy E) Dilatation and curettage
Correct Answer: A) Determination of blood type and Rh factor
Rh(D)-negative mothers are at high risk for developing anti-D antibodies if exposed to blood from an Rh(D)-positive fetus. This exposure can occur during delivery but also during episodes of fetomaternal bleeding during pregnancy, such as in threatened abortion (vaginal bleeding with closed cervical os prior to 20 weeks' gestation), as seen in this patient. If Rh(D) antigens from fetal circulation enter maternal circulation, the mother's immune system may form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen, resulting in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) if the fetus is Rh(D)-positive, as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when crossing the placenta. Rh(D) immune globulin prevents alloimmunization by binding to Rh(D)-positive cells entering maternal circulation, preventing antibody development. Administration is indicated at 28 weeks' gestation, after delivery of an Rh(D)-positive newborn, after any invasive procedure (e.g., amniocentesis), and after any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Therefore, determining blood type and Rh factor is the most appropriate next step to identify if Rh(D) immune globulin is necessary. Choice B (serum β-hCG measurement) is unnecessary as pregnancy is already confirmed with ultrasonographic evidence of a gestational sac with live fetal pole. Choice C (intramuscular medroxyprogesterone) and Choice D (oral progesterone) are hormonal contraceptives or used to prevent recurrent early pregnancy loss or preterm labor in those at increased risk, neither appropriate for this primigravid patient with a desired pregnancy. Choice E (dilatation and curettage) is inappropriate at this time for a desired pregnancy and is less time-sensitive than determining Rh status.
Source: 8A #22
A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. Amniocentesis for fetal karyotype at 16 weeks' gestation showed no abnormalities, and she received Rh(D) immune globulin intramuscularly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her blood group is B, Rh-negative. The fetal heart rate is 148/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent Rh sensitization in this patient? A) Measurement of cerebral artery flow by Doppler velocimetry B) Serum screening for atypical antibodies C) Administration of Rh(D) immune globulin D) Amniocentesis for anti-D antibody E) No further treatment is indicated
Correct Answer: C) Administration of Rh(D) immune globulin
Rh(D)-negative mothers are at high risk for developing anti-D antibodies if exposed to blood from an Rh(D)-positive fetus, which most commonly occurs during delivery. If Rh(D) antigens from fetal circulation enter maternal circulation, the mother's immune system may form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen. While initial exposure carries no significant complications, a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh(D)-positive fetus can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when they cross the placenta. Rh(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh(D)-positive cells that enter maternal circulation, preventing antibody development. Administration is recommended at 28 weeks' gestation, following delivery of an Rh(D)-positive newborn, with any invasive procedure (e.g., amniocentesis), and with any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Since Rh(D) immune globulin is effective for approximately 12 weeks, and this patient received it at 16 weeks during amniocentesis, she should receive an additional dose now at 28 weeks. Choice A (Doppler velocimetry) is used to evaluate fetal anemia but is not indicated here as this is the patient's first pregnancy with appropriate prophylaxis; it does not prevent future Rh sensitization. Choice B (serum screening for atypical antibodies) is not necessary at this time; while typically performed at labor, this patient has no increased risk as this is her first pregnancy with no transfusion history, and screening now would not alter management. Choice D (amniocentesis for anti-D antibody) is inappropriate because amniocentesis at this gestational age is dangerous to the fetus and would increase rather than decrease alloimmunization risk. Choice E (no further treatment) is incorrect because Rh(D) immune globulin administration is recommended at 28 weeks' gestation; without it, the patient is at risk for developing Rh(D) alloimmunization.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Female Infertility 6 questions
Source: 6A #8
A 42-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for the past year. She also reports hot flashes daily and vaginal dryness. Two years ago, she was diagnosed with cancer of the right breast and underwent lumpectomy, sentinel node biopsy, and four cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation therapy. There has been no evidence of recurrence. She has not had a menstrual period since beginning the second cycle of chemotherapy 18 months ago. She is in a monogamous relationship with a male partner and has frequent unprotected sexual intercourse. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m². Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination of the right breast shows a well-healed lumpectomy scar. Examination of the left breast shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Pelvic examination shows vaginal atrophy with no vulvar, vaginal, or cervical lesions. The uterus is normal sized, and there are no adnexal masses. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's infertility? A) Adrenal insufficiency B) Hyperprolactinemia C) Hypogonadism D) Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction E) Hypothyroidism
Correct Answer: C) Hypogonadism
This patient's infertility is most likely caused by hypogonadism secondary to chemotherapy-induced ovarian damage. Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are toxic to the ovaries and cause premature ovarian failure (POF), defined as depletion or dysfunction of ovarian follicles with cessation of menses in women under age 40. Although this patient is 42 years old, she is experiencing earlier-onset menopause secondary to chemotherapy-induced damage to her ovaries, resulting in ovarian follicle loss or dysfunction. Menopause is characterized by lack of ovarian estrogen production, resulting in manifestations such as vaginal atrophy, hot flashes, and infertility—all present in this patient. The timeline is consistent: amenorrhea began 18 months ago during her second chemotherapy cycle. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) presents with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, and skin hyperpigmentation from deficiency of aldosterone and cortisol. This patient's blood pressure is normal and she lacks these features. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice B) from a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, causing amenorrhea. However, it is typically associated with galactorrhea, which this patient does not have. Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (Choice D) can cause anovulation and amenorrhea through decreased GnRH, FSH, and LH. While this is a common cause of amenorrhea in young athletes, this patient's clinical presentation and history of chemotherapy make primary ovarian dysfunction more likely. Hypothyroidism (Choice E) presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, bradycardia, dry edematous skin, and delayed deep tendon reflexes. This patient lacks these additional signs. Educational Objective: Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are toxic to ovaries and cause early-onset ovarian follicle loss and dysfunction. This results in premature ovarian failure characterized by lack of ovarian estrogen production, presenting with vaginal atrophy, hot flashes, and infertility.
Source: 6A #40
A 22-year-old nulligravid woman has been unable to conceive for 18 months. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. A basal body temperature graph shows an increase in temperature on the 15th day of the cycle. Which of the following hormones is the most likely cause of the increase in basal body temperature on the 15th day? A) Estrogen B) Follicle-stimulating hormone C) Human chorionic gonadotropin D) Luteinizing hormone E) Progesterone
Correct Answer: E) Progesterone
The menstrual cycle consists of two main phases: the follicular phase (first half) and the luteal phase (second half). During the follicular phase, FSH and LH stimulate follicular development and estrogen production, leading to endometrial proliferation. Rising estrogen triggers an LH surge that causes ovulation around day 14 of a 28-day cycle. Following ovulation, the corpus luteum forms and secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining in preparation for embryonic implantation. Progesterone is thermogenic and directly increases basal body temperature, which is why a temperature elevation is observed in the luteal phase (after day 14-15). The basal body temperature rise serves as a clinical marker of ovulation and corpus luteum formation. Estrogen (Choice A) does not cause increases in basal body temperature, despite being elevated during the follicular phase and briefly after ovulation. Follicle-stimulating hormone (Choice B) is responsible for follicular maturation during the follicular phase and decreases following ovulation; it does not affect basal body temperature. Human chorionic gonadotropin (Choice C) is produced by the placenta after implantation to maintain the corpus luteum and would not be present immediately following ovulation before fertilization and implantation. Luteinizing hormone (Choice D) triggers ovulation and peaks just before ovulation but decreases thereafter; it does not directly cause an increase in basal body temperature. Educational Objective: The corpus luteum forms following ovulation and produces progesterone, which maintains the endometrial lining and causes an increase in basal body temperature. Progesterone deficiency can lead to luteal phase defect and infertility.
Source: 3A #18
A 26-year-old nulligravid woman has had infertility for 2 years. Menses occur at regular 25-day intervals. Serum progesterone concentration is 8 ng/ml (N>5) on menstrual day 21. An endometrial biopsy specimen on menstrual day 24 is most likely to show which of the following in this patient? A) Atrophic endometrium B) Decidual endometrium C) Hyperplasia of endometrium D) Proliferative endometrium E) Secretory endometrium
Correct Answer: E) Secretory endometrium
Secretory endometrium occurs during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, approximately 14 days prior to menstruation. The menstrual cycle consists of three endometrial stages: menses, proliferative, and secretory phases. During the follicular phase (first half of cycle), FSH and LH increase and stimulate follicle development. The developing follicle produces estrogen, which stimulates proliferation of the endometrium. An estrogen surge triggers an LH surge causing ovulation. Following ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the corpus luteum forms and secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining. In this patient, menses occur every 25 days, so day 24 is one day before expected menstruation. The serum progesterone of 8 ng/ml is within normal range (>5), confirming adequate luteal phase progesterone production. Therefore, the endometrium would be in the secretory phase, showing secretory changes in response to progesterone from the corpus luteum. Atrophic endometrium (Choice A) refers to decreased endometrial tissue seen in postmenopausal women due to estrogen deficiency. This patient has regular menses, making this unlikely. Decidual endometrium (Choice B) forms after embryo implantation and is stimulated by progesterone to form the maternal portion of the placenta. This patient is not pregnant. Hyperplasia of endometrium (Choice C) is excessive endometrial growth caused by unopposed estrogen. Risk factors include late menopause, nulliparity, early menarche, obesity, and exogenous estrogen use. This patient has regular cycles with adequate progesterone, making hyperplasia unlikely. Proliferative endometrium (Choice D) occurs during the follicular phase in response to estrogen. Since the biopsy is obtained on day 24 of a 25-day cycle (near menstruation), the endometrium would have transitioned to the secretory phase rather than remaining proliferative. Educational Objective: The endometrium progresses through three stages during each menstrual cycle. Proliferative endometrium occurs immediately after menses during the follicular phase due to increased estrogen. Following ovulation, approximately 14 days before menstruation, the endometrium transitions to secretory stage during the luteal phase in response to progesterone from the corpus luteum.
Source: 3A #45
A 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 3 years. Menses occur at irregular 35- to 42-day intervals and last 8 days. Laparoscopy 8 weeks ago showed spill from both fallopian tubes after methylene blue dye was instilled into the cervix; there was no evidence of endometriosis. Her husband has two children from a previous marriage. Pelvic examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable masses. Postcoital test shows many motile sperm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Clomiphene B) Danazol C) Leuprolide D) Levothyroxine E) Menotropins F) Progesterone
Correct Answer: A) Clomiphene
Clomiphene is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient's infertility. The clinical presentation indicates anovulation as the primary cause: irregular menstrual intervals (35-42 days) with heavy bleeding when menses occur, indicating unopposed endometrial proliferation. Laparoscopy confirmed patent fallopian tubes with normal dye spillage, and the postcoital test shows adequate sperm motility, ruling out tubal obstruction and male factor infertility. Clomiphene acts as a selective estrogen receptor antagonist at the hypothalamus, blocking negative feedback on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). This increases GnRH secretion and downstream release of FSH and LH, stimulating ovulation in anovulatory women. It is oral, making it ideal for initial therapy. Danazol (Choice B) is a synthetic androgen used for endometriosis, which was ruled out by laparoscopy. It has no role in treating anovulation-related infertility. Leuprolide (Choice C) is a GnRH agonist that can stimulate ovulation when used pulsatilely, but when used continuously it suppresses FSH and LH. Additionally, it is injectable, making it less suitable for initial pharmacotherapy compared to oral clomiphene. Levothyroxine (Choice D) treats hypothyroidism, which can cause anovulation and oligomenorrhea. However, this patient lacks other signs of hypothyroidism (bradycardia, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, depressed mood). Menotropins (Choice E) are gonadotropin mixtures (FSH and LH) that stimulate follicle production and are used in infertility treatment, but they are administered by injection and are typically reserved for cases not responding to oral agents. Progesterone (Choice F) is used to control irregular bleeding in anovulation but would prevent fertility through negative feedback on the pituitary gland. Educational Objective: Clomiphene is the first-line pharmacotherapy for infertility caused by anovulation. It acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist at the hypothalamus, preventing negative feedback on GnRH, thereby increasing FSH and LH concentrations and promoting ovulation.
Source: 7A #17
A 24-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 2 years. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals, and she has mild pain with menstrual periods. She has not had pain during sexual intercourse or discharge from her breasts. At the age of 18 years, she was hospitalized for management of pelvic inflammatory disease with intravenous antibiotic therapy. At that time, nucleic acid amplification testing of the cervix for Chlamydia trachomatis was positive, and testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae was negative. Her husband has a 2-year-old child from a previous relationship. Physical examination of the patient, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Hysterosalpingography shows bilateral hydrosalpinx and distal tubal occlusion. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the imaging findings? A) Congenital defect B) Ectopic endometrial tissue C) Immune response D) Ovarian cancer E) Tubal spasm
Correct Answer: C) Immune response
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract and pelvis from ascending migration of a bacterial infection of the lower genital tract. Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of PID. Complications of PID include tubal occlusion and infertility despite appropriate antibiotic treatment. Tubal occlusion is caused by an immune response to the infection and consequent scar formation. The fallopian tubes can fill with fluid to form bilateral hydrosalpinx, which prevents the passage of ova and sperm, resulting in infertility. Congenital defects (Choice A) such as uterine septations, bicornuate uterus, or Turner syndrome can cause infertility, but are an uncommon cause of hydrosalpinx and fallopian tube occlusion. Ectopic endometrial tissue (Choice B) causes endometriosis, which classically presents with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. While endometriosis can lead to tubal occlusion, this patient has no symptoms suggestive of endometriosis. Ovarian cancer (Choice D) classically presents indolently with abdominal distension, early satiety, and weight loss in postmenopausal women. Imaging typically shows a unilateral, heterogeneous mass rather than bilateral hydrosalpinx and fallopian tube occlusion. Tubal spasm (Choice E) causes only temporary tubal occlusion from smooth muscle contraction and would be unlikely to cause 2 years of infertility. Educational Objective: Pelvic inflammatory disease caused by sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia may lead to infertility despite appropriate treatment due to an immune response to the infection that causes scarring of the fallopian tubes, leading to fallopian tube occlusion and possible hydrosalpinx.
Source: 8A #4
A 42-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 16 months. She has had unprotected sexual intercourse with her partner four times weekly during this time. Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. Menses occur at regular 28- to 30-day intervals and last 4 days. She has not had nipple discharge or changes in her weight. She has no history of serious illness, operative procedures, or sexually transmitted diseases. She takes no medications. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Hysterosalpingography and semen analysis of her partner show no abnormalities. Reproductive studies obtained on day 3 of the patient's menstrual cycle are most likely to show an increase in which of the following concentrations? A) Estradiol B) Follicle-stimulating hormone C) Luteinizing hormone D) Prolactin E) Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Correct Answer: B) Follicle-stimulating hormone
In this 42-year-old nulligravid woman with 16 months of infertility, normal menses, normal physical examination, normal hysterosalpingography, and normal partner semen analysis, the most likely diagnosis is diminished ovarian reserve. As women age, there is progressive depletion and dysfunction of ovarian follicles. During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, FSH and LH concentrations increase to stimulate developing follicles. With diminished ovarian reserve, fewer follicles remain and they are less responsive, resulting in decreased estradiol production. This decreased negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis leads to compensatory elevation of FSH, particularly when measured on day 3 of the menstrual cycle (early follicular phase). This elevated FSH is a hallmark finding of diminished ovarian reserve. Estradiol (Choice A) concentrations decrease with age due to diminished ovarian reserve and reduced estradiol production from fewer follicles. The decreased estradiol provides less negative feedback, contributing to the elevated FSH. Luteinizing hormone (Choice C) may increase during menopause when estradiol is very low, but in this patient with regular menstrual cycles and normal ovulation, LH concentrations early in the follicular phase remain normal. Prolactin (Choice D) is unlikely to be elevated. Hyperprolactinemia inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone and FSH/LH, typically presenting with galactorrhea and amenorrhea. This patient has no nipple discharge and maintains regular menses, making hyperprolactinemia unlikely. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (Choice E) is elevated in hypothyroidism, which presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and oligomenorrhea or anovulation. This patient has no signs of hypothyroidism, making diminished ovarian reserve the most likely diagnosis. Educational Objective: Diminished ovarian reserve is a common cause of infertility in pre- and perimenopausal patients. The decreased secretion of estradiol from ovarian follicles leads to increased concentration of follicle-stimulating hormone, especially early in the follicular phase (day 3 of the menstrual cycle).
▶ Renal Urinary System Urinary Incontinence 6 questions
Source: 6A #22
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary incontinence for 4 weeks. Sometimes she is unable to reach a bathroom quickly enough after feeling the need to void. She recalls falling on wet grass 3 weeks ago but did not notice any injuries. She has gastroesophageal reflux disease and hypertension. Her medications include hydrochlorothiazide and famotidine. She stopped taking hydrochlorothiazide 7 days ago because she thought it was causing the incontinence, but the symptoms have continued. She takes no other medications. Her blood pressure is 137/92 mm Hg. Examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her incontinence? A) Adverse effect of medication B) Loss of progesterone effect on the bladder mucosa C) Obstruction of the bladder outlet D) Spinal cord injury E) Uninhibited bladder contractions
Correct Answer: E) Uninhibited bladder contractions
Urge incontinence most commonly occurs as a result of detrusor hyperreflexia or overactivity, leading to uninhibited bladder contractions. It typically presents with the urge to urinate followed by leakage of variable amounts of urine. It is most associated with neurologic disorders (e.g., multiple sclerosis, spinal stenosis, or spinal cord injuries) but may also be idiopathic. Although this patient experienced a fall, her symptoms began 1 week prior to this incident, making a traumatic neurologic cause less likely. Physical examination and laboratory studies disclose no abnormalities. Post-void urinary bladder residual volume will generally be within reference range. When evaluating urinary incontinence, it is important to rule out an associated urinary tract infection, especially when the urinary incontinence is new in onset. Treatment of urge incontinence includes strengthening the pelvic floor, weight loss, minimizing caffeine and alcohol intake, bladder training or timed voiding, and antimuscarinic agents (e.g., oxybutynin). Adverse effect of medication (Choice A) is a possible cause of urinary incontinence, especially with diuretics. However, this patient stopped taking hydrochlorothiazide 7 days ago and her symptoms have persisted, making this an unlikely cause. Loss of progesterone effect on the bladder mucosa (Choice B) does not typically cause incontinence. However, estrogen deficiency in menopause can cause atrophy and inflammation of the vagina and urethra, which can lead to overactive bladder or pelvic floor laxity with stress incontinence. Obstruction of the bladder outlet (Choice C) causes overflow incontinence, which presents with leakage of urine when the hydrostatic pressure of urine within the bladder overwhelms the closing pressure of the urethral sphincters or obstructing lesions. Causes include benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatic carcinoma, urethral injury, or urinary bladder cancer obstructing the urethral orifice. This patient has urge incontinence, not overflow incontinence. Spinal cord injury (Choice D) can lead to urge incontinence but more commonly leads to overflow incontinence caused by a neurogenic bladder. Spinal cord injury leading to urinary retention is unlikely in the absence of neurologic deficits, such as lower extremity weakness or perineal anesthesia. Educational Objective: Urge incontinence presents with urinary urgency and leakage of variable amounts of urine as a result of detrusor hyperreflexia, most commonly in neurologic disorders, although it can be idiopathic.
Source: 3A #13
A 50-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, aborta 1, has had loss of urine with coughing, straining, or lifting since the birth of her last child 9 years ago; the symptom has progressively worsened over the past 2 years. During examination, she loses urine in small spurts with coughing, but the anterior and posterior vaginal walls appear well supported. A cotton-tipped applicator placed in the urethra moves in an arch of 45 degrees with the horizontal during Valsalva maneuver. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cystocele B) Enterocele C) Femoral hernia D) Fourth-degree obstetric laceration E) Hiatal hernia F) Indirect inguinal hernia G) Rectocele H) Urethrocele
Correct Answer: H) Urethrocele
A urethrocele is caused by prolapse of the urethra into the anterior vaginal wall due to loss of proximal support from pelvic floor weakness. This is a common cause of stress urinary incontinence in multiparous women. The key diagnostic finding is urethral hypermobility, evidenced by deviation greater than 30 degrees from the horizontal of a cotton-tipped applicator placed in the urethra during straining (this patient demonstrates 45 degrees). Increased abdominal pressure causes the vesicourethral junction to move out of place, preventing sphincter closure and causing urine leakage. It can occur alone or with a cystocele. Incorrect answers: A cystocele involves bladder prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall with a visible bulge on examination and absent urethral hypermobility. An enterocele involves small bowel prolapse into the superior vaginal wall and is not associated with urinary incontinence. Femoral hernias present as painful masses on the anterior-superior thigh and do not cause incontinence. Fourth-degree obstetric lacerations cause fecal incontinence, not urinary incontinence. Hiatal hernias cause gastrointestinal symptoms (heartburn, dysphagia, regurgitation) but not urinary incontinence. Indirect inguinal hernias are more common in males and do not cause urinary incontinence. Rectoceles cause constipation and posterior vaginal wall bulging but not urinary incontinence.
Source: 5A #35
Seven days after undergoing an abdominal hysterectomy, a 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she has not voided since discharge 36 hours ago. She describes no unusual pain since discharge. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 112/74 mm Hg. Examination shows a clean incision and a soft symmetric mass that extends 25 cm above the symphysis. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, Leukocyte count 7800/mm³, Serum Urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, Creatinine 3 mg/dL. Serum electrolyte concentrations are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Pelvic hematoma B) Prerenal azotemia C) Retroperitoneal urinoma D) Ureteral transection E) Urinary retention
Correct Answer: E) Urinary retention
Postoperative urinary retention is a common medical complication of surgery presenting with anuria or oliguria, abdominal pain, difficulty initiating or maintaining a urine stream, incomplete bladder emptying, and a palpable suprapubic mass as seen in this patient. Laboratory evaluation shows increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine concentrations, though the ratio is typically less than 20 (in this case, 30:3 = 10:1). Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography showing a distended bladder. Treatment requires bladder catheterization. Risk factors include age >50 years, preexisting urinary retention, surgery length >2 hours, regional anesthesia, anticholinergic medications, and intravenous fluid resuscitation. Pelvic hematoma (Choice A) could present with a suprapubic mass and urinary retention if large enough to compress ureters or urethra, but would be associated with decreased hemoglobin concentration, making it unlikely here. Prerenal azotemia (Choice B) results from decreased renal blood flow causing decreased GFR in hypovolemia, hypotension, or renal hypoperfusion. It presents with fractional excretion of sodium <1% and BUN to creatinine ratio >20, as decreased tubular flow results in urea reabsorption but not creatinine reabsorption. Retroperitoneal urinoma (Choice C) typically results from kidney trauma causing urine extravasation into perirenal fat and retroperitoneum. It presents with flank pain evident on ultrasonography and CT scans, not a suprapubic mass. Ureteral transection (Choice D) is a risk during hysterectomy as ureters travel near uterine arteries bilaterally. It presents with abdominal pain from urinoma or ascites from urine leakage, nausea, vomiting, and fever, with complications including abscess formation and sepsis. It would not present with increased creatinine or a suprapubic mass. Educational Objective: Postoperative urinary retention is a common complication of surgery presenting with anuria or oliguria, a suprapubic mass on physical examination, and potential acute kidney injury. Ultrasonography is diagnostic, and treatment requires bladder catheterization.
Source: 4A #14
A 57-year-old woman, gravida 6, para 6, comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of immediate loss of urine when she coughs or exercises. Her children were born by vaginal delivery. Her last menstrual period was 10 years ago, and she has never received estrogen therapy. Pelvic examination shows a normal-sized uterus and ovaries. There is downward mobility of the urethral vesical junction with Valsalva maneuver. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cystocele B) Detrusor instability C) Stress incontinence D) Urethral prolapse E) Urethrocele F) Uterovaginal prolapse
Correct Answer: C) Stress incontinence
Stress urinary incontinence is the most likely diagnosis in this multiparous woman presenting with immediate loss of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, exercise). The key clinical finding is downward mobility of the urethral vesical junction with Valsalva maneuver, indicating urethral hypermobility. Pathophysiology: Multiple vaginal deliveries cause mechanical stress on the pelvic floor, leading to weakness of pelvic floor muscles and connective tissues. This compromises support of pelvic structures including the urethra and bladder. Increased abdominal pressure causes the vesicourethral junction to move inferiorly out of its normal position, preventing sphincter closure and resulting in urine leakage. Urethral hypermobility is typically demonstrated by deviation greater than 30 degrees from horizontal of a cotton-tipped applicator with straining. Why other options are incorrect: - Cystocele (A): Causes stress incontinence but presents with a bulge on the anterior vaginal wall and typically lacks urethral hypermobility - Detrusor instability (B): Causes urge incontinence (urge followed by variable leakage), not stress incontinence; associated with neurologic disorders; no urethral hypermobility - Urethral prolapse (D): Urethra visible at external urethral opening on examination - Urethrocele (E): Urethra palpable on vaginal wall on examination - Uterovaginal prolapse (F): Prolapse markedly evident on physical examination; causes heavy pelvic sensation, not immediate stress incontinence Treatment includes pelvic floor exercises (Kegel exercises), weight loss, pessary device placement, or surgical correction if conservative measures fail.
Source: 4A #29
A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of urinary urgency and frequency and occasional incontinence and a 2-month history of numbness below her waist. She has had to get up at least three times at night to void. She has not had fever, pain with urination, or cloudy urine. She has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; symptoms have included double vision 10 years ago and right leg weakness 3 years ago. Sensation to vibration is decreased over both feet. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ at the knees. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Her postvoid residual volume is 45 ml. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's urinary findings? A) Detrusor hyperreflexia B) Detrusor hypotonia C) External sphincter hyperactivity D) External sphincter incompetence E) Overflow incontinence secondary to bladder outlet obstruction
Correct Answer: A) Detrusor hyperreflexia
Urge incontinence most commonly occurs because of detrusor hyperreflexia or overactivity, presenting with the urge to urinate followed by leakage of variable amounts of urine. It is most commonly associated with neurologic disorders such as multiple sclerosis, spinal stenosis, or spinal cord injuries, but may also be idiopathic. Physical examination and laboratory studies show no abnormalities, and postvoid urinary bladder residual volumes are normal (as in this patient with 45 ml residual). When evaluating urinary incontinence, it is important to rule out urinary tract infection, especially when incontinence is new in onset. Treatment includes pelvic floor strengthening, weight loss, minimizing caffeine and alcohol intake, bladder training or timed voiding, and antimuscarinic agents such as oxybutynin. Detrusor hypotonia (Choice B) results in overflow incontinence caused by inadequate contraction of the detrusor muscle to overcome the urethral sphincters, commonly associated with spinal cord injury and autonomic neuropathy. Overflow incontinence may also occur secondary to external sphincter hyperactivity (Choice C), which can result in bladder outlet obstruction (Choice E), along with other potential causes such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral injury, or urinary bladder cancer. These conditions present with incontinence that manifests once urine builds up within the bladder lumen, subsequently overwhelming the pressure of the urethral sphincters or obstructing lesion, resulting in urine leakage. External sphincter incompetence (Choice D) results in stress incontinence, which typically presents with small amounts of urine leakage associated with increases in intraabdominal pressure (cough, heavy lifting). It is most common in multigravid women due to pelvic floor weakness and would be less likely to cause urinary urgency and frequency. This patient's presentation of urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, and normal postvoid residual volume in the setting of multiple sclerosis is classic for detrusor hyperreflexia causing urge incontinence.
Source: 8A #15
A 57-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening incontinence. Ten years ago, she had leaking of urine only with laughing or jogging. Now, she also has urine leakage with urgency interfering with her usual activities, and she has to wear absorbent pads all the time. She takes amitriptyline for migraine prophylaxis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a normal-appearing cervix but decreased rugation of the vaginal mucosa. The urethra appears normal. On Valsalva maneuver, the anterior vaginal wall bulges inferiorly. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's incontinence? A) Adverse effect of amitriptyline B) Detrusor overactivity C) Estrogen deficiency D) Impaired detrusor compliance E) Intrinsic sphincter deficiency
Correct Answer: E) Intrinsic sphincter deficiency
The correct answer is E) Intrinsic sphincter deficiency, though the explanation provided indicates this patient has stress urinary incontinence due to loss of urethral support (urethrocele). Stress urinary incontinence is common in multiparous women due to weakness of pelvic floor muscles and connective tissues from pregnancy-related mechanical stress. The key clinical findings are: (1) urine leakage with increased abdominal pressure (laughing, jogging), (2) anterior vaginal wall bulging on Valsalva (urethrocele), and (3) normal urethral appearance. These findings indicate urethral hypermobility and loss of proximal urethral support, causing the vesicourethral junction to move out of position during increased abdominal pressure, preventing sphincter closure. Incorrect answers: A) Amitriptyline's anticholinergic effects cause overflow incontinence from urinary retention, not stress incontinence with mechanical stress. B) Detrusor overactivity causes urge incontinence with uninhibited bladder contractions, typically associated with neurologic disorders, presenting with urge followed by variable urine leakage—not leakage with mechanical stress. C) Estrogen deficiency causes vaginal atrophy and overactive bladder (urgency, frequency, urge incontinence), but this patient's presentation with mechanical stress leakage and anterior vaginal wall prolapse is more consistent with stress incontinence. D) Impaired detrusor compliance is a far less common cause of stress incontinence, associated with spinal cord injury and radiation fibrosis. F) While intrinsic sphincter deficiency is another common cause of stress incontinence with similar risk factors, this patient's examination findings of urethrocele/cystocele more directly indicate loss of urethral support. Treatment includes pelvic floor exercises, weight loss, pessary device placement, or surgical correction for persistent incontinence.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Endometrial/Uterine Cancer 6 questions
Source: 6A #37
A 67-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of a rapidly increasing lower abdominal mass. Twenty years ago, she underwent radiation therapy of the pelvis for early cervical cancer; the uterus was not removed. She has been receiving estrogen and progesterone replacement therapy since then. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Examination shows a normal-appearing vulva, vagina, and cervix. The uterus measures 16 cm. She undergoes exploratory laparotomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Pathologic evaluation shows a uterine sarcoma. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this pathologic finding? A) Cigarette smoking B) Excessive estrogen C) Genetic predisposition D) Human papillomavirus infection E) Pelvic radiation therapy
Correct Answer: E) Pelvic radiation therapy
Uterine sarcoma is a rare malignant proliferation of the myometrium or stroma of the uterus that most commonly occurs in postmenopausal women and typically presents with postmenopausal bleeding, abdominal pain, bloating, and a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass. Physical examination discloses an enlarged uterus, and ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous mass with possible foci of internal necrosis. Evaluation includes endometrial biopsy and mass biopsy, with treatment involving total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, lymph node dissection, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy depending on disease extent. The most important risk factors for uterine sarcoma development are pelvic radiation therapy, history of retinoblastoma, and long-term tamoxifen use. This patient's prior pelvic radiation therapy for cervical cancer 20 years ago is the most likely underlying cause of her uterine sarcoma. Cigarette smoking (Choice A) increases risk for lung, urothelial, pancreatic, and squamous cell cancers (skin, cervical, anal) but does not increase risk for uterine sarcoma. Excessive estrogen (Choice B) plays a role in endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma due to its proliferative effect on the endometrium. This risk is decreased when used concomitantly with progesterone. The patient is on combined hormone replacement therapy, which provides protective effects. Genetic predisposition (Choice C) can increase uterine sarcoma risk in childhood retinoblastoma and the rare syndrome of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer. This patient is otherwise healthy except for her history of cervical cancer. Human papillomavirus infection (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted viral infection causing cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal carcinoma and condylomata acuminata, but does not increase uterine sarcoma risk. Educational Objective: Uterine sarcoma presents with a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass, abdominal pain, postmenopausal bleeding, and an enlarged uterus. Risk factors include a history of pelvic radiation, retinoblastoma, and long-term use of tamoxifen.
Source: 5A #5
A 47-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of two episodes of heavy vaginal bleeding during the past 3 months. Menarche was at the age of 11 years, and she has four to six menstrual periods each year with moderate flow. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glyburide and hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She has never received hormone therapy. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 79 kg (174 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m². Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a small amount of blood at the cervical os. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for endometrial cancer in this patient? A) Chronic anovulation B) Diabetes mellitus C) Early menarche D) Hypertension E) Nulliparity
Correct Answer: A) Chronic anovulation
Risk factors for endometrial cancer include chronically increased estrogen concentrations, unopposed estrogen therapy, chronic anovulation, obesity, estrogen-secreting tumors, and endometrial hyperplasia. Chronic anovulation is the strongest risk factor for endometrial cancer in this patient, as she presents with a history of irregular menses (four to six periods per year) for decades, indicating prolonged anovulation. Anovulation results in abnormal increased production of estrogen, as progesterone is primarily produced by the corpus luteum after ovulation. The patient's chronic anovulation has resulted in persistent, abnormal endometrial turnover, in which chronic estrogen production unopposed by progesterone causes proliferation of the endometrium, leading to endometrial hyperplasia and increased risk for endometrial carcinoma. Diabetes mellitus (Choice B) itself is not a direct risk factor for endometrial carcinoma, though obesity and insulin resistance increase risk through increased conversion of androgens to estrogen in adipose tissue. Early menarche (Choice C) and late menopause can be associated with increased endometrial cancer risk, but this association is not as strong as chronic anovulation, which directly results in unopposed estrogen production and endometrial hyperplasia. Hypertension (Choice D) has not been shown to independently increase endometrial cancer risk; comorbid factors such as obesity likely account for any association. Nulliparity (Choice E) increases endometrial cancer risk because of the lack of a gestational period, which typically provides an extended time without cyclic endometrial proliferation and menstruation. However, chronic anovulation is the strongest risk factor in this patient.
Source: 7A #27
A 42-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 3-week history of heavy vaginal bleeding. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. Menses have occurred twice yearly during the past 10 years. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. She has chronic hypertension treated with a calcium-channel blocking agent. She has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. She is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (158 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a thickened endometrial stripe and a 2 × 2-cm, simple left adnexal cyst. Results of an endometrial biopsy show well-differentiated endometrial adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition? A) Age B) BMI C) Cigarette smoking D) Hypertension E) Menstrual history
Correct Answer: E) Menstrual history
Endometrial cancer most commonly presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, although it can also present with abnormal uterine bleeding in premenopausal women. Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (e.g., bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). Risk factors include prolonged, unopposed exposure to estrogen, such as early menarche, late menopause, chronic anovulatory cycles (e.g., polycystic ovary syndrome), exogenous estrogen therapy, nulliparity, and obesity. This patient had early menarche (age 12) and has had approximately 10 years of likely anovulatory cycles (menstruating only twice yearly), which puts her at risk for prolonged, unopposed estrogen exposure. This estrogen exposure leads to endometrial growth, hyperplasia, and carcinoma. Age (Choice A) is not a risk factor for this patient; endometrial cancer primarily occurs in postmenopausal women over age 55, peaking at ages 60-70. BMI (Choice B) is a risk factor as androgens are converted to estrogens in adipose tissue, but this patient's BMI is within normal limits (24 kg/m²). Cigarette smoking (Choice C) has been associated with decreased risk for endometrial cancer development, in contrast to cervical cancer and other malignancies. Hypertension (Choice D) has not been shown to be directly associated with endometrial cancer development. Diagnosis is made with endometrial biopsy, hysteroscopy, or dilatation and curettage.
Source: 7A #38
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menstrual periods during the past year. Menses now occur at 2- to 14-week intervals and last 5 to 12 days; her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and lasted 12 days. Menses previously occurred at regular 30-day intervals and lasted 5 days. She is currently sexually active with two partners and uses condoms consistently. She is 157 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 104 kg (230 lb). BMI is 42 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following types of cancer? A) Breast B) Colon C) Endometrial D) Ovarian E) Pancreatic
Correct Answer: C) Endometrial
This patient presents with anovulation, characterized by irregular, heavy menstrual bleeding. Anovulation occurs when ovulation fails to occur, leaving the endometrium in the follicular phase with persistently high concentrations of estradiol. This chronic, unopposed estrogen exposure significantly increases the risk for endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. The patient's morbid obesity (BMI 42 kg/m²) further increases this risk, as androgens are converted to estrogens in peripheral adipose tissue, amplifying estrogen exposure. Risk factors for endometrial cancer include early menarche, late menopause, obesity, and chronic anovulation—all relevant to this patient. While breast cancer (Choice A) shares similar estrogen-related risk factors, chronic anovulation has a stronger association with endometrial cancer. Colon cancer (Choice B) is not associated with anovulation and typically presents with changes in stool frequency, gastrointestinal bleeding, or iron deficiency anemia. Ovarian cancer (Choice D) is associated with nulliparity, early menarche, and late menopause, but this patient's anovulation and obesity place her at greater risk for endometrial rather than ovarian cancer. Pancreatic cancer (Choice E) is associated with smoking, diabetes, obesity, and family history, but not specifically with anovulation. Diagnosis of endometrial cancer is made with endometrial biopsy, and treatment consists of hysterectomy plus chemotherapy or radiation depending on stage.
Source: 4A #34
A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of vaginal bleeding for 2 to 5 days every 2 weeks. The flow varies from light to heavy with passage of clots. Menses previously occurred at regular 25- to 29-day intervals and lasted for 7 days with heavy flow. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms inconsistently. Her mother died of colon cancer, and her maternal grandmother died of breast cancer. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m². Her temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The uterus is normal sized. The ovaries cannot be palpated. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. An endometrial biopsy specimen shows grade I adenocarcinoma with atypical endometrial hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Medroxyprogesterone therapy B) Oral contraceptive therapy C) Endometrial ablation D) Dilatation and curettage E) Hysterectomy
Correct Answer: E) Hysterectomy
Endometrial carcinoma often presents as abnormal uterine bleeding and is diagnosed by endometrial biopsy. Risk factors include obesity, prolonged estrogen use, early menarche or late menopause, nulliparity, advanced age, and family history. This patient has multiple risk factors: age 42, BMI 29 (overweight), and family history of cancer. The endometrial biopsy confirms grade I adenocarcinoma with atypical endometrial hyperplasia. When endometrial carcinoma is confined to the uterus, as in this patient, surgical excision is the first-line therapy. This is achieved through hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Hormonal contraceptives (medroxyprogesterone and oral contraceptives) are inappropriate in endometrial carcinoma as it is often hormonally dependent and could result in further proliferation. Endometrial ablation is a potential treatment for menorrhagia in premenopausal women but should only be performed after endometrial biopsy excludes hyperplasia or carcinoma. Dilation and curettage could debulk a portion of tumor but would not remove microscopic disease and is not appropriate treatment for endometrial carcinoma.
Source: 8A #46
A 46-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the office because of a 3-month history of painless vaginal bleeding that has required the use of a sanitary pad or tampon. Menarche was at the age of 13 years. Menses occur at 24- to 32-day intervals. She has no history of serious illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows a mildly enlarged uterus with a normal cervical os. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Combination oral contraceptive therapy B) Dilatation and curettage C) Endometrial biopsy D) Hysteroscopy E) Progestin-only oral contraceptive therapy F) Reassurance and follow-up examination in 6 months
Correct Answer: C) Endometrial biopsy
Endometrial cancer commonly presents with postmenopausal or perimenopausal vaginal bleeding, as in this 46-year-old patient with 3 months of painless bleeding. Risk factors for endometrial cancer include prolonged, unopposed exposure to estrogen such as early menarche (age 13 in this patient), late menopause, chronic anovulatory cycles (polycystic ovary syndrome), exogenous estrogen therapy, nulliparity, and obesity. The most appropriate next step in management is an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer via an office procedure. If a patient cannot tolerate the procedure or if the procedure sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilatation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed as alternative diagnostic approaches. Combination oral contraceptive therapy (Choice A) is effective for treating abnormal uterine bleeding secondary to anovulation but is inappropriate without first establishing a diagnosis in a perimenopausal patient with concerning symptoms for malignancy. Dilatation and curettage (Choice B) is more invasive, requiring anesthesia, and is typically reserved for patients unable to tolerate endometrial biopsy or when biopsy is nondiagnostic. Hysteroscopy (Choice D) is useful for visualizing structural causes like polyps and fibroids and can obtain biopsies, but it is more invasive than office endometrial biopsy. Progestin-only oral contraceptive therapy (Choice E) would be inappropriate to minimize bleeding without first establishing a diagnosis. Reassurance and follow-up examination in 6 months (Choice F) is incorrect because the patient has had heavy vaginal bleeding for 3 months significantly affecting her quality of life, and her symptoms are concerning for endometrial cancer. Delaying diagnosis would increase morbidity and mortality associated with possible underlying malignancy. Educational Objective: Endometrial cancer can present with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding or abnormal uterine bleeding in perimenopausal women. Risk factors include prolonged, unopposed estrogen exposure, early menarche, late menopause, chronic anovulatory cycles, exogenous estrogen therapy, and nulliparity. Diagnosis is made with endometrial biopsy via office procedure.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Non-Lymphogranuloma Venereum Chlamydia Trachomatis 5 questions
Source: 6A #25
A 37-year-old woman with a 2-week history of urinary frequency, urgency, and burning comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. One week ago, urinalysis showed 20-50 WBC/hpf with no protein, glucose, bacteria, ketones, or crystals. Urine dipstick showed trace blood. Her symptoms have not improved with 1 week of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy. Pelvic examination shows urethral tenderness. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis remains unchanged. In addition to urine culture, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Cytologic examination of suprapubic urine aspirate B) Gram stain of the cervical mucus C) PPD skin test D) Throat culture E) Urethral culture for chlamydia
Correct Answer: E) Urethral culture for chlamydia
A patient with persistent symptoms of urethritis (urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria) despite adequate treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole raises concern for sexually transmitted infections, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Both organisms cause urethritis and can progress to cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and tubo-ovarian abscess if untreated. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular pathogen that does not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain, resulting in absence of visualized bacteria despite significant pyuria (20-50 WBC/hpf). This presentation of pyuria without bacteriuria is classic for chlamydial urethritis. Diagnosis requires urethral culture and/or nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) to detect Chlamydia species. Treatment consists of azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone to cover potential Neisseria gonorrhoeae coinfection. Choice A (Cytologic examination of suprapubic urine aspirate) is inappropriate as suprapubic aspiration is an invasive method reserved for children unable to urinate or undergo transurethral catheterization. Choice B (Gram stain of cervical mucus) may help diagnose cervicitis but would not disclose urethritis diagnosis in a patient with isolated urethral symptoms and no mucopurulent discharge or cervical findings. Choice C (PPD skin test) evaluates tuberculosis, which presents with fever, cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, and weight loss—not urethritis. Choice D (Throat culture) is inappropriate without pharyngeal symptoms, though chlamydia can cause pharyngitis. Educational Objective: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen that does not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain. Diagnosis of chlamydial urethritis requires urethral culture and/or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves azithromycin or doxycycline combined with ceftriaxone for potential gonococcal coinfection.
Source: 3A #27
A sexually active 21-year-old college student requests an oral contraceptive. There are no contraindications based on her medical history. In addition to a Pap smear, which of the following screening tests is most appropriate? A) Test for Chlamydia trachomatis B) Liver function tests C) Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration D) Assay for serum HIV antibodies E) Serologic test for syphilis
Correct Answer: A) Test for Chlamydia trachomatis
Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis, as well as for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) for all sexually active patients under 25 years old. C. trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge, but can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Gram stain of urine or urethral/vaginal discharge typically does not reveal organisms, as C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism. Diagnosis is made with nucleic acid amplification testing, and treatment consists of azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection. Liver function tests (Choice B) are not indicated as the patient has no risk factors for or symptoms of liver dysfunction, and baseline levels are not necessary prior to initiating oral contraceptives, as liver toxicity is exceedingly rare. Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice C) is used to diagnose diabetes mellitus and is not warranted based on USPSTF guidelines for this patient's demographic, as she lacks signs or symptoms of diabetes. Assay for serum HIV antibodies (Choice D) may eventually be appropriate, as the USPSTF and CDC recommend testing for everyone between teenage years and age 65 at least once. However, this patient would benefit more from testing for C. trachomatis at this time, as it is more common and more frequently presents asymptomatically. Serologic test for syphilis (Choice E) is not recommended in asymptomatic patients. The patient is not experiencing symptoms of primary syphilis (genital lesion), secondary syphilis (maculopapular rash, condyloma lata), or tertiary syphilis (neurosyphilis or aortitis). Educational Objective: Annual screening for C. trachomatis is recommended in all sexually active patients under 25 years of age. It typically presents with urethral or vaginal discharge, dysuria, and dyspareunia if it has progressed to cervicitis. Complications include epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Treatment is azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone.
Source: 7A #24
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 5-month history of painful menstruation that causes her to occasionally miss school. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago, and her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. During questioning with her mother present, the patient says that she has never been sexually active. However, after the mother leaves the room, the patient indicates that she is sexually active. Physical and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test to obtain at this visit? A) Complete blood count B) Determination of rubella status C) Pregnancy test D) Screening for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae E) Urinalysis
Correct Answer: D) Screening for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae is recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force for all sexually active patients under age 25 years. C. trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, dyspareunia, and urethral or vaginal discharge. N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted infection that presents most commonly with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. However, both infections can also be asymptomatic, thus the recommendation for screening. Complications include cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, and long-term issues with fertility. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test. Treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline for chlamydia and ceftriaxone for gonorrhea. Choice A (Complete blood count) is not necessary in this patient. A complete blood count is useful in the evaluation of infection, which may present with leukocytosis, and in anemia. This patient has no signs of infection, with her painful menstruation more likely secondary to primary dysmenorrhea. She also has no history of menorrhagia or other health issues that would predispose her to anemia. Choice B (Determination of rubella status) is not necessary at this visit but should be determined prior to the patient becoming pregnant. This is because rubella infection of a pregnant patient can cause sensorineural deafness, neurodevelopmental delay, congenital cardiac defects, microcephaly, and extramedullary hematopoiesis in the fetus. Choice C (Pregnancy test) is also indicated for this patient but is not more appropriate at this visit than sexually transmitted infection testing based on this presentation. If the results of this patient's testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae are positive, pregnancy status should then be established to determine safe antibiotic choices. Choice E (Urinalysis) is used in the evaluation of suspected urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis. Uncomplicated cystitis presents with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort, whereas pyelonephritis causes fever and flank pain in addition to these symptoms. This patient has no symptoms of a urinary tract infection, making a urinalysis unnecessary. Educational Objective: Annual screening for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae is recommended for all sexually active patients under age 25 years. Chlamydia typically presents with urethral or vaginal discharge, dysuria, urethritis, and dyspareunia. Gonorrhea commonly causes mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. However, both infections may also remain asymptomatic. Chlamydia is treated with azithromycin or doxycycline. Gonorrhea is treated with ceftriaxone.
Source: 8A #19
A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of urinary urgency and frequency and pain with urination. She has not had fever, chills, or flank pain. She has no history of serious illness. Menses occur at regular 30-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 19 days ago. She is sexually active with one partner and uses an oral contraceptive. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent discharge on the cervix; there is no vaginal discharge. Examination of a urine sample shows 1-2 RBCs, numerous WBCs, and no bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Acyclovir B) Azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone C) Fluconazole D) Metronidazole E) Zidovudine (AZT)
Correct Answer: B) Azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone
A patient with symptoms of urethritis (urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria) and a urinalysis with no evidence of urinary tract infection raises concern for sexually transmitted infections secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Both organisms can cause urethritis and, if left untreated, can progress to cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and tubo-ovarian abscess. In urinary tract infections, urinalysis typically shows white blood cells, bacteria, and positive leukocyte esterase and/or nitrites, all of which are absent in this patient. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular pathogen and does not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain, resulting in absence of visualized bacteria. Diagnosis involves urethral culture and/or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering potential Neisseria gonorrhoeae coinfection. Acyclovir (Choice A) treats herpes genitalis caused by herpes simplex virus, which presents with multiple small painful vesicles that erode to shallow ulcers, often with fever and inguinal lymphadenopathy, but does not cause mucopurulent discharge. Fluconazole (Choice C) treats vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans, presenting with vulvar erythema, burning, vaginal pruritus, and thick white vaginal discharge, but does not cause urethritis. Metronidazole (Choice D) treats trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis. Trichomoniasis presents with pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and green, frothy, malodorous discharge. Bacterial vaginosis causes gray, thin, malodorous discharge. Neither presents with urinary frequency, urgency, or dysuria as primary symptoms. Zidovudine (AZT) (Choice E) is used in combination with other antiretroviral medications for active HIV infection, which commonly presents with flu-like illness (fever, malaise, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, sore throat). This patient's urinalysis shows no signs of infection and she has no other symptoms of HIV, making AZT treatment inappropriate. Educational Objective: Chlamydia trachomatis may cause urethritis presenting with urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria in the setting of a normal urinalysis. Because it is an obligate intracellular pathogen, it will not appear on urinalysis or Gram stain but is diagnosed with urethral culture or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering potential Neisseria gonorrhoeae coinfection.
Source: 8A #49
A 15-year-old girl is examined at a juvenile detention facility clinic for an inmate health examination. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Immunizations are up-to-date. She was sexually active with one male partner 3 months ago; they used condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. She is at the 90th percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient? A) Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis B surface antibody assays B) Human papillomavirus nucleic acid testing C) Pap smear D) Rapid plasma reagin E) Repeat hepatitis B vaccine series F) Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Correct Answer: F) Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual screening for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae for all sexually active patients under age 25 years. This patient is 15 years old and sexually active with inconsistent condom use, making her a candidate for screening. Both infections can present with urethritis, dysuria, dyspareunia, and urethral or vaginal discharge, but importantly, both can also be asymptomatic, necessitating screening. Complications include cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, and long-term fertility issues. Diagnosis is made with nucleic acid amplification testing. Treatment consists of azithromycin or doxycycline for chlamydia and ceftriaxone for gonorrhea. Incorrect choices: Hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody assays (Choice A) are not recommended for asymptomatic screening in vaccinated patients. HPV nucleic acid testing (Choice B) is typically not recommended until age 30 because infections in younger patients are often self-limited. Pap smear (Choice C) is not recommended until age 21 and is not indicated at age 15. Rapid plasma reagin (Choice D) is a serologic test for syphilis and is not recommended for asymptomatic patients without symptoms of primary, secondary, or tertiary syphilis. Repeat hepatitis B vaccine series (Choice E) is unnecessary as the patient is up-to-date on vaccinations and demonstrates immunity.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Complications of cesarean delivery 5 questions
Source: 6A #28
Immediately after cesarean delivery because of abruptio placentae, a 25-year-old woman loses consciousness. She had an estimated blood loss of 1200 ml. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Examination shows frothy pink sputum. Bilateral wheezes are heard on auscultation. The fundus is firm. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 7 g/dl, Leukocyte count 8000/mm³, Platelet count 60,000/mm³, Bleeding time 9 min, Prothrombin time 20 sec (INR=2), Partial thromboplastin time 55 sec, Thrombin time 5 sec, Plasma fibrinogen 100 mg/dl (N=200-400), Fibrin split products 80 µg/ml (N<10). An x-ray of the chest shows pulmonary edema. An ECG shows tachycardia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Amniotic fluid embolism B) Eclampsia C) Hypovolemic shock D) Pulmonary embolism E) Septic shock
Correct Answer: A) Amniotic fluid embolism
Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare and potentially fatal complication of childbirth caused by amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It most commonly occurs during delivery or in the immediate postpartum period. This patient presents with the classic triad of acute onset shortness of breath, altered mental status/unconsciousness, and bilateral wheezing immediately after cesarean delivery. Vital signs show tachycardia, hypoxia, and severe hypotension (60/40 mm Hg). Chest x-ray demonstrates pulmonary edema with frothy pink sputum consistent with acute pulmonary edema. The patient can rapidly decompensate into cardiovascular collapse and cardiopulmonary arrest. A critical finding is the coagulation abnormality pattern consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC): thrombocytopenia (60,000/mm³), prolonged PT (INR=2) and PTT (55 sec), decreased fibrinogen (100 mg/dl), and elevated fibrin split products (80 µg/ml). This consumptive coagulopathy with rapid fibrinolysis is a hallmark complication of amniotic fluid embolism. Treatment is supportive with fluids, blood products, and mechanical ventilation. Eclampsia (Choice B) presents with hypertension, proteinuria, headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, and seizures after 20 weeks' gestation or postpartum. While it can cause pulmonary edema, it would not explain the acute bilateral wheezing, frothy pink sputum, or the severe coagulation abnormalities seen here. Hypovolemic shock (Choice C) results from significant intravascular volume reduction from hemorrhage, dehydration, or gastrointestinal losses. Although this patient had 1200 ml blood loss, her hemoglobin (7 g/dl) remains above typical transfusion threshold. More importantly, hypovolemic shock would not explain the pulmonary edema or the DIC-pattern coagulation abnormalities. Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) presents with shortness of breath, tachycardia, hypoxia, and hypotension if massive, often with hemoptysis if infarction occurs. It typically originates from deep venous thrombosis of the lower extremities. It would not cause the coagulation abnormalities or DIC pattern seen in this patient. Septic shock (Choice E) results from decreased organ perfusion from overwhelming infection with hypotension. It presents with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis. The presentation is typically less abrupt (hours to days) compared to amniotic fluid embolism (minutes to hours). This patient is afebrile with normal leukocyte count, making septic shock unlikely. Educational Objective: Amniotic fluid embolism classically occurs during delivery or immediately postpartum from amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It presents with acute shortness of breath, altered mental status, hypoxia, and hypotension. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, cardiovascular collapse, and maternal or fetal death. Laboratory findings in DIC include thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, prolonged PT and PTT, and decreased fibrinogen.
Source: 5A #37
An obese 35-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, with type 2 diabetes mellitus has a cesarean delivery because of fetal macrosomia. Forty-eight hours later, there is profuse serosanguineous drainage from the midline skin incision. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Dehiscence B) Evisceration C) Hematoma D) Infection E) Vesicocutaneous fistula
Correct Answer: A) Dehiscence
Postoperative complications following an abdominal incision include bleeding, infection, dehiscence, hematoma formation, and seroma formation, as well as damage to nearby structures. Dehiscence occurs when the fascial tension is greater than the sutures holding the two layers of fascia together, which leads to disruption of the connection and leakage of the contents below the suture line. In abdominal incisions, dehiscence can occur at the fascial plane while the skin sutures remain intact. It typically presents with prominent serosanguinous drainage, along with a possible bulge at the surgical site, as seen in this patient 48 hours post-cesarean delivery. Ultrasonography and CT scans can be used to further delineate the diagnosis if there is difficulty in assessing the surgical site with physical examination. Treatment involves operative exploration of the wound site to repair the fascial dehiscence, as this places the patient at an increased risk for poor wound healing, wound infection, and evisceration, which is a surgical emergency. Risk factors include elderly age, male gender, wound infection, obesity, malignancy, hypoalbuminemia, and chronic glucocorticoid use. This patient has obesity as a significant risk factor. Evisceration (Choice B) typically occurs following a complete fascial dehiscence of an abdominal incision, in which the internal abdominopelvic organs (e.g., bowel) are expelled from the surgical site and are visible on examination. It is a surgical emergency and requires emergent operative management to close the wound. Hematoma (Choice C) typically presents with induration, pain, and bloody drainage of the wound. It can be managed expectantly or drained depending on size. It would be unlikely to present with simple serosanguinous drainage. Wound infection (Choice D) is a common complication of surgery and presents with erythema, warmth, tenderness, and induration with purulent wound drainage. It typically requires antibiotic treatment and potentially surgical debridement or irrigation depending on the severity and extent of infection. As this patient's wound is draining serosanguinous rather than purulent fluid, it is less likely a result of a wound infection. Vesicocutaneous fistula (Choice E) refers to a fistulous tract created between the bladder and outside surface of the body through the skin. It would present with the drainage of urine at the wound site, rather than serosanguinous discharge. While possible, this is a relatively unlikely complication of a cesarean delivery. Educational Objective: Postoperative wound dehiscence typically presents with serosanguinous drainage at the surgical wound site and increases the risk for evisceration, which is a surgical emergency. It requires operative management for wound closure.
Source: 5A #41
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 39 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor after spontaneous rupture of membranes. The amniotic fluid is clear, and the fetal heart tracing shows a rate of 150/min with no evidence of deceleration. Her first pregnancy ended in vaginal delivery at term, and her second pregnancy ended in cesarean delivery for breech presentation at term. Eight hours later, the cervix is 100% effaced and 10 cm dilated; the vertex is at O station. The fetal heart rate is now 140/min, but there is a sudden decrease in fetal heart rate variability followed by a prolonged fetal heart rate deceleration to 60-70/min for 3 minutes. The patient develops increasing lower abdominal pain. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A) Abruptio placentae B) Maternal supine position C) Umbilical cord compression D) Uterine rupture E) Variable fetal heart rate deceleration
Correct Answer: D) Uterine rupture
Uterine rupture is a dangerous obstetric complication wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. The clinical presentation in this case is highly suggestive: acute onset of severe lower abdominal pain during labor in a patient with a prior cesarean delivery (VBAC attempt), combined with sudden loss of fetal heart rate variability and prolonged bradycardia (60-70/min). These findings reflect both maternal and fetal hemodynamic instability. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after cesarean delivery (VBAC), multiparity, and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. The sudden loss of fetal station is a highly suggestive finding, and fetal parts may be palpable above the fundus with Leopold maneuvers. Treatment is emergent laparotomy. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) presents with abdominal or pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, and tetanic contractions. This patient has no vaginal bleeding, making abruption less likely. The acute onset of symptoms during labor with prior cesarean delivery history is more concerning for uterine rupture. Maternal supine position (Choice B) may lead to aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus, resulting in maternal hypotension, syncope, tachycardia, pallor, and diaphoresis. However, the abrupt onset of pain during delivery with sudden change in fetal hemodynamics is more consistent with uterine rupture than aortocaval compression.
