Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 16-week gestation. The fetal heart rate is 140/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Bed rest B) Cervical cerclage C) 17α-hydroxyprogesterone therapy D) Nifedipine therapy E) Terbutaline therapy
Correct Answer: C) 17α-hydroxyprogesterone therapy
This patient has a significant history of preterm delivery (at 32 and 34 weeks) and is now at 16 weeks' gestation with an uncomplicated pregnancy. For patients with a history of preterm delivery at high risk for recurrence, progesterone supplementation (17α-hydroxyprogesterone therapy) is the most appropriate preventive intervention. Progesterone is typically started at 16-20 weeks' gestation and continued until term, as it inhibits uterine contractility and helps support the developing fetus. Bed rest (Choice A) is inappropriate for prevention of preterm labor at this stage of gestation. While bed rest may be recommended for patients already in active preterm labor, it is neither practical nor effective for prevention and would not prevent preterm labor in this patient. Cervical cerclage (Choice B) is used for cervical insufficiency (the inability of the cervix to contain pregnancy without contractions or labor), not for prevention of preterm labor in patients with a history of preterm delivery. Nifedipine (Choice D) and terbutaline (Choice E) are tocolytic agents that relax uterine smooth muscle and decrease uterine contractions. These are used for treatment of active preterm labor, not for prevention in asymptomatic patients. Educational Objective: Preterm labor refers to labor onset before 37 weeks' gestation. Risk factors include prior preterm labor, maternal diabetes, extremes of age, placenta previa or abruption, cervical insufficiency, multiple gestations, and maternal tobacco use. For patients with a history of preterm delivery, progesterone supplementation (17α-hydroxyprogesterone therapy) started at 16-20 weeks' gestation and continued until term is used to prevent recurrence. For patients presenting in active preterm labor, treatment includes bed rest, hydration, tocolysis, corticosteroids (if <34 weeks), and magnesium (if <32 weeks) for neuroprotection.
Source: 4A #28
A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 41 weeks' gestation has had ruptured membranes without contractions for 8 hours. Her first infant weighed 4422 g (9 lb 12 oz) at birth. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated except for gestational diabetes, which was diagnosed at 26 weeks' gestation and has been well controlled with diet. Initial assessment shows a fundal height of 40 cm. On ultrasonography, the estimated fetal weight is 3714 g (8 lb 3 oz). The cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50% effaced. The fetal heart rate is within normal limits. Labor is induced with intravenous oxytocin. Four hours later, her cervix is 4 cm dilated and completely effaced. Continuous epidural anesthesia is administered. Two hours later, the fetal heart rate pattern demonstrates late decelerations with each contraction. The contractions occur every minute, last 45 seconds, and are 75 mm Hg at their peak. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern? A) Epidural anesthesia B) Fetal macrosomia C) Gestational diabetes D) Oxytocin administration E) Postdates pregnancy
Correct Answer: D) Oxytocin administration
The correct answer is D) Oxytocin administration. Oxytocin is used to induce or augment labor by stimulating uterine contractions. However, excessive oxytocin causes uterine tachysystole (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes) with prolonged and intensified contractions and inadequate relaxation time between contractions. This pattern is evident in this patient: contractions occurring every minute (60 per 10 minutes) lasting 45 seconds at 75 mm Hg. Tachysystole causes compression of placental blood vessels, leading to uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia, which presents as late decelerations on fetal heart tracing (gradual decreases in fetal heart rate beginning after the peak of uterine contraction). Management includes discontinuing oxytocin and monitoring the fetal heart tracing; if late decelerations persist, urgent cesarean delivery may be indicated. Uterine rupture is another potential complication of tachysystole. Epidural anesthesia (Choice A) can cause uteroplacental insufficiency only if it results in maternal hypotension and does not cause changes in uterine contraction patterns. Fetal macrosomia (Choice B) is associated with gestational diabetes and can cause shoulder dystocia, prolonged labor, and postpartum uterine atony, but does not cause tachysystole. Gestational diabetes (Choice C) increases the risk for uteroplacental insufficiency and late decelerations, and can cause preterm labor, polyhydramnios, and macrosomia, but does not cause tachysystole. Postdates pregnancy (Choice E) can be associated with macrosomia, oligohydramnios, and uteroplacental insufficiency, but given the temporal relationship between oxytocin initiation and the development of the abnormal contraction pattern with late decelerations, oxytocin administration is the more likely cause. Educational Objective: Oxytocin-induced uterine tachysystole (>5 contractions in 10 minutes) with prolonged, intense contractions and inadequate relaxation causes placental blood vessel compression, uteroplacental insufficiency, fetal hypoxemia, and late decelerations on fetal heart tracing. Management includes discontinuation of oxytocin and close fetal monitoring.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Endometriosis 4 questions
Source: 6A #46
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has had increasingly severe pelvic pain and dyspareunia over the past 8 months; during menses, the pain worsens and she has occasional episodes of diarrhea. Pelvic examination shows a normal vagina and cervix with no suspicious lesions. The uterus is normal-sized, retroverted, and fixed, and there is induration and nodularity of the posterior wall of the uterus and cul-de-sac. There are no palpable adnexal masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test? A) Measurement of serum CA 125 concentration B) Barium enema C) CT scan of the pelvis D) MRI of the pelvis E) Laparoscopy
Correct Answer: E) Laparoscopy
Endometriosis refers to the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus and classically presents with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Physical examination findings include palpable nodularity of the posterior uterus and cul-de-sac along with fixation of the uterus to nearby structures, making it immobile, as demonstrated in this patient. The gold standard diagnostic test is diagnostic laparoscopy, which directly visualizes endometriotic implant lesions on the peritoneum and confirms the diagnosis. Treatment options include oral contraceptive therapy or danazol, which acts as a synthetic androgen and partial androgen receptor agonist to prevent ovarian secretion of estradiol. Measurement of serum CA 125 concentration (Choice A) is used for suspected ovarian malignancy and monitoring disease progression, not for diagnosing endometriosis, as it is not elevated in this condition. Barium enema (Choice B) evaluates intraluminal large bowel pathology and is not appropriate for suspected endometriosis. CT scan of the pelvis (Choice C) and MRI of the pelvis (Choice D) may be used after physical examination and ultrasonography have failed to provide necessary information and may suggest the diagnosis, but neither definitively confirms endometriosis. Educational Objective: Endometriosis is caused by ectopic endometrial gland implantation presenting with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Diagnosis is definitively achieved with laparoscopy to visualize endometrial implants on the peritoneum.
Source: 5A #49
A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician with her partner because she has been unable to conceive for 18 months. She also has had moderate dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days. Examination of the patient and her partner, including physical examination, semen analysis, testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, serial urinalyses to document luteinizing hormone surge, in-phase endometrial biopsy, and hysterosalpingography, shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's infertility? A) Endometriosis B) Hyperprolactinemia C) Hypothyroidism D) Inadequate cervical mucus E) Pelvic adhesions
Correct Answer: A) Endometriosis
Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Local inflammatory responses to ectopic endometrial cells cause abdominal and pelvic pain, which may be severe and is often cyclic in response to fluctuating hormone concentrations during the menstrual cycle. The standard for diagnosis is diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for visual evidence of ectopic endometriotic implant lesions and permits obtaining samples for histology. Chronic inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes leads to infertility in many women with endometriosis. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice B) causes growth of glandular breast tissue and presents with unexpected lactation (galactorrhea), often arising from a hyperfunctioning anterior pituitary microadenoma. Dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia are not typical symptoms of hyperprolactinemia. Hypothyroidism (Choice C) presents with weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. It may result in amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea but does not explain the patient's dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia. Inadequate cervical mucus (Choice D) is a cause of infertility but is not associated with symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia, which are more suggestive of endometriosis. Pelvic adhesions (Choice E) are a delayed result of surgery, infection (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease), or chronic inflammation from severe endometriosis. While pelvic adhesions may be present and cause abdominal pain in some patients with endometriosis, infertility in most cases is directly related to ectopic endometrial tissue and associated inflammation and scarring within the fallopian tubes, rather than pelvic adhesions alone. Educational Objective: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Many patients experience infertility as a result of inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes.
Source: 7A #6
A 33-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for a premarital examination. Menses occur at regular intervals with occasional spotting 3 days before onset. She has had occasional dyspareunia over the past 8 months. Pelvic examination shows normal external genitalia and a normal-sized uterus. 1-cm tender nodules are palpated on the right uterosacral ligament. This woman is at increased risk for which of the following conditions? A) Endometrial cancer B) Endometritis C) Infertility D) Leiomyosarcoma E) Recurrent abortion
Correct Answer: C) Infertility
Infertility is the most common complication of endometriosis, which is the presence of ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus. This ectopic tissue may occur close to the uterus (on the cervix, within fallopian tubes, on the broad ligament, or on an ovary) or distantly (on visceral peritoneal surfaces of intestines or rectum, within the peritoneal cavity, or within the thorax). Endometrial tissue remains hormonally sensitive, and symptoms fluctuate cyclically as the tissue progresses through proliferative and secretory phases, then sloughs during menses. Classic symptoms include chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Pelvic examination typically shows tenderness of the uterine wall and surrounding structures with possible uterine immobility from pelvic adhesions. Endometrial implants on the cervix or vaginal wall may be visible. Infertility results from tubal obstruction or architectural changes from chronic inflammation and scarring. Definitive diagnosis is made through laparoscopy to visualize and sample endometriotic implants. Endometrial cancer (Choice A) typically presents with postmenopausal uterine bleeding and is associated with prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure, early menarche, late menopause, polycystic ovary syndrome, exogenous estrogen therapy, nulliparity, and obesity—not endometriosis. Endometritis (Choice B) is acute bacterial infection of the endometrium, commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis in young sexually active women, presenting with fever, chills, nausea, abdominal pain, uterine bleeding, and foul-smelling discharge. Endometriosis does not increase endometritis risk. Leiomyosarcoma (Choice D) is a rare uterine myometrial malignancy presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, and bloating, with risk factors including pelvic radiation, tamoxifen therapy, and familial conditions—not endometriosis. Recurrent abortion (Choice E) refers to recurrent fetal loss before 20 weeks with risk factors including age >35 years, prior fetal demise, uterine anatomic distortion, diabetes, thyroid disorders, coagulopathies, and substance abuse. While endometriosis causes infertility, it less commonly causes spontaneous abortion. Educational Objective: Endometriosis presents with chronic dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and dyschezia caused by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, with infertility being the most common complication.
Source: 4A #44
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has had increasingly severe dysmenorrhea over the past 2 years and dyspareunia and pain with defecation for 6 months. She has been unable to conceive for 2 years. Pelvic examination shows a fixed, tender, retroverted uterus, nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments, and tender adnexa bilaterally; there is a 5-cm, tender, cystic, right adnexal mass. A pregnancy test is negative. A) Adenomyosis B) Adnexal torsion C) Appendicitis D) Diverticulitis E) Ectopic pregnancy F) Endometriosis G) Endometritis H) Inflammatory bowel disease I) Leiomyomata uteri J) Ovarian carcinoma K) Pelvic inflammatory disease L) Primary dysmenorrhea M) Renal calculus N) Ruptured corpus luteum cyst O) Spontaneous abortion
Correct Answer: F) Endometriosis
Endometriosis is the presence of ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus. It may occur close to the uterus (on cervix, within fallopian tube, on broad ligament, or ovary) or distantly (on visceral peritoneal surface of intestines or rectum, within peritoneal cavity, or thorax). Endometrial tissue remains hormonally sensitive, with symptoms fluctuating cyclically as tissue progresses through proliferative and secretory phases then sloughs during menses. Classic symptoms include chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia (pain with defecation), and infertility. Physical examination findings include tenderness of affected structures, fixed retroverted uterus, nodular uterosacral ligaments, and adnexal masses (endometriomas). Diagnosis is definitively made through laparoscopy to visualize and sample endometriotic implants. Adenomyosis (A) involves endometrial glands within myometrium, typically in multiparous women, presenting with menorrhagia and enlarged boggy uterus. Adnexal torsion (B) causes acute severe pain from compromised blood supply. Appendicitis (C) presents with acute periumbilical pain migrating to right lower quadrant with fever and anorexia. Diverticulitis (D) causes left lower quadrant pain with fever and bloody bowel movements. Ectopic pregnancy (E) presents acutely with severe abdominopelvic pain and vaginal bleeding when ruptured; negative pregnancy test excludes this. Endometritis (G) is acute bacterial infection with foul-smelling discharge and fever. Inflammatory bowel disease (H) presents with chronic crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Leiomyomata uteri (I) cause menorrhagia with irregularly shaped uterus. Ovarian carcinoma (J) presents indolently in older postmenopausal patients. Pelvic inflammatory disease (K) presents acutely with fever and cervical motion tenderness. Primary dysmenorrhea (L) is painful menses without other known cause. Renal calculus (M) causes acute flank pain radiating to groin. Ruptured corpus luteum cyst (N) causes acute unilateral pain without infertility. Spontaneous abortion (O) presents with vaginal bleeding and cramping before 20 weeks. Educational Objective: Endometriosis presents with chronic dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, infertility, and dyschezia caused by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Osteoporosis 4 questions
Source: 3A #14
A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Two weeks ago, prednisone therapy was begun because of a flare-up of her disease; this is her third course of prednisone during the past 18 months. Today, the patient is feeling well. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her only other medications are vitamin D and calcium. She has no other history of serious illness, and there is no family history of serious illness. She has no known allergies. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Her pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent osteoporosis in this patient? A) Alendronate now B) Calcitonin now C) Estrogen and progesterone now D) Estrogen alone at the onset of menopause E) Raloxifene now
Correct Answer: A) Alendronate now
Glucocorticoids significantly alter calcium metabolism by decreasing gastrointestinal calcium absorption, enhancing osteoclastogenesis, and inhibiting osteoblast differentiation. Primary prevention of osteoporosis is indicated in patients with chronic glucocorticoid use to prevent premature, pathologic fragility fractures. Vitamin D and calcium are recommended for all patients at low risk of fracture. In addition to calcium and vitamin D, patients at moderate to high risk of fracture are also treated with oral bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate). Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce fracture risk and increase bone density and are the mainstay of osteoporosis treatment and prevention in patients at moderate to high risk for bone mineral density loss because of corticosteroid use. Bisphosphonates act to inhibit the action of osteoclasts, thereby preventing bone loss. Calcitonin (Choice B) is a peptide hormone that decreases osteoclast activity and osteoclast differentiation, thereby reducing bone resorption. However, it is significantly less effective than bisphosphonates and is not a first-line treatment for osteoporosis or prevention of glucocorticoid-induced bone loss. Estrogen and progesterone now (Choice C) and estrogen therapy alone at the onset of menopause (Choice D) are no longer generally recommended for the prevention or treatment of osteoporosis; the Women's Health Initiative showed that hormone therapy increases the risk of thromboembolic events in postmenopausal women. In low-risk cases, estrogen therapy may still be used for a short duration and at a low dose for treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women less than 60 years of age who have a low risk of stroke or blood clot and who wish to treat symptoms of menopause. Raloxifene (Choice E) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and as an antagonist in breast and endometrial tissue. It may be used for prevention of osteoporosis in women at high risk for breast cancer; however, it carries an increased risk for venous thromboembolic events. Therefore, it is not ideal in a patient predisposed to thrombosis due to a known inflammatory state (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) and at risk of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Educational Objective: Bisphosphonates, along with calcium and vitamin D, decrease the risk of osteoporosis and reduce bone mineral density loss in osteoporotic patients. Prolonged glucocorticoid use is a key risk factor in the development of osteoporosis due to decreased gastrointestinal calcium absorption, increased osteoclastogenesis, and diminished differentiation of osteoblasts.
Source: 5A #50
A 69-year-old nulliparous white woman has the sudden onset of severe pain in the upper back after sitting down. She has hypertension treated with a β-adrenergic blocking agent. She drinks one alcoholic beverage with dinner each night. An x-ray of the spine shows a compression fracture of the 10th thoracic vertebra. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this condition? A) Alcohol use B) Hypertension C) Nulliparity D) Race E) Use of a β-adrenergic blocking agent
Correct Answer: D) Race
Osteoporosis is a progressive loss of bone mineral density leading to decreased bone strength and fragility fractures. This patient experienced a thoracic compression fracture with minimal trauma (sitting down), characteristic of osteoporotic bone. The strongest predisposing factor is race (Caucasian ethnicity). Osteoporosis disproportionately affects postmenopausal women of Caucasian descent due to genetic factors influencing peak bone mass. Males develop higher peak bone mass during the first 30 years of life and retain higher bone mineral density longer than females. Both testosterone and estrogen stimulate osteoblasts and maintain bone mineral density; loss of estrogen in postmenopausal women accelerates bone mass loss. Other risk factors include female gender, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, endocrine disorders (hypercortisolism, hyperparathyroidism), sedentary lifestyle, and low estrogen states. Alcohol use (Choice A) has negative effects on bone mineral density primarily with heavy, chronic drinking over many years through diuretic effects and electrolyte loss including calcium, but is not the strongest factor here. Hypertension (Choice B) is associated with low bone mineral density but is not as significant a risk factor as genetic predisposition by race. Antihypertensive medications may even be protective. Nulliparity (Choice C) may be associated with low bone mineral density but to a lesser extent than conditions that reduce estrogen stimulus on bone, such as early menopause, smoking, low BMI, and late menarche. Use of β-adrenergic blocking agents (Choice E) is not a significant risk factor for osteoporosis; these agents have been associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased fracture risk. Educational Objective: Osteoporosis is a progressive loss of bone mineral density occurring with aging that can lead to fragility fractures. Major risk factors include female gender, Caucasian ethnicity, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, adrenal/thyroid/parathyroid disease, sedentary lifestyle, and low estrogen states.
Source: 4A #2
A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She has mild hypothyroidism well controlled with levothyroxine. Five years ago, she was diagnosed with stage I breast cancer; she completed tamoxifen therapy 1 year ago and is currently in remission. Menopause occurred 4 years ago. Her mother sustained a femoral fracture in a bicycle collision at the age of 55 years. The patient has smoked two cigarettes weekly for 25 years. She is 150 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Examination shows no thyromegaly. There is a small, well-healed surgical scar over the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. The remainder of the breast and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following historical findings is the greatest risk factor for osteoporotic fracture in this patient? A) BMI B) Family history of fracture C) Levothyroxine therapy D) Tamoxifen therapy E) Tobacco use
Correct Answer: A) BMI
Osteoporosis results from loss of bone mineral density through three mechanisms: failure to achieve peak bone mineral density, increased bone resorption, and decreased new bone formation. Low BMI is a key risk factor for osteoporosis because bone remodeling and formation occur in response to mechanical stress. Small stature, limited weight-bearing exercise, frailty, and limited muscle strength are highly associated with low bone density. This patient's height (less than 5 feet), weight (less than 100 pounds), and BMI at the low end of normal (19 kg/m²) all indicate frailty as an overarching syndrome that significantly raises her risk of osteoporotic fragility fracture. Family history of fracture (Choice B) in this patient may not relate to underlying osteoporosis, as the mother's fracture occurred in the setting of high-energy trauma from a bicycle collision. Levothyroxine therapy (Choice C) is associated with osteoporosis only when it leads to subclinical hyperthyroidism. This patient's hypothyroidism is described as well-controlled, so this is not a significant risk factor. Tamoxifen therapy (Choice D) is actually protective against osteoporosis because it acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in bone, preserving bone mineral density. Selective estrogen receptor modulators like raloxifene are used clinically for osteoporosis prevention. Tobacco use (Choice E) is associated with osteoporosis development, but this patient has a minimal smoking history (two cigarettes weekly), making this less contributory than her frailty, low muscle mass, and short stature. Educational Objective: Low BMI is a key risk factor for osteoporosis. Bone remodeling occurs in response to mechanical stress, and small stature, limited weight-bearing exercise, frailty, and limited muscle strength are highly associated with low bone density.
Source: 8A #21
A 37-year-old woman with a 15-year history of endometriosis comes to the physician to request information about undergoing total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. She continues to have severe pelvic pain despite treatment with various pain medications. Her mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus, and her father has prostate cancer. She read that removal of her uterus and ovaries will help control her pain. She says that she does not expect to have children because she has been unable to conceive for 8 years despite undergoing extensive treatment for infertility. During the next 10 years, this patient will be at greatest risk for which of the following if she undergoes the operation? A) Breast cancer B) Colon cancer C) Dementia, Alzheimer type D) Heart disease E) Osteoporosis
Correct Answer: E) Osteoporosis
Bilateral oophorectomy results in premature surgical menopause due to the loss of ovarian estrogen production. Estrogen stimulates osteoblasts and increases or maintains bone mineral density. The loss of ovarian estrogen leads to accelerated loss of bone mass after menopause, significantly increasing the risk for developing osteopenia or osteoporosis. This condition is often asymptomatic until a traumatic injury results in a fracture, most commonly involving the hip, distal radius, or vertebrae. Diagnosis is made using a DEXA scan once bone mineral density falls below 2.5 standard deviations of the mean for a young adult. Patients undergoing elective oophorectomy should be counseled about this increased risk for osteoporosis due to estrogen's critical role in bone mineralization and maintenance. Breast cancer (Choice A) risk is primarily related to lifetime estrogen exposure. Surgical removal of the ovaries and premature menopause would decrease this patient's lifetime estrogen exposure and actually decrease her risk for breast cancer. Colon cancer (Choice B) risk factors include low-fiber diet, excessive red or processed meat consumption, obesity, tobacco use, and hereditary cancer syndromes. While estrogen and progesterone deficiency after menopause has been linked to increased colon cancer risk, data is mixed and this correlation is not as robust as the patient's known increased risk for osteoporosis. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice C) has multiple risk factors including early menopause, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, cerebrovascular disease, sedentary lifestyle, and brain trauma. However, this patient is at higher risk for developing osteoporosis given estrogen's role in bone maintenance. Heart disease (Choice D) risk is not increased by menopause itself. If this patient were to request hormone replacement therapy to decrease osteoporosis risk, she would need counseling about increased risk for heart disease and thromboembolic events from prolonged estrogen exposure.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Ovarian Cancer 4 questions
Source: 3A #23
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of two episodes of vaginal bleeding during the past 3 weeks. Menopause occurred 12 years ago. She has hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents. She has no history of abnormal annual Pap smears. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows a normal cervix and uterus with blood at the cervical os. A 6 × 8-cm left ovarian mass is palpated. Pelvic ultrasonography confirms the results of physical examination. An endometrial biopsy specimen shows atypical complex hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Brenner tumor B) Granulosa cell tumor C) Ovarian carcinoma D) Ovarian fibroma E) Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
Correct Answer: B) Granulosa cell tumor
Vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman should raise suspicion for malignancy, including uterine or ovarian carcinoma. Ovarian sex-cord stromal tumors are a group of neoplasms which may secrete sex hormones, including estrogen or testosterone. Granulosa cell tumors are the most common sex-cord stromal tumor and present with an adnexal mass and evidence of estrogen excess such as breast tenderness and uterine bleeding. Estrogen excess is a known risk factor for atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma. In this case, the patient presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, a palpable 6 × 8-cm ovarian mass, and endometrial biopsy showing atypical complex hyperplasia—all consistent with estrogen-secreting granulosa cell tumor. Ultrasonography may reveal a large, complex ovarian mass which may contain septations or cysts. Histologic diagnosis is made by biopsy; identification of Call-Exner bodies is considered pathognomonic. Granulosa cell tumor is treated with surgical resection and may require adjuvant chemotherapy in advanced cases. Brenner tumors (Choice A) are rare tumors derived from ovarian transitional epithelial cells with a tan to yellow, firm gross appearance. They are not hormone-secreting and are less likely to present with atypical vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman. Ovarian carcinoma (Choice C) and ovarian fibroma (Choice D) both may present with a palpable adnexal mass. However, neither of these entities secrete estrogen and are unlikely to lead to atypical endometrial hyperplasia. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (Choice E) is a sex-cord stromal tumor derived from testosterone-secreting Sertoli-Leydig cells. Patients typically present at younger ages and may develop signs of androgen excess and masculinization, not estrogen excess. Educational Objective: Ovarian sex-cord stromal tumors are a group of neoplasms which secrete sex hormones, including estrogen and testosterone, and may present with evidence of androgen or estrogen excess. Excessive estrogen produced by granulosa cell tumors causes endometrial hyperplasia and abnormal, often postmenopausal, vaginal bleeding.
Source: 5A #17
During a routine health maintenance examination, an asymptomatic 65-year-old woman is found to have a second-degree cystocele, a first-degree rectocele, and a first-degree uterovaginal prolapse. The right ovary is palpable but less than 5 cm in diameter; the left ovary cannot be palpated. Which of the following findings is of most concern requiring further evaluation? A) Cystocele B) Nonpalpable left ovary C) Palpable right ovary D) Rectocele E) Uterovaginal prolapse
Correct Answer: C) Palpable right ovary
In postmenopausal women, a palpable ovary raises significant concern for ovarian malignancy and requires further evaluation. In postmenopausal women, 30% of ovarian masses are malignant. Any incidental ovarian enlargement or cyst in a woman over age 50 should be investigated with imaging and potential biopsy. Early detection is critical as ovarian cancer typically presents late in the disease course, often already metastatic and invasive at diagnosis. Presenting features are often nonspecific and may include weight loss, abdominal discomfort or distention, ascites, and gastrointestinal symptoms (early satiety, bloating, nausea, cramping, bowel obstruction). Peritoneal carcinomatosis is a common presenting diagnosis. Ovarian cancer can be hereditary, associated with BRCA 1/2 mutations and Lynch syndrome. Treatment involves surgical resection, debulking, and chemotherapy, with early diagnosis being key to maximizing survival. In contrast, pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, rectocele, uterovaginal prolapse) is a common, relatively benign condition in older women related to pelvic floor weakness from multiparity, age, obesity, hysterectomy, and chronic constipation. These can be managed conservatively with pelvic floor exercises, pessary placement, or surgical repair if symptomatic. Nonpalpable ovaries are typical and expected in postmenopausal women, as ovarian volume normally decreases after menopause.
Source: 8A #20
A 65-year-old woman comes to the office because she has had increasing abdominal girth over the past 6 months. Pelvic examination shows a 20-cm mass filling the pelvis; the mass is cystic to palpation. Ultrasonography shows a 23-cm cystic mass with multiloculated cysts that appears to involve the left ovary. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Follicular cyst of the ovary B) Ovarian tumor of endometrioid origin C) Ovarian tumor of epithelial origin D) Ovarian tumor of germ cell origin E) Ovarian tumor of stromal origin
Correct Answer: C) Ovarian tumor of epithelial origin
Ovarian cancer commonly presents indolently with abdominal distension, early satiety, and weight loss in postmenopausal women. Signs and symptoms of advanced disease may include bowel obstruction with nausea and vomiting, ascites, pleural effusions, and venous thromboembolism. Physical examination may show a palpable adnexal mass on bimanual examination or lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography is recommended to identify or characterize the lesion, with concerning features including septations, cystic components, increased blood flow, and heterogeneous structure. Further evaluation includes tumor markers (commonly serum cancer antigen 125 [CA 125]) and additional imaging to determine disease extent. Most ovarian cancers are of epithelial origin. Risk factors include family history, genetic mutation (BRCA), increased age, smoking, nulliparity, endometriosis, and pelvic radiation. Treatment includes surgical removal and chemotherapy. Follicular cyst of the ovary (Choice A) is a simple cystic structure occurring during follicle development when an egg is not appropriately released during ovulation. While patients may be asymptomatic or present with abdominal/pelvic pain if large, the 23-cm multiloculated mass with concerning ultrasonographic features is much larger and has an uncharacteristic appearance for a follicular cyst. Ovarian tumor of endometrioid origin (Choice B) is an uncommon subtype of ovarian epithelial cancer associated with endometriosis. Classic symptoms of endometriosis include dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. This patient has no symptoms of endometriosis, and this subtype is much less common than epithelial carcinoma. Ovarian tumor of germ cell origin (Choice D) includes teratomas, dysgerminomas, yolk sac tumors, and mixed germ cell tumors. They present with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, bloating, and increased hormone concentrations (B-hCG, alpha-fetoprotein, lactate dehydrogenase) with a unilateral pelvic mass. They are not typically associated with large, cystic masses. Ovarian tumor of stromal origin (Choice E) includes sex cord-stromal tumors such as granulosa cell tumors, theca cell tumors, and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. These are hormonally active and present with palpable adnexal mass, abnormal uterine bleeding, or hyperandrogenism evidence. They would be unlikely to cause symptoms solely from mass effect. Educational Objective: Ovarian cancer classically presents indolently with abdominal distension, early satiety, and weight loss in postmenopausal women. Signs of advanced disease include bowel obstruction, ascites, pleural effusions, and venous thromboembolism. The most common histology of ovarian cancer is epithelial origin.
Source: 8A #40
A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of progressive nausea and vomiting and increasing abdominal girth. Bowel sounds are hyperactive with high-pitched rushes. There is shifting dullness to palpation. Bimanual examination shows a right-sided pelvic mass. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Colon cancer B) Endometrial cancer C) Gastric cancer D) Lymphoma E) Ovarian cancer
Correct Answer: E) Ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer is the correct answer. It commonly presents indolently with abdominal distension, early satiety, and weight loss in postmenopausal women. Signs and symptoms of advanced disease include bowel obstruction with consequent nausea and vomiting, ascites (evidenced by shifting dullness), pleural effusions, and venous thromboembolism. Physical examination may reveal a palpable adnexal mass on bimanual examination or lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice and will show an ovarian mass that is heterogeneous with septations, cystic and solid components, and increased blood flow. Further evaluation includes tumor markers, commonly serum cancer antigen 125 (CA 125), and additional imaging to determine disease extent. Risk factors include family history, genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA), increased age, smoking, nulliparity, and pelvic radiation. Treatment includes surgical excision and chemotherapy. Colon cancer (Choice A) is the second most common cause of cancer deaths in the United States and is often detected on routine colonoscopy. When symptomatic, it presents with changes in stool caliber or frequency and iron deficiency anemia, not with a pelvic mass on bimanual examination. Endometrial cancer (Choice B) commonly presents with postmenopausal bleeding or abnormal uterine bleeding in premenopausal women. Risk factors include chronically increased estrogen concentrations, exogenous estrogen therapy, anovulation, obesity, and estrogen-secreting tumors. It would be less likely than ovarian cancer to cause ascites with associated nausea and vomiting. Gastric cancer (Choice C) commonly presents with weight loss, epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and occasionally gastrointestinal bleeding. Areas of metastasis include the liver and lymph nodes, and less commonly the brain or lungs. It would not cause the pelvic mass seen in this patient. Lymphoma (Choice D) presents with weight loss, fevers, and night sweats in the setting of lymphadenopathy, with additional symptoms based on tumor location. It does not typically present with a pelvic mass. Educational Objective: Ovarian cancer classically presents indolently with abdominal distension, early satiety, and weight loss in a postmenopausal woman. Signs of advanced disease include bowel obstruction, ascites, pleural effusions, and venous thromboembolism. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice and will show an ovarian mass that is heterogeneous with septations, as well as both cystic and solid components. Treatment includes surgical excision and chemotherapy.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Primary Amenorrhea 4 questions
Source: 3A #30
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has never had a menstrual period. She is otherwise healthy. Both of her older sisters had normal pubertal development. Examination shows absent breast development and scant pubic hair. Her serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is 105 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test B) Karyotype analysis C) Measurement of serum electrolyte concentrations D) Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration E) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
Correct Answer: B) Karyotype analysis
Turner syndrome (45,XO) is a common cause of primary amenorrhea resulting from ovarian dysgenesis. The clinical presentation of absent breast development, scant pubic hair, and primary amenorrhea in a 17-year-old with elevated FSH (105 mIU/mL) is classic for Turner syndrome. The elevated FSH indicates hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to lack of negative feedback from estrogen. Diagnosis is definitively made through karyotype analysis, which will reveal the 45,XO genotype. Additional features of Turner syndrome include short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, hand/foot swelling, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney, and infertility. Choice A (GnRH stimulation test) is used to diagnose central precocious puberty or occasionally delayed puberty in younger patients, not for establishing the diagnosis of Turner syndrome, which is a form of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Choice C (serum electrolyte concentrations) is not indicated as Turner syndrome is not characterized by electrolyte abnormalities. Choice D (serum LH concentration) would help differentiate hypergonadotropic from hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but the elevated FSH already indicates hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and does not establish the specific diagnosis of Turner syndrome. Choice E (serum TSH concentration) may be helpful in diagnosing thyroid disorders, which can cause irregular menses, but thyroid disease is an uncommon cause of primary amenorrhea and is not suggested by this clinical presentation. Educational Objective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is a common cause of primary amenorrhea due to ovarian dysgenesis. Diagnosis is made by karyotype analysis. Elevated LH and FSH concentrations result from absent negative feedback from estrogen. Associated features include absent secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, webbed neck, cardiac and renal abnormalities, and infertility.
Source: 5A #44
An otherwise healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period. She is 150 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. The cervix is visualized, and the vaginal mucosa is hypoestrogenized. Serum studies show a luteinizing hormone concentration of 22 mIU/mL, follicle-stimulating hormone concentration of 33 mIU/mL, and prolactin concentration of 9 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Anorexia nervosa B) Congenital absence of the uterus C) Gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome) D) Hyperprolactinemia E) Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism F) Polycystic ovarian syndrome G) Pregnancy
Correct Answer: C) Gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome)
Turner syndrome (45,XO) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea due to ovarian dysgenesis. This patient presents with classic features: short stature (150 cm), primary amenorrhea, Tanner stage 3 breast and pubic hair development (incomplete secondary sexual characteristics due to low estrogen), and hypoestrogenized vaginal mucosa. The elevated LH (22 mIU/mL) and FSH (33 mIU/mL) are characteristic findings resulting from absent negative feedback from estrogen on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype analysis. Other associated features include cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) causes amenorrhea through hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis suppression but presents with extremely low body weight and fear of weight gain; this patient has an overweight BMI of 28 kg/m². Congenital absence of the uterus (Choice B) results from Müllerian system developmental error but patients have functional ovaries with adequate secondary sexual characteristic development, unlike this patient's incomplete Tanner staging. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice D) causes amenorrhea and galactorrhea through inhibition of GnRH, resulting in decreased FSH and LH; this patient's prolactin is normal at 9 ng/mL. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Choice E) presents with low FSH and LH; this patient has elevated levels. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Choice F) presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, irregular menses, elevated LH-to-FSH ratio, and ovarian cysts on ultrasound; it typically causes secondary oligomenorrhea rather than primary amenorrhea. Pregnancy (Choice G) causes secondary amenorrhea in sexually active patients, not primary amenorrhea.
Source: 5A #47
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of nausea, urinary frequency, and fatigue for 2 months. She has never had a menstrual period. Breast development is Tanner stage 4. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Complete blood count B) Measurement of serum estrogen concentration C) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone concentrations D) Pregnancy test E) Progesterone challenge test
Correct Answer: D) Pregnancy test
Pregnancy should always be considered as a potential etiology of presumed primary amenorrhea and should be excluded before considering other causes. Early symptoms of pregnancy include fatigue, nausea, urinary frequency, and irregular menstruation. Clinicians should maintain a low threshold of suspicion for pregnancy in adolescent and teenage patients who are at high risk for unintended pregnancy. A careful history should be taken, including menstrual history, sexual activity, contraceptive usage, and the possibility of pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test should be obtained if it is possible that the patient may be pregnant. Choice A (Complete blood count) is useful in diagnosing anemia, which may present with lightheadedness, diaphoresis, and pallor, but does not address the primary clinical presentation. Choice B (Serum estrogen concentration) may reflect abnormalities in ovarian estrogen production and disclose causes of primary amenorrhea such as Turner syndrome (45,X). However, this patient presents with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics, suggesting normal estrogen concentrations. Choice C (FSH and LH concentrations) may disclose hypothalamic or pituitary disorders leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and primary amenorrhea. Patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism typically do not present with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics. Choice E (Progesterone challenge test) is useful for distinguishing outflow tract disorders from hormonal etiologies of amenorrhea, but should only be performed after pregnancy has been excluded.
Source: 4A #15
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of constant severe abdominal pain. During the past year, she has had 10 episodes of cramps; each episode lasts 3 to 5 days. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has never had a menstrual period. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they do not use contraception. She is at the 80th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Breast and genital development is Tanner stage 5. Abdominal examination shows moderate tenderness. A mass is palpated in the suprapubic region at the midline. Pelvic examination shows normal-appearing external genitalia and lower vagina. The cervix cannot be visualized because of bluish bulging vaginal tissue that obscures the upper vagina. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy B) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy C) Oral contraceptive therapy D) Transvaginal incision and drainage E) Laparotomy
Correct Answer: D) Transvaginal incision and drainage
This patient presents with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and a bulging pelvic mass in an adolescent with otherwise normal sexual development (Tanner stage 5), which is classic for transverse vaginal septum. The transverse vaginal septum results from failure of canalization of the vaginal canal, preventing excretion of menstrual blood. The bluish bulging vaginal tissue represents hematocolpos—significant accumulation of menstrual blood products that gives the bulging hymen a blue appearance. The cyclic nature of her pain (10 episodes over the past year, each lasting 3-5 days) reflects menstrual cycling with blood accumulation. Diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography. Treatment is transvaginal incision and drainage with resection of the septum and evacuation of accumulated blood. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy (Choice A) is used for menorrhagia or endometriosis but does not address the anatomic obstruction. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy (Choice B) treats primary dysmenorrhea but does not address the underlying structural problem or the primary amenorrhea. Oral contraceptive therapy (Choice C), while appropriate for contraception in this sexually active patient, does not address the hematocolpos and anatomic obstruction. Laparotomy (Choice E) is unnecessary as hematocolpos can be easily approached vaginally with better cosmetic outcomes and lower morbidity than abdominal surgery.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Preconception counseling and care 4 questions
Source: 7A #25
A healthy 28-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation presents for her second prenatal visit. She has no significant past medical history, takes no medications, and has no allergies. Her vital signs are stable, and her physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient at this time? A) Return for another prenatal visit in 4 weeks B) Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration C) Administration of Rho(D) immune globulin D) Administration of rubella vaccine E) Administration of varicella vaccine
Correct Answer: A) Return for another prenatal visit in 4 weeks
For uncomplicated pregnancies, the standard prenatal visit schedule is every 4 weeks until 28 weeks' gestation, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks' gestation, and then every week until delivery. At 12 weeks' gestation, this patient is in the early pregnancy period and should return in 4 weeks for her next visit. Prenatal visits allow healthcare providers to recognize risk factors for increased maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality, optimize medical issues, treat infections and asymptomatic bacteriuria, and perform appropriate screenings. Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice B) is recommended for patients with known diabetes mellitus or increased risk for its development, neither of which applies to this patient. Gestational diabetes screening via oral glucose tolerance test is typically performed between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation and can lead to macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress, and newborn hypoglycemia if untreated. Administration of Rho(D) immune globulin (Choice C) is recommended for Rh(D)-negative mothers at 28 weeks' gestation (not at 12 weeks), following delivery of an Rh(D)-positive newborn, after invasive procedures such as amniocentesis, and after episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. It prevents development of anti-D antibodies that could cause erythroblastosis fetalis in subsequent pregnancies. Administration of rubella vaccine (Choice D) is contraindicated in pregnancy as it is a live attenuated virus. Live vaccines can infect the fetus. Rubella infection in unvaccinated pregnant patients can cause fetal defects including sensorineural deafness, neurodevelopmental delay, congenital cardiac defects, microcephaly, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Vaccination should occur after delivery if the patient is not immune. Administration of varicella vaccine (Choice E) is contraindicated in pregnancy as it is a live virus. Varicella infection in early pregnancy causes congenital varicella syndrome with severe birth defects including microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, cerebral cortical atrophy, intellectual disability, seizures, ocular defects (microphthalmia, cataracts, chorioretinitis), limb hypoplasia, and cicatrizing skin lesions. Vaccination should occur after delivery if the patient is not immune.
Source: 7A #41
A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for counseling prior to conception. She and her husband would like to conceive within the next year. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days. The patient and her husband are both healthy, take no medications, and are in a stable marital relationship. Neither has used tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. She has a strong family history of alcohol use disorder, and her father had Guillain-Barré syndrome. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 80 kg (176 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 122/84 mm Hg. A grade 1/6 systolic flow murmur is heard. Examination shows multiple diffuse nodularity of the breasts with no discrete masses. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. There is a large verruca plantaris on the left foot. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice for this patient before conception? A) Genetic counseling B) Weight loss C) Chemical dependency evaluation D) Mammography E) Folic acid supplementation F) Removal of the verruca plantaris
Correct Answer: E) Folic acid supplementation
Prepregnancy visits optimize a patient's chances for a successful pregnancy and healthy child by identifying and intervening on risks to mother and fetus. Key assessments include medical conditions, social behaviors, teratogen exposure, genetic conditions/family history, and vaccination records. Laboratory evaluation includes rubella and varicella serology and STI screening when indicated. Critical interventions include folic acid supplementation, substance use abstinence, medication optimization, and vaccinations. Folic acid supplementation is essential as deficiency causes neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Neural tube formation occurs early in pregnancy, often before patients realize they are pregnant. The recommended dose for previously unaffected patients is 0.4 mg daily, starting at least 1 month prior to pregnancy. Patients with previous neural tube defect-affected children or family history should take 1-4 mg daily starting 1-3 months prior to conception. Genetic counseling (A) is indicated only if the patient or partner has personal or family history of inherited diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anemia). This patient and partner are healthy; alcohol use disorder is not inherited, and Guillain-Barré syndrome is acquired, not inherited. Weight loss (B) is unnecessary. While slightly overweight (BMI 28), she has no consequent health issues or ovulation problems. During pregnancy, she should be counseled about appropriate weight gain expectations for her BMI. Chemical dependency evaluation (C) is not recommended. Although she has a strong family history of alcohol use disorder, she has no personal history of substance use. Mammography (D) is not warranted. It is indicated for palpable breast masses (which she lacks) or as screening after age 40. Her diffuse nodularity without discrete masses does not require mammography. Removal of verruca plantaris (F) is unnecessary prior to conception. While it may be offered, it does not affect pregnancy ability or outcomes. Educational Objective: Prepregnancy visits optimize chances for successful pregnancy with healthy child. Important aspects include ascertaining varicella and rubella immunity, encouraging substance use abstinence, changing teratogenic medications, and prescribing folic acid supplementation to prevent neural tube defects. Folic acid supplementation should begin 1-3 months prior to conception.
Source: 8A #2
A 27-year-old primigravid white woman at 9 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. There is no family history of genetic disorders, thrombophilia, or intellectual developmental disorder. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 9-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient? A) Cystic fibrosis screening B) Diabetes mellitus screening C) Serum lipid studies D) Thalassemia screening E) Chorionic villus sampling
Correct Answer: A) Cystic fibrosis screening
The first prenatal visit is used to establish baseline medical and gynecologic history, date the pregnancy, and perform laboratory and genetic screening for potential maternal or fetal health issues. Genetic carrier screening for heritable disorders present in specific populations is a key component. In white patients, routine genetic screening includes cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs disease, and spinal muscular atrophy. Screening for additional disorders can be tailored based on the patient's ethnicity and the disorders found in that population (e.g., Amish, Ashkenazi Jewish, African American). Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by failure to pass meconium in infancy, recurrent sinus and pulmonary infections, digital clubbing, bronchiectasis, and pancreatic insufficiency due to deficient trafficking of a membrane chloride channel. Cystic fibrosis carrier state increases the risk that the child may have the disorder if the father is either a carrier or affected. Diabetes mellitus screening (Choice B) is not routinely performed at the first prenatal visit in asymptomatic patients without risk factors such as a history of pregestational prediabetes, obesity, or prior gestational diabetes. This patient should be offered a 1-hour glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks. Serum lipid studies (Choice C) are not routinely recommended during pregnancy and do not often change management, as statin therapy is contraindicated in pregnancy. Lipid panels can be discussed after postpartum recovery if risk factors develop. Thalassemia screening (Choice D) is not routinely offered at the first prenatal visit for white patients unless risk factors are present, such as a history of recurrent pregnancy loss. If initial laboratory studies show microcytic anemia lower than expected physiologic anemia of pregnancy (<10.5 g/dL), screening for hemoglobinopathies including thalassemia should be offered. Chorionic villus sampling (Choice E) is an invasive test used to identify genetic abnormalities of the fetus. As it carries risk to the fetus, it is reserved for further evaluation of abnormalities on aneuploidy screens or ultrasonography. There is no indication of genetic abnormality in this patient, making it inappropriate at this time. Educational Objective: The first prenatal visit is used to establish baseline history, evaluate maternal health, and screen for genetic disorders prevalent in that patient's population. Genetic screening in the United States for white patients routinely includes aneuploidies, cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and Tay-Sachs disease. Screening for additional disorders can be tailored to the patient's family history and ethnicity.
Source: 8A #24
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician for counseling prior to conception. She would like to conceive within the next year, but she and her 38-year-old husband are concerned about the risk for fetal death. Her first pregnancy ended in the delivery of a 3175-g (7-lb) stillborn infant at 34 weeks' gestation. The infant appeared normal, and autopsy did not show any congenital malformations. There was no evidence of umbilical cord compression or fetal-maternal hemorrhage. She and her husband are both healthy, take no medications, and are in a stable marital relationship. Neither has used tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Her 37-year-old brother has type 1 diabetes mellitus, and her 60-year-old father has type 2 diabetes mellitus. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 65 kg (143 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. A grade 1/6 soft systolic murmur is heard. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice for this patient prior to conception? A) HLA typing of the patient and her husband B) Karyotype analysis of the patient and her husband C) Measurement of the patient's fasting serum glucose concentration D) Semen analysis E) Hysterosalpingography
Correct Answer: C) Measurement of the patient's fasting serum glucose concentration
In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly a result of chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease. Risk factors for uteroplacental insufficiency include pregestational or gestational diabetes, pregestational or gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, cocaine use, smoking, coagulopathies, severe anemia, placental abruption, and intrauterine infection. This patient has a significant family history of diabetes mellitus (brother with type 1 diabetes, father with type 2 diabetes), normotension, no history of drug use, no history of fetal insults, and no history of prior fetal abnormalities. Given the late third-trimester stillbirth and strong family history, occult pregestational diabetes should be suspected and screened for with measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration. Patients with pregestational diabetes require tight glucose control during conception and pregnancy to minimize effects of hyperglycemia on the fetus, including macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, congenital malformations (cardiac, caudal regression), preeclampsia, preterm labor, intrauterine growth restriction due to uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal mortality. After birth, the fetus synthesizes excess insulin but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose, leading to neonatal hypoglycemia. HLA typing (Choice A) is less likely to reveal the cause of late pregnancy loss, as HLA mismatch is primarily a risk factor for earlier miscarriage. Karyotype analysis (Choice B) could determine gonadal mosaicism or Robertsonian translocations but is typically used when other evaluations are normal given the relatively low prevalence of abnormal parental karyotypes; chromosomal abnormality is less likely than pregestational diabetes in this case. Semen analysis (Choice D) is useful for male infertility evaluation but is not indicated here as maternal factors contributing to placental insufficiency should be evaluated first. Hysterosalpingography (Choice E) evaluates uterine cavity and fallopian tube structure and patency but is less likely to identify the cause than pregestational diabetes in a patient with late third-trimester loss and strong family history of diabetes.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Bartholin Gland Abscess 3 questions
Source: 6A #2
A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a third episode of a Bartholin gland abscess over the past 5 years. Culture of the abscess cavity is most likely to show which of the following? A) Bacteroides fragilis B) Chlamydia trachomatis C) β-Hemolytic streptococcus D) Neisseria gonorrhoeae E) Mixed enteric and skin flora
Correct Answer: E) Mixed enteric and skin flora
Bartholin gland abscesses are commonly polymicrobial infections that develop when a Bartholin gland becomes obstructed and infected. The Bartholin glands are located on each side of the introitus and provide vaginal lubrication. Obstruction of the ducts leads to cyst formation, which can become infected with abscess formation presenting as painful, fluctuant swelling with erythema and tenderness over the posterior labium majus. The most common culture finding is mixed enteric and skin flora, as organisms originate from both the gastrointestinal tract and normal skin microbiota. If a single organism is identified, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most likely pathogen, but polymicrobial infection is more common than monobacterial infection. Treatment involves incision and drainage with catheter placement for complete evacuation, followed by antibiotic therapy. Incorrect answers: Bacteroides fragilis (Choice A) is an anaerobic gram-negative bacillus that causes infections only when displaced from the colon (post-surgery, rupture, or trauma). Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice B) causes urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease but is not a typical cause of Bartholin duct abscess. β-Hemolytic streptococcus (Choice C), including S. pyogenes and S. agalactiae, may contribute to polymicrobial infection but would not typically cause monobacterial abscess. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice D) is a possible cause but is less common than polymicrobial flora. Educational Objective: Bartholin gland abscesses are commonly polymicrobial with organisms from both skin and enteric flora. If a single organism is identified, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is most likely, but mixed flora is the most common culture result.
Source: 3A #40
A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painful vulvar swelling for 2 days. She has had three episodes of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection treated successfully with oral antibiotics over the past 5 years. Examination shows a 4-cm, tender, fluctuant mass of the labium majus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Bacterial vaginosis B) Bartholin duct abscess C) Human papillomavirus infection D) Lichen sclerosus E) Urethral diverticulum F) Vulvar vestibulitis
Correct Answer: B) Bartholin duct abscess
A Bartholin duct abscess is the correct diagnosis. Bartholin glands are located on each side of the introitus and provide vaginal lubrication. When the ducts become obstructed, a Bartholin cyst can form, presenting as a small area of painful, fluctuant swelling over the posterior aspect of the labium majus. With ongoing obstruction and inflammation, infection develops, leading to a Bartholin gland abscess characterized by erythema and tenderness to palpation. Abscesses are commonly polymicrobial, but Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a frequently isolated aerobe, which is particularly relevant given this patient's history of recurrent gonorrheal infections. Treatment involves incision and drainage, often with catheter placement to promote complete evacuation. Bacterial vaginosis (Choice A) is caused by Gardnerella vaginalis or anaerobic bacterial overgrowth presenting with thin, malodorous, gray-white discharge, not vulvar abscesses. Human papillomavirus (Choice C) is a sexually transmitted viral infection causing cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal carcinoma and condylomata acuminata, not vulvar abscesses or labial swelling. Lichen sclerosus (Choice D) occurs in postmenopausal women with thinning and fibrosis of genital skin, presenting with pruritic white plaques and ulcerations, not abscess formation. Urethral diverticulum (Choice E) is an outpouching of the urethra presenting with recurrent urinary tract infections, urethritis, incontinence, and incomplete bladder emptying, not vulvar abscesses. Vulvar vestibulitis (Choice F) presents with erythema and hypersensitivity of the vestibule causing dyspareunia, not vulvar abscesses. Educational Objective: Bartholin gland cysts and duct abscesses present with unilateral, painful, fluctuant swelling of the labia majus, with abscesses marked by erythema and tenderness to palpation. They are most often polymicrobial but N. gonorrhoeae is a commonly isolated aerobe. They are typically treated with incision and drainage.
Source: 8A #35
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of a tender mass at the entrance to the vagina. During the past week, she has had some pain in this area during sexual intercourse. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms. Pelvic examination shows a 4-cm, fluctuant, moderately tender mass located at the 7-o'clock position relative to the opening of the vagina. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Bacterial infection B) Fungal infection C) Neoplasia D) Trauma E) Viral infection
Correct Answer: A) Bacterial infection
A Bartholin abscess occurs when a Bartholin gland becomes obstructed and infected. Bartholin glands are located on each side of the introitus at the 5- and 7-o'clock positions relative to the vaginal opening and produce secretions that lubricate the vagina. When the ducts become obstructed, a Bartholin cyst can form, presenting as painful, fluctuant swelling over the posterior aspect of the labium majus. With ongoing obstruction and inflammation, infection develops, leading to a Bartholin abscess characterized by erythema and tenderness. Abscesses are commonly polymicrobial bacterial infections with organisms from both skin and enteric flora. If a single organism is identified, it is usually Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial sources are more common. Treatment includes incision and drainage with catheter placement and antibiotic therapy. Fungal infection (Choice B) typically presents with vulvar erythema, vaginal pruritus, and thick white vaginal discharge from Candida species, not a fluctuant mass near the introitus. Neoplasia (Choice C) such as vulvar carcinoma commonly presents with a pruritic patch rather than a large fluctuant mass. Trauma (Choice D) could cause a vulvar or vaginal hematoma presenting as a tender, fluctuant, discolored mass, but this patient has no history of trauma, making this less likely than a Bartholin abscess. Viral infection (Choice E) such as herpes simplex virus causes small, painful vesicular lesions and is not causative of Bartholin abscesses. Educational Objective: Bartholin abscesses present with a large, tender, fluctuant area over the posterolateral vaginal entrance as polymicrobial bacterial infections. Treatment includes incision and drainage with catheter placement and antibiotic therapy.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Bacterial Vaginosis 3 questions
Source: 6A #3
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a foul-smelling vaginal discharge for 10 days. She is sexually active with one partner. She had a bilateral tubal ligation 7 years ago. Examination shows a watery vaginal discharge with vulvar irritation. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis? A) Culture for Candida albicans B) DNA probe for Chlamydia trachomatis of the cervix C) Serologic testing for syphilis D) Vaginal culture for Gardnerella vaginalis E) Wet mount preparation
Correct Answer: E) Wet mount preparation
Bacterial vaginosis is a common gynecologic condition characterized by a shift of vaginal flora and overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis, a Gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. The condition presents with gray, thin, malodorous (foul-smelling) vaginal discharge, elevated vaginal pH (>4.5), and a fish-like odor upon KOH testing. The identification of clue cells on wet mount preparation is the most appropriate confirmatory test. Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells with bacteria adherent to their borders, creating a stippled appearance. Metronidazole is first-line therapy. Bacterial vaginosis is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, and treatment of asymptomatic sexual partners is not recommended. Choice A (Culture for Candida albicans) is useful for evaluating Candida vulvovaginitis, which presents with vaginal pruritus, vulvar erythema, and thick white discharge—not the foul-smelling watery discharge seen here. Choice B (DNA probe for Chlamydia trachomatis) is indicated for cervicitis evaluation. C. trachomatis presents with thin watery discharge and cervical motion tenderness, but this patient lacks cervicitis on examination. Choice C (Serologic testing for syphilis) detects antibodies against Treponema pallidum and is not indicated for this presentation. Choice D (Vaginal culture for Gardnerella vaginalis) is not diagnostic because G. vaginalis is part of normal vaginal flora found in many healthy females. Wet mount with clue cells is more diagnostically useful and also excludes motile trichomonads suggestive of trichomoniasis. Educational Objective: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by vaginal overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and presents with gray, thin, malodorous discharge, vaginal pH >4.5, and fish-like odor on KOH testing. Identification of clue cells on wet mount microscopy is the confirmatory test of choice.
Source: 7A #8
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-week history of malodorous vaginal discharge. She has not had abdominal pain, pain with urination, or fever. Her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 3 days; flow is normal. Three months ago, she had vulvovaginal candidiasis that resolved after treatment with clotrimazole. Her only current medication is a combination oral contraceptive. She is sexually active with two male partners; they use condoms inconsistently. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 120/82 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a moderate amount of homogeneous, gray-white discharge in the vagina; the vagina otherwise appears normal. The cervix appears normal. There is no cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness. The adnexa are not enlarged. Wet mount preparation of the vaginal discharge is performed. Addition of KOH produces a fishy odor. Microscopic examination shows clue cells; no other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Diluted vinegar douche B) Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for the patient and oral doxycycline for her sexual partners C) Oral fluconazole for the patient only D) Oral metronidazole for the patient and her sexual partners E) Intravaginal metronidazole for the patient
Correct Answer: E) Intravaginal metronidazole for the patient
Bacterial vaginosis is a common gynecologic condition characterized by a shift of vaginal flora and overgrowth of bacterial species, commonly Gardnerella vaginalis, a gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. It presents with gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge, vaginal pH greater than 4.5, and a fishy odor detected on KOH testing. The identification of clue cells on wet mount preparation is the most appropriate confirmatory test. Metronidazole is the first-line therapy and may be delivered orally or intravaginally. Bacterial vaginosis is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, and treatment of asymptomatic sexual partners is not recommended. Choice A (Diluted vinegar douche) is inappropriate because douching increases the risk for infection and chemical vaginitis and would not treat the underlying infection. Choice B (Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline for the patient and oral doxycycline for her sexual partners) is used for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, which present with urethritis, dysuria, and cervicitis. These infections do not present with clue cells on microscopic examination. Choice C (Oral fluconazole for the patient only) is used for vulvovaginal candidiasis, which presents with vaginal pruritus, vulvar erythema, and thick white discharge. Candidiasis shows normal vaginal pH, negative KOH testing, and pseudohyphae rather than clue cells on microscopy. Choice D (Oral metronidazole for the patient and her sexual partners) is not necessary because treatment of sexual partners is not indicated, as bacterial vaginosis is not a sexually transmitted infection.
Source: 4A #22
A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of increasingly severe vaginal burning and discharge. She has been sexually active with one partner for 1 year, and they use condoms consistently for contraception. Examination shows normal external genitalia and a gray frothy vaginal discharge. The pH of the vaginal discharge is 5; microscopic examination shows squamous epithelial cells coated with bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Hydrogen peroxide douches B) Oral azithromycin C) Vaginal estrogen D) Vaginal metronidazole gel E) Vaginal miconazole
Correct Answer: D) Vaginal metronidazole gel
Bacterial vaginosis is a common gynecologic condition characterized by a shift of vaginal flora and overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis, a Gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. The clinical presentation includes gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge with vaginal pH greater than 4.5 and a fishy odor upon KOH testing. The identification of clue cells (squamous epithelial cells coated with bacteria) on wet mount preparation is diagnostic. Metronidazole is the first-line therapy and may be applied as a vaginal gel. Bacterial vaginosis is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, and treatment of asymptomatic sexual partners is not recommended. Incorrect choices: Hydrogen peroxide douches (A) are less effective than antibiotic therapy and are no longer recommended. Oral azithromycin (B) is used for Chlamydia trachomatis infection, not bacterial vaginosis. Vaginal estrogen (C) is used for vulvovaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women and has not been demonstrated to be effective for bacterial vaginosis when applied vaginally. Vaginal miconazole (E) is an antifungal used for Candida vulvovaginitis and has no antimicrobial activity against Gardnerella. Educational Objective: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by vaginal overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis, a Gram-variable, facultative anaerobe. It presents with gray, thin, malodorous vaginal discharge, vaginal pH greater than 4.5, and a fishy odor upon KOH testing. Metronidazole is the first-line treatment.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Fibrocystic Changes 3 questions
Source: 6A #11
A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of breast tenderness that is worse just prior to the onset of menses. Her menses occur at regular 28-day intervals, and she is currently on day 26 of her menstrual cycle. Examination shows multiple, bilateral, firm cystic areas of the breasts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Reexamination after menses B) Cytology of expressed nipple discharge C) Mammography D) Aspiration of the cysts E) Biopsy of the cysts
Correct Answer: A) Reexamination after menses
Fibrocystic changes of the breast occur most commonly in premenopausal women and present with various sites of breast pain and lumps that may be bilateral. The condition is characterized by cysts, stromal fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia on histology, believed to occur in response to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle.
