Reexamination after menses is the most appropriate next step because the size of fibrocystic changes should subside after menses, distinguishing it from other causes. On examination, the cysts may appear blue. Fibrocystic change is benign and does not generally convey increased cancer risk except for certain subtypes, though it can result in recurrent mastalgia. Supportive care using NSAIDs and a well-fitting brassiere is appropriate; oral contraceptive therapy has not been shown to relieve symptoms. Cytology of expressed nipple discharge (Choice B) may be useful for evaluating ductal carcinoma, but mammography or fine needle biopsy are preferred. This patient's bilateral, cyclic mastalgia is more suggestive of fibrocystic disease. Mammography (Choice C) is the preferred screening method for breast carcinoma, with USPSTF recommending screening for all women beginning at age 50. This patient's findings are not suggestive of malignancy, and mammography subjects the patient to an uncomfortable test that may lead to unnecessary biopsy. Aspiration of the cysts (Choice D) may help alleviate mastalgia in fibrocystic disease patients. However, reexamination after menses is more reasonable for confirming diagnosis prior to more invasive treatments. Biopsy of the cysts (Choice E) is not usually necessary for fibrocystic changes. If reexamination after menses does not demonstrate reduction in size, biopsy may be performed to evaluate for other possible causes. Educational Objective: Fibrocystic change of the breast is a benign condition occurring in menstruating women that presents with multiple, bilateral, painful breast cysts. Reexamination after menses should demonstrate a reduction in size of the fibrocystic changes, which distinguishes the diagnosis from other causes.
Source: 3A #47
An otherwise healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 weeks after noticing a tender mass in her left breast during breast self-examination. She has a history of similar smaller masses that resolved spontaneously within a few weeks. She feels well and takes no medications. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 3½ weeks ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no lymphadenopathy. The breasts are symmetric, and there are no skin changes. Examination of the left breast shows several 1-cm, smooth, soft, mobile masses and a 3-cm, mobile, soft, tender mass in the upper outer quadrant. Examination of the right breast shows tenderness to deep palpation and small masses similar to the left breast. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abscess B) Fat necrosis C) Fibroadenoma D) Fibrocystic changes of the breast E) Galactocele F) Intraductal papilloma G) Lipoma H) Mammary ductal ectasia I) Mastitis
Correct Answer: D) Fibrocystic changes of the breast
Fibrocystic changes of the breast occur most commonly in premenopausal women over age 35 but can occur in younger patients of reproductive age. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: a 27-year-old menstruating woman with multiple, bilateral, tender, mobile breast masses that have a history of spontaneous resolution. The condition is characterized by cysts, stromal fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia on histology, believed to result from hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle. Cysts may appear blue on examination. Fibrocystic change is benign and does not generally increase cancer risk (except certain subtypes). Treatment includes supportive care with NSAIDs and well-fitting brassieres; cyst aspiration can relieve symptoms and yields benign fluid (clear, milky, yellow, green, or brown). Oral contraceptives have not been shown to relieve symptoms. Incorrect answers: Abscess (Choice A) occurs as a complication of mastitis in breastfeeding women with indurated, fluctuant, erythematous tissue. Fat necrosis (Choice B) presents as palpable nodularity in areas of previous trauma with peripheral calcifications on imaging. Fibroadenoma (Choice C) presents as a unilateral, nontender, mobile, rubbery mass in younger women. Galactocele (Choice E) is a painless breast lump of retained milk following lactation cessation. Intraductal papilloma (Choice F) is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge. Lipoma (Choice G) presents as a solitary, painless, soft, mobile subcutaneous mass. Mammary ductal ectasia (Choice H) occurs in perimenopausal women with widening of lactiferous ducts near the nipple. Mastitis (Choice I) presents with erythema, induration, and warm tender skin, classically in breastfeeding mothers.
Source: 8A #25
A previously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of increasing pain of both breasts. The pain is worse immediately prior to the onset of her menstrual periods. She states that she does not perform monthly breast self-examinations because of the pain and numerous lumps. A paternal aunt has a history of breast cancer. Her menstrual period was 16 days ago. Examination of the breasts shows bilateral diffuse tenderness and nodularity; no masses can be palpated. There is no galactorrhea, nipple discharge, or axillary adenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Reexamination of the breasts on day 9 of the next menstrual cycle B) Measurement of serum prolactin concentration C) Mammography D) Ultrasonography of the breasts E) MRI of the breasts
Correct Answer: A) Reexamination of the breasts on day 9 of the next menstrual cycle
Fibrocystic changes of the breast occur most commonly in premenopausal women and present with various sites of breast pain and lumps, which may be bilateral. The condition is characterized by cysts, stromal fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia on histology, believed to occur in response to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle. Reexamination after menses (day 9 of the next menstrual cycle) is the most appropriate next step because the size of fibrocystic changes should subside after menses, distinguishing it from other causes. On examination, the cysts may appear blue. Fibrocystic change is benign and does not generally convey increased cancer risk except for certain subtypes, though it can result in recurrent mastalgia. If discomfort is associated, aspiration can be performed to relieve symptoms. Cyst aspiration yields fluid that is clear, milky, yellow, green, or brown—all benign. Supportive care with NSAIDs and a well-fitting bra is appropriate. Measurement of serum prolactin concentration (Choice B) is useful in evaluating galactorrhea and menstrual cycle irregularities (oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea) due to prolactin's inhibition of gonadotropin-releasing hormone. This patient has no galactorrhea, making this test unnecessary. Mammography (Choice C) is primarily used as a screening modality for early breast cancer detection and to aid in diagnosis of palpable breast masses. However, ultrasonography is more commonly used for patients under age 35 years, as their breast tissue is often too dense for adequate mammographic evaluation. Ultrasonography of the breasts (Choice D) is frequently used to evaluate breast lesions in patients under age 35 years and can determine the need for fine-needle aspiration or further imaging. However, this patient has no palpable breast lump, making ultrasonography ineffective for evaluating her symptoms. If performed, it would likely show multiple small cystic lesions. MRI of the breasts (Choice E) may be used for evaluating breast lumps in patients under age 35 years but is more commonly reserved for patients with breast implants or those at high risk for breast cancer (BRCA mutation carriers). This patient may require additional imaging in the future but should first have repeat examination on day 9 of her next menstrual cycle. Educational Objective: Fibrocystic change of the breast is a benign condition occurring in menstruating women that presents with multiple, bilateral, painful breast cysts. Reexamination after menses should show a decrease in size of the fibrocystic changes, which distinguishes the diagnosis from other causes.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Abnormal Uterine Bleeding, Including Perimenopausal 3 questions
Source: 6A #12
A previously healthy 47-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of excessive vaginal bleeding with the passage of clots. During this time, she has had to change her sanitary pad every 2 hours. She has had occasional hot flashes during the past 6 months. Her menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals until 1 year ago. She now has 2 weeks of bleeding every 2 months. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Six months ago, a Pap smear showed no abnormalities. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Pap smear B) Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration C) Measurement of serum testosterone concentration D) CT scan of the pelvis E) Endometrial biopsy
Correct Answer: E) Endometrial biopsy
Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (e.g., bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endocrine dysfunction (e.g., thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens), and may be iatrogenic or idiopathic. This 47-year-old perimenopausal woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by irregular intervals (every 2 months) and heavy flow requiring pad changes every 2 hours. She has no stigmata or history of thyroid disorder, coagulopathy, polycystic ovarian syndrome, or ovulatory dysfunction. In patients over the age of 45 who are perimenopausal or postmenopausal, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The next appropriate step in evaluation is an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. Hysteroscopy with sampling allows for more complete evaluation of the endometrium (e.g., polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities). A Pap smear (Choice A) would not be appropriate as a recent Pap smear 6 months ago showed no abnormalities; repeat Pap smear would be indicated 12 months after the previous one if abnormalities were present. Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone (Choice B) or serum testosterone concentration (Choice C) would not be the next best step; while LH is increased in postmenopausal patients and testosterone concentrations are decreased, neither is useful in the evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. CT scan of the pelvis (Choice D) would not be helpful in initial evaluation of uterine bleeding as it does not adequately evaluate the endometrium; ultrasonography would be a more helpful initial imaging modality to evaluate for polyps, adenomyosis, and endometrial hyperplasia.
Source: 3A #15
A 47-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual flow during the past 3 months. Previous menses were normal with regard to flow. She has mild hypertension treated with diuretics and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemics. She has no history of abnormal Pap smears. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 146/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. A Pap smear is reported as atypical glandular cells. Colposcopy shows no abnormalities. Endocervical curettage shows benign cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Second Pap smear in 6 months B) Human papillomavirus testing C) Pelvic ultrasonography D) Endometrial biopsy E) Loop electrosurgical excision of the cervical transformation zone
Correct Answer: D) Endometrial biopsy
Abnormal uterine bleeding in a 47-year-old woman with atypical glandular cells on Pap smear requires evaluation for endometrial pathology. The patient has already undergone appropriate cervical evaluation with colposcopy and endocervical curettage, both of which were normal, ruling out cervical malignancy as the source of the atypical glandular cells. In patients over 45 years of age, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy. The presence of atypical glandular cells on Pap smear, combined with abnormal uterine bleeding and age >45, necessitates endometrial biopsy to evaluate for endometrial cancer or hyperplasia. If the patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. Hysteroscopy with sampling allows for more complete evaluation of the endometrium including polyps, myomas, and structural abnormalities. Incorrect answers: Second Pap smear in 6 months (Choice A) is inappropriate because atypical glandular cells (not ASC-US) warrant further investigation, not repeat cytology. Repeat Pap smear and HPV testing (Choice B) are appropriate for atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), not atypical glandular cells. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice C) can be helpful in evaluating endometrial thickness, polyps, and myomas, but given the presence of glandular cells on sampling, direct tissue biopsy is superior to imaging. Loop electrosurgical excision (Choice E) would only be appropriate if colposcopy or endocervical curettage showed cervical pathology, which they did not. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding may be caused by structural, neoplastic, coagulopathic, infectious, endocrine, or iatrogenic sources. After an abnormal Pap smear showing atypical glandular cells, appropriate evaluation includes colposcopy and endocervical curettage. If these are normal, endometrial biopsy is necessary to evaluate for endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy, particularly in women over 45 years of age.
Source: 5A #19
A previously healthy 42-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of severe pelvic pain and heavy bleeding during her menstrual periods. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 6 days. The pain begins 2 days before the onset of menses and lasts for 4 days; treatment with ibuprofen does not control the pain. She takes no other medications. She has had two cesarean deliveries; delivery of her second child was complicated by deep venous thrombosis. She and her husband do not want to have any more children, and he is planning on undergoing vasectomy. Physical examination of the patient, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a normal uterus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Combination oral contraceptive therapy B) Placement of a copper IUD C) Endometrial ablation D) Dilatation and curettage E) Uterine artery embolization
Correct Answer: C) Endometrial ablation
Abnormal uterine bleeding refers to irregular menstrual bleeding that may be abnormal in quality, duration, or timing. For patients who are unable to take combination oral contraceptives, do not desire future pregnancy, or fail medical management, endometrial ablation is the appropriate option for treatment of heavy uterine bleeding. Endometrial ablation involves resection and destruction of the endometrial lining of the uterus and is contraindicated only in patients who desire future pregnancy or those with endometrial hyperplasia or cancer. This patient is an ideal candidate: she has completed childbearing (gravida 2, para 2), her husband is undergoing vasectomy (no future pregnancy desired), has normal pelvic ultrasound excluding structural pathology, and has failed conservative management with NSAIDs. Combination oral contraceptive therapy (Choice A) is contraindicated due to her history of deep venous thrombosis, as estrogen-progestin contraceptives increase thromboembolism risk. Other contraindications include migraines with aura, smoking, breast malignancy, hypertension, and history of coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease. Placement of a copper IUD (Choice B) would be inappropriate because copper IUDs contain no hormones to decrease endometrial proliferation and may actually cause irregular vaginal bleeding, increased menstrual flow, and increased menstrual pain. Dilatation and curettage (Choice D) is used for incomplete or missed abortions, as an adjunct for endometrial biopsies in postmenopausal bleeding evaluation, or when endometrial polyps are suspected. It is not used for definitive treatment of abnormal uterine bleeding. Uterine artery embolization (Choice E) is used for abnormal uterine bleeding associated with uterine leiomyomas. Since this patient has a normal uterus on examination and ultrasonography without leiomyomas, this procedure would not be appropriate.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Polyhydramnios 3 questions
Source: 6A #14
A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of shortness of breath at rest. She has gestational diabetes treated with diet. She measures her blood glucose concentrations four times daily; her 1-hour postprandial concentrations have averaged 144 mg/dL. Ultrasonography at 18 weeks' gestation showed a fetus with normal anatomy consistent in size with gestational age. The patient is Rh-negative and received Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation; antibody screening was negative. Her pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 22/min. The lungs are clear to auscultation and percussion. Examination shows a fundal height of 44 cm. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and 50% effaced; the vertex is at -2 station. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Anencephaly B) Incorrect gestational age C) Polyhydramnios D) Rh isoimmunization E) Twin gestation
Correct Answer: C) Polyhydramnios
Polyhydramnios refers to an excess of amniotic fluid (amniotic fluid index >25 on ultrasound) and is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. The clinical presentation is classic: a 31-week primigravida with gestational diabetes (a major risk factor for polyhydramnios) presenting with dyspnea at rest. The physical examination reveals a fundal height of 44 cm, which greatly exceeds the expected 31 cm for 31 weeks' gestation, indicating significant uterine enlargement from excess amniotic fluid. The dyspnea results from the enlarged gravid uterus preventing normal diaphragmatic excursion and reducing lung capacity. Polyhydramnios is associated with fetal developmental defects that impair swallowing (anencephaly, esophageal atresia, duodenal atresia), maternal diabetes mellitus, maternofetal Rh incompatibility, and congenital infections. In this case, the patient's gestational diabetes is the primary risk factor. The normal fetal anatomy on 18-week ultrasound makes a major structural defect less likely. Treatment is supportive; severe cases may require amniocentesis for symptom relief. Anencephaly (Choice A) is a frequent cause of polyhydramnios due to impaired fetal swallowing, but was ruled out by normal anatomy on 18-week ultrasound. While it could indirectly cause dyspnea through polyhydramnios, it is not the direct cause here. Incorrect gestational age (Choice B) could explain some discrepancy between uterine size and dates, but would not account for such a large discrepancy (44 cm fundal height at stated 31 weeks) and is less likely given the patient's specific risk factors for polyhydramnios. Rh isoimmunization (Choice D) occurs when an Rh-negative mother becomes sensitized to Rh-positive fetal blood, potentially leading to hemolytic disease of the newborn and hydrops fetalis. However, this patient's antibody screening was negative and she received appropriate Rh immune globulin prophylaxis, making isoimmunization unlikely. Additionally, Rh isoimmunization does not commonly cause polyhydramnios or significant uterine enlargement. Twin gestation (Choice E) would have been detected on the 18-week ultrasound, making this diagnosis unlikely. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios is an excess of amniotic fluid (AFI >25) associated with fetal swallowing impairment, maternal diabetes mellitus, Rh incompatibility, and congenital infections. It presents with maternal dyspnea due to diaphragmatic compression from uterine enlargement. Diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound; treatment is supportive with amniocentesis for severe symptomatic cases.
Source: 3A #48
A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports a 4-day history of mild difficulty breathing, especially when in the reclining position. She has no history of serious illness; her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The fundal height is 37 cm. Pelvic examination shows no cervical dilation or effacement. Ultrasonography shows a normal-appearing fetus. The amniotic fluid index is 35 cm (N=10-20). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Complete bed rest until delivery B) Recommendation to limit dietary sodium intake C) Antenatal testing D) Diuretic therapy E) Weekly amniocentesis for removal of fluid
Correct Answer: C) Antenatal testing
Polyhydramnios refers to excessive levels of amniotic fluid volume, indicated by an amniotic fluid index (AFI) greater than 20 cm. This patient has an AFI of 35 cm, confirming polyhydramnios. The condition is associated with increased risk of fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infections (parvovirus B19), twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly). Fetal anomalies are the most common cause. The appropriate management is antenatal testing including fetal ultrasonography with biophysical profile to evaluate for underlying fetal anomalies, along with amniocentesis to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities if ultrasonography is nondiagnostic. Incorrect answers: Complete bed rest (A) is not recommended for polyhydramnios and would not improve pregnancy prognosis; further testing is needed to evaluate for fetal abnormalities. Limiting dietary sodium intake (B) and diuretic therapy (D) have no role in treating polyhydramnios, as maternal sodium intake and diuretics have minimal to no effect on amniotic fluid volume. Weekly amniocentesis for fluid removal (E) is reserved for severe polyhydramnios causing severe shortness of breath or abdominal discomfort; this patient has only mild difficulty breathing, making it inappropriate. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios is excessive amniotic fluid volume associated with increased risk of fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. Antenatal testing including fetal monitoring, biophysical profile, fetal ultrasonography, amniotic fluid index measurement, and amniocentesis are appropriate to assess for underlying fetal structural or genetic abnormalities.
Source: 7A #21
A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. Two weeks ago, she fell off her bicycle and had no visible injuries, so she did not seek treatment. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated. The patient's blood group is A, Rh-positive. Current medications are a prenatal vitamin and iron supplementation. Vital signs are within normal limits. Fundal height is 28 cm. Ultrasonography shows polyhydramnios and no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Fetal esophageal atresia B) Fetal growth restriction C) Fetal renal agenesis D) Fetal Rh alloimmunization E) Maternal trauma
Correct Answer: A) Fetal esophageal atresia
Polyhydramnios refers to an excess of amniotic fluid, defined sonographically as an amniotic fluid index greater than 25. It is associated with fetal developmental defects that result in impaired swallowing, such as esophageal atresia, anencephaly, or duodenal atresia. Risk factors also include maternal diabetes mellitus, maternofetal Rh incompatibility, and congenital infections. In this patient, the gravid uterus is enlarged beyond expected size for gestational age, which can lead to maternal symptoms of dyspnea through prevention of diaphragmatic excursion. Diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasonography showing an enlarged pool of amniotic fluid. Treatment is supportive, though patients with severe symptoms may undergo amniocentesis. Complications include cord prolapse and placental abruption on rupture of membranes. Fetal growth restriction (Choice B) presents with decreased muscle mass and minimal subcutaneous fat at birth with very low birth weight. This patient's ultrasound showed no evidence of fetal growth restriction. Fetal renal agenesis (Choice C) would cause oligohydramnios rather than polyhydramnios due to lack of appropriate urine production, which comprises a significant portion of amniotic fluid. Other causes of oligohydramnios include prelabor rupture of membranes, uteroplacental insufficiency, and other congenital genitourinary malformations. Fetal Rh alloimmunization (Choice D) could occur if an Rh-negative fetus was exposed to maternal Rh-positive blood, typically during delivery or fetomaternal bleeding episodes. However, the fetal immune system is too immature to create a strong enough antibody response for clinical significance. Maternal trauma (Choice E) does not frequently lead to polyhydramnios. It more commonly causes placental abruption or fetomaternal bleeding. While fetomaternal bleeding could lead to polyhydramnios if the mother was Rh-negative with alloimmunization to Rh(D) antigens causing hydrops fetalis, this patient is Rh-positive, making maternal trauma an unlikely cause.

Source: 6A #20
A 27-year-old woman at 22 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because of fractures of right ribs 4-10 sustained in a motor vehicle collision. She is intubated. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, and urine output is 50 ml/h. Fetal monitoring shows no fetal heart tones. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 30%, Leukocyte count 9500/mm³, Platelet count 70,000/mm³, Prothrombin time 16 sec, Partial thromboplastin time >100 sec, Plasma fibrinogen 50 mg/dL (N=200-400). Fibrin split products are present in the serum at a 1:160 dilutional titer. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows free fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) CT scan of the abdomen B) Exchange transfusion C) Platelet transfusion D) Transfusion of packed red blood cells E) Cesarean removal of the fetus
Correct Answer: E) Cesarean removal of the fetus
This patient presents with antepartum intrauterine fetal demise (confirmed by absent fetal heart tones on monitoring and ultrasonography) following significant blunt abdominal trauma from a motor vehicle collision. The trauma likely caused placental abruption or uterine rupture. The critical finding is that the patient has developed disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), evidenced by: thrombocytopenia (70,000/mm³), prolonged prothrombin time (16 sec) and partial thromboplastin time (>100 sec), decreased fibrinogen (50 mg/dL, normal 200-400), and presence of fibrin split products at 1:160 dilution. DIC occurs when the fetus is retained following intrauterine demise due to release of tissue factor (thromboplastin) from the placenta. Urgent delivery is warranted to prevent further coagulation complications. Since the patient is intubated and not in active labor, cesarean delivery is the most appropriate next step. Choice A (CT scan) would delay necessary delivery and offers no additional information beyond what ultrasonography has already provided. Choice B (Exchange transfusion) is used for sickle cell disease and severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, not DIC. Choice C (Platelet transfusion) is indicated only when platelet count falls below 10,000/mm³ without bleeding or 50,000/mm³ with active bleeding or surgical need; this patient does not meet criteria. Choice D (Packed RBC transfusion) is indicated when hematocrit falls below 21% or with evidence of end-organ damage or hypotension; this patient's hematocrit of 30% does not warrant transfusion. Educational Objective: Retention of the fetus following intrauterine demise can lead to acute disseminated intravascular coagulation with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, increased D-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration. Development of DIC requires urgent delivery of the fetus via vaginal or cesarean delivery.
Source: 5A #26
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports that she has felt little movement of the fetus during the past 18 hours. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated. She weighed 59 kg (130 lb) prior to her pregnancy; BMI was 22 kg/m². She has had a 9.5-kg (28-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy. Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. The fundal height is 29 cm. No fetal heart tones are heard on Doppler. On pelvic examination, the cervix is closed and not effaced. Urine dipstick shows no glucose or protein. Ultrasonography confirms the absence of fetal cardiac activity in an otherwise normal-appearing male fetus. The patient and her husband choose to return home to await spontaneous labor. Four weeks later, the patient comes to the physician because of an episode of light vaginal bleeding but no contractions. External electronic monitoring shows mild irregular contractions every 20 to 30 minutes. The cervix is closed and not effaced, and the presenting part is soft and at -2 station. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, Hematocrit 32%, Platelet count 90,000/mm³, Plasma fibrinogen 250 mg/dL (N=20-400). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Induction of labor B) Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma C) Transfusion of platelets D) Cesarean delivery E) Dilatation and curettage
Correct Answer: A) Induction of labor
Stillbirth refers to fetal demise after 20 weeks' gestation and can occur before or during delivery. Antepartum intrauterine fetal demise commonly presents with decreased fetal movement and lack of fetal heart tones on examination, as confirmed by ultrasonography in this case. In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly caused by chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease. Delivery for antepartum intrauterine fetal demise is based on the mother's wishes, with options for immediate induction or delayed natural delivery in the absence of complicating medical issues. Labor typically begins 1 to 2 weeks after fetal demise. However, coagulation abnormalities can occur with delayed delivery because of the release of tissue factor (thromboplastin) from the placenta, potentially leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Given this patient's early mild contractions, closed cervix, prolonged retention of a nonviable fetus (4 weeks post-demise), and risk for developing coagulation abnormalities, induction of labor is the most appropriate next step to prevent further complications. Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma (Choice B) is typically performed in patients with established coagulation abnormalities such as supratherapeutic INR or DIC, which this patient has not yet developed. Transfusion of platelets (Choice C) is indicated when platelets fall below 10,000/mm³ or below 50,000/mm³ when actively bleeding or requiring surgical intervention; this patient's platelets are 90,000/mm³, making transfusion inappropriate. Cesarean delivery (Choice D) is not typically required for intrauterine fetal demise, as the collapse and maceration of the fetal body allows most fetuses to undergo successful vaginal delivery. Dilation and curettage (Choice E) is used for elective abortion or to remove remaining fetal tissue in missed or incomplete spontaneous abortion, but at 32 weeks, the fetus is too large for this procedure.
Source: 8A #3
A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 25 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because of a 24-hour history of absent fetal movement. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated with no contractions, vaginal spotting, or loss of fluid. She received routine prenatal care. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Fundal height is 25 cm. Fetal heart tones cannot be heard on auscultation. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) Fetal nonstress test B) Kleihauer-Betke (acid elution) test C) Measurement of maternal serum B-hCG concentration D) Ultrasonography E) Amniocentesis
Correct Answer: D) Ultrasonography
Antepartum intrauterine fetal demise commonly presents with decreased fetal movement and lack of fetal heart tones on examination. Ultrasonography confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating the absence of cardiac activity and intrauterine fetal demise. In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly the result of chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease, whereas in low-income countries it is more commonly the result of maternal infection, preeclampsia, or obstructed labor. Delivery for antepartum intrauterine fetal demise is based on the mother's wishes, with immediate induction or delayed natural delivery both feasible options in the absence of any complicating medical issues. Labor typically begins 1 to 2 weeks after fetal demise. Coagulation abnormalities can occur with delayed delivery due to the release of tissue factor (thromboplastin) from the placenta, which can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation presenting with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times, increased D-dimer concentrations, and decreased fibrinogen. Fetal nonstress test (Choice A) measures fetal heart rate and its response to fetal movements but is ineffective when no fetal heart tones are present. Kleihauer-Betke test (Choice B) quantifies fetal blood exposure to maternal circulation for Rh(D) immune globulin dosing and plays no role in confirming fetal demise. Measurement of maternal serum B-hCG concentration (Choice C) is used in pregnancy diagnosis and choriocarcinoma surveillance but would not change substantially shortly after fetal demise. Amniocentesis (Choice E) is an invasive procedure inappropriate at 25 weeks due to increased fetal injury risk and would not indicate fetal viability.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Gestational Trophoblastic Disease 3 questions
Source: 6A #24
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, is brought to the emergency department because of headaches for 4 days and slurred speech for 3 hours. She also has had fatigue and intermittent vaginal bleeding since delivering a healthy newborn at term 4 months ago; the bleeding has been heavy at times. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a closed cervical os. Ultrasonography shows a slightly enlarged uterus with a small clot in the endometrial cavity. There are bilateral, 8-cm, cystic, ovarian masses. Neurologic examination shows right-sided weakness. Her hematocrit is 28%, and serum β-hCG concentration is 530,000 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Choriocarcinoma B) Ectopic pregnancy C) Germ cell ovarian tumor D) Hydatidiform mole E) Threatened abortion
Correct Answer: A) Choriocarcinoma
Choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblastic tissue that can develop after pregnancy, including both molar pregnancies and full-term or preterm pregnancies. It is highly aggressive and typically presents with distant metastases, with a predilection for the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. Symptoms are secondary to bleeding from the primary tumor or metastases, including vaginal bleeding, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headache, seizures, and stroke-like symptoms. This patient's presentation of headaches, slurred speech, right-sided weakness, and vaginal bleeding 4 months postpartum with markedly elevated β-hCG (530,000 mIU/mL) and bilateral theca lutein cysts is classic for choriocarcinoma with brain metastases. Physical examination may disclose an enlarged uterus and bilateral adnexal masses. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a hypervascular uterine mass. Chest x-ray evaluates for lung metastases, and further imaging such as CT or MRI is warranted based on clinical symptoms. Treatment involves chemotherapy and surgical resection, with serial β-hCG monitoring. Ectopic pregnancy presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominopelvic pain, abnormal ultrasonography without an intrauterine fetal pole, and abnormally low β-hCG that should double every 48 hours—not the markedly elevated level seen here. Germ cell ovarian tumors present with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, bloating, and unilateral pelvic mass with increased hormones, but would not cause neurologic symptoms. Hydatidiform moles present with persistent nausea and vomiting, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size out of proportion to gestational age, with diffuse echogenic structures in the uterus on ultrasonography. They are precursors to choriocarcinoma but typically present earlier. Threatened abortion presents with vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks' gestation with fetal cardiac activity and closed cervical os, and would not explain the neurologic symptoms or markedly elevated β-hCG in a patient 4 months postpartum.
Source: 3A #32
A 19-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of nausea and persistent vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 15 weeks ago, but she has had daily vaginal bleeding for the past month. She has not received prenatal care. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows pedal edema. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation; there is no adnexal tenderness. A serum pregnancy test is positive. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein. Ultrasonography shows bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts and echogenic structures in the uterus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Combined ectopic and intrauterine pregnancy B) Hydatidiform mole C) Multiple gestation D) Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome E) Placenta accreta F) Polyhydramnios
Correct Answer: B) Hydatidiform mole
Hydatidiform moles result from abnormal fertilization: complete moles from fertilization of an empty egg by a single sperm with paternal DNA duplication (46 chromosomes), or incomplete moles from dual fertilization of a normal ovum (69 chromosomes). Neither form is viable. The clinical presentation includes hyperemesis gravidarum or persistent nausea and vomiting due to abnormally elevated β-hCG, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size greater than expected for dates. Pelvic examination may reveal cystic molar clusters in the vagina. Laboratory findings show markedly elevated β-hCG. Ultrasonography characteristically shows bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts (theca-lutein cysts) and diffuse echogenic structures in the uterus (hydatidiform moles), as seen in this patient. No fetal heartbeat is found on Doppler. Treatment involves dilation and curettage followed by sequential β-hCG monitoring to detect malignant gestational trophoblastic disease (invasive moles or choriocarcinoma), which requires chemotherapy. Choice A (Combined ectopic and intrauterine pregnancy) is extremely rare and would present with abdominal pain and show a viable intrauterine pregnancy plus an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy on ultrasound. Choice C (Multiple gestation) can present with hyperemesis gravidarum from elevated β-hCG but would show multiple viable fetuses on ultrasound. Choice D (Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome) results from exaggerated follicular response to injected gonadotropins used in infertility treatment. This patient has not received such treatment. Choice E (Placenta accreta) involves abnormal placental attachment to myometrium with risk factors including prior cesarean delivery, increased maternal age, and multiparity. It presents with postpartum hemorrhage risk, not the clinical picture here. Choice F (Polyhydramnios) is excessive amniotic fluid associated with maternal diabetes, multiple gestations, and fetal malformations. It is typically asymptomatic and associated with a viable pregnancy, which is absent here. Educational Objective: Hydatidiform moles present with persistent nausea and vomiting, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size disproportionate to expected gestational age. Markedly elevated β-hCG and characteristic ultrasound findings of diffuse echogenic uterine structures and bilateral ovarian theca-lutein cysts are diagnostic. Hydatidiform moles can progress to malignant trophoblastic disease requiring chemotherapy.
Source: 8A #27
A 38-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 12 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of heavy vaginal bleeding and moderate abdominal pain. She also feels jittery and as if her heart were racing. Her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and ended in vaginal deliveries at term. Her last menstrual period was 3 months ago. Menses previously occurred at irregular 3- to 4-month intervals. Abdominal examination reveals moderate tenderness. Pelvic examination shows a large amount of dark blood in the vaginal vault with bleeding from the nondilated cervix. Her hematocrit is 29%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abruptio placentae B) Ectopic pregnancy C) Endometritis D) Gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole) E) Placenta accreta F) Uterine rupture G) Vasa previa
Correct Answer: D) Gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole)
Hydatidiform moles (molar pregnancies) are caused by either fertilization of an empty egg by a single sperm followed by duplication of paternal DNA resulting in 46 chromosomes (complete mole) or dual fertilization of a normal ovum resulting in 69 chromosomes (incomplete mole). This patient presents with classic features of a molar pregnancy: first trimester vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and symptoms of hyperthyroidism (jitteriness, tachycardia). The irregular menstrual history and uterine size greater than expected for dates are also consistent with this diagnosis. The significant vaginal bleeding has caused anemia (hematocrit 29%) with associated hemodynamic changes (tachycardia). Increased β-hCG concentrations stimulate thyroid hormone secretion, causing hyperthyroid symptoms. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) occurs after 20 weeks' gestation, not at 12 weeks. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice B) would not remain asymptomatic for 12 weeks and typically presents with rupture earlier. Endometritis (Choice C) presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and mucopurulent discharge, which are absent here. Placenta accreta (Choice E) is typically asymptomatic until delivery and is associated with prior cesarean delivery. Uterine rupture (Choice F) does not present spontaneously in early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding. Vasa previa (Choice G) requires rupture of membranes to cause symptoms, and membranes are intact here. Molar pregnancies can progress to malignant trophoblastic disease including invasive moles or choriocarcinoma, requiring close follow-up with β-hCG monitoring.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Polycystic Ovary Syndrome 3 questions
Source: 6A #29
A 39-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes for a routine health maintenance examination. Menses have occurred at irregular intervals since menarche at the age of 14 years. Her last menstrual period occurred 6 months ago and was extremely heavy. She has declined to take hormones to regulate menses because she does not want to have a monthly menstrual period. Her only child was conceived 8 years ago after she was treated with clomiphene. She has had mild hirsutism since adolescence. Which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to be increased? A) Follicle-stimulating hormone B) Progesterone C) Testosterone D) Thyroid-stimulating hormone E) Thyroxine (T4)
Correct Answer: C) Testosterone
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, and hirsutism, often in patients with increased body weight. Diagnosis requires two of the following: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism. PCOS is associated with insulin resistance and an abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback response, leading to increased luteinizing hormone (LH) compared to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), as well as markedly increased androgen production from theca lutein cells. This results in increased serum testosterone concentration. The patient's presentation of irregular menses since menarche, amenorrhea for 6 months with prior heavy menstrual bleeding, infertility requiring clomiphene treatment, and hirsutism are classic for PCOS. Choice A (FSH) is increased in menopause and premature ovarian failure, which present with irregular menstruation or amenorrhea, hot flashes, and night sweats. This is less likely in a woman of reproductive age with signs of hyperinsulinemia, hyperandrogenism, and obesity. Choice B (Progesterone) is increased during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Increased progesterone would more likely present with amenorrhea due to endometrial atrophy rather than irregular menstruation. Choice D (TSH) is increased in primary hypothyroidism, which presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, bradycardia, dry skin, and delayed deep tendon reflexes. It is less likely to cause chronic oligo/anovulation and hirsutism. Choice E (T4) is increased in hyperthyroidism, which presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, but is not associated with hyperandrogenism. Treatment of PCOS includes weight loss, combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism, clomiphene for those desiring pregnancy, and metformin or insulin if diabetes mellitus develops. A potential complication is endometrial cancer from chronic anovulation resulting in unopposed estrogen exposure.
Source: 7A #36
An otherwise asymptomatic 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of irregular vaginal bleeding since she underwent tubal ligation 2 years ago. An abnormality of which of the following serum concentrations is most consistent with the suspected diagnosis? A) Estradiol B) Follicle-stimulating hormone C) Prolactin D) Testosterone E) Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Correct Answer: D) Testosterone
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, and hirsutism, often in patients with increased body weight. Diagnosis requires two of the following: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism. PCOS is associated with signs of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans and increased blood glucose concentrations. PCOS is associated with an abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback response, which leads to increased luteinizing hormone (LH) in comparison to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), as well as markedly increased androgen production from the theca lutein cells. This results in an increased serum concentration of testosterone. Treatment includes weight loss, oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, and spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism. Clomiphene stimulates ovulation and can be used for patients desiring pregnancy. If the patient is diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, oral medications (e.g., metformin) or insulin may be necessary. A potential complication of long-standing PCOS is endometrial cancer due to chronic anovulation resulting in prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen. Estradiol (Choice A) concentration varies based on the menstrual cycle phase. Patients with PCOS typically have normal estradiol concentration for their cycle phase, but spend more time in the follicular phase due to anovulation, resulting in higher long-term estradiol exposure. Follicle-stimulating hormone (Choice B) is increased in menopause and premature ovarian failure but is frequently normal in PCOS. LH, in contrast, is increased in PCOS as a result of decreased inhibition from the hypothalamic feedback loop. This increased LH is partly responsible for excessive androgen production in PCOS. Prolactin (Choice C) abnormalities occur in prolactinomas or prolactin-secreting pituitary tumors. Hyperprolactinemia inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, presenting with oligomenorrhea but often associated with galactorrhea, headaches, or visual changes—none present in this patient. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (Choice E) evaluates hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. Hypothyroidism presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, oligomenorrhea, bradycardia, dry and edematous skin, and delayed deep tendon reflexes. Hyperthyroidism presents with heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations, diaphoresis, and diarrhea. While both may cause oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, the patient has no other signs or symptoms suggesting thyroid disease. Educational Objective: Polycystic ovary syndrome presents with chronic anovulation, signs of androgen excess, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. Laboratory studies show increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone and testosterone. Treatment includes weight loss and oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, along with antihyperglycemic medications or insulin for concomitant diabetes mellitus management if diagnosed.
Source: 4A #17
A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of increasingly irregular menses. Menses had occurred at irregular 45- to 60-day intervals since menarche at the age of 14 years, but now her cycle interval is up to 90 days. Her menstrual periods typically last 2 to 7 days. She is otherwise asymptomatic and has no history of serious illness. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 103 kg (227 lb); BMI is 39 kg/m². Her pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows velvety pigmented skin over the axillae and groin. Which of the following serum hormone concentrations is most likely to be increased in this patient? A) Cortisol B) Follicle-stimulating hormone C) Progesterone D) Testosterone E) Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Correct Answer: D) Testosterone
This patient presents with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), characterized by irregular menses, obesity (BMI 39), acanthosis nigricans (velvety pigmented skin indicating insulin resistance), and signs of hyperandrogenism. PCOS requires two of the following for diagnosis: oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism. The condition is caused by abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback, leading to increased luteinizing hormone relative to follicle-stimulating hormone and markedly increased androgen production (particularly testosterone) from theca lutein cells. Testosterone is the most likely elevated hormone in this patient. Cortisol (Choice A) is increased in Cushing syndrome, which presents with fatigue, hypertension, truncal obesity, hyperglycemia, and abdominal striae—less likely given the chronic abnormal uterine bleeding pattern and absence of typical Cushing features. Follicle-stimulating hormone (Choice B) is increased in menopause and premature ovarian insufficiency, presenting with irregular menstruation, hot flashes, and night sweats from anovulation and low estrogen. This is less likely in a reproductive-age woman with signs of hyperinsulinemia and obesity. Progesterone (Choice C) is increased during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. High progesterone would more likely cause amenorrhea from endometrial atrophy (as seen with progestin-based contraceptives) rather than irregular menstruation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (Choice E) is increased in primary hypothyroidism, presenting with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and oligomenorrhea. This is less likely given the patient's signs of insulin resistance and chronic oligo/anovulation pattern. Educational Objective: PCOS presents with menstrual irregularities, signs of androgen excess, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography. Treatment includes weight loss, combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism, and antihyperglycemic medications or insulin if diabetes mellitus develops. A potential complication is endometrial cancer from prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Dysmenorrhea 3 questions
Source: 6A #30
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of an 18-month history of increasingly severe menstrual cramps associated with diarrhea and vomiting. The symptoms cause her to miss 2 days of school each month, and her school performance is beginning to decline. Menarche was at the age of 13 years. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. She is not sexually active. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m². Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows normal-appearing external genitalia, vagina, and cervix. The uterus is small, mobile, and nontender. There are no adnexal masses or nodularity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Adenomyosis B) Endometrial polyps C) Endometriosis D) Leiomyomata uteri E) Primary dysmenorrhea
Correct Answer: E) Primary dysmenorrhea
Primary dysmenorrhea is defined as menstrual pain that accompanies each menstrual cycle but is not associated with any underlying pathology. To diagnose primary dysmenorrhea, causes of secondary dysmenorrhea must be ruled out, including endometriosis, leiomyomata uteri (fibroids), adhesions, pelvic inflammatory disease, and adenomyosis. This patient's normal pelvic examination effectively excludes these secondary causes. Primary dysmenorrhea typically presents with lower abdominal and pelvic pain that may radiate to the lower back or thighs, often accompanied by nausea, diarrhea, headaches, and flushing. The pathophysiology involves uterine vasoconstriction in response to excess prostaglandin. Treatment targets this pathway with NSAIDs and topical heat therapy, with combined oral contraceptives or progestin IUD as options for persistent symptoms. Adenomyosis (Choice A) is the presence of glandular endometrial tissue in the myometrium, presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain, typically in multiparous women aged 40-50 years. On examination, a large, globular uterus may be palpated—findings absent in this patient. Endometrial polyps (Choice B) may cause irregular or unpredictable uterine bleeding not associated with usual premenstrual symptoms and do not typically cause dysmenorrhea. This patient has regular menses without menometrorrhagia, a common feature of endometrial polyps. Endometriosis (Choice C) denotes endometrial tissue outside the uterus, classically presenting with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Diagnosis requires diagnostic laparoscopy. Pelvic examination often discloses tenderness of the uterine wall and surrounding structures with possible uterine immobility from pelvic adhesions—not found in this patient. Leiomyomata uteri (Choice D), or uterine fibroids, are benign myometrial neoplasms causing abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain. They are typically visible on ultrasonography and may be palpated if large—not evident on this patient's examination.
Source: 3A #7
A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of increasingly severe pain during her menstrual periods. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 to 7 days with light flow. Her last menstrual period was 25 days ago. She underwent a loop electrosurgical excision of the cervical transformation zone for cervical dysplasia 6 months ago; examination of the biopsy specimen showed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 with negative margins. She is sexually active and uses condoms and spermicidal foam. Pelvic examination shows a normal vagina and a small, scarred cervical os. The uterus is slightly enlarged and tender. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Cervical stenosis B) Endometritis C) Premenstrual syndrome D) Recurrent dysplasia E) Threatened abortion
Correct Answer: A) Cervical stenosis
Cervical stenosis is the most likely diagnosis. It is caused by scar tissue narrowing the cervical os, which in this patient resulted from loop electrosurgical excision performed 6 months ago. The clinical presentation of increasingly severe dysmenorrhea with light menstrual flow and an enlarged, tender uterus is classic for cervical stenosis. The obstruction of menstrual flow through the scarred cervical os leads to retrograde or stagnant flow of menses, causing cyclical pelvic pain and hematometra (blood accumulation in the uterus). If scarring extends into the uterine cavity, amenorrhea, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss may occur. Any inflammatory or scarring process affecting the cervix—including endometriosis, radiation, chronic infection, trauma, or previous instrumentation—can cause cervical epithelial erosions that heal by forming scar tissue. Gradual cervical dilation may be an effective treatment. Endometritis (Choice B) presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, foul-smelling discharge, and pelvic pain from acute or chronic endometrial inflammation, typically associated with pelvic inflammatory disease. This does not fit the clinical picture of regular menses with light flow and a scarred cervical os. Premenstrual syndrome (Choice C) is characterized by physical or psychological symptoms occurring for at least 5 days prior to menses for at least three consecutive cycles that impair function. While the patient has menstrual-related symptoms, the progressive nature and association with a scarred cervix point to cervical stenosis rather than PMS. Recurrent dysplasia (Choice D) is unlikely after excision of CIN 2 with negative margins, especially only 6 months post-procedure. Patients require surveillance with cervical cancer screening at 6 months and colposcopy if results are abnormal, but recurrent dysplasia would not explain the acute worsening of dysmenorrhea. Threatened abortion (Choice E) involves vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks' gestation with fetal cardiac activity present and a closed cervical os. This is unlikely given the patient's regular menstrual cycles and use of contraception. Educational Objective: Cervical stenosis results from any inflammatory or scarring process of the cervix and presents with dysmenorrhea or cyclical pelvic pain associated with light menstrual flow. When stenosis involves the uterine cavity, it may also cause amenorrhea, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss.
Source: 4A #38
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of painful episodes of menstrual cramping over the past 5 months; the pain has caused her to miss several days of school monthly. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. Her last menstrual period was 5 days ago. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her pain? A) Dermoid cyst B) Endometriosis C) Ovarian torsion D) Prostaglandin production E) Psychological factors
Correct Answer: D) Prostaglandin production
Primary dysmenorrhea is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy adolescents and young women, occurring in the absence of secondary causes such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. This patient presents with the classic presentation: cramping lower abdominal or pelvic pain beginning several days prior to menses and persisting for several days, along with associated symptoms including fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and headache. The pain is caused by endometrial sloughing accompanied by prostaglandin production, which stimulates painful uterine contractions. Treatment typically involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes and limit prostaglandin synthesis, or oral hormonal contraceptives. Dermoid cyst (Choice A), a mature cystic teratoma, is a benign ovarian tumor that may present with abdominal fullness and pain or ovarian torsion, but does not typically cause cyclic pelvic pain. Endometriosis (Choice B) is a common cause of pelvic and abdominal pain from ectopic endometrial cells and presents with dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. While it should be excluded in this patient, it is less likely than primary dysmenorrhea given the cyclic nature and absence of other typical features. Ovarian torsion (Choice C) presents with sharp, severe, unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain often accompanied by nausea and vomiting, but is not cyclic and would typically show abnormalities on examination. Psychological factors (Choice E) can contribute to dysmenorrhea severity but are less likely as the primary cause in this patient given the absence of history suggestive of stress, depression, anxiety, or other psychological factors.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Breast Cyst, Solitary 3 questions
Source: 6A #34
A 23-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain of the left breast over the past 3 days. She now describes the pain as excruciating. Five days ago, she delivered a 3700-g (8-lb 3-oz) newborn vaginally after an uncomplicated labor. Her pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios, and labor was induced at 39 weeks' gestation. Her postpartum course has been uncomplicated. She is breast-feeding. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F). Examination shows a tender, edematous area on the lateral aspect of the left breast that is not erythematous or warm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Application of heat to the area B) Aminoglycoside therapy C) Dicloxacillin therapy D) Needle aspiration and culture E) Incision and drainage
Correct Answer: A) Application of heat to the area
This patient presents with a painful breast lump that coincided with breastfeeding, consistent with a galactocele diagnosis. Galactoceles are retention cysts that form as a result of obstruction of a lactiferous duct. They may be painful or painless and tend to appear during lactation or shortly after cessation of lactation. The key clinical features supporting this diagnosis are: (1) recent postpartum period with active breastfeeding, (2) tender, edematous area without erythema or warmth, (3) normal temperature (37.5°C), and (4) absence of systemic signs of infection. Diagnosis is facilitated with mammography and ultrasonography. Treatment is primarily supportive with massage and application of heat. Patients with refractory symptoms may benefit from therapeutic fine needle aspiration. Incorrect answers: Aminoglycoside therapy (B) is useful for bacterial infections but is not first-line for mastitis or breast abscess and carries risks of sensorineural hearing loss and nephrotoxicity. This patient lacks fever and erythema/calor, arguing against infection. Dicloxacillin therapy (C) is appropriate first-line for mastitis and breast abscess, but again, the absence of fever and localized signs of inflammation argue against an infectious process. Needle aspiration and culture (D) may be helpful for refractory galactoceles but is not indicated as initial management, and culture is not usually necessary. Incision and drainage (E) is more invasive than fine needle aspiration with increased scarring and unfavorable cosmetic outcomes and is not preferred for management of galactoceles or breast abscess.
Source: 7A #28
A 32-year-old woman presents with a firm, fluctuant, painless mass in the subareolar area of her breast. She discontinued breast-feeding 2 months ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals a discrete, mobile mass without overlying skin changes, erythema, or warmth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Breast abscess B) Fibroadenoma C) Galactocele D) Inflammatory carcinoma E) Mastitis
Correct Answer: C) Galactocele
A galactocele is a benign retention cyst of the mammary glands caused by obstruction to lactiferous duct outflow. It occurs in lactating patients or those who recently discontinued lactation. Galactoceles present as firm, fluctuant, painless or mildly tender masses, most commonly in the subareolar area, with normal vital signs. Although typically filled with milky fluid, they can contain clear fluid. Diagnosis is usually clinical but can be confirmed with mammography or ultrasonography showing a cystic mass. Treatment is primarily supportive with massage and heat application. Persistent, symptomatic cases may benefit from aspiration or excision. Complications are uncommon but include superimposed infection, abscess formation, rupture, and inflammation. Breast abscesses (Choice A) are infections presenting as tender, fluctuant, erythematous masses with fever and purulent nipple discharge. They can develop from galactoceles if bacteria are introduced but this patient's presentation lacks signs of infection. Fibroadenoma (Choice B) presents as a unilateral, nontender, mobile, rubbery mass typically in younger women and is benign. Inflammatory carcinoma (Choice D) presents with unilateral breast edema, erythema, pain, and characteristic 'peau d'orange' appearance from dermal lymphatic invasion; it does not present with a discrete mass and is often misdiagnosed as mastitis. Mastitis (Choice E) is cellulitis of breast tissue caused by bacterial introduction at the nipple, presenting with unilateral erythematous, indurated, edematous, warm, tender breast tissue and fever. It does not present with a discrete mass unless progressed to abscess. Educational Objective: Galactoceles are benign retention cysts of the breast caused by obstruction of lactiferous ducts in patients who are lactating or shortly after cessation of lactation. They present as fluctuant, painless masses in the subareolar area and most self-resolve with supportive care including massage and heat application. Refractory cases may require therapeutic fine-needle aspiration.
Source: 8A #10
A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician 1 week after she noticed a tender lump in her right breast during routine breast self-examination. She has no significant medical history, and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. Physical examination reveals a smooth, rubbery, freely mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast; there is no nipple discharge. Ultrasonography of the right breast shows a cystic lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Second breast examination in 6 months B) Mammography C) Fine-needle aspiration D) True-cut needle biopsy E) Lumpectomy
Correct Answer: C) Fine-needle aspiration
This premenopausal patient with a tender cystic lesion likely has a breast cyst, a benign lesion that may be found in isolation or as part of fibrocystic changes. Breast cysts are hormonally responsive and may fluctuate in size during menses. However, thorough evaluation is necessary for any patient presenting with a breast mass, as this can be the first presenting sign of breast cancer, the most common nondermatologic cancer in women. Evaluation should include a thorough history (including family history) and physical examination. Benign lesions typically present as smooth, rubbery, freely mobile masses with no coexisting skin changes, lymphadenopathy, or nipple discharge, whereas malignant lesions often present with irregular, firm, adherent masses. Further evaluation includes diagnostic imaging with either mammography or ultrasonography. When ultrasonography shows a cystic lesion, fine-needle aspiration should be completed to determine if the mass resolves and to treat the patient's associated symptoms. If the cyst disappears and fluid analysis is benign, no further treatment is warranted. If it does not resolve, biopsy should be performed to rule out malignancy. Choice A (Second breast examination in 6 months) is incorrect because any patient presenting with a breast mass should be evaluated to rule out malignancy to decrease morbidity and mortality associated with delayed diagnosis. This patient requires further testing with fine-needle aspiration to ensure her breast lesion is benign. Choice B (Mammography) would not benefit this patient. Ultrasonography is typically used for breast lesions in women under age 35 years, as their breast tissue is often too dense for adequate mammographic assessment. Ultrasonography has already evaluated this lesion, and fine-needle aspiration is the next appropriate step. Choice D (True-cut needle biopsy) is not useful for this patient's lesion. True-cut needle biopsy obtains a core biopsy of a mass, which is more beneficial for diagnosing solid rather than cystic lesions. Fine-needle aspiration is more helpful in managing this patient's symptoms and confirming the diagnosis. Choice E (Lumpectomy) is used for breast masses concerning for malignancy. It is a surgical excision of a breast lump sent for pathologic evaluation and is more invasive than fine-needle aspiration, which may cause resolution of this patient's mass. Educational Objective: Breast cysts present commonly in premenopausal women as large, rubbery, tender masses without accompanying lymphadenopathy, overlying skin changes, or nipple discharge. Ultrasonography shows a cystic lesion. Treatment includes fine-needle aspiration.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Pelvic Relaxation 3 questions
Source: 6A #38
A 77-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 5, aborta 2, comes to the physician because of a mass protruding from the vagina for 1 week; she feels something moving within the mass. She has also had severe low back pain for 6 months. Eight years ago, she underwent a vaginal hysterectomy and anterior and posterior colporrhaphy for treatment of uterovaginal prolapse. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cystocele B) Enterocele C) Femoral hernia D) Indirect inguinal hernia E) Sigmoid intussusception F) Urethrocele
Correct Answer: B) Enterocele
Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) occurs secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction and weakness, resulting in the herniation of abdominopelvic organs causing mass effect and protrusion along the vaginal wall. POP is more common in individuals with multiple childbirths, advancing age, and obesity—all risk factors for pelvic floor dysfunction. Even though this patient had her uterus removed with anterior and posterior colporrhaphy for prior uterovaginal prolapse, additional viscera may still prolapse through other portions of the pelvic floor. When intestines herniate through the pelvic floor and impress upon the vaginal canal, this is called an enterocele. The small bowel typically prolapses into the superior wall of the vagina with a visible bulge on physical examination. The patient's sensation of peristalsis causing the feeling of something moving within the mass is pathognomonic for enterocele. POP tends to be slowly progressive if untreated. Cystocele (Choice A) involves bladder prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall, associated with stress urinary incontinence, and presents with a bulge on the anterior vaginal wall. Femoral hernias (Choice C) occur below the inguinal ligament presenting as a painful mass on the anterior thigh, more common in women and prone to strangulation. Indirect inguinal hernias (Choice D) occur through the internal inguinal ring, are more common in males, and do not cause vaginal protrusion. Sigmoid intussusception (Choice E) involves telescoping of the sigmoid colon, more common in children, and presents with bowel obstruction symptoms. Urethrocele (Choice F) involves urethral prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall and is a common cause of stress urinary incontinence in multiparous women. Educational Objective: Pelvic organ prolapse occurs secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction and weakness, resulting in herniation of pelvic viscera into the vaginal wall. Urethrocele (urethral prolapse), cystocele (bladder prolapse), enterocele (small bowel prolapse), and rectocele (rectal prolapse) are the primary subtypes of POP.
Source: 5A #25
An 87-year-old woman who is a nursing home resident is brought to the physician 1 week after the staff noticed a vaginal mass. She has dementia, Alzheimer type, and appears disoriented. Examination shows partial prolapse of the uterine cervix through the introitus. The uterus can be easily pushed back into the pelvis. There is no cervical ulceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Pelvic ultrasonography B) Endometrial biopsy C) Insertion of a vaginal pessary D) Cervical amputation E) Vaginal hysterectomy
Correct Answer: C) Insertion of a vaginal pessary
Pelvic support defects causing urogenital prolapse result from loss of connective tissue and muscular support of the uterus, paravaginal tissue, bladder wall, urethra, or distal rectum. Risk factors include collagen and connective tissue disorders, vaginal delivery, menopause, prior pelvic surgery, and increased intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, chronic constipation). Signs and symptoms include vaginal mass, vaginal pressure, perineal discomfort, and urinary or fecal retention or incontinence. Management begins with noninvasive therapies, including insertion of a vaginal pessary (a mechanical device providing pelvic support) along with pelvic floor exercises. Surgical treatment with reconstruction, fixation, uterine suspension, or hysterectomy is reserved for cases where noninvasive management fails and is particularly difficult to justify ethically in elderly patients with dementia depending on goals of care and surgical safety. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice A) has no role in diagnosing pelvic support defects; evaluation is primarily clinical with speculum examination and may include urinalysis, cystoscopy, or post-void residual volume assessment. Endometrial biopsy (Choice B) is used for abnormal uterine bleeding evaluation, particularly in women over 45 or postmenopausal women for investigation of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, not for prolapse. Cervical amputation (Choice D) and vaginal hysterectomy (Choice E) are surgical options considered only after noninvasive management fails and are not appropriate as initial management, especially in this elderly patient with dementia.
Source: 8A #44
An 80-year-old nursing home resident presents with a mass protruding out of her vagina for 10 years. A 10 x 6-cm mass with a 1-cm ulcer on the dependent portion is protruding from the area of the vagina. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Bartholin duct cyst B) Complete procidentia C) Urethral caruncle D) Vaginal myoma E) Vulvar carcinoma
Correct Answer: B) Complete procidentia
Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) occurs secondary to pelvic floor dysfunction and weakness, resulting in herniation of abdominopelvic organs through the vaginal wall. Complete procidentia is a severe form of POP that includes herniation of the entire anterior, posterior, and apical vaginal compartments through the introitus, with cystocele (bladder prolapse), rectocele (rectal prolapse), and enterocele (intestinal prolapse) caused by descent of the pelvic organs. All or a portion of the cervix and uterus may be visible externally at the introitus. POP is more common with multiple childbirths, advancing age, and obesity. These herniations can result in urinary, defecatory, and sexual dysfunction, as well as an external mass that may show ulceration and bleeding, as seen in this patient. Diagnosis is made with physical examination; treatment includes pelvic floor exercises, vaginal pessaries, and surgical correction. Bartholin duct cyst (Choice A) presents as a small, painful, fluctuant swelling over the posterior labium majus from obstruction of a Bartholin gland. It would not cause perineal bleeding or such a large mass at the introitus. Urethral caruncle (Choice C) most commonly presents with perineal bleeding in postmenopausal women and can cause overflow urinary incontinence. However, these are small outgrowths on the posterior urethra, not large protruding vaginal masses. Vaginal myoma (Choice D) is a benign vaginal wall tumor that may present with a palpable mass and vaginal bleeding. However, these tumors are extraordinarily rare compared to complete procidentia. Vulvar carcinoma (Choice E) most commonly presents as a vulvar lesion on the labia majora that is pruritic or friable, leading to bleeding and pain. Risk factors include tobacco use, HPV infection, and immunocompromised status. This patient has a large mass protruding from the vagina rather than a plaque or ulcer on the labia majora.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Human Papillomavirus Infection, Genital/Venereal/Anal Warts, Condylomata Acuminata 3 questions
Source: 6A #44
A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine pelvic examination. She has had multiple sex partners. Perianal examination shows two venereal warts. Cervical examination shows no abnormalities. A Pap smear shows epithelial cells with an irregular nuclear contour and a distinct halo around the nucleus with a dense outer rim of cytoplasm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the cytologic abnormalities? A) Infection with Chlamydia trachomatis B) Infection with cytomegalovirus C) Infection with herpes simplex virus 2 D) Infection with human papillomavirus E) Invasive cervical carcinoma
Correct Answer: D) Infection with human papillomavirus
The clinical presentation of soft, pink, papillary lesions on the external genitalia (perianal warts) is consistent with condyloma acuminata (genital warts) associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Multiple sexual partners are a risk factor for HPV transmission. The Pap smear findings of epithelial cells with irregular nuclear contours and a distinct perinuclear halo with dense outer rim of cytoplasm are pathognomonic for koilocytes, which are virally infected cells characteristic of HPV infection. Low-risk HPV strains (6 and 11) typically cause condyloma acuminata with low oncogenic potential. High-risk strains (16, 18, 31, 33) can infect cervical epithelium and cause dysplasia and malignancy. The cytologic atypia observed on this Pap smear is caused by active HPV viral infection. Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice A) causes urethritis, dysuria, and discharge but does not produce cytologic atypia. Cytomegalovirus (Choice B) causes mononucleosis-like illness with atypical lymphocytes, not koilocytes.
