Herpes simplex virus 2 (Choice C) causes painful vesicles and erosions but does not cause cytologic atypia. Invasive cervical carcinoma (Choice E) requires demonstration of invasion on biopsy and cannot be diagnosed on cytology alone; the findings here represent active viral infection rather than invasion. Screening recommendations include Pap smears every 3 years for women aged 21-29 years and every 5 years with HPV co-testing (or every 3 years without co-testing) for women aged 30-65 years. Abnormal cytology is typically evaluated by colposcopy with biopsy of suspicious lesions.
Source: 5A #38
A 22-year-old college student comes to student health services because of vulvar irritation for 14 days. She is sexually active and has had three partners since the age of 15 years; she uses an oral contraceptive. Examination shows multiple 5- to 10-mm soft pink papillary lesions with areas of pigmentation on the labia minora and posterior fourchette. The vagina and cervix appear normal, and there is no vaginal discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient? A) Acyclovir therapy B) Azithromycin therapy C) Interferon therapy D) Podophyllum resin therapy E) Zidovudine (AZT) therapy F) Radiation therapy
Correct Answer: D) Podophyllum resin therapy
Soft, pink, papillary lesions on the external genitalia are consistent with condyloma acuminata (genital warts) associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Multiple sexual partners and failure to use condoms are risk factors for development. The most implicated strains are HPV 6 and 11, which have low oncogenic potential, though high-risk strains (16, 18, 31, 33) may also be present and indicate higher risk for cervical dysplasia and malignancy. Diagnosis is made by examination or biopsy showing papillomatous lesions with koilocytes in the epidermis. The goal of treatment is to destroy affected cells. First-line therapy options include topical formulations of podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid, fluorouracil, or liquid nitrogen. Immune therapy with topical imiquimod stimulates local innate immunity through toll-like receptors, leading to recognition of viral particles and adaptive immune response. Incorrect answers: Acyclovir (Choice A) treats herpes simplex virus (HSV) genital infection, characterized by painful vesicles and ulcers, not papillary lesions. Azithromycin (Choice B) treats Chlamydia trachomatis, presenting with urethritis, dysuria, and discharge. Interferon therapy (Choice C) is reserved for severe, refractory condyloma acuminata and is expensive. Zidovudine/AZT (Choice E) is used for HIV infection; while HIV and HPV often co-infect, there are no signs of current HIV infection in this patient. Radiation therapy (Choice F) is used for neoplastic vulvar disease, not condyloma acuminata. Educational Objective: Soft, pink, papillary lesions on the external genitalia are consistent with condyloma acuminata associated with HPV. Treatment goals involve destroying affected cells using topical formulations (podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid, fluorouracil, liquid nitrogen) or immune therapy (imiquimod) as first-line options.
Source: 4A #3
A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of vaginal discharge. She is sexually active with one partner, and they use condoms inconsistently. She reports that he was recently treated for syphilis. Physical examination of the patient shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows white verrucous lesions over the upper vaginal wall and cervix. A Pap smear is reported as atypical squamous cells. Human papillomavirus testing is negative for high-risk types. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Bacterial vaginosis B) Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 C) Condylomata acuminata D) Herpes simplex E) Secondary syphilis
Correct Answer: C) Condylomata acuminata
Condylomata acuminata are genital warts presenting as soft, fleshy, verrucous growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly strains 6 and 11, which have low oncogenic potential. They can appear on the vagina, vulva, penis, and/or anal canal. High-risk HPV subtypes (16, 18, 31, 33) may also be present and indicate higher risk of progression to cervical dysplasia and malignancy. Diagnosis is made by examination and/or biopsy if necessary. Treatment aims to destroy affected cells using topical podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid, fluorouracil, liquid nitrogen, or immune therapy with imiquimod, which stimulates local innate immunity through toll-like receptors. Bacterial vaginosis (Choice A) is caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis presenting with thin, malodorous, gray-white discharge, not verrucous papules. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 (Choice B) is a moderate-grade cervical lesion associated with high-risk HPV strains (16, 18, 31, 33), which are absent in this case. Colposcopy shows whitening with trichloroacetic acid but not verrucous lesions. Herpes simplex (Choice D) presents with painful vesicles in the genital area that lyse into shallow, painful ulcers with erythematous borders, not verrucous lesions. Secondary syphilis (Choice E) presents with a scaly rash classically involving palms and soles, along with condyloma lata—whitish-gray, flat-topped lesions that differ from the verrucous papules of condylomata acuminata. Educational Objective: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) are soft, verrucous papules caused by HPV strains 6 and 11. High-risk strains (16, 18, 31, 33) confer increased risk of cervical dysplasia and carcinoma.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Ovarian Cyst 3 questions
Source: 6A #47
A previously healthy, asymptomatic 25-year-old woman comes to the physician for contraceptive advice. She takes no medications. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last approximately 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 20 days ago. Pelvic examination shows a 5-cm mobile mass in the right adnexa; the mass is moderately painful to palpation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract B) Adenocarcinoma of the ovary C) Distended urinary bladder D) Diverticulitis E) Ectopic pregnancy F) Endometrioma G) Hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst H) Lymphoma I) Tuba-ovarian abscess
Correct Answer: G) Hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst
The corpus luteum develops from the mature follicle after ovulation during the menstrual cycle. In some instances, the corpus luteum can form a cyst that may rupture. A ruptured corpus luteum cyst classically presents with unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain that is sudden in onset and severe, most commonly after sexual intercourse or other physical activity. Physical examination may show a unilateral adnexal mass that may be tender. Pelvic ultrasonography will show a complex cystic mass or free fluid in the pelvis if ruptured, which may include hemorrhagic components (hemoperitoneum). Culdocentesis typically produces serosanguinous fluid, as the corpus luteum is highly vascular. It is typically managed with observation and supportive therapy. Incorrect answers: Adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract typically presents with constipation, decreased stool caliber, hematochezia or melena, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia; it is more common in older patients. Adenocarcinoma of the ovary is more common in postmenopausal women and presents late with weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and bloating. Distended urinary bladder presents with abdominal pain, decreased urinary output, and a suprapubic mass, typically in the setting of urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction. Diverticulitis presents with left lower quadrant pain, diarrhea, fever, and left lower quadrant tenderness, not an adnexal mass. Ectopic pregnancy presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, abnormal ultrasonography without an intrauterine fetal pole, and abnormally low serum β-hCG; it is unlikely with a recent last menstrual period 20 days ago. Endometrioma is formed from ectopic endometrial tissue and presents with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia; endometriomas are generally adherent and less likely to be freely mobile. Lymphoma presents with weight loss, fevers, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy, not typically a pelvic mass. Tuba-ovarian abscess presents as a sequela of pelvic inflammatory disease with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and cervical/adnexal tenderness; it is less likely given the absence of mucopurulent discharge and fever. Educational Objective: A hemorrhagic corpus luteum can be asymptomatic but, once ruptured, typically presents with severe, acute-onset, unilateral pelvic pain in an otherwise hemodynamically stable, premenopausal woman.
Source: 8A #23
A 15-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of severe pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Her menses started the day before; her previous menses began 6 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F). She has right adnexal tenderness. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, show normal findings. Serum β-hCG testing is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Appendicitis B) Endometrioma C) Endometriosis D) Intestinal colic E) Ruptured ovarian cyst F) Spontaneous abortion
Correct Answer: E) Ruptured ovarian cyst
A ruptured ovarian cyst typically presents with severe, acute onset of unilateral pelvic pain, most commonly after sexual intercourse or physical activity, in an otherwise hemodynamically stable patient. The most common cysts are follicular and corpus luteal/hemorrhagic cysts. Follicular cysts are simple cystic structures that occur when an egg is not appropriately released during ovulation. A corpus luteum cyst, which can be hemorrhagic, forms following ovulation. Either type can rupture, presenting with sudden, severe pelvic or lower abdominal pain. Physical examination may show unilateral adnexal tenderness. Laboratory studies are typically within normal ranges, and pelvic ultrasonography will show a simple or complex cystic ovarian mass or free fluid in the pelvis if ruptured, which may include hemorrhagic components. Treatment consists of observation and supportive therapy. Appendicitis (Choice A) typically presents with periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and gradually worsening course over hours to days. This patient has no fever or leukocytosis to suggest infection. Endometrioma (Choice B) is a cyst formed from ectopic endometrial tissue within the adnexa in patients with endometriosis. Endometriosis (Choice C) refers to ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and commonly presents with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. This patient has no previous symptoms of endometriosis, and neither condition presents with acute onset of severe pain. Intestinal colic (Choice D) refers to intermittent abdominal pain with associated nausea, emesis, diarrhea, anorexia, and bloating, more common in irritable bowel disease and inflammatory bowel diseases. This patient's pain is constant rather than intermittent with no associated symptoms. Spontaneous abortion (Choice F) presents with acute vaginal bleeding and cramping prior to 20 weeks' gestation. This patient has a negative serum β-hCG concentration, making spontaneous abortion incorrect.
Source: 8A #36
A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. Menses had previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. Abdominal examination shows right lower quadrant tenderness. The uterus is consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. There is right adnexal tenderness. Her quantitative serum B-hCG concentration is 10,000 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a gestational sac in the uterus containing a yolk sac; there is a 3-cm, complex right adnexal mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Corpus luteum cyst B) Ectopic pregnancy C) Endometrioma D) Hydatidiform mole E) Ovarian germ cell tumor
Correct Answer: A) Corpus luteum cyst
The corpus luteum develops from the mature follicle after ovulation and enlarges during pregnancy to secrete progesterone until the placenta takes over. An enlarged corpus luteum can form a cyst that may rupture. A ruptured corpus luteum cyst classically presents with sudden onset, severe unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain, most commonly after sexual intercourse or physical activity. Physical examination may reveal a unilateral adnexal mass that is tender. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a complex cystic mass or free fluid in the pelvis if ruptured, potentially with hemorrhagic components (hemoperitoneum). Culdocentesis typically produces serosanguineous fluid due to the corpus luteum's high vascularity. These cysts are managed with observation and supportive therapy. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice B) occurs outside the endometrial cavity, often in the fallopian tube, and presents with acute severe abdominopelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, and peritoneal inflammation signs. However, this patient has an intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac, confirming a normal intrauterine pregnancy with an associated corpus luteum cyst. Endometrioma (Choice C) forms from endometrial tissue in patients with endometriosis and presents with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. This patient has no prior endometriosis symptoms, and endometriomas do not cause acute pain. Hydatidiform mole (Choice D) presents with persistent nausea/vomiting, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size disproportionate to gestational age. Ultrasonography would show diffuse echogenic structures in the uterus and bilateral ovarian theca-lutein cysts, not an intrauterine yolk sac. Ovarian germ cell tumor (Choice E) includes teratomas, dysgerminomas, yolk sac tumors, and mixed germ cell tumors, presenting with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, bloating, and elevated B-hCG, alpha-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase. While this patient has elevated B-hCG, it is secondary to her normal intrauterine pregnancy, not a germ cell tumor. Educational Objective: Corpus luteum cysts are common in pregnancy as the corpus luteum must enlarge to support fetal development. These cysts can rupture, presenting with acute onset and severe unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain. Ultrasonography may reveal a complex cystic mass or free fluid in the pelvis. Management consists of observation and supportive therapy.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Candidiasis of the Vulva or Vagina 3 questions
Source: 3A #12
A 21-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of a small amount of vaginal discharge and itching; her symptoms began immediately before her last menstrual period. She has had two sexual partners over the past 2 months and uses an oral contraceptive. One month ago, she had pain on urination and urinary frequency that resolved after a 7-day course of cephalexin. Examination shows a red introitus and vulva with erythematous vaginal walls and a normal amount of vaginal discharge. The cervix and cervical discharge are normal. Vaginal pH is 4.5. The addition of KOH to the discharge produces no odor. A wet mount preparation shows no motile organisms. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Candida albicans B) Chlamydia trachomatis C) Gardnerella vaginalis D) Neisseria gonorrhoeae E) Trichomonas vaginalis
Correct Answer: A) Candida albicans
The patient's presenting signs and symptoms of vaginal pruritus, vulvar erythema, and odorless discharge on KOH testing are suggestive of vulvovaginitis from Candida albicans. While Candida species compose an element of normal vaginal flora, overgrowth can occur and lead to vulvovaginitis. C. albicans is the most frequently associated species. Candida vulvovaginitis can be distinguished from other causes by abnormal, often white, vaginal discharge with normal vaginal pH (≤4.5), negative KOH testing (no fishy odor), and absence of motile organisms on wet mount preparation. Risk factors include use of antibiotics (which disrupts normal flora), oral contraceptives, intravaginal or intrauterine contraceptive devices, and immunocompromised states. Treatment includes intravaginal antifungal agents such as clotrimazole, miconazole, or nystatin, or oral fluconazole. Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice B) most commonly presents with cervicitis, thin watery discharge, and cervical motion tenderness. The absence of cervicitis on examination makes this less likely. Gardnerella vaginalis (Choice C) causes bacterial vaginosis, characterized by gray, thin, malodorous discharge with vaginal pH >4.5 and a positive fishy odor on KOH testing. Clue cells are identified on wet mount. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice D) typically presents with mucopurulent cervical discharge and can cause cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease. The absence of abnormal cervical discharge makes this less likely. Trichomonas vaginalis (Choice E) is a flagellated protozoan causing green, frothy, malodorous discharge with vaginal pH >4.5 and motile organisms visible on wet mount preparation. This patient has no motile organisms and normal pH. Educational Objective: Vaginal candidiasis involves overgrowth of normal Candida flora, presenting with pruritus, erythema, and white discharge with normal vaginal pH and negative KOH testing.
Source: 5A #20
A previously healthy 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 7-day history of vulvar and vaginal itching. She has had no vaginal bleeding or discharge. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She currently takes no medications. She is not sexually active. Examination shows mild erythema and excoriation of the labia majora; there are no lesions. Results of the vaginal smear are consistent with Candida. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Oral clindamycin B) Oral metronidazole C) Vaginal clindamycin D) Vaginal metronidazole E) Vaginal miconazole
Correct Answer: E) Vaginal miconazole
The patient presents with vulvovaginitis caused by Candida albicans, evidenced by vulvar pruritus, erythema, and excoriation of the labia majora. Candida species are part of normal vaginal flora but can overgrow to cause symptomatic vulvovaginitis. Key diagnostic features include white vaginal discharge, normal vaginal pH, pseudohyphae on microscopy, and absence of motile organisms on wet mount. Candida vulvovaginitis is not sexually transmitted and is not associated with the risk factors mentioned in this case (antibiotics, oral contraceptives, immunocompromise). Treatment involves intravaginal antifungal agents such as miconazole, clotrimazole, or nystatin, or oral fluconazole. Vaginal miconazole is the most appropriate choice among the options provided. Oral clindamycin is used for bacterial pelvic infections like endometritis and tubo-ovarian abscess. Oral metronidazole, vaginal clindamycin, and vaginal metronidazole are all used for bacterial vaginosis, which presents with gray, thin, malodorous discharge, elevated vaginal pH >4.5, fish-like odor on KOH testing, and clue cells on wet mount—none of which are present in this patient. Educational Objective: Vaginal candidiasis results from Candida overgrowth and presents with vaginal pruritus, vulvar erythema, and white, thick discharge. Treatment includes intravaginal antifungal agents (miconazole, clotrimazole, nystatin) or oral fluconazole.
Source: 8A #1
A woman receives a 6-day course of oral ampicillin for acute cystitis. One week later, she has vaginal pruritus, burning, and dyspareunia. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of these symptoms? A) Candida albicans B) Gardnerella vaginalis C) Mycoplasma hominis D) Neisseria gonorrhoeae E) Trichomonas vaginalis
Correct Answer: A) Candida albicans
This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of vaginal pruritus, burning, and dyspareunia after a recent course of antibiotics are suggestive of vulvovaginitis from Candida albicans. While Candida species compose an element of normal vaginal flora, overgrowth can occur and lead to vulvovaginitis. C. albicans is the most frequently associated species. Candida as a cause of vulvovaginitis can be distinguished from other potential causes by abnormal, often white, vaginal discharge with normal vaginal pH, negative KOH testing, and absence of motile organisms on wet mount preparation. Microscopy will show pseudohyphae, which can confirm the diagnosis. Risk factors for Candida vulvovaginitis include the use of medications, especially antibiotics and oral contraceptives, use of intravaginal or intrauterine contraceptive devices, and an immunocompromised state. Candida vulvovaginitis is treated with intravaginal antifungal agents such as clotrimazole, miconazole, or nystatin, or with oral fluconazole. Gardnerella vaginalis (Choice B) is the most common causative organism of bacterial vaginosis, which occurs as a result of a shift of vaginal flora, allowing its overgrowth. Bacterial vaginosis presents with gray, thin, malodorous discharge and clue cells on wet mount preparation. It does not cause vulvar pruritus or burning. Mycoplasma hominis (Choice C) is a normal bacterium of the urogenital flora in men and women. While colonization is common, M. hominis is a rare cause of urogenital infection in nonpregnant individuals and would not be expected to cause the vaginal pruritus, burning, and dyspareunia found in this patient. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted bacterium that classically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus, although it may be asymptomatic. It does not typically cause vaginal burning and would be less likely than vulvovaginal candidiasis to present immediately after a course of antibiotics. Trichomonas vaginalis (Choice E) is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan that causes vaginal trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection. It presents with pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and abnormal discharge that is described as green, frothy, and malodorous. While this patient does have pruritus and dyspareunia, she has no abnormal discharge, making trichomoniasis unlikely. Educational Objective: Vulvovaginal candidiasis involves the overgrowth of normal vaginal Candida flora, most commonly Candida albicans. Symptoms include vulvar pruritus and erythema, burning, dyspareunia, and a thick, white vaginal discharge. A frequent risk factor is recent antibiotic use. Treatment includes intravaginal antifungal agents or oral fluconazole.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Gestational diabetes 3 questions
Source: 3A #17
At 37 weeks' gestation, a 28-year-old woman with gestational diabetes delivers a 4500-g (10-lb) newborn who develops hyaline membrane disease. The mother had postprandial serum glucose concentrations of 180-200 mg/dL during the last half of pregnancy. The macrosomia and pulmonary disease are most closely related to an increased serum concentration of which of the following in the fetus? A) Cortisol B) Growth hormone C) Human placental lactogen D) Insulin E) Reverse triiodothyronine (rT3)
Correct Answer: D) Insulin
Excessive fetal exposure to insulin in utero causes both macrosomia and hyaline membrane disease (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome). In gestational diabetes, human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. When the mother's body cannot generate enough insulin to overcome this resistance, maternal serum glucose concentrations rise (180-200 mg/dL postprandially in this case). Elevated maternal glucose crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperglycemia, which stimulates the fetus to produce excess insulin. Fetal insulin acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia (excessive fetal growth). Additionally, insulin inhibits surfactant production in fetal lungs, causing relative surfactant deficiency that leads to increased alveolar surface tension, alveolar collapse, and hyaline membrane disease characterized by respiratory distress, hypoxia, rhonchi, and diffuse alveolar infiltrates. Cortisol (A) is synthesized in the adrenal cortex and increases blood pressure, insulin resistance, and gluconeogenesis, but does not cause macrosomia or hyaline membrane disease. Growth hormone (B) increases insulin resistance and causes gigantism/acromegaly but requires prolonged exposure and would not be evident immediately at birth. Human placental lactogen (C) is produced by the placenta and increases maternal insulin resistance, playing a role in gestational diabetes development, but does not directly cause macrosomia or hyaline membrane disease. Reverse triiodothyronine (E) is the inactive isomer of T3 with no physiologic activity and is associated with euthyroid sick syndrome, not gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes occurs in the second half of pregnancy with risk factors including obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), previous gestational diabetes, and African American, Asian American, Hispanic, Native American, and Pacific Islander ethnicity. Complications include macrosomia, hyaline membrane disease, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycemia, and fetal mortality.
Source: 5A #32
A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has no history of operative procedures, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has a 3-year history of hypothyroidism well controlled with levothyroxine. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. She weighed 77 kg (169 lb) prior to her pregnancy; BMI was 29 kg/m². She has had a 14-kg (31-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Fundal height is 30 cm. Ultrasonography shows moderate polyhydramnios. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Excessive maternal hydration B) Fetal aneuploidy C) Fetal myotonic dystrophy D) Fetal renal agenesis E) Undiagnosed maternal diabetes mellitus
Correct Answer: E) Undiagnosed maternal diabetes mellitus
Polyhydramnios refers to excessive amniotic fluid volume with increased uterine size relative to gestational age. It is associated with increased risk for fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. It should be suspected when fundal height exceeds expected measurements for gestational age. Diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasonography by measuring the amniotic fluid index (AFI); an AFI greater than 24 cm indicates polyhydramnios. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection (parvovirus B19), twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (duodenal atresia, anencephaly, esophageal atresia). While fetal anomalies are the most common cause overall, they are typically apparent on ultrasonography. Given this patient's uncomplicated pregnancy until this point with no apparent fetal anomalies on ultrasound, undiagnosed maternal diabetes mellitus is the most likely cause. The patient's pre-pregnancy BMI of 29 kg/m² (overweight) is a risk factor for gestational diabetes. Incorrect answers: (A) Excessive maternal hydration may cause peripheral edema and hypervolemic hyponatremia but would not alter amniotic fluid volume. (B) Fetal aneuploidy can present with polyhydramnios but would be expected to show apparent congenital abnormalities on ultrasonography; for example, trisomy 18 presents with intrauterine growth restriction, rounded feet, cystic hygroma, neural tube defects, facial defects, omphalocele, and cardiac abnormalities. (C) Fetal myotonic dystrophy presents with hypotonia, joint contractures, respiratory muscle weakness, and bilateral facial paralysis; while polyhydramnios is common, inheritance is autosomal dominant and would be unlikely without family history. (D) Fetal renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios due to absent urine production, not polyhydramnios.
Source: 8A #48
A healthy 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She feels well, and fetal movement has been appropriate. Her blood group is A, Rh-positive. Her only medication is multivitamins. At her first prenatal visit, her hemoglobin concentration was 11.2 g/dL. Rubella testing showed immunity, and hepatitis and HIV antibody tests were negative. Urine cultures and testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis were negative, and a Pap smear showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography 1 month ago showed a fetus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. Examination today shows a uterine fundus measuring 25 cm from symphysis to fundus. The fetal heart rate is 155/min. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient at this visit? A) Antibody screening B) Glucose tolerance test C) Repeat testing for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis D) Repeat urine culture E) Repeat ultrasonography
Correct Answer: B) Glucose tolerance test
A 1-hour maternal glucose tolerance test is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient at 24 weeks' gestation. Screening for gestational diabetes is typically performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Although this test can be done at the first prenatal visit if there is suspicion of underlying or preexisting diabetes or in patients with a BMI ≥25 kg/m² plus another risk factor (such as first-degree relatives with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, previous macrosomia or gestational diabetes, or history of impaired glucose tolerance), routine screening at 24 weeks is standard practice. Gestational or preexisting diabetes mellitus can lead to increased risk for congenital anomalies, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Neonatal effects include hypoglycemia from sudden changes in maternal-fetal glucose balance, hyperbilirubinemia, polycythemia, and increased risk for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Early recognition allows for appropriate treatment, decreased average blood glucose concentrations, and improved neonatal outcomes. Antibody screening (Choice A) should be performed at the first prenatal visit for all patients, but repeat screening is not indicated for this Rh-positive patient with an uncomplicated pregnancy. Repeat testing for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis (Choice C) is not indicated for this asymptomatic patient with no high-risk sexual behavior. Repeat testing may be considered only if symptoms of cervicitis develop or if high-risk sexual behavior occurs. Repeat urine culture (Choice D) is not indicated for this asymptomatic patient with a negative routine urine culture screen. It may be considered only for patients with UTI symptoms or those at high risk (recurrent UTIs, urinary tract anomalies, or diabetes mellitus). Repeat ultrasonography (Choice E) is not yet indicated. The patient had a normal 20-week ultrasound for anatomic survey and growth monitoring. Routine ultrasonography is not recommended until 28 weeks' gestation or later for monitoring fetal growth and amniotic fluid index.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Congenital Parvovirus B19 Infection 3 questions
Source: 3A #20
A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 19 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She works in a preschool. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated except for mild gastrointestinal symptoms 6 weeks ago. She has an abnormal triple screen study prompting ultrasonography that shows fetal hydrops and ascites. A) Alcohol use B) Amphetamine use C) Cigarette smoking D) Cocaine use E) Cystic fibrosis carrier state F) Folic acid deficiency G) Gametic nondisjunction H) Heroin use I) Iodine deficiency J) Marijuana use K) Parvovirus B19 infection L) Rh sensitization M) Rubella infection N) Tay-Sachs carrier state
Correct Answer: K) Parvovirus B19 infection
Parvovirus B19 acquired during pregnancy typically presents with a mild viral syndrome including fever, chills, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, or respiratory symptoms. When acquired in the second or third trimester, it can have serious fetal consequences. Parvovirus B19 has tropism for bone marrow where it infects erythroid progenitor cells, causing fetal anemia that presents as fetal tachycardia, hydrops, high-output heart failure, and potentially fetal death. It also causes fetal myocarditis. This patient's occupational exposure in a preschool is a significant risk factor, as parvovirus B19 is a common cause of childhood erythema infectiosum. Alcohol use causes fetal alcohol syndrome with craniofacial dysmorphism, microcephaly, developmental delay, and learning disabilities. Amphetamine use is associated with cleft palate, cardiac malformation, intrauterine growth restriction, and fetal tachycardia. Cigarette smoking causes premature birth, placental abruption, low birth weight, and neurocognitive abnormalities. Marijuana carries similar risks. Cocaine is strongly associated with fetal demise through placental abruption and intrauterine growth restriction. Cystic fibrosis and Tay-Sachs carrier states increase risk only if the father is a carrier or affected; neither is associated with fetal hydrops. Folic acid deficiency is associated with neural tube defects like spina bifida. Gametic nondisjunction leads to trisomies with dysmorphism and structural heart disease. Heroin use causes neonatal abstinence syndrome but not hydrops. Iodine deficiency presents with neonatal hypothyroidism and cretinism. Rh sensitization causes fetal hemolytic anemia primarily in subsequent pregnancies. Rubella infection presents with sensorineural deafness, neurodevelopmental delay, congenital cardiac defects, and microcephaly. Educational Objective: Parvovirus B19 infects fetal bone marrow, causing anemia, heart failure, and hydrops.
Source: 3A #35
A 23-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She reports that her daughter had a flu-like illness 2 months ago that resolved without medical treatment. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated, and results of prenatal laboratory studies have been within the reference ranges. Examination shows a fundal height of 34 cm. Ultrasonography shows polyhydramnios, fetal ascites, and skin thickening. Infection with which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Adenovirus B) Coxsackievirus A C) Cytomegalovirus D) Herpes simplex virus E) Parvovirus B19
Correct Answer: E) Parvovirus B19
Polyhydramnios, fetal ascites, and skin thickening caused by subcutaneous edema are characteristic of hydrops fetalis. Hydrops fetalis is diagnosed by the combination of fluid accumulation in at least two extravascular compartments (e.g., pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, ascites, or subcutaneous edema). It is also associated with placentomegaly and polyhydramnios. Parvovirus B19 infection in a gravid woman is associated with spontaneous abortion and fetal nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Symptoms of parvovirus B19 infection in children can include fever, upper respiratory tract symptoms, headache, and rash, which is usually self-limited. The patient's daughter's recent flu-like illness 2 months ago is consistent with parvovirus B19 infection, which can be transmitted to the pregnant patient. Adenovirus (Choice A) is a common virus that causes upper respiratory tract symptoms, fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis but does not have known deleterious fetal effects. Coxsackievirus A (Choice B) is an enterovirus that causes hand, foot, and mouth disease characterized by fever, painful blisters in the mouth and throat, and a macular rash especially on the hands and feet. It does not have known deleterious fetal effects. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Choice C) can often be asymptomatic or cause a short, febrile, flu-like illness. CMV is associated with intrauterine growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephaly, seizures, periventricular calcifications, and rash. While fetal hydrops is a potential complication of CMV infection, parvovirus B19 infection is the more likely cause given the clinical presentation. Herpes simplex virus infection (Choice D) in an adult is characterized by tender vesicles with ulceration followed by crusting. It may pass to a newborn during delivery, and neonatal encephalitis is a severe complication, but it is not the typical cause of hydrops fetalis. Educational Objective: Hydrops fetalis is diagnosed by the combination of fluid accumulation in at least two extravascular compartments (e.g., pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, ascites, and subcutaneous edema), and it is associated with placentomegaly and polyhydramnios. Parvovirus B19 infection in a gravid woman is a common infectious cause of hydrops fetalis.
Source: 5A #16
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 34 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports that 1 week ago, she had malaise for 2 days followed by a bright rash over her cheeks that resolved within 3 days. A rash has now developed on her arms and legs. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and pulse is 90/min. Examination shows a marble-appearing rash over the upper and lower extremities. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft. Fundal height is 35 cm. The fetal heart rate is 160/min. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Cytomegalovirus B) Herpes simplex virus 1 C) Human papillomavirus D) Parvovirus E) Rubella
Correct Answer: D) Parvovirus
Parvovirus B19 is the correct answer. In adults, parvovirus B19 presents as a mild viral syndrome that may include a variable rash (less likely to show the characteristic red-cheeked appearance seen in children), fever, chills, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, or mild respiratory symptoms. The clinical presentation in this case—initial facial rash followed by extremity involvement—is consistent with parvovirus B19 infection. The virus has tropism for bone marrow and infects erythroid progenitor cells, causing fetal anemia when acquired during pregnancy, particularly in the second or third trimester. Fetal anemia from parvovirus B19 can manifest as fetal tachycardia (as seen in this case with fetal heart rate of 160/min), high-output heart failure, hydrops fetalis, and potentially fetal death. Parvovirus B19 can also cause fetal myocarditis. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) typically does not present with rash and is associated with intrauterine growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephaly, and chorioretinitis in the fetus. Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) is characterized by tender vesicles followed by ulceration and crusting, most commonly around the mouth or genital area, not the marble-appearing rash described. Fetal infection causes localized lesions of skin, eyes, and mouth with potential for disseminated disease. Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is usually asymptomatic and does not typically present with a skin rash. Chronic infections with high-risk strains can lead to cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal cancer. Rubella can present with erythematous rash, arthralgias, and fever, but the clinical presentation and fetal complications (sensorineural deafness, neurodevelopmental delay, congenital cardiac defects, microcephaly) differ from the presentation in this case. Educational Objective: Parvovirus B19 in pregnant patients presents as a mild viral syndrome with variable rash and can cause hydrops fetalis secondary to fetal anemia and high-output cardiac failure, especially when infection occurs in the second or third trimester.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Ectopic pregnancy 3 questions
Source: 3A #29
A previously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramps. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one partner, and they use condoms for contraception consistently. She takes no medications. Her pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen and lower quadrant tenderness. Speculum examination shows moderate vaginal bleeding and a closed cervical os. A pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a fluid-filled endometrial cavity and no gestational sac. Her quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 2500 mIU/mL. Forty-eight hours later, a second measurement of quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 2800 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Blighted ovum B) Complete spontaneous abortion C) Ectopic pregnancy D) Hydatidiform mole E) Normal intrauterine pregnancy
Correct Answer: C) Ectopic pregnancy
Ectopic pregnancy is the most likely diagnosis in this case. The key diagnostic features are: (1) positive pregnancy test with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain; (2) transvaginal ultrasonography showing a fluid-filled endometrial cavity but NO gestational sac despite β-hCG of 2500 mIU/mL (which should be sufficient to visualize an intrauterine gestational sac, as transvaginal ultrasound can detect intrauterine pregnancy once β-hCG exceeds 1000-2000 mIU/mL); and (3) abnormally slow rise in β-hCG (only 300 mIU/mL increase over 48 hours, or 12% increase). In normal intrauterine pregnancy, β-hCG doubles approximately every 48 hours in early pregnancy. The suboptimal rise in β-hCG combined with absence of intrauterine gestational sac is pathognomonic for ectopic pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy where the fertilized ovum implants in a non-endometrial location, most commonly the fallopian tube, but also the ovary, peritoneal cavity, or cervix. It is not viable and requires treatment with either medical management (methotrexate for small, early pregnancies) or surgical intervention (salpingectomy or laparoscopic evacuation). Complications include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum. Blighted ovum (Choice A) is an anembryonic pregnancy with a gestational sac but no embryo; β-hCG would decrease over time, not increase. Complete spontaneous abortion (Choice B) would show decreasing β-hCG, not the slow rise seen here. Hydatidiform mole (Choice D) typically produces β-hCG in excess of what would be expected for gestational age and shows characteristic cystic structures on ultrasound without fetal parts. Normal intrauterine pregnancy (Choice E) would show appropriate doubling of β-hCG every 48 hours and visualization of an intrauterine gestational sac on transvaginal ultrasound at this β-hCG level.
Source: 5A #3
A 21-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, aborta 1, comes to the emergency department because of vaginal spotting and lower abdominal pain for 3 hours. She is sexually active and does not use contraception. Menarche was at the age of 13 years. Menses occur at regular 30-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. Pelvic examination shows slightly blood-tinged vaginal discharge. There is cervical motion tenderness with a firm cervix and a closed cervical os. The uterus is firm and tender and consistent in size with a 6-week gestation. The right adnexa is tender. Urine pregnancy test is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Appendicitis B) Ectopic pregnancy C) Hemorrhagic corpus luteal cyst D) Hydatidiform mole E) Pelvic inflammatory disease
Correct Answer: B) Ectopic pregnancy
Ectopic pregnancy is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. An ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in a non-endometrial location, most commonly the fallopian tube, but can also occur on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or other sites. It is nonviable and cannot support a pregnancy. Key clinical features supporting ectopic pregnancy in this case: - Positive urine pregnancy test with 6-week missed menstrual period - Vaginal bleeding/spotting - Abdominopelvic pain - Right adnexal tenderness - Closed cervical os with cervical motion tenderness - Uterus consistent with 6-week gestation size Diagnostic findings in ectopic pregnancy include: - Serum β-hCG concentrations that do not increase as expected (should double approximately every 48 hours in normal pregnancy) - Absence of a fetal pole within the endometrial cavity on transvaginal ultrasonography - An intrauterine gestational sac should be visible by 5 weeks gestational age when β-hCG exceeds 1000-2000 mIU/mL Management options include medical management with methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, or surgical intervention (salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy) for larger pregnancies, treatment failure, or complications. Complications include rupture, bleeding, hemoperitoneum, and potentially hemorrhagic shock. Why other options are incorrect: - Appendicitis (A): While it can present with right lower quadrant pain, it would not explain the positive pregnancy test and vaginal bleeding - Hemorrhagic corpus luteal cyst (C): Can cause abdominopelvic pain but would be less likely with vaginal bleeding and positive pregnancy test - Hydatidiform mole (D): Presents with vaginal bleeding and positive pregnancy test but typically shows uterine size out of proportion to gestational age and lacks adnexal findings - Pelvic inflammatory disease (E): Typically presents with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and would not explain the positive pregnancy test
Source: 8A #6
A 15-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of pain in the midline and right abdomen for 3 hours. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She has had nausea and vomiting for 1 hour. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 130/68 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows severe tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Ultrasonography shows an ill-defined 4-cm mass in the right lower quadrant. A pregnancy test is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Admission to the hospital for laparoscopy B) Admission to the hospital for laparotomy C) CT scan of the pelvis D) Limited-stay observation E) MRI of the pelvis F) Uterine evacuation in the operating room
Correct Answer: A) Admission to the hospital for laparoscopy
Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in a nonendometrial location, most commonly the fallopian tube, but also on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or elsewhere. It is a nonviable pregnancy. This patient presents with classic features: abdominal pain, positive pregnancy test, missed/delayed period (7 weeks), nausea and vomiting, and an ill-defined right lower quadrant mass on ultrasonography. Ectopic pregnancies are not viable and require treatment. For small, early pregnancies, methotrexate can be used. For larger pregnancies or cases of medical treatment failure, laparoscopy with salpingectomy or evacuation is indicated. Complications include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum. Given this patient's large 4-cm mass and acute presentation with severe tenderness, urgent laparoscopy is the most appropriate next step to remove the ectopic pregnancy and prevent life-threatening complications. Laparotomy (Choice B) is unnecessarily invasive compared to laparoscopy and is associated with greater postoperative pain and complications. While laparotomy may occasionally be needed during a laparoscopic approach, laparoscopy is usually sufficient for treating ectopic pregnancy. CT scan (Choice C) and MRI (Choice E) would delay appropriate treatment and increase rupture risk. Although these imaging modalities offer better resolution, they would not change the treatment strategy and are unnecessary given the clinical presentation and ultrasonographic findings. Limited-stay observation (Choice D) is inappropriate because delaying laparoscopic treatment increases the risk for rupture, bleeding, and hemodynamic instability. This patient requires urgent intervention. Uterine evacuation (Choice F) is ineffective because ectopic pregnancies implant outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Uterine evacuation would not address the underlying pathology. Educational Objective: Ectopic pregnancy is a nonviable pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, typically in the fallopian tube. It presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with a positive pregnancy test. Ultrasonography aids diagnosis. Treatment includes methotrexate for small early pregnancies and laparoscopy for larger or complicated pregnancies.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Anovulation 3 questions
Source: 3A #36
An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses over the past 3 months; menses occur at 14- to 40-day intervals. Menstrual flow varies from spotting to heavy cramping and bleeding; the latter symptoms have caused her to miss school. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Menarche was at the age of 12 years, and menses had occurred at regular 28-day intervals for 6 years. She has a sedentary lifestyle. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (139 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Conjugated estrogen therapy B) Cyclic progesterone therapy C) Hysteroscopy D) Endometrial biopsy E) Dilation and curettage
Correct Answer: B) Cyclic progesterone therapy
Cyclic progesterone therapy is the most appropriate treatment for anovulation in this young woman. The patient presents with classic anovulatory bleeding: irregular menstrual intervals (14-40 days) with variable flow (spotting to heavy bleeding) after 6 years of regular 28-day cycles. This pattern is consistent with dysfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, a common cause of anovulation in young women. Progesterone therapy works by: (1) inhibiting FSH and LH secretion to prevent ovulation, (2) maintaining the endometrial lining and transitioning it from a proliferative to secretory phase, and (3) causing withdrawal bleeding when discontinued if anovulation is due to hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis irregularity. Incorrect options: Conjugated estrogen therapy (A) is used for menopausal vasomotor symptoms and carries risks of breast cancer, hypercoagulability, and cardiovascular morbidity; it would not treat anovulation and increases endometrial cancer risk without progestins. Hysteroscopy (C) evaluates structural causes like polyps or fibroids but is not indicated when symptoms are consistent with anovulation. Endometrial biopsy (D) is reserved for postmenopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium on ultrasound to rule out hyperplasia or carcinoma, not for young patients with anovulatory bleeding. Dilation and curettage (E) is a more invasive intervention reserved for heavy bleeding unresponsive to medical management or for removing fetal tissue/retained products of conception. Educational Objective: Cyclic progesterone therapy is the first-line treatment for anovulatory irregular menses. It transitions the endometrium from proliferative to secretory phase, inhibits FSH and LH, and produces withdrawal bleeding when discontinued if anovulation is related to irregular gonadotropin release. It will not produce bleeding if there is structural uterine abnormality or estrogen deficiency.
Source: 3A #38
A 12½-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period for 5 months. Menarche was at the age of 11 years, and menses had occurred at irregular 30- to 90-day intervals and lasted 1 to 5 days. She plays softball in the spring and participates in physical education class at school two times weekly. She is not sexually active. She is at the 60th percentile for height and 40th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Anorexia nervosa B) Athletic amenorrhea C) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia D) Hyperthyroidism E) Hypothyroidism F) Polycystic ovarian syndrome G) Prolactin-secreting tumor H) Normal development
Correct Answer: H) Normal development
Normal development of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis takes time. It is not uncommon for adolescent girls to have irregular periods for the first one to two years after beginning menstruation due to immaturity of the HPO axis, resulting in irregular and noncyclic gonadotropin-releasing hormone release from the hypothalamus. This causes varying follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations, leading to anovulation and amenorrhea, as well as varying degrees of secondary sexual characteristic progression. Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) presents with amenorrhea due to malnutrition effects on cyclic gonadotropin release, but also presents with low body weight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²), lanugo, and electrolyte imbalances not seen in this patient. Athletic amenorrhea (Choice B) occurs with suppression of the HPO axis from increased energy demands and decreased gonadotropin-releasing hormone production, most commonly in thin females undergoing rigorous exercise regimens. This patient's average amount of exercise would not be expected to cause this. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Choice C) is a disorder of cortisol synthesis with symptoms including virilization, ambiguous genitalia, salt-wasting, hirsutism, precocious puberty, and abnormal uterine bleeding depending on subtype. It would be less likely in this young, otherwise healthy patient. Hyperthyroidism (Choice D) presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. This patient lacks additional signs suggesting hyperthyroidism. Hypothyroidism (Choice E) presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and occasionally heavy or irregular periods, with physical examination findings of bradycardia, dry edematous skin, and delayed deep tendon reflexes. This patient lacks these findings. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Choice F) most commonly presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses due to anovulation from increased androgen concentration, with ultrasonography showing multiple intraparenchymal follicular cysts. This patient's presentation is more consistent with normal development. A prolactin-secreting tumor (Choice G) can inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, presenting with amenorrhea often associated with galactorrhea. This would be a less common cause of amenorrhea than normal development in this patient.
Source: 8A #8
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of heavy vaginal bleeding and passage of plum-sized clots over the past menstrual period, which was 2.5 months ago. She is not sexually active. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall with pubic hair development at sexual maturity rating stage 4. Examination shows a 50-mL clot in the vaginal vault; the cervical os is closed. The uterus is normal in size and contour. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient? A) Clomiphene therapy B) Leuprolide therapy C) Oral contraceptive therapy D) Dilatation and curettage E) No treatment indicated
Correct Answer: C) Oral contraceptive therapy
This patient presents with anovulation secondary to immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, a common cause of heavy menstrual bleeding in adolescents. Anovulation results in unopposed estrogen production, leading to continued endometrial development and heavy vaginal bleeding when menses occur. The immature HPO axis causes irregular and noncyclic GnRH release, resulting in varying FSH and LH concentrations, which prevents normal ovulation and progesterone production. Oral contraceptive therapy is the first-line treatment because it normalizes the menstrual cycle and stabilizes the endometrium by providing exogenous estrogen and progesterone, thereby decreasing menstrual bleeding. This is particularly important given this patient's anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL) and ongoing bleeding. Clomiphene therapy (Choice A) is used to treat infertility caused by anovulation by acting as an estrogen receptor antagonist to increase FSH and LH, promoting ovulation. It would not effectively normalize the menstrual cycle or decrease bleeding in this patient. Leuprolide therapy (Choice B) is a GnRH agonist useful for treating menorrhagia or endometriosis but is typically reserved for patients who fail oral contraceptive therapy and is less practical as an injectable medication for initial management. Dilatation and curettage (Choice D) is an invasive surgical option reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients or those who fail conservative management with oral contraceptives. No treatment (Choice E) is inappropriate given the patient's significant bleeding, anemia, and risk of further hemoglobin decline without intervention. Educational Objective: Heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding in adolescents is often secondary to anovulation from an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Oral contraceptives are first-line therapy to normalize the menstrual cycle and stabilize the endometrial lining.
▶ Male Reproductive Genital Herpes 3 questions
Source: 3A #41
A 47-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of increasing pain with urination. Five days ago, she began treatment with a sulfonamide antibiotic by her primary physician after a phone consultation; she has not had relief of her symptoms. She has no history of serious illness, abnormal Pap smears, or sexually transmitted diseases. She currently takes no medications. She states that she has had increasing stress during the past month. Pelvic examination shows an exquisitely tender ulcer on the lower labium minus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Candidiasis B) Condyloma acuminatum C) Herpes simplex virus 1 D) Molluscum contagiosum E) Paget disease
Correct Answer: C) Herpes simplex virus 1
Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) genital infection is characterized by painful vesicles in the genital area (vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum) and is associated with pain during urination. Most cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, but HSV-1 also causes genital herpes infection. The condition typically begins with vesicle formation, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border. This painful rash is exacerbated during urination when acidic urine passes over open vesicles or ulcers. The dysuria may be misinterpreted as a urinary tract infection and treated with sulfonamide antibiotics, which are ineffective against HSV. HSV is treated with acyclovir or valacyclovir, guanosine analogs that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, reducing the duration of viral shedding and symptoms. Vulvovaginal candidiasis presents with erythema, itching, burning, and excoriation with thick white coarse discharge and pseudohyphae on microscopy, but does not cause ulcerations or vesicles. Condyloma acuminatum (genital warts) from human papillomavirus presents as soft, fleshy growths. Molluscum contagiosum from poxvirus presents as small painless papules with central umbilication. Paget disease of the vulva is a skin cancer appearing as a pink or red well-demarcated raised lesion that can be pruritic. Educational Objective: HSV-1 and HSV-2 can both cause genital herpes, characterized by painful vesicles and ulcers on an erythematous base. Symptoms typically include local pain and itching, dysuria, and tender lymphadenopathy.
Source: 5A #2
A previously healthy 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever, chills, and severe burning vulvar pain with urination. She is sexually active with one male partner and does not use contraception. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral, tender, firm inguinal lymphadenopathy. There are several erythematous, coalescing labial vesicles bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Chlamydia trachomatis B) Gardnerella vaginalis C) Haemophilus ducreyi D) Herpes simplex virus E) Neisseria gonorrhoeae F) Treponema pallidum G) Trichomonas vaginalis
Correct Answer: D) Herpes simplex virus
This patient presents with classic features of genital herpes caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). The key clinical findings are erythematous, coalescing labial vesicles bilaterally, fever, chills, severe burning vulvar pain with urination, and bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. HSV-1 and HSV-2 are double-stranded DNA, enveloped viruses. Genital herpes is most commonly caused by HSV-2 but can also be caused by HSV-1. The infection typically begins with vesicle formation, which then lyse to form shallow, painful ulcers with erythematous borders. Genital herpes causes vulvar pain with urination due to irritation of vesicles and ulcers. HSV may remain latent in sacral ganglia and reactivate to cause recurrent painful vesicles and erosions with associated inguinal lymphadenopathy. Systemic manifestations can include viral meningitis and encephalitis. Treatment involves guanosine analogs such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, which inhibit viral DNA polymerase. Incorrect answers: Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice A) causes lymphogranuloma venereum with painless genital ulcers, not painful vesicles. Gardnerella vaginalis (Choice B) causes bacterial vaginosis presenting with gray, malodorous discharge and clue cells, not vesicles. Haemophilus ducreyi (Choice C) causes chancroid with exudative painful ulcers but not vesicular lesions. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice E) causes cervicitis and urethritis but does not produce painful vesicles. Treponema pallidum (Choice F) causes syphilis with a painless chancre in primary stage, not painful vesicles. Trichomonas vaginalis (Choice G) causes trichomoniasis with green malodorous discharge and motile organisms on wet mount, not vesicles. Educational Objective: Genital herpes infections present with painful vesicles and erosions accompanied by dysuria, fever, chills, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. HSV-2 followed by HSV-1 are the most common viral culprits.
Source: 7A #11
A 24-year-old woman presents with fever, malaise, multiple painful blisters on the vulva, and difficulty voiding. She is sexually active with multiple partners. Examination shows multiple tender vesicles on the vulva and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chancroid B) Chlamydia trachomatis infection C) Genital Herpes Simplex Virus D) Lymphogranuloma venereum E) Molluscum contagiosum F) Trichomoniasis
Correct Answer: C) Genital Herpes Simplex Virus
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) genital infection is a sexually transmitted infection characterized by painful vesicles in the genital area (vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum). Most cases are caused by HSV-2, though HSV-1 can also cause genital herpes. The condition typically begins with pain and paresthesia, followed by formation of vesicles that lyse and progress to shallow, round, painful ulcers with an erythematous border. The painful rash is exacerbated during urination as acidic urine passes over open vesicles or ulcers. Erosions are frequently accompanied by fever, chills, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Treatment includes acyclovir or valacyclovir, which decrease the duration of viral shedding and symptoms. Incorrect answers: Chancroid (Choice A) is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and typically presents with a single painful exudative ulcer rather than multiple vesicles. Chlamydia trachomatis infection (Choice B) presents with urethritis, dysuria, and discharge but does not cause painful genital ulcers. Lymphogranuloma venereum (Choice D), caused by Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L1-L3, presents with small nonpainful genital ulcers and severe inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) but not painful vesicles. Molluscum contagiosum (Choice E), caused by poxvirus, presents with small painless papules with central umbilication, not painful lesions. Trichomoniasis (Choice F) causes vaginitis with pruritus, dyspareunia, and frothy green discharge but does not cause genital lesions. Educational Objective: Herpes genitalis is characterized by painful vesicles and ulcers on an erythematous base with symptoms including local pain, itching, dysuria, and tender lymphadenopathy. Treatment includes acyclovir or valacyclovir.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Leiomyomata Uteri 3 questions
Source: 5A #6
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes for a routine health maintenance examination. She has used a copper-containing IUD for contraception for 2 years. Examination shows an enlarged uterus and a visible IUD string. Pelvic ultrasonography shows the IUD to be near the fundus adjacent to a 4-cm intramural leiomyoma uteri; the endometrial cavity is normal in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Leave the IUD in place, but inform the patient that the leiomyoma may cause heavier menses B) Remove the IUD, and recommend another contraceptive method C) Remove the IUD, and recommend removal of the leiomyoma D) Replace the IUD with an IUD of a different shape E) Reposition the IUD farther from the leiomyoma to maintain the effectiveness of the IUD
Correct Answer: A) Leave the IUD in place, but inform the patient that the leiomyoma may cause heavier menses
Leiomyomata uteri (uterine fibroids) are benign neoplasms of uterine myometrial smooth muscle and common tumors in women. They are classified as subserosal (most common, alter exterior diameter), intramural (within myometrial wall), or submucosal (extend into uterine cavity, alter endometrial shape). They typically present with vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, miscarriage, or infertility, though they can be asymptomatic. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus. Pelvic ultrasonography visualizes fibroids well. They are estrogen-responsive, increasing in size with pregnancy and decreasing with menopause. Treatment for symptomatic fibroids includes NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives, GnRH agonists, myomectomy, or hysterectomy. In this case, the patient's 4-cm intramural fibroid is asymptomatic with a normal endometrial cavity. The IUD is positioned appropriately in the endometrial cavity and its T-shape is unaltered by the fibroid. IUD efficacy is not affected by the presence of fibroids when there is no endometrial cavity alteration. Therefore, the IUD should remain in place for long-term contraception, but the patient should be counseled that the fibroid may cause heavier menses. Choice B is incorrect because IUD removal is unnecessary when the device is appropriately positioned and endometrial cavity is normal; efficacy is not compromised. Choice C is incorrect because neither IUD removal nor fibroid removal is necessary in an asymptomatic patient. Choice D is incorrect because the T-shape of the copper IUD is unaltered by the intramural fibroid, making replacement unnecessary. Choice E is incorrect because repositioning is not needed, as the fibroid does not affect IUD effectiveness when the endometrial cavity remains normal. Educational Objective: Intrauterine device efficacy is not affected by the presence of fibroids in the absence of endometrial cavity alteration. Asymptomatic intramural fibroids do not require intervention.
Source: 5A #30
A 42-year-old woman with leiomyomata uteri comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has not had vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, or loss of urine. Examination shows no abnormalities except for a uterus consistent in size with a 15-week gestation. Her hematocrit is 41%. Pelvic ultrasonography confirms leiomyomata uteri. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Observation only B) Intravenous pyelography C) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy D) Oral contraceptive therapy E) Myomectomy
Correct Answer: A) Observation only
In this patient with asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri (uterine fibroids), the most appropriate management is observation only. Leiomyomata uteri are common benign tumors of the uterine smooth muscle that may be asymptomatic or cause abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain/pressure, and reproductive dysfunction. Since this patient has no symptoms (no vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, or urinary loss) and normal hematocrit, and because leiomyomata are benign and may regress over time or with menopause, asymptomatic lesions should be managed expectantly with observation. For symptomatic leiomyomata uteri, treatment options include hysteroscopic or abdominal myomectomy (first-line for those desiring pregnancy), oral contraceptive therapy, GnRH agonist therapy, or hysterectomy (for those not desiring pregnancy). However, these interventions are only indicated for symptomatic disease. Intravenous pyelography (Choice B) visualizes the urinary tract using iodine contrast dye and is not indicated for evaluating the uterus. Myomectomy (Choice E) is a first-line treatment for symptomatic uterine fibroids but is not appropriate for asymptomatic disease. GnRH agonist therapy (Choice C) and oral contraceptive therapy (Choice D) are treatment options for symptomatic leiomyomata uteri in patients not desiring pregnancy, but these are not indicated in asymptomatic patients and can cause rebound symptoms when discontinued. Educational Objective: Leiomyomata uteri are common benign smooth muscle tumors. Asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri are managed expectantly with observation, while symptomatic disease can be treated with myomectomy, oral contraceptive therapy, GnRH agonists, or hysterectomy depending on patient preferences regarding fertility preservation.
Source: 4A #25
A widowed 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, whose youngest child is 10 years old, has had increasingly heavy but regular menstrual periods for the past 3 years. Her last menses occurred 2½ weeks ago. She reports a 2-day history of labor-like pains accompanied by a small amount of vaginal bleeding. Speculum examination shows that the cervix is moderately effaced and 2 cm dilated, with some beefy red tissue at the os. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Carcinoma of the cervix B) Carcinoma of the endometrium C) Incomplete abortion D) Pedunculated submucous leiomyoma uteri E) Sarcoma of the uterus
Correct Answer: D) Pedunculated submucous leiomyoma uteri
Leiomyomata uteri (uterine fibroids) are benign neoplasms of the uterine myometrium and the most common tumor in women. They commonly present with vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, and miscarriage or infertility, and are more common in African American patients. Physical examination typically shows an enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus. In the case of pedunculated intracavitary fibroids that grow on a stalk, pressure on the internal cervical os causes dilation and effacement of the cervix with protrusion of the fibroid through the os, as seen in this patient. Laboratory studies may show iron deficiency anemia if uterine bleeding is significant. Fibroids are typically well-visualized on pelvic ultrasonography. They are estrogen-responsive, increasing in size with pregnancy and decreasing with menopause. Treatment includes NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists, and surgical options such as myomectomy or hysterectomy. Carcinoma of the cervix (Choice A) presents with vaginal bleeding, classically postcoital, and is associated with HPV high-risk strains. Physical examination shows an exophytic lesion, not a mass protruding through the cervical os. Carcinoma of the endometrium (Choice B) commonly presents as postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium on ultrasound. It does not present with a mass at the cervical os, and pelvic pain is uncommon. Incomplete abortion (Choice C) occurs when a fetus expires with partial expulsion of fetal tissue through an open cervical os. Given the patient's last menses was 2½ weeks ago, pregnancy is unlikely. Sarcoma of the uterus (Choice E) is a rare malignant tumor of the myometrium presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, and bloating. It is unlikely to present with cervical dilation and effacement as seen here.
▶ Renal Urinary System Pyelonephritis 3 questions
Source: 5A #14
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 31 weeks' gestation has had constant moderate pain in the right flank for 12 hours. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.4°F). A catheterized urine specimen shows 15-20 RBC/hpf and 30-40 WBC/hpf. Ultrasonography of the kidneys shows no abnormalities. The ureters are markedly dilated, the right more than the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Bilateral ureteral obstruction B) Hemorrhagic cystitis C) Pyelonephritis D) Renal vein thrombosis E) Ureteral calculus
Correct Answer: C) Pyelonephritis
Pyelonephritis is the most likely diagnosis. The classic presentation includes fever (38.6°C), flank pain, pyuria (30-40 WBC/hpf), and hematuria (15-20 RBC/hpf). Pyelonephritis results from retrograde spread of urinary tract infection to the kidney. Pregnant patients are at significantly higher risk due to progesterone-induced decreased ureteral tone and motility, combined with mechanical compression of the ureters by the gravid uterus at the pelvic brim, bladder, and ureteral orifices. Urinalysis typically shows >10 WBC/hpf, RBCs from mucosal inflammation, and white blood cell casts. Gram-negative rods are the most common pathogens. Physical examination findings include high fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Bilateral ureteral obstruction (Choice A) can occur from mechanical compression by the gravid uterus but would not cause fever, hematuria, or pyuria unless complicated by infection. Hemorrhagic cystitis (Choice B) presents with hematuria and pyuria from lower urinary tract infection with symptoms of dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic pain. Systemic symptoms like fever and chills are less likely, and vital signs are typically normal. Renal vein thrombosis (Choice D) may present with flank pain and hematuria but would not cause fever or dysuria. It occurs in patients with underlying thrombophilia. Ureteral calculus (Choice E) presents with colicky, unilateral flank pain radiating to the groin with gross or microscopic hematuria. RBCs without casts are common on urinalysis. It would not cause fever, dysuria, or pyuria unless there was concomitant infection. Educational Objective: Pyelonephritis typically presents with fevers, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness. It most commonly results from ascending urinary tract infections. Pregnant patients are at higher risk due to progesterone-induced decreased ureteral tone and motility, and mechanical compression of the ureters by the gravid uterus.
Source: 5A #18
A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 27 weeks gestation is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate back pain, fever, and nausea. Pregnancy has been complicated by a positive urine culture for Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) infection at 8 weeks gestation that resolved with ampicillin therapy and iron deficiency anemia with a hemoglobin concentration of 9.9 g/dL. She has not adhered to her medication regimen of iron supplementation and a prenatal vitamin. She appears moderately anxious. Her temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and right costovertebral angle tenderness. The uterus is soft and nontender. Fundal height is 26 cm. The baseline fetal heart rate is 180/min with decreased variability. Contractions occur every 10 to 15 minutes and last 20 seconds. Pelvic examination shows clear mucoid discharge from the cervical os. The cervix is not dilated or effaced. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.7 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the fetal tachycardia? A) Fetal anemia B) Fetal dehydration C) Maternal anemia D) Maternal anxiety E) Maternal fever
Correct Answer: E) Maternal fever
Maternal fever is the most likely cause of fetal tachycardia in this clinical scenario. Fetal tachycardia is defined as a heart rate greater than 160/min and can be caused by maternal fever, fetal hypoxia, fetal anemia, intra-amniotic infection, and maternal medications. In the setting of maternal infection, fetal tachycardia is most likely secondary to maternal fever. This patient presents with classic signs of pyelonephritis: fever, back pain, right costovertebral angle tenderness, and elevated blood pressure. The fetal heart rate of 180/min with decreased variability is consistent with a maternal febrile state. Fetal anemia (Choice A) can present with tachycardia but is also likely to be associated with ascites, pericardial fluid, pleural effusions, and an increased middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, making it less likely in this case. Fetal dehydration (Choice B) is uncommon and unlikely in the absence of signs of maternal dehydration. Maternal anemia (Choice C) is common in pregnancy due to physiologic adaptations such as increased plasma volume and increased risk for iron deficiency. However, severe maternal anemia can cause premature birth and low birth weight but does not typically cause fetal tachycardia. Maternal anxiety (Choice D) can cause fetal tachycardia if severe due to release of catecholamines that cross the placenta. However, this patient is experiencing only moderate anxiety, and her high fever is a more likely cause of the fetal tachycardia. Educational Objective: Causes of fetal tachycardia (heart rate >160/min) include maternal fever, fetal hypoxia, fetal anemia, intra-amniotic infection, and maternal medications. In the setting of maternal infection, fetal tachycardia is most likely secondary to maternal fever.
Source: 4A #7
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 27 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of painful contractions every 5 minutes. She has not had vaginal discharge or itching. During her first prenatal visit, routine urine culture grew 10,000 colonies/ml of Streptococcus agalactiae (group B). She was not treated at that time because she was asymptomatic. She has no history of serious illness. Pregnancy had been otherwise uncomplicated. She takes no medications and has an allergy to penicillin. Her first pregnancy ended in spontaneous vaginal delivery at 33 weeks' gestation. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows tenderness to percussion over the right flank. The uterus is nontender and consistent in size with a 27-week gestation. The fetal heart rate is 160/min. Uterine contractions occur every 5 minutes and last 45 seconds. On pelvic examination, the cervix is 2 cm dilated and 75% effaced; the vertex is at O station. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Chorioamnionitis B) Cervical insufficiency C) Premature rupture of membranes D) Pyelonephritis E) Sepsis
Correct Answer: D) Pyelonephritis
