Pyelonephritis is an infection of the upper urinary tract and kidneys typically caused by retrograde spread of bacterial infection from the lower urinary tract. It is characterized by fever, leukocytosis, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral angle (flank) tenderness—all present in this patient. In pregnancy, asymptomatic bacteriuria significantly increases the risk for pyelonephritis. This patient had asymptomatic bacteriuria with group B Streptococcus at her first prenatal visit and was not treated, placing her at high risk. Pyelonephritis increases the risk of obstetric complications including preterm labor, defined as contractions with cervical change occurring after 20 weeks and before 37 weeks' gestation. The clinical presentation—fever (37.8°C), tachycardia (100/min), hypotension (90/50 mm Hg), right flank tenderness on percussion, and preterm contractions—is classic for pyelonephritis with secondary preterm labor. Treatment requires hospital admission for intravenous antibiotics, followed by suppressive antibiotics throughout the remainder of pregnancy. Chorioamnionitis (Choice A) is a bacterial infection of fetal membranes that commonly occurs with premature or prolonged rupture of membranes. While it presents with maternal fever and leukocytosis, the uterus is typically tender to palpation. This patient's infection preceded preterm labor without membrane rupture. Cervical insufficiency (Choice B) is the inability of the cervix to contain pregnancy products without contractions or labor, typically presenting in the second or early third trimester with feelings of pelvic fullness in the absence of contractions. It would not explain the patient's fever or costovertebral angle tenderness. Premature rupture of membranes (Choice C) is rupture of the amniotic sac before labor onset. Patients typically report a gush or steady leakage of vaginal fluid. This patient has no reported vaginal discharge or fluid leakage. Sepsis (Choice E) is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection. While acute pyelonephritis can cause sepsis, the clinical picture here is more consistent with uncomplicated pyelonephritis with secondary preterm labor rather than sepsis-induced organ dysfunction. Educational Objective: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is a significant risk factor for pyelonephritis, which increases the risk for preterm labor and/or premature rupture of membranes. All pregnant women should be screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria and treated if positive. Gravid women with acute pyelonephritis require hospital admission for close monitoring and intravenous antibiotics, with suppressive antibiotic therapy continued throughout pregnancy to prevent recurrence.
▶ Respiratory System Pulmonary Embolism 3 questions
Source: 5A #28
Two days after spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy newborn at term, a previously healthy 37-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has left-sided pleuritic chest pain and progressive shortness of breath. Her pulse is 94/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 96/55 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. Examination of the extremities shows mild edema and no tenderness. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.1 g/dL, and leukocyte count is 15,500/mm³. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.45, PaCO2 21 mm Hg, and PaO2 85 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Bronchial smooth muscle contractions B) Exudates in the alveoli C) Fetal squamous cells in the pulmonary veins D) Mucus trapping in the bronchioles E) Thrombus within the pulmonary arteries
Correct Answer: E) Thrombus within the pulmonary arteries
Pulmonary embolism (PE) classically presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and clear breath sounds—exactly as seen in this patient. The postpartum period is a significant hypercoagulable state, and pelvic venous congestion during pregnancy is a common source of deep venous thrombosis. The arterial blood gas findings are pathognomonic: acute respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.45, PaCO2 21 mm Hg) from hyperventilation due to hypoxemia, and hypoxemia (PaO2 85 mm Hg) resulting from ventilated but not perfused lung segments. The clear breath sounds help exclude pneumonia and other airway diseases. The mild hypotension (96/55 mm Hg) suggests a large embolus with hemodynamic compromise. Diagnosis is confirmed with CT pulmonary angiography, though ventilation-perfusion scanning is preferred in pregnancy due to lower fetal radiation exposure. Treatment includes anticoagulation or surgical thrombectomy depending on bleeding risk. Incorrect answers: (A) Bronchial smooth muscle contractions describe asthma/reactive airway disease, which presents with wheezing and respiratory distress on examination—this patient has clear breath sounds. (B) Exudates in the alveoli describe pneumonia or ARDS, which present with cough, fever, focal rhonchi, and egophony—not seen here. (C) Fetal squamous cells in pulmonary veins describe amniotic fluid embolism, a rare intrapartum complication presenting with acute severe dyspnea, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, and DIC—unlikely 2 days postpartum. (D) Mucus trapping in bronchioles describes acute/chronic bronchitis or cystic fibrosis, presenting with productive cough and rhonchorous breath sounds—not present in this patient.
Source: 7A #4
Two days after undergoing cesarean delivery because of failure to progress, a 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has mild chest pain and dyspnea after walking to the nursery to see her newborn. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.2°C, heart rate is 110/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Physical examination shows a clean, dry incision. Cardiopulmonary exam is unremarkable. Abdomen is moderately tender. Pelvic examination shows moderate lochia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Abdominal ultrasonography B) Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities C) Echocardiography D) Spiral CT angiography of the chest E) MRI of the abdomen
Correct Answer: D) Spiral CT angiography of the chest
This patient presents with acute-onset dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia (110/min), tachypnea (28/min), and hypoxia (90% on room air) two days after cesarean delivery, which is highly suggestive of pulmonary embolus (PE). Pregnancy and the postpartum period represent hypercoagulable states due to overexpression of coagulation factors I, II, VII, VIII, IX, and X, while anticoagulant protein S is underexpressed. Additionally, hormonal changes and compression by the gravid uterus lead to venous stasis and pooling of blood in the lower extremities and pelvis, increasing risk for deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and subsequent PE. ECG typically shows sinus tachycardia without ST segment changes. The most appropriate next diagnostic step is spiral CT angiography of the chest to confirm PE diagnosis. For postpartum patients, spiral CT angiography is preferred; for gravid patients, nuclear medicine ventilation-perfusion scans are preferred due to lower fetal radiation exposure. Abdominal ultrasonography (Choice A) is useful for acute abdominal pain evaluation (biliary pathologies, appendicitis) but this patient's presentation is highly suspicious for pulmonary pathology requiring chest imaging. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities (Choice B) can confirm DVT but will not confirm PE diagnosis and delays treatment of the acute presentation. Echocardiography (Choice C) evaluates cardiac pathologies and may be indicated if right heart strain is suspected, but spiral CT angiography should be performed first to confirm PE diagnosis. MRI of the abdomen (Choice E) can evaluate postpartum abdominal pain if other imaging is nondiagnostic, but this patient's pulmonary findings require prompt chest imaging. Educational Objective: Pulmonary embolus presents with acute-onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Gravid and postpartum patients are at increased risk for DVT and PE due to hypercoagulability and venous stasis. For postpartum patients, diagnosis is confirmed with spiral CT angiography of the chest; for gravid patients, nuclear medicine ventilation-perfusion scans are preferred due to lower fetal radiation exposure.
Source: 4A #1
A previously healthy 39-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of acute pain in the left hemithorax. She says that the pain is exacerbated by breathing. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Fetal heart tones are 170/min. Examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows nonspecific changes. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.43, PCO2 35 mm Hg, PO2 70 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Angina pectoris B) Costochondritis C) Myocardial infarction D) Pulmonary embolus E) Viral pneumonia
Correct Answer: D) Pulmonary embolus
This patient's presenting findings of acute onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia (PO2 70 mm Hg) are highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism. A minority of patients with PE present with mild fever, which can create diagnostic confusion. ECG commonly shows sinus tachycardia without ST segment depression or elevation. Pregnancy represents a hypercoagulable state in which coagulation factors I, II, VII, VIII, IX, and X are overexpressed, while anticoagulant protein S is under-expressed. Hormonal changes and compression by the gravid uterus lead to venous stasis and pooling of blood in the lower extremities and pelvis, common sites of venous thrombosis. Gravid patients are at increased risk for deep vein thrombosis and subsequent pulmonary embolism throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period. Further evaluation should include ventilation-perfusion scan (preferred in pregnancy) or CT pulmonary angiography (rapid and sensitive but carries fetal radiation risk). Angina pectoris (Choice A) is characterized by exertional or stress-triggered chest pain that improves with rest or nitroglycerin, often radiating to neck, jaw, or arm. Anginal pain does not typically change with respiration or position. Costochondritis (Choice B) involves inflammation of costochondral or chondrosternal junctions. While symptoms may worsen during deep inspiration due to chest wall expansion, localized tenderness to palpation helps differentiate it from pleuritic chest pain. Costochondritis does not typically produce hypoxia. Myocardial infarction (Choice C) classically presents with acute-onset chest pain radiating to neck, jaw, or arm, along with shortness of breath, nausea, and/or lightheadedness. The pain is non-pleuritic, and ECG typically shows ST segment depression or elevation. Viral pneumonia (Choice E) presents with dyspnea, cough, tachypnea, and fever with possible pleuritic chest pain. Symptom onset occurs over hours or days rather than suddenly. Chest x-rays typically show lobar opacification or patchy, multifocal infiltrates. Given normal x-rays, this presentation is more consistent with pulmonary embolism. Educational Objective: Pulmonary embolism presents with acute onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Gravid patients are at increased risk for deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism due to hypercoagulability and venous stasis. A high index of suspicion should be maintained for gravid patients presenting with acute onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Pelvic Inflammatory Disease 3 questions
Source: 5A #33
A previously healthy 19-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, aborta 1, comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of severe pelvic pain and a pus-like vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. She has had two sexual partners during the past month and uses an oral contraceptive. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows tenderness to palpation of the lower quadrants with no guarding or rebound. Speculum examination shows irritated vaginal and cervical mucosa with copious purulent discharge coming from the cervical os. Bimanual examination shows cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Rectovaginal examination shows a fluctuant mass in the cul-de-sac. In addition to testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Pap smear B) Herpes simplex virus test C) HIV antibody test D) Human papillomavirus test E) Hysterosalpingography
Correct Answer: C) HIV antibody test
This patient presents with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and/or Chlamydia trachomatis, characterized by mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness, fever, and a fluctuant mass in the cul-de-sac suggesting a tuba-ovarian abscess. Risk factors for PID include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and lack of barrier contraception. Patients diagnosed with PID should be tested for other common sexually transmitted infections, including HIV and syphilis. Compromised mucosal barriers from genital infections provide an entry point for HIV transmission, making HIV testing essential in this clinical context. Pap smear (Choice A) is used for routine cervical cancer screening to detect dysplasia caused by HPV, not for diagnosis of acute sexually transmitted infections. Herpes simplex virus testing (Choice B) is indicated when genital herpes is suspected, presenting with painful vesicles and dysuria, which is not the clinical picture here. Human papillomavirus testing (Choice D) is performed in conjunction with Pap smear cytology for cervical cancer screening, not for acute STI diagnosis. Hysterosalpingography (Choice E) is used in infertility evaluation to assess fallopian tube patency and detect intrauterine abnormalities, not for acute infection diagnosis. Educational Objective: Patients diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease caused by gonorrhea or chlamydia should be tested for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV and syphilis, as compromised mucosal barriers from genital infections increase the risk of HIV acquisition.
Source: 4A #19
A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of moderate lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting that began after her last menstrual period 2 weeks ago. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. She underwent a first trimester elective abortion 8 months ago and has been using an oral contraceptive since then. She has been sexually active with one male partner for 1 year. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness. Pelvic examination shows blood-tinged discharge at the cervical os. There is cervical motion and mild uterine tenderness. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Chlamydia trachomatis infection B) Endometrial polyp C) Levonorgestrel-induced endometrial atrophy D) Retained products of conception E) Trichomoniasis
Correct Answer: A) Chlamydia trachomatis infection
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract and pelvis from upward migration of bacterial infection from the lower genital tract. Clinical manifestations include abnormal uterine bleeding, cervical and vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and uterine tenderness. Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of PID and endometritis (inflammation of the uterine lining). C. trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted infection in young adults, and the USPSTF recommends testing for C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in all sexually active patients under 25 years old. While C. trachomatis can present with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge, it can also be asymptomatic. Diagnosis is made with nucleic acid amplification testing, and treatment consists of azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone. When endometritis is present (indicated by uterine tenderness), 10-14 days of antibiotic therapy is recommended. Endometrial polyps (B) may cause irregular or unpredictable uterine bleeding but would not cause cervical motion tenderness or uterine tenderness. Levonorgestrel-induced endometrial atrophy (C) from hormonal contraception would not cause the patient's cervical motion tenderness or uterine tenderness, and she is using oral contraceptives rather than a hormonal IUD. Retained products of conception (D) could cause endometritis but would be expected to present shortly after the abortion 8 months prior, not at this time. Trichomoniasis (E) causes vaginitis and cervicitis with pruritus, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and characteristic green, frothy, malodorous discharge, but does not typically cause the degree of uterine tenderness seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of endometritis in young, sexually active women. Endometritis is characterized by inflammation of the uterine wall and causes abnormal uterine bleeding, discharge, abdominal pain, and cervical and uterine tenderness on examination.
Source: 8A #37
A 42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-year history of progressively irregular and increasingly painful menstrual periods. During this time, she also has had pain during sexual intercourse. Menses occur at 18- to 23-day intervals and last 10 days. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. The patient has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is sexually active and monogamous with her husband, who had a vasectomy 10 years ago. The patient is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). Physical examination shows uterine tenderness to palpation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An endometrial biopsy specimen obtained 20 days after her last menstrual period shows secretory endometrium with plasma cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chronic endometritis B) Endometrial cancer C) Endometrial hyperplasia D) Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism E) Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism F) Pelvic inflammatory disease
Correct Answer: A) Chronic endometritis
Chronic endometritis is inflammation of the uterine lining that is most commonly idiopathic or inflammatory. Less common causes include pelvic radiation therapy, infection, IUDs, fibroids, and polyps. The key clinical presentation includes abnormal uterine bleeding (irregular, unpredictable bleeding not associated with usual menstrual signs) and abdominal/pelvic pain, with possible uterine or cervical motion tenderness on examination. The pathognomonic finding on endometrial biopsy is the presence of plasma cells in the endometrium, which is exactly what this patient demonstrates. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may include antibiotic therapy, removal of foreign bodies, or surgical excision of intrauterine growths. Endometrial cancer and endometrial hyperplasia typically present with postmenopausal bleeding and would show increased glandular density with atypical nuclei or malignant cells with stromal invasion on biopsy, not plasma cells. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure) presents with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility in younger women with elevated FSH/LH, not abnormal uterine bleeding with plasma cells on biopsy. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism causes anovulation or amenorrhea with decreased FSH/LH levels, not the histologic findings seen here. Pelvic inflammatory disease is acute endometritis caused by ascending Chlamydia or Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, presenting with fever, mucopurulent discharge, and neutrophils (not plasma cells) on endometrial biopsy. This patient's chronic presentation with plasma cells on biopsy and absence of acute infection signs distinguishes chronic endometritis as the correct diagnosis.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Intrapartum fetal evaluation 3 questions
Source: 4A #21
A 34-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted because of a blood pressure of 160/95 mm Hg. She has chronic hypertension and is being treated with methyldopa. Ultrasonography shows fetal growth restriction. Four hours after induction of labor with oxytocin, the cervix is 6 cm dilated. A fetal heart tracing is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the findings shown in the fetal heart tracing? A) Compensated fetal stress B) Umbilical cord compression C) Pressure on the fetal head D) Uteroplacental insufficiency E) Normal fetal heart rate
Correct Answer: D) Uteroplacental insufficiency
Uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia present with late decelerations on the fetal heart tracing. Late decelerations are defined as gradual decreases in fetal heart rate that begin after the peak of uterine contraction and reach the nadir more than 30 seconds after initiation of heart rate decline. Risk factors for uteroplacental insufficiency include hypertension (present in this patient), diabetes, anemia, cocaine use, smoking, coagulopathies, late-term pregnancy, and uterine infection. Fetal hypoxemia can also result from severe uterine contractions and maternal hypotension or hypoxia. This patient has chronic hypertension and fetal growth restriction, both predisposing factors. Treatment includes supplemental oxygenation, positioning the patient on her left side or all fours, and intravenous fluids. If late decelerations persist, urgent cesarean delivery is indicated to prevent fetal harm. Compensated fetal stress (Choice A) would not show such significant changes on fetal heart tracing; late decelerations indicate uncompensated fetal hypoxemia. Umbilical cord compression (Choice B) presents with variable decelerations—abrupt decreases of at least 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds to 2 minutes without specific relation to uterine contractions. Pressure on the fetal head (Choice C) occurs during labor engagement and presents with early decelerations that mirror uterine contractions; this is a normal finding requiring no intervention. Normal fetal heart rate (Choice E) ranges 110-160 bpm with 6-25 beats of variability and frequent accelerations; variable and early decelerations may be acceptable during labor, but late decelerations indicate fetal distress requiring intervention.
Source: 4A #43
A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 41 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Contractions occur every 3 minutes. The cervix is 100% effaced and 4 cm dilated; the vertex is at +1 station. The membranes rupture yielding moderately thick meconium-stained fluid. The fetal heart rate has a baseline of 130/min with variable decelerations lasting 45 seconds and decreasing to 60/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) External cephalic version B) Forceps delivery C) Amnioinfusion D) Amniocentesis E) Cordocentesis
Correct Answer: C) Amnioinfusion
Variable decelerations following rupture of membranes are suggestive of umbilical cord compression. Amnioinfusion is the process of instilling fluid into the amniotic cavity and is useful for alleviating umbilical cord compression by increasing the volume of amniotic fluid. Although amnioinfusion is the most appropriate response among the options provided, evidence for its benefit in improving outcomes related to meconium-stained amniotic fluid remains controversial. External cephalic version (Choice A) is a technique for repositioning the fetus in breech presentation after 37 weeks' gestation and is not routinely used for managing umbilical cord compression; it carries risk of worsening compression or cord entanglement. Forceps delivery (Choice B) assists vaginal delivery but is not appropriate for persistent umbilical cord compression due to fetal distress. Emergency cesarean delivery is the preferred method in this scenario. Amniocentesis (Choice D) involves ultrasonography-guided needle aspiration of amniotic fluid and is useful for diagnosing fetal chromosomal abnormalities and chorioamnionitis. Removal of further amniotic fluid in cord compression would worsen compression and fetal hypoxia and should not be performed. Cordocentesis (Choice E) involves ultrasonography-guided needle aspiration of blood from the fetal umbilical cord. Fetal blood sampling carries significant risk and should only be used when less invasive techniques provide inadequate information. It is not appropriate for diagnosing or managing umbilical cord compression. Educational Objective: Variable decelerations following rupture of membranes indicate umbilical cord compression. Amnioinfusion alleviates fetal cord compression by increasing amniotic fluid volume.
Source: 4A #47
A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks' gestation has had ruptured membranes for 5 hours without contractions. Her prenatal course was uncomplicated. Her cervix is 80% effaced and 2 cm dilated. The fetal position is right occipitoposterior. The fetal heart rate pattern is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern? A) Chorioamnionitis B) Fetal sleep state C) Occipitoposterior position D) Umbilical cord compression E) Uteroplacental insufficiency
Correct Answer: B) Fetal sleep state
Minimal variability, defined as less than six beats per minute variation from the baseline heart rate, can be caused by fetal sleep state, hypoxia, opioids, and magnesium. When caused by hypoxia, the fetal heart tracing typically shows either tachycardia or bradycardia (depending on severity) along with late or variable decelerations. In this case, the patient shows no signs of distress, the fetal heart rate is normal, and there has been no administration of opioids or magnesium, making fetal sleep state the most likely explanation. Chorioamnionitis (Choice A) is a bacterial infection of fetal membranes commonly occurring with prolonged rupture of membranes. It presents with maternal fever and leukocytosis, and the fetal heart tracing would likely show tachycardia from maternal fever. Occipitoposterior position (Choice C) is a fetal malposition that increases risk for arrest of descent but does not cause decreased fetal heart rate variability unless accompanied by labor complications. Umbilical cord compression (Choice D) typically presents with variable decelerations associated with contractions and would be unexpected prior to contractions except in cord prolapse. It does not typically cause minimal variability without severe hypoxia. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) typically presents with late decelerations associated with contractions in conditions like preeclampsia, placental abruption, or intrauterine infection. It does not cause minimal variability without severe hypoxia. Educational Objective: Minimal variability in fetal heart rate can be caused by fetal sleep state, hypoxia, opioids, and magnesium. When the fetal heart rate is normal with no other signs of fetal or maternal distress, the most common cause is a fetal sleep state.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Lochia 2 questions
Source: 6A #4
A 25-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of almost continuous vaginal bleeding since delivery 5 days ago. She underwent a cesarean delivery because of a breech presentation at 40 weeks' gestation. She has had no difficulty breast-feeding. She is afebrile. Approximately 5 ml of old blood is visible in the vagina. The cervix is closed, and the uterus is firm and approximately 10 cm in length. Her hematocrit is 37%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Observation B) Coagulation profile C) Administration of methylergonovine D) Administration of oxytocin E) Dilatation and curettage
Correct Answer: A) Observation
Vaginal discharge (lochia) following delivery is a normal physiologic process that may last during the puerperium for 4 to 6 weeks. Lochia progresses through three stages: lochia rubra (bloody, lasting up to 10 days), lochia serosa (serous), and lochia alba (white to yellow). This patient presents with stable hemodynamics, normal hematocrit (37%), a firm uterus, closed cervix, and only a small amount of old blood on examination—all findings consistent with normal lochia rubra. No intervention is necessary; observation is appropriate. Significant postpartum hemorrhage would present with hemodynamic instability, falling hematocrit, and larger volumes of bleeding, prompting evaluation for causes such as uterine atony, lacerations, retained products of conception, or coagulopathy. Coagulation profile (Choice B) is indicated only if coagulopathy is suspected in cases of significant hemorrhage. Methylergonovine (Choice C) and oxytocin (Choice D) are ergot alkaloids and uterotonic agents used to treat postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony by increasing uterine smooth muscle contraction and tone; they are not indicated for normal lochia. Dilation and curettage (Choice E) is reserved for postpartum hemorrhage secondary to retained placental fragments, which would present with significant bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, and malodorous discharge. Educational Objective: Normal lochia is not significant bleeding and does not require intervention. Significant postpartum bleeding should raise suspicion for delayed postpartum hemorrhage and prompt immediate evaluation for underlying causes.
Source: 8A #50
A 20-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of vaginal discharge since an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her newborn at term 1 week ago. Initially the discharge was red, but it is now white. She is breast-feeding without difficulty. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a thick, white vaginal discharge. No vaginal lacerations are noted. The cervix is closed, and the uterus is consistent in size with a 12-week gestation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Bacterial vaginitis B) Candidiasis C) Lochia alba D) Retained products of conception E) Undiagnosed vaginal laceration
Correct Answer: C) Lochia alba
Lochia is normal vaginal discharge following delivery caused by the shedding of the superficial decidua and lasts during the puerperium for 4 to 6 weeks. It progresses through three stages: lochia rubra (early discharge containing blood lasting up to 10 days), lochia serosa (serous discharge lasting 2-3 weeks), and lochia alba (white to yellow discharge). This patient's presentation of white discharge 1 week postpartum is consistent with the transition from lochia rubra to lochia alba. Physical examination, laboratory studies, and diagnostic imaging are not typically performed as lochia is a physiologic rather than pathologic condition. Bacterial vaginitis (Choice A) presents with gray, thin, malodorous discharge, vaginal pH >4.5, fish-like odor on KOH testing, and clue cells on wet mount. This patient has thick, white discharge without these features. Candidiasis (Choice B) presents with vaginal pruritus, vulvar erythema, thick white discharge, normal vaginal pH, and negative KOH testing. While this patient has white discharge, she lacks pruritus, erythema, and risk factors (diabetes, recent antibiotics, or corticosteroids). Retained products of conception (Choice D) can cause secondary postpartum hemorrhage (bleeding 24 hours to 12 weeks after delivery) and infection with abdominal pain, fever, and malodorous discharge. This patient has no signs of bleeding or infection. Undiagnosed vaginal laceration (Choice E) would present with delayed vaginal bleeding rather than white discharge. While most lacerations are diagnosed immediately due to ongoing bleeding, an undiagnosed laceration would not cause the white discharge observed here. Educational Objective: Lochia is normal postpartum vaginal discharge caused by decidual shedding. Lochia rubra (first stage) contains blood and lasts up to 10 days, progressing to lochia serosa (serous), and finally lochia alba (white to yellow discharge).
▶ Human Development Preventive and travel medicine in adulthood 2 questions
Source: 6A #17
A 47-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance examination. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years but quit 1 year ago. She has had one lifetime sexual partner and has not been sexually active for 3 years. Pap smear and mammography showed normal findings 8 months ago. Her mother died of breast cancer at age 60 years. Physical and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for this patient? A) Pap smear B) X-ray of the chest C) Mammography D) Colonoscopy E) No screening indicated
Correct Answer: E) No screening indicated
Screening tests are used to identify potentially treatable conditions early in their course to prevent long-term morbidity or mortality. The decision to perform screening tests for malignancy is based on patient age and specific cancer risk factors. Screening tests decrease in value with repeated performance, particularly when recent results are normal. For this 47-year-old woman: Pap smear (Choice A): Recommended every 3 years for ages 21-29 and every 5 years with HPV co-testing (or every 3 years without) for ages 30-65. Since this patient had a normal Pap smear 8 months ago, repeat screening is not indicated at this time. X-ray of the chest (Choice B): Not used for lung cancer screening. The USPSTF recommends low-dose CT scans for adults aged 55-80 with a 30-pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. This patient does not meet age criteria yet, though she will be eligible at age 55 given her 30-pack-year history. Mammography (Choice C): Recommended by ACOG every 1-2 years after age 40 for average-risk women. Before age 40, screening decisions are individualized considering lower incidence, decreased sensitivity, and potential harms from false positives. This patient had normal mammography 8 months ago, so repeat screening is not indicated at this time. Colonoscopy (Choice D): Screening should begin at age 50 in patients without family history of colorectal cancer, occurring every 10 years. This patient is only 47 years old and does not meet age criteria for screening colonoscopy. Educational Objective: At age 47, this patient does not require any cancer screening at this time. Recent normal Pap smear and mammography (within 8 months) preclude repeat screening. Colonoscopy screening begins at age 50, and lung cancer screening with low-dose CT begins at age 55. Appropriate screening intervals and age-based recommendations prevent unnecessary testing while maintaining effective cancer detection.
Source: 4A #33
An asymptomatic 52-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Her last visit to a physician was 4 years ago. Menses occur at regular 30- to 32-day intervals; there is no bleeding between menses. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily but quit 5 years ago; she drinks one to two glasses of wine per week. In addition to a Pap smear, mammography, and cholesterol testing, which of the following tests is most appropriate at this time? A) X-rays of the chest B) Pelvic ultrasonography C) Sputum cytology D) Bone densitometry E) Colonoscopy
Correct Answer: E) Colonoscopy
The U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends routine screening for colorectal carcinoma in all adults between 50 to 75 years of age. Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer death in the United States. Early detection and treatment have been shown to reduce mortality. A variety of screening techniques are commonly employed, including colonoscopy performed every 10 years, test of the stool for occult blood or fecal immunochemical testing performed annually, or stool DNA testing with fecal immunochemical testing performed every 1 to 3 years. Colonoscopy carries the benefit that any visualized colonic polyps can be immediately excised and sent for histologic evaluation, making it both a diagnostic and therapeutic modality. X-rays of the chest (Choice A) and sputum cytology (Choice C) have been used in the past to screen for lung cancer in smokers. However, these methods have poor sensitivity and specificity and are no longer recommended as screening tests for lung cancer. The preferred method for detection of lung cancer is a low-dose CT scan, which is recommended by the USPSTF in current smokers between 50 to 80 years of age with a 30 pack-year smoking history or those who have quit within the past 15 years. This patient quit 5 years ago and does not meet current screening criteria. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice B) can be useful for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer. However, the USPSTF does not currently recommend routine screening for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic women. Bone densitometry (Choice D) is recommended by the USPSTF as routine screening in women over 65 years of age and in those at risk for osteoporosis. Osteoporosis risk can be assessed using standardized calculation tools such as the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool. This patient is 52 years old and does not yet meet age-based screening criteria. Educational Objective: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer deaths in the United States. The mortality of colorectal cancer can be reduced by early detection and treatment. The U.S. Preventative Services Task Force currently recommends routine colorectal cancer screening in all adults between 50 and 75 years of age, which may be performed with colonoscopy or several alternative methods.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Postpartum sepsis 2 questions
Source: 6A #21
A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of moderate abdominal pain and cramping. She has no history of serious illness or operative procedures. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Vital signs are within normal limits. On pelvic examination, the cervix is 6 cm dilated and 100% effaced; the presenting part is at +1 station. Ultrasonography shows a fetus in a breech presentation and consistent in size with a 26-week gestation. The patient undergoes an emergent cesarean delivery. Twenty-four hours after delivery, the patient's temperature is 41°C (105.8°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation over the uterus. Urinalysis shows 2+ RBCs and trace leukocyte esterase. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Pneumonia B) Puerperal sepsis C) Pyelonephritis D) Retained placental fragments E) Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Correct Answer: B) Puerperal sepsis
Puerperal sepsis refers to sepsis presenting immediately after delivery and is typically characterized by fever, abdominal pain, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, or septic shock. This patient presents with classic features: fever (41°C), tachycardia (130/min), tachypnea (30/min), hypotension (80/40 mm Hg indicating septic shock), and moderate uterine tenderness 24 hours post-cesarean delivery. Risk factors for puerperal sepsis include cesarean delivery, premature rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, and manual removal of the placenta. Septic shock is a form of distributive shock characterized by decreased organ perfusion from overwhelming infection, presenting with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and signs of infection on examination. Pneumonia (Choice A) is characterized by fever, productive cough, malaise, and chest discomfort with abnormal lung sounds on examination. This patient has no respiratory symptoms or abnormal cardiopulmonary findings. Pyelonephritis (Choice C) typically presents with fevers, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis typically shows >10 WBC/hpf, red blood cells, white blood cell casts, and bacteria. This patient's urinalysis shows only trace leukocyte esterase and 2+ RBCs without significant pyuria, effectively ruling out pyelonephritis. Retained placental fragments (Choice D), also called retained products of conception, are a potential cause of postpartum hemorrhage. While they can cause fever, the clinical presentation and vital signs are more consistent with septic shock from infection rather than hemorrhage. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (Choice E) is a rare sequela of endometritis that presents with pelvic pain and fever that is often widely variable in course. This condition typically develops as a complication of inadequately treated endometritis and puerperal sepsis, not as the initial presentation. Diagnosis typically occurs through blood cultures and imaging. If this patient were persistently febrile despite appropriate antibiotic treatment, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis should be considered. Educational Objective: Puerperal sepsis refers to sepsis presenting immediately after delivery and is typically characterized by fever, abdominal pain, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, or septic shock. Risk factors include cesarean delivery, premature rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, and manual removal of the placenta. Prophylactic antibiotics are typically given at the time of cesarean delivery to prevent this complication.
Source: 6A #26
A 30-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has had fever and lower abdominal pain for 24 hours. Two days ago, she underwent a low transverse cesarean delivery because of failure to progress in labor after 18 hours. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). The lungs are clear to auscultation. The incision is mildly tender and pink. The fundus is near the umbilicus and extremely tender. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this infection? A) Gram-negative aerobes B) Gram-negative anaerobes C) Gram-positive aerobes D) Gram-positive anaerobes E) Mixed aerobes and anaerobes
Correct Answer: E) Mixed aerobes and anaerobes
This patient presents with postpartum endometritis, an acute polymicrobial infection of the uterine endometrium. The clinical presentation is classic: fever (39°C), severe uterine fundal tenderness, and recent cesarean delivery (a major risk factor). During labor and delivery, microbes from the genital tract enter the uterine cavity and cause infection. Postpartum endometritis characteristically involves a mixture of both aerobic and anaerobic organisms from the normal genital flora, making mixed aerobes and anaerobes the correct answer. Risk factors include prolonged labor (18 hours in this case), cesarean delivery, premature or prolonged rupture of membranes, bacterial vaginosis, Group B Streptococcus colonization, and manual placental removal. Treatment requires broad-spectrum antibiotics such as clindamycin and gentamicin for appropriate coverage of both aerobic and anaerobic organisms. While gram-negative aerobes (such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) can cause endometritis, they more commonly cause cervicitis and are unlikely primary causes of postpartum endometritis. Gram-negative anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) and gram-positive anaerobes (Clostridium) are rare and unlikely sole causes. Gram-positive aerobes can cause endometritis in toxic shock syndrome but are typically associated with prolonged tampon use, not the postpartum setting. The polymicrobial nature of postpartum endometritis is the key distinguishing feature.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Hyperemesis gravidarum 2 questions
Source: 6A #31
A previously healthy 23-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation has had nausea and vomiting for 4 weeks. She can tolerate small amounts of food intermittently but usually vomits 3 to 4 times daily. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall; she has lost 1.8 kg (4 lb) and currently weighs 54 kg (119 lb). Ultrasonography shows a viable fetus consistent with a 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most likely effect of her condition on the fetus? A) Developmental delay B) Premature birth C) Pulmonary hypoplasia D) Spontaneous abortion E) No significant adverse effect
Correct Answer: E) No significant adverse effect
Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) presents with severe, often intractable nausea and vomiting preventing adequate oral intake, leading to dehydration and starvation ketosis. Associated findings include ketonuria and ketonemia, hyponatremia, and hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Laboratory studies may show ketones in blood and urine. Treatment consists of vitamin B6, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and total parenteral nutrition if necessary. It is important to exclude molar pregnancy with pelvic ultrasonography and β-hCG assessment. With appropriate treatment, there are generally no long-term adverse effects on the developing fetus, making E the correct answer. Developmental delay (A) is associated with chromosomal abnormalities, lysosomal storage disorders, neurologic disorders, and vitamin deficiencies, but not HG. Premature birth (B) occurs before 37 weeks and is increased by maternal diabetes, placental abnormalities, cervical insufficiency, and maternal tobacco use; while untreated HG may increase preterm labor risk, appropriate treatment makes this less likely. Pulmonary hypoplasia (C) typically results from oligohydramnios with fetal urogenital tract defects causing thoracic compression and inadequate lung development, not from maternal HG. Spontaneous abortion (D) most commonly results from chromosomal abnormalities, intrauterine infection, uterine structural abnormalities, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and maternal endocrinopathy; it is less likely with appropriate HG treatment.
Source: 3A #46
A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation has had severe nausea and has been unable to keep anything in her stomach for 48 hours. She has had mild nausea and vomiting for 6 weeks. Examination shows normal findings. Ultrasonography shows a normal 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Complete blood count B) Measurement of serum bilirubin concentration C) Measurement of serum glucose concentration D) Measurement of urinary ketones E) Measurement of urinary protein
Correct Answer: D) Measurement of urinary ketones
Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) presents with severe, often intractable nausea and vomiting that prevents adequate oral intake in a pregnant patient, leading to dehydration and starvation ketosis. The most appropriate diagnostic test is measurement of urinary ketones, which reflects the starvation state and ketogenesis occurring from prolonged inability to maintain adequate nutrition. Associated findings include ketonuria and ketonemia, electrolyte abnormalities (hypoosmolar hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia), acid-base disturbances (hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis or metabolic acidosis), and volume contraction. HG typically extends past the first trimester when typical morning sickness resolves, and is commonly associated with molar pregnancy, making β-hCG measurement and pelvic ultrasonography important confirmatory studies. Treatment consists of vitamin B6 supplementation, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and in severe cases, total parenteral nutrition. Incorrect choices: Complete blood count (A) would not necessarily be affected by HG; while leukocytosis could suggest infection, this is less likely given the prolonged pregnancy-associated symptoms. Serum bilirubin (B) would be appropriate for suspected hemolysis, liver disease, or preeclampsia, but this patient has no risk factors for hepatitis and HG is more likely. Serum glucose (C) may provide nonspecific information about nutritional status but would not establish the diagnosis. Urinary protein (E) would be indicated for nephrotic/nephritic syndrome or preeclampsia, but urinary ketones are more specific for HG and proteinuria is not necessarily increased.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Amnionitis 2 questions
Source: 6A #36
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3, at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital 8 hours after premature rupture of membranes. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Previous pregnancies were uncomplicated with spontaneous vaginal delivery of 3430-g, 3629-g, and 3770-g newborns at 37 to 39 weeks' gestation. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/65 mm Hg. The cervix is 1 cm dilated and 80% effaced. Labor augmentation with oxytocin is begun and results in contractions 2 to 3 minutes apart. The cervix is now 8 cm dilated and 100% effaced; the vertex is at +2 station. Her temperature now is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 105/58 mm Hg. The baseline fetal heart rate is 175/min with mild variable decelerations. The uterus is tender. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Antibiotic therapy B) Increased oxytocin therapy C) Forceps delivery D) Vacuum extraction E) Immediate cesarean delivery
Correct Answer: A) Antibiotic therapy
Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of the fetal membranes that commonly occurs with premature or prolonged rupture of membranes due to migration of vaginal flora into the uterus. Risk factors include repeated digital vaginal examinations, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and genital tract infections. This patient presents with classic signs of chorioamnionitis: maternal fever (39°C), tachycardia (110/min), tachypnea (22/min), tender uterus, and fetal tachycardia (175/min). Further evaluation of amniotic fluid may show positive Gram stain with culture, numerous leukocytes, and low glucose concentration. Complications include uterine atony, wound infections, pelvic abscess, and sepsis. Treatment consists of delivery and intravenous antibiotics. Since this patient is in active labor with appropriate cervical progression (8 cm dilated, 100% effaced), the addition of intravenous antibiotics and careful monitoring of labor progression are warranted. Increased oxytocin therapy (B) is unnecessary as the patient demonstrates adequate labor progression with contractions every 2-3 minutes and significant cervical change. Forceps delivery (C) and vacuum extraction (D) are indicated for prolonged second stage of labor or fetal distress and require an engaged occiput; this patient is progressing appropriately through the active stage. Immediate cesarean delivery (E) is occasionally required if there is evidence of fetal or maternal instability, but this patient is progressing appropriately through active labor with no signs of fetal distress (mild variable decelerations are not concerning at this stage). The educational objective is that chorioamnionitis presents with fever, tender uterus, purulent amniotic fluid, and leukocytosis, with risk factors including prolonged or premature rupture of membranes, and requires intravenous antibiotics and delivery.
Source: 5A #22
A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She had spontaneous rupture of membranes 32 hours ago. At 35 weeks' gestation, results of a rectovaginal culture for group B streptococcal infection were positive. Her temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). The lungs are clear to auscultation. The uterus is tender to palpation. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. A fetal heart tracing is shown. The cervix is 80% effaced and 3 cm dilated; the vertex is at -1 station. Her leukocyte count is 19,200/mm³ with a left shift. Microscopic examination of a catheterized urine specimen shows no WBCs or bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this fetal heart tracing pattern? A) Chorioamnionitis B) Oligohydramnios C) Pyelonephritis D) True knot in the umbilical cord E) Uteroplacental insufficiency
Correct Answer: A) Chorioamnionitis
Fetal tachycardia (heart rate >160/min) is the key finding on the fetal heart tracing. Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of the fetal membranes that commonly occurs with prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours). This patient has multiple classic findings: fever (38.8°C), uterine tenderness on palpation, leukocytosis (19,200/mm³ with left shift), and prolonged rupture of membranes (32 hours). Fetal tachycardia results from intrauterine infection. Risk factors include young maternal age, smoking, low socioeconomic status, and history of STIs. Treatment involves broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) and labor induction. The neonate requires close monitoring for infection (pneumonia, bacteremia) and typically needs antibiotic therapy. Oligohydramnios (Choice B) presents with low amniotic fluid index and causes variable decelerations (not tachycardia) due to umbilical cord compression. Pyelonephritis (Choice C) would present with dysuria, flank pain, and urinalysis findings (pyuria, nitrites, bacteria), but this patient's catheterized urine is negative for infection and lacks costovertebral angle tenderness. True knot in the umbilical cord (Choice D) is rare and typically causes fetal distress during descent through the vaginal canal, not sustained tachycardia. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) causes late decelerations and would not explain the fever, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis. Educational Objective: Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of fetal membranes commonly associated with prolonged rupture of membranes, presenting with fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis. It causes fetal tachycardia on monitoring and requires prompt antibiotic therapy and delivery.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Intrauterine Device 2 questions
Source: 3A #16
A 37-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, with recently diagnosed breast cancer comes to the physician for advice regarding contraception. She will begin chemotherapy and radiation therapy in 6 weeks. She had been using a combination oral contraceptive for 3 years but discontinued it 8 weeks ago on advice of her oncologist and began using condoms. Since discontinuing oral contraceptive therapy, she has had one menstrual period that lasted 4 days. Previously, menses occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted 3 to 4 days. She delivered her first child 18 months ago and wishes to have another child in the future. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. Her blood pressure is 115/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding contraception for this patient? A) Progestin-only oral contraceptive B) Diaphragm C) Placement of a copper IUD D) Depot medroxyprogesterone E) Etonogestrel implant
Correct Answer: C) Placement of a copper IUD
Placement of a copper IUD is the most appropriate contraceptive option for this patient with breast cancer. Breast cancers may express estrogen, progesterone, or HER2 receptor positivity. Depending on receptor status, hormonal contraceptives may be harmful and increase the risk for breast cancer progression, making them contraindicated in breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. The copper IUD provides effective contraception without hormones. Copper is spermicidal and inhibits sperm motility and the acrosomal reaction necessary for fertilization. It also induces local inflammatory changes of the endometrium and increases cervical mucus production, further decreasing the chance of successful sperm passage or embryonic implantation. The IUD can be kept in place for up to ten years with a pregnancy rate less than 1%. Potential complications include increased menstrual flow and dysmenorrhea. Contraindications include copper allergy, Wilson disease, endometrial cancer, and undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding. Incorrect options: Progestin-only oral contraceptives (A), depot medroxyprogesterone (D), and etonogestrel implant (E) are all hormonal contraceptives contraindicated in breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. A diaphragm (B) is a barrier method that is less effective than an IUD and carries increased risk of urinary tract infection due to pressure on the urethra and spermicide use, which would be unsuitable in a patient undergoing immunosuppressive chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Educational Objective: Hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. A copper IUD is an effective, hormone-free long-acting reversible contraceptive that is spermicidal and suitable for patients with breast cancer.
Source: 4A #48
A 42-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 5, comes to the physician requesting advice regarding contraception. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 3 days ago. She has hypertension treated with a β-adrenergic blocking agent, but she often forgets to take it. At the age of 21 years, she was treated for Chlamydia trachomatis infection. During her second pregnancy, a Pap smear was reported as a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; after delivery, a follow-up Pap smear showed no abnormalities. Since that time, she has had no abnormal Pap smears. She is sexually active and monogamous with her husband. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. She desires the most effective contraception that she will easily remember to use. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding contraception for this patient? A) Condoms B) Oral contraceptive C) Diaphragm D) Depot medroxyprogesterone E) Placement of an IUD
Correct Answer: E) Placement of an IUD
An intrauterine device (IUD) is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient because it is a long-acting reversible contraceptive that does not require active patient compliance, which is critical given her history of medication non-adherence with her antihypertensive agent. IUD Mechanism and Efficacy: Both copper and levonorgestrel IUDs are available. Copper IUDs provide contraception without hormones through spermicidal effects, inhibition of sperm motility and the acrosomal reaction, and induction of local endometrial inflammatory changes that increase cervical mucus production. Hormonal IUDs cause cervical mucous thickening and induce glandular atrophy of the endometrium, preventing implantation. IUDs are highly reliable with failure rates as low as 1% and can remain in place for up to 10 years depending on type. Why Other Options Are Suboptimal: Condoms (Choice A): Available in male and female varieties but must be placed prior to intercourse. While they provide STI protection, they have higher failure rates than hormonal or IUD contraception and are not ideal for a patient seeking maximum effectiveness. Oral Contraceptives (Choice B): Require daily compliance, making them unsuitable for a patient with documented medication non-adherence. Additionally, hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in patients with certain conditions including thromboembolic disorders, liver dysfunction, and hormone receptor-positive breast malignancy. Diaphragm (Choice C): A barrier method that must be placed prior to intercourse and left in place for 6-8 hours after use, typically with spermicide. It is less effective than an IUD at preventing pregnancy and requires patient compliance with proper placement. Depot Medroxyprogesterone (Choice D): Although administered only every 14 weeks (approximately 3 months), it is still a hormonal contraceptive requiring periodic compliance for re-injection and is not optimal for a patient with compliance concerns. It carries the same contraindications as other hormonal methods. Educational Objective: IUDs are among the most reliable forms of contraception because they do not depend on patient compliance, making them ideal for patients with medication adherence issues. Their low failure rates and long duration of action make them an excellent choice for women seeking effective, long-term contraception.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Perimenopause 2 questions
Source: 3A #19
A 47-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue, constipation, night sweats, anxiety, and mood lability over the past year; she has had a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight gain during this period. Her last menstrual period was 6 months ago. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical and pelvic examinations show normal findings. Which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to be increased? A) ACTH B) Follicle-stimulating hormone C) Parathyroid hormone D) Thyroid-stimulating hormone E) Thyrotropin-releasing hormone
Correct Answer: B) Follicle-stimulating hormone
This 47-year-old woman presents with classic symptoms of perimenopause/menopause: amenorrhea (6 months without menses), night sweats, mood lability, irritability, fatigue, constipation, and weight gain. Menopause is defined by 12 months of amenorrhea, but symptoms begin during the perimenopausal transition. The pathophysiology involves exhaustion of ovarian follicles leading to anovulation and decreased estrogen production. In response to low estrogen, FSH and LH lose negative feedback inhibition and increase significantly in the serum. While menopause is typically a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms and amenorrhea, elevated FSH and LH can confirm the diagnosis when uncertain. Incorrect answers: ACTH (Choice A) is elevated in Cushing syndrome, which presents with central obesity, skin striae, moon facies, and hypertension—features not present in this patient. Parathyroid hormone (Choice C) is elevated in hyperparathyroidism, presenting with abdominal/bone pain, psychological changes, and nephrolithiasis—not consistent with this presentation. TSH and TRH (Choices D and E) are elevated in primary hypothyroidism, which causes fatigue, weight gain, constipation, and oligomenorrhea, but notably does NOT cause night sweats. The presence of night sweats and amenorrhea in a woman in her late 40s makes menopause the most likely diagnosis. Educational Objective: Menopause commonly presents in women aged 40-50 with amenorrhea, night sweats, irritability, mood lability, and weight gain due to exhaustion of ovarian follicle reserves and decreased estrogen. While primarily a clinical diagnosis, increased serum FSH and LH concentrations can confirm the diagnosis. Hormone replacement therapy can treat vasomotor symptoms but carries increased risks of breast cancer, hypercoagulability, and cardiovascular mortality; SSRIs/SNRIs are alternative options.
Source: 8A #7
An otherwise healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of irregular menses, hot flashes, occasional night sweats, and irritability. Her last menstrual period was 5 months ago. Menses had previously occurred at irregular 8- to 13-week intervals. She is sexually active and uses condoms for contraception. She has had no other symptoms and takes no medications. She has two children, ages 14 and 18 years. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (146 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a slightly enlarged uterus and normal ovaries. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum estradiol concentration B) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration C) Measurement of serum β-hCG concentration D) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration E) Progestin challenge test
Correct Answer: C) Measurement of serum β-hCG concentration
In a woman of reproductive age presenting with signs of menopause (irregular menses, hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes), pregnancy must be ruled out first as the underlying cause of amenorrhea and symptoms, especially with a slightly enlarged uterus on examination. Measurement of serum β-hCG concentration is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step. Amenorrhea can result from pregnancy, menopause, primary ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis abnormalities, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. While this patient's presentation is consistent with early menopause (occurring before age 45), the slightly enlarged uterus raises concern for pregnancy, which must be excluded before proceeding with other evaluations. Estradiol (Choice A) varies with menstrual cycle phase and is difficult to interpret in isolation. FSH (Choice B) is elevated in menopause but decreased in pregnancy; while confirmatory for menopause, it should not be the first test given the need to rule out pregnancy. TSH (Choice D) should be measured if thyroid disease is suspected, but this patient lacks signs of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. The progestin challenge test (Choice E) is contraindicated before ruling out pregnancy as it could negatively affect an existing pregnancy. Educational Objective: When amenorrhea and menopausal symptoms occur in women younger than age 45 years, serum β-hCG concentration should be measured first to exclude pregnancy before pursuing other diagnostic tests for menopause or other etiologies.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Antepartum fetal evaluation 2 questions
Source: 3A #22
A 38-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, is admitted to the hospital at 33 weeks' gestation because of suspected pyelonephritis as evidenced by temperatures to 38.9°C (102°F) and back pain. She has had costovertebral angle tenderness for 10 days and mild contractions for 4 hours. Intravenous ampicillin therapy is started. Urinalysis is consistent with a urinary tract infection. The fetal heart rate pattern is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern? A) Fetal hypoxia B) Maternal age C) Maternal fever D) Preterm gestation E) Reaction to antibiotics
Correct Answer: C) Maternal fever
Maternal fever can cause fetal tachycardia, which is defined as a fetal heart rate greater than 160/min. Other causes of fetal tachycardia include hypoxia and fetal anemia. Conversely, bradycardia is defined as a fetal heart rate less than 110/min and can be caused by congenital heart malformations, as well as hypoxia or fetal distress. Decreased variability in the fetal heart tracing also indicates fetal distress. Given this patient's presentation with pyelonephritis and fever, it is most likely that the fetal tachycardia is secondary to maternal fever as there are no other signs or symptoms to suggest fetal hypoxemia or anemia. Fetal hypoxia (Choice A) can cause fetal tachycardia or bradycardia depending on severity. However, the mother is not showing signs of hypoxia, hypotension, or hypoperfusion, making fetal hypoxia unlikely as the contributing factor. Additionally, there are no late decelerations to suggest uteroplacental insufficiency or variable decelerations to suggest umbilical cord compression. Maternal age (Choice B) would not be expected to affect the fetal heart rate in utero. Preterm gestation (Choice D) would not be expected to affect the fetal heart rate, as the expected fetal heart rate is similar throughout pregnancy. Reaction to antibiotics (Choice E) would be unlikely to cause isolated fetal tachycardia without signs of an allergic reaction (e.g., hives, rash, pruritus) in the mother. Educational Objective: Causes of fetal tachycardia (fetal heart rate >160/min) include maternal fever, fetal hypoxia, and fetal anemia. In cases of maternal infection, fetal tachycardia is most likely secondary to maternal fever.
Source: 5A #12
An 18-year-old primigravid woman at 18 weeks' gestation comes for her second prenatal visit. Abdominal examination shows a uterus that measures 23 cm above the pubic symphysis. She has gained 4.5 kg (10 lb) since her last visit 4 weeks ago. Her blood pressure is 120/72 mm Hg. Fetal heart tones are 160/min. Urine dipstick is negative for protein and trace positive for glucose. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Schedule an appointment in 1 week B) Nutritional counseling C) Measurement of serum estriol concentration D) Glucose tolerance test E) Ultrasonography for dating
Correct Answer: E) Ultrasonography for dating
Fundal height is used to estimate gestational age, with the distance in centimeters between the pubic symphysis and the top of the uterine fundus approximating gestational age in weeks. When there is a discrepancy between fundal height measurement and calculated gestational age from the last menstrual period, ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step to assess gestational age through objective fetal parameters including crown-rump length, biparietal diameter, femur length, and abdominal circumference. Ultrasonography-guided measurements are most accurate during the first trimester and can also identify other causes of larger-than-expected fundal height, including multiple gestations, hydatidiform moles, and fetal macrosomia. Choice A (scheduling an appointment in 1 week) is inappropriate given the uncertainty about fetal gestational age from the discrepancy between LMP dating and fundal height. Choice B (nutritional counseling) is not necessary as the patient is gaining appropriate weight for pregnancy (4.5 kg in 4 weeks is within normal range; typical total weight gain for normal BMI is 11.3-15.9 kg over entire gestation). Choice C (serum estriol concentration) is part of the quad screen used to assess for genetic disorders and is measured at 15-22 weeks, but accurate gestational dating via ultrasonography must be established first since quad screen reference ranges depend on gestational age. Choice D (glucose tolerance test) is typically performed at 24-28 weeks' gestation to screen for gestational diabetes. At 18 weeks by LMP or 23 weeks by fundal height, this patient is too early for this screening. Educational Objective: Ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step when there is a discrepancy between fundal height and calculated gestational age based on last menstrual period, providing accurate dating through objective fetal parameters and assessing for multiple gestations, hydatidiform moles, and macrosomia.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Ovarian Failure, Premature Menopause 2 questions
Source: 3A #24
A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has been amenorrheic and has had hot flashes for the past 6 months. She takes thyroid medication for chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease). After using an oral contraceptive for 2 years, she discontinued taking it 3 years ago. Serum studies show: Follicle-stimulating hormone 62 mlU/mL, Estradiol 15 pg/ml (N=20-60), Thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.5 µU/ml, Prolactin 5 ng/ml. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Autoimmune ovarian failure B) Hypothalamic dysfunction C) Inadequate control of hypothyroidism D) Post-pill amenorrhea E) Pure gonadal dysgenesis
Correct Answer: A) Autoimmune ovarian failure
Autoimmune ovarian failure, also known as primary ovarian insufficiency, classically presents in a woman of reproductive age with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility, along with signs of early menopause such as hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular bleeding. It is caused by autoimmune inflammation and destruction within the ovaries, leading to decreased estrogen production, diminished follicle reserve, and loss of ovarian stromal cells. The elevated FSH (62 mlU/mL) and low estradiol (15 pg/ml) reflect appropriate compensatory increase in gonadotropins due to lack of negative feedback from estrogen on the anterior pituitary. This condition is most often idiopathic but is more common in women with karyotype abnormalities or other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto thyroiditis, which this patient has. Hypothalamic dysfunction (Choice B) would present with decreased FSH and LH due to reduced GnRH, not the elevated FSH seen here. Inadequate control of hypothyroidism (Choice C) can cause amenorrhea, but the patient's TSH is normal (1.5 µU/ml), indicating adequate thyroid supplementation. Post-pill amenorrhea (Choice D) typically resolves within months of discontinuing oral contraceptives; this patient stopped 3 years ago, making persistent post-pill amenorrhea unlikely. Pure gonadal dysgenesis (Choice E) presents with amenorrhea and absent secondary sexual characteristics from birth or early development; this patient previously conceived, ruling out this diagnosis. Educational Objective: Autoimmune ovarian failure or primary ovarian insufficiency presents in reproductive-age women with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility. Laboratory studies show decreased estrogen and increased FSH and LH concentrations. It is commonly associated with other autoimmune disorders or karyotype abnormalities.
Source: 7A #14
A 32-year-old woman comes to the office because she has not had a menstrual period for 8 months; she has had hot flashes and vaginal discomfort with coitus during this time. Her last child was born 4 years ago. Menarche occurred at the age of 12 years, and menses occurred at regular monthly intervals until the age of 25 years. From the age of 25 years until she stopped menstruating, her periods became progressively less frequent. Two years ago, oral progesterone caused her to have a menstrual period, but an identical dose failed to cause a menstrual period 3 months ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Endometrial biopsy B) Hysteroscopy C) Measurement of serum estradiol-17B concentration D) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration E) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
Correct Answer: D) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration
This patient presents with premature ovarian failure (primary ovarian insufficiency), characterized by secondary amenorrhea, hot flashes, and vaginal atrophy in a reproductive-age woman. The progressive decrease in menstrual frequency from age 25 and the failure of progesterone withdrawal to induce bleeding 3 months ago (despite success 2 years prior) indicate declining ovarian reserve and estrogen deficiency. Measurement of serum FSH concentration (Choice D) is the most appropriate next diagnostic step. In premature ovarian failure, FSH and LH concentrations are appropriately elevated due to loss of negative feedback from decreased estrogen production. Elevated FSH (typically >40 mIU/mL) confirms the diagnosis of primary ovarian insufficiency. The progesterone withdrawal test helps differentiate causes of amenorrhea: bleeding occurs with hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis dysfunction (anovulation), but not with structural uterine abnormalities or estrogen deficiency. This patient's lack of bleeding with progesterone withdrawal indicates estrogen deficiency, consistent with ovarian failure. Premature ovarian failure is most often idiopathic but is more common in women with karyotype abnormalities or autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto thyroiditis. Incorrect choices: Endometrial biopsy (A) is used for endometrial cancer evaluation in women with abnormal bleeding, not amenorrhea. Hysteroscopy (B) evaluates structural uterine causes but is not indicated for amenorrhea from ovarian failure. Serum estradiol-17B (C) would be low but does not establish the diagnosis; FSH elevation is diagnostic. TSH measurement (E) could evaluate thyroid disease as a cause of menstrual irregularity, but this patient lacks other signs of thyroid dysfunction. Educational Objective: Premature ovarian failure presents with anovulation, amenorrhea, and signs of early menopause (hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal atrophy) in reproductive-age women. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated FSH and LH with decreased estrogen. Progesterone withdrawal test shows no bleeding due to estrogen deficiency. The condition is associated with autoimmune disorders and karyotype abnormalities.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Postmenopausal Atrophic Vaginitis 2 questions
Source: 3A #26
A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of urinary urgency. She often has a strong urge to void but passes only a small amount of urine. Sometimes she is unable to reach a bathroom quickly enough after feeling the sudden need to void. She says she often feels hot at night and occasionally during the day. She has not had any other symptoms. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her last menstrual period was 12 months ago. She is not sexually active. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows moderate tenderness and vaginal atrophy. The uterus is normal sized. There are no vulvar, vaginal, or cervical lesions or adnexal masses. The remainder of the examination, including rectal examination, shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. A wet mount preparation of vaginal fluid shows numerous leukocytes. Urine culture is negative. Her postvoid residual volume is 50 ml. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings? A) Atonic bladder B) Estrogen deficiency C) Prolapse of the pelvic floor D) Trichomoniasis E) Urinary tract infection
Correct Answer: B) Estrogen deficiency
Estrogen deficiency in menopause causes atrophy and inflammation of the vagina and urethra, leading to an overactive bladder with urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence. This inflammation results in leukocytes within the urine and vaginal fluid in the absence of infection. The patient's symptoms of hot flashes and amenorrhea for 12 months are consistent with menopause and estrogen deficiency. Pelvic examination typically shows vaginal atrophy and tenderness without other abnormalities, as seen in this patient. The normal postvoid residual volume (50 ml) rules out atonic bladder, which presents with increased post-void residual from incomplete emptying. Prolapse of the pelvic floor causes stress incontinence triggered by increased intra-abdominal pressure (lifting, sneezing, Valsalva), not the urge incontinence seen here. Trichomoniasis presents with green, malodorous vaginal discharge and motile trichomonads on wet mount, neither present in this patient. Urinary tract infection can cause overactive bladder but is ruled out by negative urine culture; patients also typically experience dysuria and suprapubic pain. Treatment options for urge incontinence include bladder training, Kegel exercises, and antimuscarinic medications. Supplemental estrogens are no longer widely recommended due to increased risk of gynecologic and breast malignancies and venous thromboembolic disease. Educational Objective: In postmenopausal women, estrogen deficiency can cause symptoms of overactive bladder including urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence.
