Trisomy 21 (Choice E) is another cause of fetal growth restriction, which can be further evaluated with karyotyping. Fetal ultrasonography typically shows increased nuchal thickness in fetuses with trisomy 21, which was not demonstrated in this patient. Educational Objective: Preeclampsia may lead to fetal growth restriction by causing placental hypoperfusion and fetal hypoxia. Fetal growth restriction may be identified by a smaller than expected fundal height, a fetus that is below the 10th percentile of weight for its gestational age, and oligohydramnios.
Source: 4A #39
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, at 34 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Pregnancy had been complicated by blurred vision and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight gain over the past week. Her last routine prenatal visit 1 month ago showed no abnormalities. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 150/110 mm Hg. Examination shows retinal arteriolar spasms and pedal edema. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Leukocyte count 8000/mm³, Platelet count 200,000/mm³, Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Urine protein 2+. This patient's fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following obstetric complications? A) Brachial plexus injury B) Fetal growth restriction C) Hydrops D) Macrosomia E) Pulmonary hypoplasia F) Sepsis
Correct Answer: B) Fetal growth restriction
This patient presents with classic findings of preeclampsia: hypertension (150/110 mm Hg), proteinuria (2+), and end-organ dysfunction (elevated creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, blurred vision from retinal arteriolar spasms, thrombocytopenia at 200,000/mm³) occurring after 20 weeks' gestation. Preeclampsia results from abnormalities of placental spiral arteries and poor trophoblastic invasion, leading to placental hypoperfusion and production of vasoactive hormones that cause generalized endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability, and vasospasm. The resulting uteroplacental insufficiency places the fetus at greatest risk for fetal growth restriction. If untreated, preeclampsia can progress to eclampsia with maternal seizures, potentially causing maternal stroke, cardiac arrest, renal failure, or maternal/fetal death. Treatment includes antihypertensive agents, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis, and delivery of the fetus and placenta. Incorrect answers: Brachial plexus injury (A) occurs secondary to shoulder dystocia during delivery, not from preeclampsia. Hydrops (C) results from fetal anemia, hemolysis, intrauterine infections, cardiac abnormalities, or chromosomal abnormalities—not preeclampsia. Macrosomia (D) is associated with gestational diabetes; preeclampsia is more commonly associated with small-for-gestational-age fetuses. Pulmonary hypoplasia (E) results from oligohydramnios as part of Potter sequence, not preeclampsia. Sepsis (F) may result from preterm rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis, not preeclampsia itself.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Factor V Leiden 2 questions
Source: 4A #23
A 23-year-old primigravid woman at 33 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital because she has not felt fetal movement for 2 days. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness. Her sister has had three spontaneous abortions. The patient's temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a soft uterus consistent in size with a 33-week gestation. Fundal height is 34 cm. Fetal heart tones cannot be auscultated. Ultrasonography confirms intrauterine fetal demise. Laboratory studies show the patient to be a homozygote for the factor V Leiden mutation. Thrombosis of which of the following is the most likely cause of the fetal demise? A) Fetal cerebral arteries B) Fetal ductus arteriosus C) Maternal lower extremity D) Umbilical cord E) Uteroplacental artery
Correct Answer: E) Uteroplacental artery
Factor V Leiden is an autosomal dominant condition wherein coagulation factor V is resistant to inactivation by protein C, leading to a hypercoagulable state. This hypercoagulable state creates an increased risk of thromboembolic events in the maternal vasculature, including within the uteroplacental arteries, leading to placental infarction and intrauterine fetal demise. Thromboembolism is most likely to occur within the maternal vasculature and affect the uteroplacental arteries. The relationship between maternal factor V Leiden and fetal vascular thromboembolic disease is less clear unless the fetus has also inherited the mutant allele. Thrombosis of the fetal cerebral arteries (Choice A) is uncommon and may lead to fetal ischemic stroke and cerebral palsy, but the pathogenesis is poorly understood and this location is less likely. Fetal ductus arteriosus (Choice B) allows circulating blood to bypass the fetal lungs by creating an anastomosis between the pulmonary arterial trunk and the descending aorta and is an unlikely location of thrombosis. Maternal lower extremity venous thrombosis (Choice C) would be consistent with deep venous thrombosis; while women with factor V Leiden are at increased risk, this is not a likely cause of fetal demise. Umbilical cord thrombosis (Choice D) is an unlikely source of placental infarction given that it is within the fetal rather than maternal circulation and most commonly affects the umbilical vein following cordocentesis.
Source: 8A #47
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 10 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. She delivered her last child 9 months ago; the pregnancy was complicated by deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of the left lower extremity documented by venous Doppler ultrasonography. Her mother and sister also had DVT during pregnancy, and her maternal grandfather and uncle died of cerebral infarction in their 40s. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for this patient? A) Measurement of plasma fibrinogen concentration B) Measurement of prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times C) Measurement of serum factor VIII antigen concentration D) Factor V Leiden mutation analysis E) Repeat venous Doppler ultrasonography
Correct Answer: D) Factor V Leiden mutation analysis
Factor V Leiden is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a point mutation in the F5 gene of factor V, wherein coagulation factor V is resistant to inactivation by protein C, leading to a hypercoagulable state. It is the most common inherited cause of hypercoagulability in white patients. Pregnancy causes a hypercoagulable state due to overexpression of coagulation factors I, II, VII, VIII, IX, and X, underexpression of anticoagulant protein S, and venous stasis in the pelvis and lower extremities caused by hormonal changes and compression by the gravid uterus. Thromboembolic events during pregnancy or the postpartum period are a common presentation of Factor V Leiden. Other presentations include thromboembolic events within the uteroplacental arteries, leading to placental infarction and possible intrauterine fetal demise, and cerebral vein thrombosis. A heritable coagulation disorder should be suspected in this patient with a history of provoked DVT in combination with an extensive family history of thromboembolic events. Diagnosis can be confirmed with genetic testing or a functional assay evaluating activated protein C resistance. Venous thromboembolic event prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g., enoxaparin) is indicated for gravid patients with Factor V Leiden and personal history of thrombosis/thromboembolism. Warfarin is a teratogen and should be avoided. Novel oral anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban and apixaban are not recommended because of fetal safety concerns. Measurement of plasma fibrinogen concentration (Choice A) is indicated in evaluation of coagulopathy and will be decreased in consumptive coagulopathies such as disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. Fibrinogen is overexpressed in pregnancy, but acquired hyperfibrinogenemia would not explain this patient's extensive family history of VTE. Measurement of prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times (Choice B) evaluates function of the extrinsic and intrinsic coagulation pathways in patients with coagulopathy. Partial thromboplastin time may be decreased or normal in Factor V Leiden; genetic or functional testing are more sensitive and specific. Measurement of serum factor VIII antigen concentration (Choice C) may be performed for diagnosis of hemophilia A, an X-linked coagulopathy. This patient's history is suspicious for an inherited thrombophilia, not coagulopathy. Acquired increased factor VIII concentration is found in pregnancy, malignancy, and hyperthyroidism, but the association with VTE is weak. Repeat venous Doppler ultrasonography (Choice E) would be indicated if this patient presented with features of DVT such as unilateral lower extremity pain, erythema, edema, and tenderness. This asymptomatic patient requires genetic testing for suspected inherited thrombophilia in the setting of her significant family history and current pregnancy.
▶ Endocrine System Congenital hypothyroidism 1 question
Source: 6A #1
A 2-week-old newborn is brought for an initial examination. She was born at home to a 25-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents say that it takes a long time to feed the newborn, and she usually does not finish her bottle. They are also concerned that she may be constipated. She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight and 90th percentile for head circumference. She has a hoarse cry. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows large anterior and posterior fontanelles, a large protruding tongue, and a small umbilical hernia. The skin is dry and slightly mottled. There is mild hypotonia. Which of the following is most likely to have predicted these findings? A) Routine newborn screening B) Fetal monitoring C) Paternal karyotype analysis D) Prenatal ultrasonography E) Maternal glucose tolerance testing
Correct Answer: A) Routine newborn screening
Congenital hypothyroidism can be caused by maternal hypothyroidism, thyroid agenesis, thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, or iodine deficiency. The clinical presentation in this newborn is classic for congenital hypothyroidism, with characteristic findings including lethargy, hoarse cry, hypotonia, myxedematous facies, macroglossia (large protruding tongue), large fontanelles, dry and mottled skin, constipation, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Routine newborn screening has been specifically developed to detect congenital hypothyroidism by measuring thyroxine (T4) or thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels. Early detection and treatment with levothyroxine is critical to prevent neurocognitive deficits and intellectual disability. Fetal monitoring (Choice B) using non-stress tests and biophysical profiles is used for assessment of fetal well-being in high-risk pregnancies but would not detect congenital hypothyroidism. Paternal karyotype analysis (Choice C) is used in infertility evaluation or recurrent pregnancy loss, not in uncomplicated pregnancies. Prenatal ultrasonography (Choice D) evaluates fetal anatomy, growth, and development but cannot diagnose congenital hypothyroidism. Maternal glucose tolerance testing (Choice E) screens for gestational diabetes between 24-28 weeks and would not predict congenital hypothyroidism in the newborn. Educational Objective: Signs and symptoms of congenital hypothyroidism include lethargy, hoarse cry, hypotonia, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, dry skin, hypothermia, constipation, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Routine newborn screening has been developed to detect congenital hypothyroidism by measuring T4 or TSH.
▶ Male Reproductive Chancroid 1 question
Source: 6A #6
A previously healthy 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of vulvar pain. She is sexually active with three male partners, and they use condoms inconsistently. Examination shows a tender, nonindurated ulcer on the right labium majus that bleeds easily when touched. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Calymmatobacterium granulomatis B) Chlamydia trachomatis C) Haemophilus ducreyi D) Human papillomavirus E) Treponema pallidum
Correct Answer: C) Haemophilus ducreyi
The clinical presentation of a tender, nonindurated, easily bleeding genital ulcer with a 2-day history in a sexually active woman is classic for chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The key distinguishing feature is that the ulcer is PAINFUL and TENDER, which differentiates it from other sexually transmitted infections that cause genital ulcers. A variety of sexually transmitted infections may cause genital ulcers, but they differ in clinical presentation. Painful genital ulcers are caused by HSV (genital herpes) and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid). The ulcer of chancroid is typically exudative and accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. In contrast, nontender genital ulcers are caused by: - Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L1, L2, and L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum) - Treponema pallidum (primary syphilitic chancre, which is painless with a clean base) - Klebsiella (Calymmatobacterium) granulomatis (granuloma inguinale/donovanosis, which is red, friable, and painless) Incorrect options: A) Calymmatobacterium granulomatis causes granuloma inguinale, which presents as a painless ulcer, not painful. B) Chlamydia trachomatis typically causes urethritis, dysuria, and discharge, not genital ulcers. D) Human papillomavirus causes condylomata acuminata and carcinoma, not genital ulcers. E) Treponema pallidum causes a painless chancre in primary syphilis, not a painful ulcer. Educational Objective: HSV and Haemophilus ducreyi both cause painful genital ulcers, while Chlamydia trachomatis (LGV), Treponema pallidum (syphilis), and Klebsiella granulomatis (granuloma inguinale) cause painless genital ulcers. The ulcer of chancroid is exudative and accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Toxic Shock Syndrome 1 question
Source: 6A #7
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after the sudden onset of loss of consciousness. She has a 1-day history of temperatures to 39.4°C (103°F), vomiting, watery diarrhea, and a rash over her face, trunk, and arms. Her last menstrual period started 5 days ago; she routinely uses tampons. Her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 30/min, and her palpable systolic blood pressure is 70 mm Hg. Examination shows erythema of the conjunctivae and pharynx. Pelvic examination shows 10 to 15, 0.5-cm ulcers over the vaginal mucosa. Culture of a lesion scraping grows Staphylococcus aureus. This patient is at greatest risk for mortality from which of the following complications? A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome B) Hemorrhage C) Hepatic failure D) Pulmonary embolism E) Renal failure
Correct Answer: A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome
This patient has toxic shock syndrome (TSS) caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen that triggers massive cytokine release (IL-1, IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-α). TSS is classically associated with prolonged tampon use and presents with fever, diffuse erythematous macular rash, and distributive shock from endothelial dysfunction causing fluid leakage and vasodilation. The resulting inflammatory state leads to multiorgan failure affecting multiple systems: gastrointestinal (abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hepatic failure), renal (elevated creatinine, electrolyte derangements, oliguria), hematologic (anemia, DIC), and neurologic (encephalopathy, confusion, seizures). Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a serious complication of TSS characterized by diffuse inflammatory lung injury resulting in dyspnea and hypoxic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Patients with ARDS are critically ill with significantly increased mortality rates, making it the greatest mortality risk among the options. Hemorrhage (Choice B) is unlikely as the hypotension results from cytokine-mediated endothelial dysfunction causing distributive shock, not hemorrhage or hypovolemia. Hepatic failure (Choice C) and renal failure (Choice E) are potential consequences from hypoperfusion and end-organ damage but carry lower mortality risk than ARDS. Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) is not a known complication of TSS. Educational Objective: Toxic shock syndrome secondary to Staphylococcus aureus exotoxin production causes fever, diffuse erythematous macular rash, hypotension/distributive shock, and multiorgan system failure. ARDS is a serious complication of TSS with increased mortality rates.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Ovarian Torsion 1 question
Source: 6A #13
An 18-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea and vomiting. During a routine visit 2 weeks ago, pelvic examination showed an 8-cm right adnexal mass. Ultrasonography showed an 8-cm, mature cystic teratoma on the right ovary. Abdominal examination today shows severe rebound tenderness with guarding in the right lower quadrant. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute appendicitis B) Ectopic pregnancy C) Ovarian torsion D) Pelvic inflammatory disease E) Renal calculi
Correct Answer: C) Ovarian torsion
Ovarian torsion describes a condition in which the ovary twists on its ligamentous support. The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains the ovarian artery and vein; if twisted, it can lead to impaired blood supply resulting in ovarian infarction. Ovarian teratomas are typically unilateral and can rapidly grow, leading to complications such as pain, hemorrhage, necrosis, and ovarian torsion. While ovarian torsion may occur in patients with normal ovaries, an ovarian mass or cyst significantly increases the risk for torsion, and as the size of an ovarian mass increases, the risk for torsion also increases. Malignant masses that adhere to the pelvis may be at lower risk for torsion. Signs and symptoms of ovarian torsion include acute, severe unilateral pelvic pain, abdominopelvic tenderness and guarding, an adnexal mass, nausea, and vomiting. This patient's presentation of acute, severe abdominal pain with a known 8-cm ovarian cyst is classic for ovarian torsion. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, but Doppler ultrasonography evaluation of the ovary can be used to confirm torsion. Treatment involves emergent surgery for detorsion of the ovary in an attempt to conserve it. Acute appendicitis (Choice A) typically presents with periumbilical abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. It typically has a gradually worsening course over hours to days, whereas this patient's acute, severe pain with a known large ovarian cyst is more consistent with torsion. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice B) refers to abnormal implantation of the embryo outside the uterine endometrium (fallopian tube, cervix, myometrium, ovary, or peritoneum). It should be suspected in a patient with a positive urine pregnancy test presenting with vaginal bleeding and acute abdominopelvic pain in the first trimester. There is no mention of pregnancy in this case. Pelvic inflammatory disease (Choice D) typically presents with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and cervical or adnexal tenderness. Adnexal tenderness may be present in cases of tuba-ovarian abscess, but the acute presentation with a known ovarian mass is more consistent with torsion. Renal calculi (Choice E) may present with unilateral flank pain that is colicky and sometimes radiates to the groin with associated hematuria. It would typically not cause abdominal tenderness on physical examination, and urinalysis would show red blood cells without casts.
▶ Endocrine System Diabetes mellitus, type 1 1 question
Source: 6A #16
A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician for counseling prior to conception. She feels well. She is recently married, and she and her husband wish to start a family immediately. She has a 10-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with an insulin pump. During the past 3 years, she has been hospitalized twice for ketoacidosis. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum glucose concentration is 180 mg/dL in the physician's office. Which of the following measures will have the greatest impact on the success of this patient's pregnancy? A) Adding an oral hypoglycemic to the regimen B) Exercise program C) Prenatal vitamin supplementation D) Tighter glucose control E) Weight gain
Correct Answer: D) Tighter glucose control
Tight glucose control during conception and pregnancy in a patient with pre-gestational diabetes mellitus (type 1 or 2) is critical for minimizing the effects of hyperglycemia on the fetus. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance, especially in insulin-dependent patients, leading to increased glucose concentrations in both maternal and fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia causes the fetus to produce excess insulin and decrease gluconeogenesis. Insulin acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia, and inhibits surfactant production, causing respiratory distress syndrome. After birth, the fetus continues synthesizing excess insulin but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose, resulting in neonatal hypoglycemia. Other complications of uncontrolled diabetes in pregnancy include congenital malformations (cardiac, caudal regression), fetal demise, preeclampsia, preterm labor, intrauterine growth restriction from uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal mortality. Choice A (oral hypoglycemic) is ineffective for type 1 diabetes mellitus, which lacks endogenous insulin production. Oral hypoglycemics are also avoided in pregnancy due to insufficient fetal safety data. Choice B (exercise program) alone is unlikely to be effective without insulin dose adjustments in a patient with type 1 diabetes and absent endogenous insulin production. Choice C (prenatal vitamin supplementation) should be recommended to reduce congenital malformations such as neural tube defects, but does not address the complications of poor glucose control. Choice E (weight gain) is less important than tight glucose control. While inadequate weight gain increases risk for fetal growth restriction and preterm birth, and excess weight gain increases risk for macrosomia and preeclampsia, glucose control remains the primary concern in pre-gestational diabetes. Educational Objective: Tight maternal blood glucose control in patients with pre-gestational diabetes mellitus decreases the risk for macrosomia, respiratory distress syndrome, postnatal hypoglycemia, congenital malformations, preeclampsia, preterm labor, and maternal and fetal mortality.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Breech presentation 1 question
Source: 6A #18
A 30-year-old multigravid woman at 37 weeks' gestation is admitted in labor 6 hours after the onset of regular uterine contractions. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. By abdominal palpation, her fetus is thought to be in breech presentation. Her amniotic membranes are intact. Her cervix is 2 cm long and 1 cm dilated; the presenting part is at -3 station but is difficult to palpate. Ultrasonography shows a double footling breech presentation. During labor, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications? A) Chorioamnionitis B) Fetal shoulder dystocia C) Hemorrhage D) Prolapse of the fetal umbilical cord E) Uterine rupture
Correct Answer: D) Prolapse of the fetal umbilical cord
Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os, preventing proper head engagement in the pelvis for descent. This can also occur in polyhydramnios when excess amniotic fluid prevents any body part from presenting at the cervical os until membrane rupture. A serious complication of fetal malpresentation is umbilical cord prolapse. Because the occiput is not engaged at the cervical os, the umbilical cord can protrude through the cervix following rupture of membranes before the fetus descends into the pelvic opening. Subsequent contractions cause cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Given the high risk associated with vaginal deliveries in fetal malpresentation, elective cesarean delivery is typically performed when the condition is known. Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate cesarean delivery. Chorioamnionitis (Choice A) is a bacterial infection of fetal membranes commonly occurring with premature or prolonged rupture of membranes, characterized by maternal fever and leukocytosis, but is not a common complication of fetal malpresentation. Fetal shoulder dystocia (Choice B) occurs after delivery of the fetal head when shoulders are impacted behind the pubic symphysis or sacral promontory, leading to brachial nerve injury, asphyxia, and death. It is associated with macrosomia, post-term pregnancy, and maternal obesity—not breech presentation. Postpartum hemorrhage (Choice C) is most commonly caused by uterine atony in macrosomia, multiple gestations, prolonged labor, or uterine infection, and can result from cervical or vaginal laceration and retained products of conception. Uterine rupture (Choice E) occurs when the muscular uterine wall tears, presenting with severe abdominal pain, hemodynamic instability, and loss of fetal station. Risk factors include previous cesarean deliveries and labor induction, not breech presentation. Educational Objective: Rupture of membranes when there is no palpable presenting fetal body part or when fetal malpresentation exists carries high risk for umbilical cord prolapse, which can lead to cord compression and fetal hypoxia.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Neural tube defects 1 question
Source: 6A #27
A 37-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She conceived 17 weeks ago by in vitro fertilization. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The uterus is consistent in size with a 17-week gestation. Her maternal serum α-fetoprotein concentration is 7.3 multiples of the median. Which of the following is the most likely fetal abnormality? A) Cystic fibrosis B) Down syndrome C) Myelomeningocele D) Tay-Sachs disease E) Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: C) Myelomeningocele
Myelomeningocele is a neural tube defect where the neural crest arch fails to fully form posteriorly, resulting in protrusion of the dura and spinal cord out of the spinal canal. It is associated with abnormalities in folate metabolism or inadequate folic acid concentrations to support neural crest cell differentiation and neural tube development. Maternal diabetes is an additional risk factor. The condition results in nerve dysfunction and paralysis distal to the lesion. Myelomeningocele is commonly diagnosed prenatally with increased α-fetoprotein on prenatal maternal serum screening (as seen in this case with 7.3 multiples of the median), evidence of malformation on fetal ultrasonography, and the presence of acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid. Incorrect answers: Cystic fibrosis (Choice A) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by failure to pass meconium, recurrent infections, digital clubbing, bronchiectasis, and pancreatic insufficiency; it is detected on newborn screening and is not associated with elevated α-fetoprotein. Down syndrome (Choice B) is caused by trisomy 21 and presents with characteristic facies, intellectual disability, single palmar creases, and cardiac defects; it is associated with increased human chorionic gonadotropin and inhibin A, but decreased α-fetoprotein and estriol on second trimester screening. Tay-Sachs disease (Choice D) is a lysosomal storage disorder presenting with developmental delay, neurologic deficits, and cherry red spot on the macula; it is not associated with increased serum α-fetoprotein. Ventricular septal defect (Choice E) is a non-cyanotic congenital heart lesion with no relation to α-fetoprotein concentration. Educational Objective: α-Fetoprotein concentration is increased in maternal serum in the setting of neural tube defects, such as meningocele and myelomeningocele.
▶ Behavioral Health Medication-Induced Depressive Disorder 1 question
Source: 6A #32
A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of a migraine. She has a history of migraines treated with sumatriptan. She reports that she has not taken any pain relief medication for her headache because of concern regarding possible harm to her fetus. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Acetaminophen B) Butalbital C) Ergotamine D) Meperidine E) Sumatriptan
Correct Answer: A) Acetaminophen
Migraine headache is a frequent occurrence during pregnancy. Acetaminophen is considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding and is the most appropriate choice for treating acute pain associated with migrainous headache. Acetaminophen selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes in the central nervous system, resulting in analgesia, with the primary adverse effect being hepatotoxicity if taken in excess. It has no teratogenic effects and is well-evidenced as safe in pregnancy. Butalbital (Choice B) is a barbiturate with addictive properties that has been shown to cause fetal birth defects including neural tube defects, tetralogy of Fallot, and cardiac septal defects, with maximum susceptibility during the first trimester as in this patient. Ergotamine (Choice C) is an ergot alkaloid contraindicated in all trimesters of pregnancy due to uterotonic and vasoconstrictive properties that can cause fetal distress, birth defects, and miscarriage. Meperidine (Choice D) is a synthetic opioid that should not be used in pregnancy due to risks of maternal and fetal dependence and addiction, as well as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Sumatriptan (Choice E), while useful for migraine treatment, has evidence of increased incidence of behavioral problems when used in the first trimester. Although there is no conclusive evidence of birth defects, acetaminophen remains the safer, well-evidenced choice. Importantly, migrainous or tension headaches must be distinguished from other serious conditions that may present similarly during pregnancy, including preeclampsia, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and pituitary apoplexy. Educational Objective: Selection of analgesics during pregnancy must account for fetal susceptibility to teratogens during the first trimester and addictive properties of certain medications. Acetaminophen is generally considered safe for treatment of acute pain during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Fetal growth assessment 1 question
Source: 6A #39
A healthy 27-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well and has not had any uterine contractions. The baby has been very active. She has had a 1-kg (2-lb) weight gain since her last visit 2 weeks ago. She does not drink alcohol and quit smoking after learning she was pregnant. She works as a bartender. Blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a fundal height of 28 cm. Fetal heart tones are 150/min. Leopold maneuvers confirm a cephalic presentation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Follow-up visit in 2 weeks B) Fetal ultrasonography C) Induction of labor D) Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling E) Amniocentesis F) Cesarean delivery
Correct Answer: B) Fetal ultrasonography
Fundal height is used to estimate gestational age, with the distance in centimeters between the pubic symphysis and top of the uterine fundus approximating gestational age in weeks. At 32 weeks' gestation, expected fundal height should be approximately 32 cm; this patient's fundal height of 28 cm represents a 4-cm discrepancy, suggesting the fetus is smaller than expected for gestational age. When there is a discrepancy between fundal height and expected gestational age, the most appropriate next step is ultrasonography to assess the fetus through objective parameters for accurate dating and to evaluate for causes of small fundal height such as intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), incorrect dating, or oligohydramnios. Fetal measurements including crown-rump length, biparietal diameter, femur length, and abdominal circumference can accurately assess fetal size and dating. In this case, the patient is likely experiencing IUGR, which can be secondary to uteroplacental insufficiency, congenital infections, or maternal substance use (she works as a bartender with potential secondhand smoke exposure). Follow-up in 2 weeks (A) would be appropriate for a healthy gestation at 36 weeks but is inadequate when IUGR is suspected. Induction of labor (C) may be indicated after IUGR is confirmed but should not precede diagnostic confirmation. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (D) is invasive, carries risks of fetal bleeding, fetomaternal bleeding, infection, and fetal loss, and is reserved for confirmation of severe fetal anemia or when amniocentesis/chorionic villus sampling are nondiagnostic. Amniocentesis (E) is typically performed at 15-20 weeks for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities and, while potentially useful in determining IUGR etiology, should only be considered after ultrasonographic confirmation of the diagnosis. Cesarean delivery (F) is not indicated for IUGR alone and is reserved for fetal malpresentation, macrosomia, placenta previa, and arrest of labor.
▶ Social Sciences Advance care planning 1 question
Source: 6A #42
A 66-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of decreased level of consciousness and dyspnea. Two years ago, she was diagnosed with stage IV epithelial ovarian cancer. The patient initially responded to surgical debulking and chemotherapy, but she has not responded to the past three chemotherapy regimens. Her last CT scan of the abdomen showed an increase in peritoneal tumor burden. The patient does not have an advance directive. She appears thin and is in moderate respiratory distress. She is unconscious and does not respond to verbal stimuli. Her temperature is 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Breathing is labored, and breath sounds are decreased in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Her serum CA 125 concentration is 1236 U/ml (N<35); 1 month ago, it was 247 U/ml. The physician requests a family meeting with her two daughters. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial statement by the physician? A) "Do you want your mother to be an organ donor?" B) "What do you think is happening with your mother?" C) "Who is in charge of making decisions about your mother's care?" D) "Would you like your mother to be put on life support?" E) "Your mother will not live through the night."
Correct Answer: B) "What do you think is happening with your mother?"
Physicians should begin end-of-life discussions with open-ended questions to assess the understanding of patients or family members of the gravity of the situation. This approach allows the physician to tailor further discussion to address emotional needs or knowledge gaps. Family members may not realize that the patient may die imminently and require education and time to process this information before making decisions about care. Choice A (organ donor) inappropriately focuses on potential organ recipients rather than the patient and family's needs and emotional support. Choice C (decision-maker) is an important early step but should follow assessment of family understanding, as they may not yet realize the patient has likely lost decision-making capacity permanently and may die soon. Choices D and E (life support and prognosis) may shock family members who do not yet appreciate the gravity of the situation and preclude effective further discussion about end-of-life decisions. Educational Objective: Physicians should begin end-of-life discussions with open-ended questions to assess understanding of the gravity of the situation, then tailor discussion to address emotional needs and knowledge gaps of patients and family members.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Elder Abuse 1 question
Source: 6A #43
An 82-year-old woman with dementia, Alzheimer type, is brought to the physician by her daughter because of blood on her underwear. The patient is confused and smells of urine. She is not oriented to place or time, but she knows her name. Pelvic examination shows severe vaginal atrophy. There is a 3-cm, tender laceration and an erythematous, edematous vaginal perineal body. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Acute allergic reaction B) Lichen planus C) Sexual assault D) Squamous cell carcinoma in situ E) Urinary incontinence
Correct Answer: C) Sexual assault
This patient presents with perineal erythema, vaginal bleeding, and a genital laceration most likely secondary to mechanical trauma from sexual assault. The odor of urine likely indicates neglect. Elder abuse, neglect, and mistreatment is common, particularly in vulnerable populations with cognitive impairment. Sexual abuse specifically may present with pain in the genital area, vaginal or rectal bleeding, and bruises or lacerations of the vulva or breasts. Skin tears, lacerations, and bruises in unusual locations suggest elder abuse. Elder abuse can exacerbate cognitive impairment and may explain this patient's confusion and incontinence. Elderly patients who demonstrate signs of abuse should be interviewed without their caregiver present. An acute allergic reaction such as contact dermatitis of the vagina may present with erythema, pruritus, burning, or soreness, but lacerations and vaginal bleeding would be atypical. Vulvar lichen planus is an uncommon inflammatory condition presenting with vulvar soreness, intense pruritus, and burning, with the erosive form demonstrating narrowing of the introitus and loss of the labia minora; this patient's vaginal bleeding and lacerations are inconsistent with this diagnosis. Squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the vulva would present with an often raised, pruritic lesion, not with perineal erythema, vaginal bleeding, and genital laceration. Urinary incontinence could lead to vulvar erythema and skin peeling, but linear lacerations and vaginal bleeding would be atypical. Physicians are mandated by many states to report abuse of vulnerable adults to protective agencies. Sexual abuse of elderly patients may present with pain in the genital area, vaginal or rectal bleeding, and lacerations or bruises of the vulva or breasts.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Peripheral Nerve Injury 1 question
Source: 6A #45
Three days after a moderately difficult forceps delivery, a 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of numbness and tingling of the anterior lower right leg. She also has had buckling of the right knee when she attempts to walk. Epidural anesthesia was administered during labor. After 4 hours of pushing in stirrups during the second stage of labor, spinal anesthesia was administered for the forceps delivery. Examination shows decreased sensation along the anterior, anteromedial, and medial aspect of the right thigh, knee, and upper leg. There is some weakness of the quadriceps femoris muscle. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Adverse effect of epidural anesthesia B) Adverse effect of spinal anesthesia C) Injury to the femoral nerve D) Injury to the genitofemoral nerve E) Injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Correct Answer: C) Injury to the femoral nerve
The patient's clinical presentation is consistent with femoral nerve injury. Nerve compression injuries result from prolonged pressure against a nerve fiber, causing nerve ischemia and demyelination that may be reversible depending on the extent of ischemia. The most commonly injured nerves in the lithotomy position (with feet in stirrups) are the femoral nerve and the peroneal nerve. The femoral nerve can be compressed under the inguinal ligament when the hip is flexed greater than 90 degrees, leading to numbness of the anterior and medial aspects of the thigh and weakness of the quadriceps muscle, exactly as seen in this patient. After 4 hours of pushing in stirrups, the patient's prolonged positioning caused this compression injury. Recovery depends on the length of time the nerve was exposed to ischemia, and physical therapy can be useful. Adverse effects of epidural anesthesia (Choice A) and spinal anesthesia (Choice B) include back pain, headache, hematoma formation, infection (e.g., epidural abscess), urinary retention, hypotension, and neuropathy. However, the risk for anesthesia-related neuropathy is low and would more likely present bilaterally and in the distribution of a dermatome rather than within the territory of an individual nerve. Injuries to the genitofemoral nerve (Choice D) and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (Choice E) can occur during open pelvic surgeries as they run along the pelvic sidewall. Genitofemoral nerve injury presents with numbness of the upper medial thigh and scrotum or labia, whereas lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injuries present with pain along the anterior and lateral aspects of the thigh—neither matching this patient's presentation. Educational Objective: Prolonged positioning with hips flexed greater than 90 degrees can lead to femoral nerve injury, which presents with numbness of the anterior and medial aspects of the thigh, as well as weakness of the quadriceps muscle.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Morning-After Pill 1 question
Source: 6A #49
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because she is concerned that she may be pregnant. She was sexually active with her husband 2 days ago, and they did not use contraception. She wants to prevent an unintended pregnancy. She is breast-feeding their 7-month-old infant. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. She has a 5-year history of migraines and a history of hepatitis B. She was treated for Chlamydia trachomatis infection at the age of 17 years. She takes no medications and has no known drug allergies. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is a contraindication for the use of levonorgestrel as emergency contraception in this patient? A) Breast-feeding B) History of Chlamydia trachomatis infection C) History of hepatitis B D) History of migraines E) There are no contraindications
Correct Answer: E) There are no contraindications
Levonorgestrel is an emergency contraceptive that prevents ovulation and can be taken up to 72 hours after intercourse. It has no significant contraindications and is safe to use in breastfeeding women. Breast-feeding is not a contraindication to levonorgestrel, although combined oral contraceptives are usually avoided in breastfeeding patients due to risk of prolactin inhibition and impaired milk production. History of Chlamydia trachomatis infection plays no role in the choice of emergency contraceptive; however, active infections would preclude use of a copper intrauterine device. History of hepatitis B is not a contraindication to levonorgestrel despite the drug being primarily metabolized in the liver. Hepatitis B can be sexually transmitted but does not affect the ability to use emergency contraception. History of migraines commonly precludes the use of estrogen-based contraception but does not affect the ability to use levonorgestrel, which is a progestin-only method. Adverse effects of levonorgestrel include nausea, irregular menstrual bleeding, lower abdominal pain, and fatigue. Alternative emergency contraceptive methods include ulipristal (an anti-progesterone effective up to 5 days after intercourse) and the copper intrauterine device (most effective form, effective if placed within 5 days of intercourse, with contraindications including active uterine infection or anatomic abnormalities).
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Prenatal risk assessment and prevention 1 question
Source: 3A #1
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 17 weeks ago. Examination shows a uterine fundus that is palpated midway between the pubic symphysis and umbilicus. Her serum α-fetoprotein concentration is 2.6 multiples of the median. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Repeat measurement of serum α-fetoprotein concentration B) Serum studies for fetal erythrocytes C) Ultrasonography D) Amniocentesis E) Pregnancy termination
Correct Answer: C) Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step when maternal serum α-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated. The most common causes of increased AFP include inaccurate gestational dating, multiple gestations, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele), and neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida). Ultrasonography allows accurate assessment of gestational age, identification of multiple gestations, and detection of fetal structural abnormalities. Amniocentesis can be performed after ultrasonography if neural tube defect is suspected, to assess for amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase. Repeat AFP measurement (Choice A) is unnecessary given the significantly elevated result of 2.6 multiples of the median, making false positive unlikely. Serum studies for fetal erythrocytes (Choice B) would assess for maternal-fetal blood mixing, for which there is no clinical evidence based on elevated AFP alone. Testing for fetal anemia requires invasive umbilical cord sampling and should not be performed without specific clinical indication. Amniocentesis (Choice D) is invasive and carries risks including fetal-maternal hemorrhage, premature rupture of membranes, and chorioamnionitis. It should be reserved for after ultrasonography if neural tube defect is suspected, not as an initial diagnostic test. Pregnancy termination (Choice E) is a highly individualized decision that should only be considered after determining the cause of elevated AFP, particularly given the possibility of gestational dating error. Educational Objective: Common causes of increased α-fetoprotein concentration in maternal serum are inaccurate gestational dating, multiple gestations, and abdominal wall or neural tube defects. Initial evaluation is performed with ultrasonography to evaluate gestational age accuracy, number of fetuses, and presence of fetal structural abnormalities.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Imperforate Hymen 1 question
Source: 3A #2
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has never had a menstrual period. She also has had moderate lower abdominal pain during the past 5 months. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m². Breast development is Tanner stage 4. Examination shows coarse pubic and axillary hair. The external genitalia appear normal. The vaginal canal cannot be visualized. Rectal examination shows an anterior tender, central mass. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Androgen insensitivity syndrome B) Complete mullerian agenesis C) Hormonally active ovarian tumor D) Imperforate hymen E) Normal development
Correct Answer: D) Imperforate hymen
Imperforate hymen is a common congenital disorder wherein the hymenal opening is absent, leading to obstruction of the vaginal canal and preventing excretion of menstrual blood. It presents with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and a bulging pelvic mass in an adolescent with otherwise normal sexual development. Significant accumulation of menstrual blood products may give the bulging hymen a blue appearance and may be palpated through the rectum, a condition known as hematocolpos. Diagnosis is made by ultrasonography, and treatment involves surgical hymenotomy and evacuation of accumulated blood. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (Choice A) presents with primary amenorrhea and a blind vaginal pouch in XY karyotype patients with androgen receptor mutations. These patients have sparse or absent axillary and pubic hair, and imaging shows testes with absence of uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vaginal canal—inconsistent with this patient's coarse hair and normal external genitalia. Complete mullerian agenesis/Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome (Choice B) results from failure of mullerian duct development with varying degrees of vaginal and uterine agenesis. Functioning ovaries are present with normal secondary sexual characteristics, but a tender midline mass would not be present. Hormonally active ovarian tumors (Choice C), such as granulosa cell tumors or Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, may present with palpable adnexal mass, abnormal uterine bleeding, or hyperandrogenism. This patient's clinical findings are more consistent with imperforate hymen with hematocolpos. Normal development (Choice E) is contradicted by delayed menarche. Menarche typically occurs between ages 11-14; failure to develop menarche by age 16 indicates primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Imperforate hymen is a congenital absence of the hymenal opening presenting with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and bulging pelvic mass in adolescents with otherwise normal sexual development. Surgical hymenotomy and evacuation of accumulated menstrual blood is curative.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Fetal growth restriction 1 question
Source: 3A #4
A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 36 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital after fetal growth restriction is found during a routine prenatal visit. She has a 6-year history of mild chronic essential hypertension controlled with β-adrenergic blocking agents that were discontinued at 8 weeks' gestation. At 10 weeks' gestation, a 24-hour urine collection shows a protein concentration of 50 mg and creatinine clearance of 110 mL/min. Ultrasonography and amniocentesis at 18 weeks' gestation showed no abnormalities; the estimated fetal weight was at the 50th percentile. Her temperature today is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a fundal height of 30 cm. Ultrasonography shows a fetal head circumference consistent with 35-week gestation and an abdominal circumference consistent with 30-week gestation. The estimated fetal weight is at the 9th percentile. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to determine the risk of intrauterine fetal demise? A) Determination of nuchal thickness B) Fetal fibronectin test C) Glucose tolerance test D) Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery E) Determination of amniotic fluid glucose concentration
Correct Answer: D) Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery
Fetal growth restriction (FGR) occurs when the fetus fails to reach its full genetic growth potential and is defined as an estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile. FGR is classified as symmetrical (restriction of fetal head, abdomen, and extremities indicating early impairment) or asymmetrical (normal fetal head development with restricted abdominal and extremity growth). Symmetrical FGR is caused by intrauterine infections, chromosomal abnormalities, and maternal drug or toxin exposures. Asymmetrical FGR typically occurs in the third trimester from causes such as maternal hypertension, chronic kidney disease, preeclampsia, or smoking, and is usually due to placental insufficiency. This patient demonstrates asymmetrical FGR with a normal head circumference (35 weeks) but restricted abdominal circumference (30 weeks) at 36 weeks' gestation, consistent with placental insufficiency from her history of hypertension. Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery is the most appropriate test to assess for placental insufficiency and fetal well-being in the third trimester by evaluating umbilical artery waveforms. This test has been shown to decrease perinatal morbidity and mortality in FGR. Determination of nuchal thickness (Choice A) is used to screen for chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 21, not for FGR evaluation. Fetal fibronectin test (Choice B) via vaginal swab indicates leakage of fibronectin at the chorioamnion-decidua interface and predicts impending preterm labor, not FGR risk. Glucose tolerance test (Choice C) diagnoses maternal gestational diabetes, which more commonly causes fetal macrosomia rather than FGR; it does not evaluate placental insufficiency. Determination of amniotic fluid glucose concentration (Choice E) is useful for identifying gestational diabetes or chorioamnionitis, not FGR. Educational Objective: Fetal growth restriction with estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile occurring in the third trimester may indicate fetal hypoxia secondary to maternal vascular risk factors. Umbilical Doppler ultrasonography is the best test to evaluate for uteroplacental insufficiency as a cause of FGR.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Asymptomatic urinary tract infection in pregnancy 1 question
Source: 3A #5
A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of pain and burning with urination. Two years ago, she had similar symptoms that resolved with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy. She is sexually active and uses an oral contraceptive. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows no costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows bacteria and pus. She requests advice about preventing future episodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation? A) Drinking 6 ounces of cranberry juice daily B) Voiding immediately after coitus C) Antibiotic prophylaxis only after coitus D) Daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis E) No preventive measures available
Correct Answer: B) Voiding immediately after coitus
Lower urinary tract infections (UTIs) present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. They occur more frequently in women than in men because of a shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth. Risk factors include urinary catheters, anatomic genitourinary defects, diabetes, pregnancy, and frequent or recent sexual intercourse. Urinalysis typically shows bacteriuria, white blood cells, positive leukocyte esterase, and positive nitrites depending on the organism. Treatment of uncomplicated UTIs consists of outpatient antibiotic management with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, or cephalexin. Preventive measures for UTIs include voiding immediately after coitus, oral hydration, and improvement of feminine hygiene practices to reduce bacterial introduction to the urethra. Voiding after coitus is the most appropriate initial recommendation for this patient who has had only two UTIs in two years, as it avoids unnecessary antibiotic exposure and associated adverse effects. Cranberry juice (Choice A) has not been shown to decrease the frequency of recurrent UTIs. Antibiotic prophylaxis only after coitus (Choice C) or daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (Choice D) are adequate regimens for recurrent UTIs but are better reserved for patients with more frequent infections who do not respond to conservative measures. No preventive measures available (Choice E) is incorrect, as behavioral and medical interventions can reduce recurrent UTI risk.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Abnormal Cervical Cytology 1 question
Source: 3A #6
A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Six weeks ago, she underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for leiomyomata uteri. She has no history of abnormal Pap smears. Examination today shows a well-healing incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding future Pap smears for this patient? A) Annually B) Annually for 3 years and then every 3 years C) Every 3 years D) In 1 year and then no longer indicated E) No longer indicated
Correct Answer: E) No longer indicated
Pap smear testing uses a cervical swab to collect cells from the transformation zone of the cervix for screening of cervical carcinoma. USPSTF guidelines recommend cervical cancer screening every 3 years in women aged 21-29, and every 3 years (or every 5 years with HPV co-testing) in women aged 30-65. However, total abdominal hysterectomy involves surgical removal of both the uterus and cervix. Patients who have undergone this procedure for benign indications such as uterine fibroids no longer require cervical cancer screening with Pap smears because they no longer have cervical tissue. Annual screening (Choice A) or annually for 3 years then every 3 years (Choice B) are intensified regimens reserved for high-risk patients with history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, HIV, or diethylstilbestrol exposure—not applicable here. Every 3 years (Choice C) is standard for women aged 21-29 or women 30-65 without HPV co-testing, but is inappropriate after total abdominal hysterectomy for benign disease. Screening in 1 year then no longer (Choice D) is also inappropriate as the patient has no cervical tissue remaining. Educational Objective: Total abdominal hysterectomy involves surgical removal of the uterus and cervix. Patients who have undergone this procedure for a benign condition do not require further screening for cervical cancer.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Lactation problems 1 question
Source: 3A #8
One month after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a 3400-g (7-lb 8-oz) newborn, a 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 7-day history of a tender mass in her left breast. Her pregnancy had been complicated by abdominal trauma sustained in a motor vehicle collision. A second-degree midline vaginal laceration was repaired without difficulty after delivery. She is breast-feeding. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows a 3 x 3-cm, fluctuant mass in the lateral aspect of the left breast. The mass is mildly tender to palpation. The breast is not warm or erythematous. The breasts are symmetric. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abscess B) Breast engorgement C) Galactocele D) Mastitis E) Supernumerary breast
Correct Answer: C) Galactocele
A galactocele is a benign cyst of the mammary glands caused by obstruction of lactiferous duct outflow. It occurs in lactating women or those who recently discontinued lactation and presents with a firm, fluctuant mass that is painless or mildly tender, most commonly in the subareolar area. Vital signs are within normal limits. Diagnosis is typically clinical but can be confirmed with ultrasonography showing a cystic mass. Galactoceles generally resolve spontaneously but can be aspirated or excised if persistent and symptomatic. Complications include superimposed infection, abscess formation, rupture, and subsequent inflammation. Breast abscesses (Choice A) are infections presenting as palpable, tender, fluctuant, erythematous masses with fever and purulent nipple discharge. They can develop from galactoceles if bacteria are introduced through nipple abrasions, but this patient's galactocele has not progressed to abscess. Breast engorgement (Choice B) occurs from increased milk production relative to release, causing bilateral painful swelling with possible fever—neither present here. Mastitis (Choice D) is cellulitis of breast tissue from bacterial introduction at the nipple, presenting with unilateral erythematous, indurated, edematous, warm, tender tissue and fever. It does not present with a unilateral mass unless progressed to abscess. A supernumerary breast (Choice E) is an extra breast present from birth, not developing after lactation. Educational Objective: Galactoceles are benign breast cysts caused by obstruction of lactiferous ducts in lactating women, presenting with a firm, fluctuant, painless mass typically in the subareolar area. Most self-resolve; persistent symptomatic cases can be treated with aspiration or excision.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Birth trauma 1 question
Source: 3A #9
A 20-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She reports severe abdominal pain and has received no prenatal care. Leopold maneuvers indicate a fetus at term. The cervix is 10 cm dilated and 100% effaced; the vertex is at +2 station. After pushing for 3 hours, low-forceps-assisted delivery is performed because of nonreassuring fetal heart tones, severe variable decelerations, and maternal exhaustion. The operative vaginal delivery of a 4200-g newborn is complicated by shoulder dystocia that requires 8 minutes to reduce. On examination, the newborn does not move the right arm. The forearm is pronated, and the arm is adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings in this newborn? A) Fracture of the clavicle B) Hypoxic injury to the motor area of the precentral gyrus C) Injury to the eighth cervical root and first thoracic root D) Injury to the fifth and sixth cervical roots E) Partial dislocation of the elbow
Correct Answer: D) Injury to the fifth and sixth cervical roots
Erb palsy is characterized by a pronated, adducted, and internally rotated arm secondary to injury of the upper brachial plexus, specifically the fifth and sixth cervical roots (C5, C6). This occurs during complicated deliveries when lateral traction is placed on the neck, such as during shoulder dystocia or forceps-assisted delivery. The C5 and C6 roots innervate the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii muscles. Loss of function of these muscles results in: (1) adduction of the arm due to failure of the deltoid and supraspinatus to abduct; (2) medial (internal) rotation due to failure of the infraspinatus to externally rotate; and (3) extension and pronation due to failure of the biceps brachii to flex and supinate the forearm. This clinical presentation is pathognomonic for Erb palsy. Fracture of the clavicle (Choice A) can occur during shoulder dystocia but typically causes pain and decreased movement that heals within 1-2 weeks, not the characteristic nerve palsy pattern seen here. Hypoxic injury to the motor area of the precentral gyrus (Choice B) would present with paralysis of the contralateral face and extremities, not the specific peripheral nerve distribution pattern observed in this case. Injury to the eighth cervical root and first thoracic root (Choice C) constitutes Klumpke palsy, which results from upward traction on the arm and causes dysfunction of intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei, hypothenar muscles), not the proximal arm findings seen here. Partial dislocation of the elbow (Choice E) presents with pain with elbow movement but does not produce the characteristic muscle palsy pattern associated with C5-C6 nerve root injury. Educational Objective: Erb palsy is a brachial plexus injury of the C5 and C6 nerve roots caused by lateral traction of the neck during delivery. This results in dysfunction of the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii muscles, presenting as characteristic arm adduction, internal rotation, extension, and pronation.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Necrotizing fasciitis 1 question
Source: 3A #10
A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus has had increasingly severe perineal pain over the past 3 days. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Pelvic examination shows a 5 x 5-cm tense cystic mass in the posterior right labium majus with cellulitis extending past the right pubic hairline. Which of the following is the most serious complication of this condition? A) Bartholin gland abscess B) Chlamydial sepsis C) Gram-positive sepsis D) Necrotizing fasciitis E) Perirectal abscess
Correct Answer: D) Necrotizing fasciitis
A perineal abscess presenting as an erythematous, edematous, tender, cystic mass can be complicated by necrotizing fasciitis if left untreated. Necrotizing fasciitis is a severe bacterial infection involving the fascial plane between skin and muscle, most commonly caused by mixed anaerobic and aerobic bacteria. It classically presents with erythema or purple discoloration over the skin, bullae, crepitus, and exquisite tenderness on palpation. The infection spreads along the deep fascial plane causing rapid extension that is often difficult to appreciate visually. Vital signs may disclose fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Risk factors include previous trauma to the infected site and systemic diseases such as diabetes, renal failure, and liver failure. When occurring in the perineum, necrotizing fasciitis is known as Fournier gangrene. It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and fluid resuscitation. Bartholin gland abscess (Choice A) typically follows a Bartholin gland cyst and presents as a swollen mass at the introitus. While it can progress to an abscess with erythema and tenderness, formation of another abscess would not be as serious as necrotizing infection. Chlamydial sepsis (Choice B) is uncommon and would present with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and leukocytosis. Chlamydia trachomatis typically presents with vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding, and dysuria, not perineal abscess. Gram-positive sepsis (Choice C) can result from skin infections or indwelling catheters. While possible, a more pressing complication would be necrotizing fasciitis, which requires emergent surgical debridement. Perirectal abscess (Choice E) presents as an erythematous, fluctuant, tender mass around the rectum. While the infection could spread to the perirectal area, this would be less worrisome than necrotizing fasciitis as it could be treated with non-emergent incision and debridement plus antibiotics. Educational Objective: Necrotizing fasciitis is a severe infection of the deep fascial planes presenting with erythema, tenderness, and rapid expansion leading to bullae, purple discoloration, and crepitus. Risk factors include systemic diseases such as diabetes, liver failure, and renal failure. Treatment requires emergent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 1 question
Source: 3A #11
A 32-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician at 30 weeks' gestation because of a 10-day history of decreased appetite, intermittent nausea, and generalized itching. She has no history of serious illness, and her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated. Her pulse is 98/min and regular, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. Examination shows excoriations on the left shoulder. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the left sternal border. The uterus is consistent in size with a 30-week gestation. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 86 µm³, Leukocyte count 10,200/mm³, Platelet count 114,000/mm³, Red cell distribution width 13% (N=13%-15%), Total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 206 U/L, AST 30 U/L, ALT 26 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her symptoms? A) Acute fatty liver B) HELLP syndrome C) Intrahepatic cholestasis D) Mastocytosis E) Normal pregnancy
Correct Answer: C) Intrahepatic cholestasis
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, also known as cholestasis of pregnancy, is a common liver disease in pregnancy that typically occurs in the late second or third trimesters and quickly resolves following delivery. Rising estrogen and progesterone concentrations, in addition to potential genetic susceptibility, are hypothesized to result in impaired bile flow. Patients typically present with generalized pruritus and can also exhibit right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Physical examination usually shows excoriations from generalized scratching and possible jaundice depending on severity. Laboratory studies typically show increased serum bile acid concentration and abnormal liver function tests (LFTs), with increased alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin concentrations being common; hepatic aminotransferase activity may also be abnormal. Ursodeoxycholic acid is often administered to relieve pruritus and to prevent neonatal complications related to maternal bile acids crossing the placenta (e.g., preterm birth, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and intrauterine demise). Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (Choice A) occurs because of abnormal fatty acid metabolism leading to fatty acid accumulation in the liver. It presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and jaundice. In severe cases, patients show signs of acute liver failure such as ascites. Increased aminotransferase activity is common, and laboratory studies may show indirect hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and coagulopathy. Pruritus is an uncommon symptom of acute fatty liver of pregnancy. HELLP syndrome (Choice B), which stands for hemolysis, increased liver enzymes (aminotransferase activity), and low platelet count, is a condition of the third trimester in which microangiopathy and intravascular coagulation occur in the liver. Patients typically present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and malaise. Hypertension and proteinuria are also common, as the syndrome may be related to preeclampsia. The syndrome is associated with anemia with schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, thrombocytopenia, increased serum indirect bilirubin, and increased serum aminotransferase activity. Mastocytosis (Choice D) is a rare disorder of mast cell proliferation in the skin or other organs. In cutaneous mastocytosis, lesions manifest as a pruritic maculopapular or urticarial rash. In systemic mastocytosis, mast cells can invade the bone marrow, liver, or gastrointestinal tract, presenting with cytopenias, portal hypertension, and/or nausea. Serum tryptase activity is typically increased. This patient has no specific skin lesions other than excoriation. Normal pregnancy (Choice E) is not characterized by pruritus or nausea in the third trimester, though nausea in early pregnancy is common. This patient also has an atypically high bilirubin concentration. In normal pregnancy, maternal alkaline phosphatase activity can be increased by placental isoenzyme activity. Additionally, plasma volume increases in late pregnancy, resulting in a systolic flow murmur and dilutional thrombocytopenia and anemia. Educational Objective: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is associated with pruritus and nausea in late pregnancy and can feature increased serum bile acid concentrations and abnormal LFTs. Pruritus and increased serum bile acid concentrations distinguish intrahepatic cholestasis from acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Abruptio placentae 1 question
Source: 3A #21
A 19-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and lethargy for 4 hours. She has had no prenatal care. She is unable to give a history. Her pulse is 112/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 190/108 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a fundal height of 27 cm. The abdomen is rigid and tender to palpation. For each patient with a fetus or newborn with abnormalities, select the maternal condition most likely associated with these findings. A) Alcohol use B) Amphetamine use C) Cigarette smoking D) Cocaine use E) Cystic fibrosis carrier state F) Folic acid deficiency G) Gametic nondisjunction H) Heroin use I) Iodine deficiency J) Marijuana use K) Parvovirus B19 infection L) Rh sensitization M) Rubella infection N) Tay-Sachs carrier state
Correct Answer: D) Cocaine use
Cocaine use in pregnancy is associated with placental abruption (abruptio placentae), the premature separation of the placenta from the uterus. Abruptio placentae presents with vaginal bleeding, severe uterine pain, and tetanic contractions, typically in the third trimester. It commonly results from lower abdominal trauma, smoking, or cocaine use. In cases of cocaine use, patients typically present with sympathomimetic toxicity evidenced on vital signs by hypertension, tachycardia, and tachypnea. The uterus is typically exquisitely tender to palpation and may present similarly to peritonitis, with severe pain disproportionate to exam findings, and abdominal rigidity. Because of the compromised fetal blood supply, this is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate cesarean delivery and Rh0(D) immune globulin if the maternal blood type is Rh-negative. Alcohol use causes fetal alcohol syndrome with craniofacial dysmorphism, microcephaly, developmental delay, and learning disabilities. Amphetamine use is associated with cleft palate, cardiac malformation, intrauterine growth restriction, and fetal tachycardia. Cigarette smoking increases risk of premature birth and low birth weight but would not cause hypertension. Cystic fibrosis and Tay-Sachs carrier states increase risk of disease in offspring if the father is a carrier or affected. Folic acid deficiency is associated with neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Gametic nondisjunction leads to trisomies but is not associated with placental abruption. Heroin use is associated with neonatal abstinence syndrome but does not classically cause placental abruption. Iodine deficiency presents with neonatal hypothyroidism or cretinism. Marijuana use carries similar risks to cigarette smoking. Parvovirus B19 infects fetal bone marrow causing anemia and hydrops. Rh sensitization develops when an Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood. Rubella infection presents with sensorineural deafness, neurodevelopmental delay, congenital cardiac defects, and microcephaly.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Prolonged pregnancy 1 question
Source: 3A #34
A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for labor induction. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness. On admission, her temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 130/72 mm Hg. Fetal nonstress testing is reactive. Pelvic examination shows a closed, long, posterior cervix. The amniotic fluid index is 3.2 cm (N=9-31). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Discharge home and readmit in 1 week B) Administer betamethasone C) Administer a prostaglandin D) Begin amnioinfusion E) Perform an immediate cesarean delivery
Correct Answer: C) Administer a prostaglandin
Postterm pregnancy is defined as gestation extending to or beyond 42 weeks and is associated with increased rates of maternal and neonatal complications, including meconium aspiration and fetal demise. While expectant management may be offered to select patients, the presence of an unfavorable cervix or oligohydramnios (as indicated by a low amniotic fluid index of 3.2 cm, normal 9-31 cm) are indications for induction of labor. Oligohydramnios in postterm pregnancy results from changes in maternal-fetal circulation due to placental aging and is associated with umbilical cord compression. Induction of labor is achieved by administering a prostaglandin analogue (dinoprostone or misoprostol) or oxytocin, or through nonpharmacologic methods such as membrane stripping or rupture of the amniotic sac. Choice A (discharge home) is inappropriate given the presence of oligohydramnios in postterm pregnancy. While uncomplicated postterm pregnancies may be managed expectantly, complications such as oligohydramnios mandate labor induction to reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Choice B (betamethasone) is a corticosteroid that stimulates fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, appropriate only in preterm pregnancies. It has no role in managing complicated postterm pregnancy. Choice D (amnioinfusion) instills fluid into the amniotic cavity and may be useful for oligohydramnios when fetal heart rate monitoring reveals variable decelerations suggesting cord compression. However, amnioinfusion does not address the underlying cause of oligohydramnios in postterm pregnancy (placental aging and maternal-fetal circulatory changes). Labor induction is therefore more appropriate. Choice E (immediate cesarean delivery) exposes mother and fetus to unnecessary surgical risks. Induction of labor is the appropriate initial step, with cesarean delivery reserved for cases where induction leads to fetal distress. Educational Objective: Postterm pregnancy (≥42 weeks) is associated with maternal and fetal complications. An unfavorable cervix or complications such as oligohydramnios are indications for labor induction using prostaglandin analogues (dinoprostone or misoprostol) or oxytocin.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Premature separation of placenta 1 question
Source: 3A #42
A 37-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 4, aborta 2, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Spontaneous rupture of membranes along with severe abdominal pain occurred 4 hours ago. The pain is constant and sharp, unlike the labor pains of her previous pregnancies. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Her last pregnancy ended in cesarean delivery at term for breech presentation. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 122/68 mm Hg. The fundal height is 28 cm. Leopold maneuvers show fetal small parts above the fundus. External monitoring shows fetal tachycardia with late decelerations and loss of beat-to-beat variability. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abruptio placentae B) Chorioamnionitis C) Placenta previa D) Umbilical cord prolapse E) Uterine rupture
Correct Answer: E) Uterine rupture
Uterine rupture is a dangerous complication of pregnancy wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. Severe, constant sharp pain is a common initial finding, unlike typical labor pains. Hemodynamic instability can manifest in the mother with tachycardia and hypotension, and in the fetus with late decelerations, tachycardia, bradycardia, or loss of beat-to-beat variability. If uterine rupture occurs during labor, sudden loss of fetal station is a highly suggestive finding. Fetal parts may be palpable above the fundus with Leopold maneuvers, as seen in this patient. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after cesarean delivery (this patient had prior cesarean for breech), multiparity (gravida 7, para 4), and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. Uterine rupture is treated with emergency laparotomy.
