Abruptio placentae presents with abdominal or pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, and tetanic contractions, but the uterine wall remains intact and fetal parts will not be palpable above the fundus. Chorioamnionitis is a bacterial infection of fetal membranes characterized by maternal fever and leukocytosis with uterine tenderness, not the acute severe pain and fetal distress pattern seen here. Placenta previa is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue overlying the internal cervical os, typically detected on prenatal ultrasound and presenting with painless third trimester vaginal bleeding, not acute pain. Umbilical cord prolapse presents with fetal bradycardia as a common finding, not the tachycardia with late decelerations seen in this case. Educational Objective: Uterine rupture is a dangerous obstetric complication where the uterine wall tears. Acute severe pain, loss of fetal station, fetal parts palpable above the fundus, and both maternal and fetal hemodynamic instability (fetal tachycardia with late decelerations and loss of beat-to-beat variability) are suggestive findings. Treatment is with emergency laparotomy.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Cervical Cancer 1 question
Source: 3A #49
A 77-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding. Each episode lasts 3 to 4 days and is not associated with trauma or sexual intercourse. Menopause occurred 26 years ago, and she has never received hormone therapy. Her last gynecologic examination was 38 years ago following the birth of her youngest child. She takes no medications. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a 2-cm, exophytic lesion on the cervix. There is no enlargement of the uterus or evidence of blood in the vagina. Results of a biopsy specimen of the lesion are most likely to show which of the following? A) Adenocarcinoma B) Carcinosarcoma C) Clear cell carcinoma D) Papillary serous carcinoma E) Squamous cell carcinoma
Correct Answer: E) Squamous cell carcinoma
An exophytic lesion on the cervix is highly concerning for cervical cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histological type, accounting for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases. It arises from the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) between the ectocervix and endocervix, which is the target region for Pap smear screening. Risk factors for cervical cancer include HPV infection (high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, 33), early sexual activity, tobacco use, oral contraceptive use, immunosuppression, and HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Cervical cancer classically presents with vaginal bleeding with or without intercourse. Advanced disease may invade the bladder or rectum and cause hydronephrosis through ureteral obstruction. Metastatic spread commonly involves the lungs. Incorrect answers: Adenocarcinoma (Choice A) comprises only ~25% of invasive cervical cancers and is less common than squamous cell carcinoma, though it has similar treatment. Carcinosarcoma (Choice B) is a rare malignant mixed Müllerian tumor found in the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes, not the cervix. Clear cell carcinoma (Choice C) is a histological variant of adenocarcinoma with poorer chemotherapy response, seen in renal and endometrial cancers. Papillary serous carcinoma (Choice D) is a rare uterine malignancy with higher propensity for lymphatic spread, not a cervical lesion. Educational Objective: An exophytic mass on the cervix is highly suggestive of cervical cancer, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most common derivation, comprising 70% of cervical cancer cases.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Retained products of conception 1 question
Source: 5A #1
Thirty minutes after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a newborn at term, a 22-year-old primigravid woman has the sudden onset of heavy vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy and labor were uncomplicated. Prior to the onset of bleeding, the placenta delivered spontaneously with a nontapering vessel extending to the margin of the membranes. Examination now shows no vaginal or cervical lacerations. The uterus has moderate tone and is consistent in size with a 24-week gestation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abruptio placentae B) Placenta accreta C) Placenta percreta D) Placenta previa E) Succenturiate placental lobe
Correct Answer: E) Succenturiate placental lobe
Succenturiate placental lobes are accessory lobes of the placenta that develop separately from the main placenta but are connected via fetal vessels. One or more accessory lobes may be present. This condition is associated with first trimester bleeding, polyhydramnios, placenta previa, vasa previa, abruptio placentae, and postpartum hemorrhage caused by retained placental tissue. Risk factors include advanced maternal age, leiomyomata, and previous uterine surgery. Diagnosis is made by ultrasonography, and management typically involves cesarean delivery if discovered antepartum due to high risk for maternal and fetal mortality from hemorrhage. If undiagnosed until delivery, the mother may require oxytocin and manual extraction of the placenta and accessory lobes. The clinical presentation in this case is classic for succenturiate placental lobe: the presence of a nontapering vessel extending to the margin of the membranes indicates a separate accessory lobe connected by fetal vessels, and the sudden postpartum hemorrhage results from retained placental tissue. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) presents with vaginal bleeding, severe uterine pain, tetanic contractions, and often fetal demise, typically in the third trimester, commonly resulting from lower abdominal trauma, smoking, or cocaine use. Placenta accreta (Choice B) and placenta percreta (Choice C) refer to abnormal attachment of the placenta to the myometrium or through to the serosa and potentially adjacent organs (e.g., bladder), respectively, rather than to the decidualized endometrium. While they can present with postpartum hemorrhage from retained placental tissue, they are typically diagnosed prenatally on ultrasonography and do not present with the characteristic vessel extending to the membrane margin. Placenta previa (Choice D) is abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or entirely overlies the internal cervical os. It is usually detected on routine prenatal ultrasonography, and its most common presenting symptom is third trimester painless vaginal bleeding, not immediate postpartum hemorrhage after spontaneous placental delivery.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Achondroplasia 1 question
Source: 5A #4
A healthy 32-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. She has achondroplasia. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or drugs. She works as a chef 10 to 12 hours daily. She is 107 cm (3 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 36 kg (80 lb). Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 106/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Examination of the pelvis shows a conjugate diameter of 7 cm, intraspinous diameter of 5 cm, and intertuberous diameter of 5 cm. Ultrasonography shows a fetus at 9 weeks' gestation. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.9 g/dl. Urinalysis shows trace protein. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following? A) Cesarean delivery B) Fetal achondroplasia C) Preeclampsia D) Renal failure E) Uterine rupture
Correct Answer: A) Cesarean delivery
Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder of abnormal long bone growth caused by a mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), and is the most common cause of dwarfism. The disease affects long bones but has minimal effect on the cranium. This patient's fetus has a 50% chance of developing achondroplasia with associated macrocephaly. Normal adult female pelvic measurements are 10-12 cm conjugate diameter, 9.5-11.5 cm intraspinous diameter, and 10-12 cm intertuberous diameter. This patient's pelvic measurements (7 cm conjugate, 5 cm intraspinous, 5 cm intertuberous) are significantly smaller than normal, creating severe cephalopelvic disproportion. This anatomic constraint will likely necessitate cesarean delivery regardless of whether the fetus has achondroplasia, as the small pelvis cannot accommodate successful passage of the fetus through the pelvic inlet and outlet during vaginal delivery, placing the patient at greatest risk for fetal arrest of descent during labor. Fetal achondroplasia (Choice B) has a 50% likelihood given autosomal dominant inheritance, but cesarean delivery will be necessary regardless of fetal achondroplasia status due to maternal pelvic size. Preeclampsia (Choice C) presents with hypertension, edema, and proteinuria typically after 20 weeks of gestation. Achondroplasia does not increase preeclampsia risk. This patient's blood pressure is normal and proteinuria is only trace. Renal failure (Choice D) presents with uremia symptoms (fatigue, nausea, pruritus, altered mental status), hyperkalemia, and hypervolemia. It is not a typical complication of pregnancy in achondroplasia. Uterine rupture (Choice E) occurs when the muscular uterine wall tears, presenting with severe abdominal pain, hemodynamic instability, and loss of fetal station. Risk factors include previous cesarean delivery, multiparity, and labor induction, but not achondroplasia. Educational Objective: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder of abnormal long bone growth. Pregnant patients with achondroplasia frequently require cesarean delivery because of their small pelvic size, resulting in severe cephalopelvic disproportion.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Tay-Sachs Disease 1 question
Source: 5A #8
A 25-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician with her husband for counseling prior to conception. They are planning to start a family next year and would like to know their risk for having a child with Tay-Sachs disease. She is French-Canadian and has some distant cousins who died during early childhood. Her husband is Jewish but not of Ashkenazi descent. He has no known relatives with Tay-Sachs disease. Examination of the patient shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the risk for Tay-Sachs disease in this patient's future children? A) Testing of the husband first; if positive, no further testing is indicated B) Testing of the wife first; if negative, no further testing is indicated C) Testing of the wife first; if positive, no further testing is indicated D) No testing is indicated
Correct Answer: B) Testing of the wife first; if negative, no further testing is indicated
Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by a genetic mutation leading to deficiency of the hexosaminidase A (Hex A) enzyme, resulting in accumulation of the cell membrane glycolipid GM2 ganglioside within neuronal lysosomes. Preconception testing is recommended for patients from high-risk populations, including Ashkenazi Jewish, French-Canadian, Pennsylvania Dutch, and Cajun populations. Since this patient is French-Canadian with a family history of premature childhood deaths (distant cousins), she is at high risk for being a carrier and should be tested first. If the high-risk patient tests negative (indicating a wild-type allele for Hex A enzyme), no further testing of the spouse is indicated because the child would have no chance of developing Tay-Sachs disease due to its autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. A negative test in the high-risk individual means she will produce enough Hex A enzyme to degrade GM2 ganglioside. If either spouse tests positive, testing of the other spouse would be indicated to determine the child's risk. Tay-Sachs disease presents with normal motor development in the first few months of life followed by progressive loss of motor skills, muscle spasticity, macrocephaly, and a characteristic cherry red macular spot. The disease ultimately leads to blindness, seizures, and fatal aspiration pneumonia from pharyngeal muscle weakness, typically limiting life expectancy to 2-5 years. Choice A is incorrect because if the husband tests positive, the wife's status must still be determined. Choice C is incorrect because if the wife tests positive, the husband must be tested to assess risk. Choice D is incorrect because the wife's French-Canadian background and family history of premature childhood death are definitive reasons to undergo preconception testing.
▶ Human Development Routine vaccinations in adulthood 1 question
Source: 5A #11
A 52-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well and has no history of serious illness. Menses occur at regular 30-day intervals. She has received all appropriate childhood immunizations but none since that time. She has never been sexually active but plans on becoming sexually active with her boyfriend soon. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Prior to discussing contraceptive options with this patient, which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at this time? A) Hepatitis A B) Human papillomavirus C) Influenza virus D) Meningococcal E) Varicella
Correct Answer: C) Influenza virus
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends annual influenza vaccination for all patients older than 6 months of age. The influenza vaccine is available in inactivated, recombinant, and live-attenuated forms. The only absolute contraindication to receiving influenza vaccination is a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous dose. The live-attenuated vaccine should not be used in immunocompromised patients (HIV, immunosuppressant medications, asplenia), pregnant women, or those with cochlear implants. Seasonal influenza causes significant morbidity and mortality through complications including pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome, myositis, myocarditis, and multisystem organ failure. Annual vaccination is necessary due to the high mutation rate of influenza virus, which decreases host immunity. Hepatitis A vaccination (Choice A) is recommended for immunosuppressed patients, those traveling to endemic areas, intravenous drug users, healthcare workers, and men who have sex with men—not routine for this patient. Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination (Choice B) is recommended for patients aged 9-26 years and occasionally up to 45 years for prevention of high-risk strains (16, 18, 31, 33) that cause cervical, vulvar, penile, and anal cancers. At age 52, this patient is outside the recommended age range. Meningococcal vaccination (Choice D) is recommended for those in shared housing (college dorms, military barracks), with asplenia, or traveling to endemic regions—not indicated for this patient. Varicella vaccination (Choice E) is recommended for patients lacking immunity (born after 1980 without prior chickenpox). At age 52, this patient would have natural immunity and does not require this vaccine. Educational Objective: Annual influenza vaccinations are recommended for all patients older than 6 months. The only absolute contraindication is a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous influenza vaccine dose.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Postpartum hemorrhage 1 question
Source: 5A #13
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, delivers a full-term, 4082-g (9-lb) newborn vaginally. The pregnancy was uncomplicated. Despite receiving oxytocin therapy in the recovery room, she has excessive vaginal bleeding and a boggy uterus. The bleeding continues after uterine massage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Measurement of plasma fibrinogen concentration, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and factor VIII B) Ergonovine therapy C) Endometrial curettage D) Uterine artery embolization E) Exploratory laparotomy
Correct Answer: B) Ergonovine therapy
Uterine atony presents with postpartum hemorrhage and a boggy uterus on physical examination, as demonstrated in this patient. Initial management involves intravenous fluid administration, uterine massage, and oxytocin infusion. When uterine atony persists despite these interventions, pharmacologic agents such as methylergonovine (methergine), an ergot alkaloid, or carboprost tromethamine, a prostaglandin, should be administered. Ergonovine works directly on uterine smooth muscle, inducing increased uterine tone through sustained tetanic contraction, which reduces blood loss and is highly effective for postpartum uterine atony. Important contraindications to ergonovine include a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, or cerebrovascular disease due to risk of arterial vasospasm. Carboprost is contraindicated in asthmatic patients as it may induce bronchospasm. Risk factors for uterine atony include macrosomia, multiple gestations, prolonged labor, uterine infection, and spinal anesthesia. Choice A (coagulation studies) may be appropriate to rule out bleeding diatheses, but these tests take time to process and it is more important to stop bleeding quickly with medical management first. Choice C (endometrial curettage) is useful for retained products of conception or abnormal bleeding unresponsive to other interventions, but does not address uterine atony. Choices D (uterine artery embolization) and E (exploratory laparotomy for hysterectomy) are reserved for uncontrolled bleeding despite optimal medical management and are not the most appropriate next step when medical options remain available. Educational Objective: Uterine atony presents with postpartum hemorrhage and a boggy uterus. Initial management includes uterine massage and oxytocin, followed by ergonovine therapy (contraindicated in hypertension, coronary artery disease, and cerebrovascular disease) or carboprost tromethamine (contraindicated in asthma).
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Fibroadenoma 1 question
Source: 5A #15
An otherwise healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the physician 4 months after noticing a painless lump in her right breast during breast self-examination. She notes that the lump has increased in size. She feels well. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no lymphadenopathy. Examination of the right breast shows a raised area in the upper outer quadrant; there are no skin changes. A 4-cm, firm, smooth, mobile mass is palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Examination of the left breast shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abscess B) Fat necrosis C) Fibroadenoma D) Fibrocystic changes of the breast E) Galactocele F) Intraductal papilloma G) Lipoma H) Mammary ductal ectasia I) Mastitis
Correct Answer: C) Fibroadenoma
Fibroadenomas are benign breast masses composed of epithelial and fibroblastic stromal tissue and are the most common breast tumor of young women. They present in women between ages 25 and 40 as painless, mobile breast lumps that are typically small (less than 3 cm in diameter), mobile, and have a rubbery consistency. This patient's presentation of a painless, firm, smooth, mobile 4-cm mass in a 22-year-old woman is classic for fibroadenoma. Diagnosis is facilitated with ultrasonography or mammography, with definitive diagnosis requiring biopsy showing a well-circumscribed mass composed of hypercellular stromal cells with bland, uniform appearance without atypia and epithelial cells. Fibroadenomas usually decrease in size over time and have little malignant potential, so treatment is with regular observation. Abscess (Choice A) is a complication of mastitis occurring in breastfeeding women, presenting with localized indurated, fluctuant, erythematous, tender tissue—not applicable here as the patient is not breastfeeding and the mass is not tender. Fat necrosis (Choice B) is detected as palpable nodularity in an area of previous trauma with peripheral calcifications on imaging—this patient has no history of trauma. Fibrocystic changes (Choice D) are a benign, cyclic etiology of breast pain occurring most commonly in premenopausal women over age 35, presenting with various sites of bilateral breast pain and lumps—this patient is younger and has a single painless mass. Galactocele (Choice E) is a retained collection of breast milk presenting as a painless breast lump typically following cessation of lactation—this patient is not lactating. Intraductal papilloma (Choice F) is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge, not a palpable mass. Lipoma (Choice G) presents as a solitary, painless, soft (not firm), mobile subcutaneous mass, often on the torso—the firmness and location in breast tissue make this less likely. Mammary ductal ectasia (Choice H) occurs in perimenopausal women and involves widening of lactiferous ducts near the nipple—this patient is too young and the mass is in the upper outer quadrant. Mastitis (Choice I) presents with erythema and induration of tender, warm skin, classically in breastfeeding mothers—this patient is not breastfeeding and has no signs of infection.
▶ Behavioral Health Cocaine Use Disorder 1 question
Source: 5A #27
A 25-year-old primigravid woman is in labor at 24 weeks' gestation. Treatment with a tocolytic agent is ineffective. She has used crack cocaine during the pregnancy. Cocaine most likely altered her uterine contractility by which of the following mechanisms? A) Decreasing catecholamine B) Decreasing parasympathetic tone C) Increasing catecholamine D) Increasing norepinephrine reuptake E) Increasing parasympathetic tone
Correct Answer: C) Increasing catecholamine
Crack cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that increases sympathetic tone through inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. This results in increased synaptic norepinephrine concentration and consequent increased adrenergic receptor activation. The increased sympathetic tone activates α-adrenergic receptors on uterine myometrial smooth muscle myocytes, leading to increased contraction and abnormally increased, unregulated uterine smooth muscle contraction that can result in preterm labor onset. Tocolytic therapy with agents such as terbutaline (β-mimetic), magnesium sulfate, prostaglandin inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers are often ineffective because they do not directly inhibit the sympathetic activation of uterine myocytes, which is increased with cocaine use. Cocaine use in pregnancy also causes uteroplacental insufficiency with low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, miscarriage, and abruptio placentae due to sympathetic stimulation and resultant vasoconstriction. Choice A is incorrect because decreasing catecholamines would cause uterine smooth muscle relaxation, not the contraction seen here. Cocaine is a sympathomimetic that inhibits norepinephrine reuptake, increasing sympathetic tone and uterine contractility. Choice B is incorrect because while decreasing parasympathetic tone may lead to smooth muscle contraction due to relative increase in sympathetic tone, this is not the mechanism of crack cocaine action. Choice D is incorrect because increasing norepinephrine reuptake would decrease norepinephrine available for adrenergic receptor stimulation, causing decreased sympathetic stimulation and decreased smooth muscle contraction. Cocaine does the opposite—it inhibits norepinephrine reuptake. Choice E is incorrect because increasing parasympathetic tone would lead to uterine smooth muscle relaxation rather than the contraction observed in this patient, and this is not the mechanism of crack cocaine. Educational Objective: Crack cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic due to inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. In pregnancy, this increased sympathetic tone increases risk for abnormal uterine smooth muscle contractions and preterm labor. Cocaine is also associated with increased risk for uteroplacental insufficiency, miscarriage, low birth weight, and abruptio placentae.
▶ Male Reproductive Syphilis 1 question
Source: 5A #31
A 19-year-old woman comes to student health services because of a 5-day history of an ulcer on the inner side of the right vulva. Six weeks ago, she was diagnosed with herpes simplex virus 2 involving the left side of the vulva. At that time, testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae was negative. HIV antibody testing and rapid plasma reagin were also negative. She has completed a 10-day course of valacyclovir therapy. She has not been sexually active since her last examination. Today, she reports that her herpes sores are gone. Pelvic examination shows a 1 x 2.5-cm nontender ulcer with slightly raised edges and a shallow base on the perineum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Repeat HIV antibody test B) Repeat rapid plasma reagin C) Repeat testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae D) Viral culture of the ulcer E) Excision of the ulcer
Correct Answer: B) Repeat rapid plasma reagin
A variety of sexually transmitted infections cause nontender genital ulcers, including lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes L1, L2, L3), primary syphilitic chancre (Treponema pallidum), and granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis). In contrast, genital herpes (HSV) and chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) cause painful genital ulcers. The ulcer described in this case—nontender, 1 x 2.5 cm, with slightly raised edges and shallow base—is most consistent with primary syphilis. The chancre of primary syphilis is characteristically shallow with a clean base and painless. Serologic testing for syphilis begins with nontreponemal tests such as rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or VDRL. During early primary syphilis, these tests may be negative; therefore, repeat RPR testing is indicated given the clinical presentation. If positive, confirmation with a treponemal test (FTA-ABS) should follow. Choice A (Repeat HIV antibody test) may be warranted in the future as coinfection can occur, but is not necessary for current diagnosis since the presentation is more consistent with syphilis. Choice C (Repeat Chlamydia/Neisseria testing) is unnecessary without repeat sexual activity since the first negative tests; moreover, lymphogranuloma venereum presents with exudative ulcers and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. Choice D (Viral culture) is appropriate for HSV lesions, which present with painful vesicles and erosions, not the nontender ulcer described. Choice E (Excision) is inappropriate for infectious ulcers as it does not treat the underlying infection; excision is reserved for neoplastic ulcers.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Rh isoimmunization affecting maternal management 1 question
Source: 5A #43
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. She had a fracture of the right femur 12 months ago that required open reduction and a blood transfusion. Her current partner is the father of all her children. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Her blood group is O, Rh-negative. Indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for anti-Kell antibody at a titer of 1:256. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) 24-Hour urine collection for measurement of protein and creatinine clearance B) Kell typing of the father's blood C) Liver function tests D) Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid E) Intravenous IgG therapy F) Intravenous Rh0(D) immune globulin therapy
Correct Answer: B) Kell typing of the father's blood
A mother can develop antibodies against red blood cell (RBC) antigens after exposure to fetal blood antigens during delivery or from a previous blood transfusion. In this case, the patient likely developed antibodies to the Kell RBC antigen from her blood transfusion 12 months ago. Because maternal IgG antibodies can cross the placenta, it is critical to determine whether the fetus has Kell-positive or Kell-negative RBCs. If the fetus is Kell-positive, maternal anti-Kell antibodies would cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes, leading to severe fetal hemolytic anemia (erythroblastosis fetalis) and potential fetal demise. The most efficient initial approach is to determine the Kell antigen status of the father. If he is Kell-negative, the fetus will definitely be Kell-negative and there is no risk for erythroblastosis fetalis. If he is Kell-positive, there is a possibility the fetus will be Kell-positive and at risk for hemolytic disease. Incorrect answers: (A) 24-hour urine collection for protein and creatinine clearance is used to diagnose preeclampsia, which typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation, not at 8 weeks. (C) Liver function tests assess for HELLP syndrome, which also typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. (D) Measurement of bilirubin in amniotic fluid can assess fetal hemolysis but is unnecessary if paternal Kell typing shows he is Kell-negative, making it an inappropriate initial step. (E) Intravenous IgG therapy might have prevented Kell antibody development if given at the time of transfusion but plays no role in preventing erythroblastosis fetalis with active anti-Kell antibodies. (F) Intravenous Rh0(D) immune globulin is used to prevent alloimmunization to the Rh(D) antigen in Rh-negative women but is not indicated for anti-Kell antibodies. Educational Objective: Fetal RBC antigens depend on the antigens inherited from each parent. When a mother has antibodies against a specific RBC antigen (from prior pregnancy or transfusion), the fetus is at risk for erythroblastosis fetalis if it carries that antigen, since maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta. The first step in determining potential fetal RBC antigens is to determine the antigen type of each parent.
▶ Renal Urinary System Urethral Obstruction 1 question
Source: 7A #3
An 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of urinary urgency; during this period, she has noticed that the toilet paper is blood-tinged after urinating. At times she loses small amounts of urine unrelated to any precipitating events. She has a strong urge to urinate almost all the time. She voids small amounts every 30 minutes during the day and awakens approximately two times nightly to urinate. A photograph of the genitalia shows a large, friable mass near the urethral opening. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows no RBCs, WBCs, bacteria, or protein. A Gram stain of urine shows no bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Urethral carcinoma B) Urethral diverticulum C) Urethritis secondary to estrogen deficiency D) Urethrocele E) Urethrovaginal fistula
Correct Answer: A) Urethral carcinoma
This patient presents with overflow urinary incontinence (unprecipitated urine leakage and inability to empty the bladder) secondary to obstruction from a large, friable mass near the urethral opening, most consistent with urethral carcinoma. Urethral carcinoma is a rare cancer more common in men than women. In women, it most commonly presents with lower urinary tract symptoms such as dysuria or dyspareunia. The most common type in women is squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors include age, chronic inflammation, urethral diverticulum, and human papillomavirus infection. Evaluation includes physical examination with bimanual examination, laboratory studies to rule out urinary tract infection, and imaging such as CT/MRI or cystourethroscopy. Treatment involves surgical resection with chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending on disease extent. Urethral diverticulum (Choice B) is an outpouching of the urethra presenting with recurrent urinary tract infections, urethritis, urinary incontinence, and incomplete bladder emptying, but would not cause the large external pelvic mass observed. Urethritis secondary to estrogen deficiency (Choice C) occurs in postmenopausal women with urgency, frequency, and urge or stress incontinence due to vaginal and urethral atrophy from lack of estrogen. This patient has overflow incontinence from physical obstruction rather than urge incontinence. Urethrocele (Choice D) results from urethral prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall, causing stress urinary incontinence from urethral hypermobility, particularly in multiparous women. This patient's symptoms result from obstructive effect of the tumor rather than hypermobility. Urethrovaginal fistula (Choice E) creates a tract between the urethra and vaginal canal causing painless urine leakage from the vagina, typically from gynecologic surgery or radiation therapy. This patient has overflow incontinence rather than constant urine leakage and lacks surgical/radiation history. Educational Objective: Urethral carcinoma is a rare pelvic malignancy associated with increased age, chronic inflammation, and human papillomavirus infection. It is more common in men than women. A mass near the urethral opening may be present on examination with signs of overflow incontinence from physical obstruction. Treatment includes surgical resection with chemotherapy and radiation therapy depending on stage.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Streptococcus agalactiae infection in pregnancy 1 question
Source: 7A #5
A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 16 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of moderate pain with urination during the past 2 days. She has no history of serious illness, and pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 16-week gestation. Urine culture grows greater than 100,000 colonies/mL of group B streptococcus, sensitive to penicillin. In addition to antibiotic therapy now, which of the following is the most appropriate management? A) Screening for group B streptococcal infection at 35 weeks' gestation B) Screening for group B streptococcal infection at the onset of labor C) Maternal antibiotic therapy at 35 weeks' gestation D) Maternal antibiotic therapy during labor E) Elective cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation
Correct Answer: D) Maternal antibiotic therapy during labor
Group B streptococcus (GBS) frequently colonizes the urethra, vagina, and rectum and rarely causes infection in immunocompetent non-pregnant adults. However, in pregnancy, GBS infection is not uncommon and can cause asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis, chorioamnionitis, and endometritis. Maternal colonization and infection significantly increase the risk for neonatal transmission, which can lead to neonatal sepsis—a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. Current recommendations include screening with a urine culture early in pregnancy and an anovaginal swab at 36 to 38 weeks' gestation. Importantly, if a patient develops a documented GBS infection during pregnancy (as in this case), they should receive intrapartum antibiotic therapy during labor to prevent neonatal transmission, regardless of subsequent screening results. Choice A and B are incorrect because screening is not recommended for this patient who already has a known GBS infection; screening would likely remain positive even after appropriate antibiotic therapy due to common GBS colonization. Choice C is incorrect because antibiotic therapy at 35 weeks' gestation would be ineffective. Neonatal transmission occurs during delivery when the fetus is exposed to GBS in the vagina, so intrapartum antibiotics are necessary, not antepartum therapy. Choice E is incorrect because elective cesarean delivery is not required for a history of GBS infection. While it would reduce neonatal exposure, early elective cesarean delivery carries more complications than spontaneous vaginal delivery and is not indicated. Educational Objective: GBS is a common cause of asymptomatic bacteriuria and other infections in pregnant patients. Maternal colonization or infection increases neonatal transmission risk and consequent neonatal sepsis. Management includes urine culture early in pregnancy and screening at 36-38 weeks' gestation. Patients with positive cultures or symptomatic GBS infection during pregnancy require intrapartum antibiotic therapy to decrease neonatal transmission.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Appendicitis in Pregnancy 1 question
Source: 7A #23
A 31-year-old primigravid woman at 23 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of moderate lower abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and nausea. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 100/90 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation of the right mid abdomen. The uterus is consistent in size with a 23-week gestation. There is no bleeding or fluid discharge. Her leukocyte count is 15,000/mm³, serum AST activity is 45 U/L, and serum ALT activity is 48 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Abruptio placentae B) Appendicitis C) Braxton Hicks contractions D) Hepatitis E) Preterm labor
Correct Answer: B) Appendicitis
Appendicitis typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, with associated nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. In pregnancy, the enlarging uterus displaces the appendix superiorly (cephalad) compared to non-pregnant patients, which can limit the classic presentation. Initial periumbilical pain is attributed to vague visceral innervation of the appendix being referred to the midline; once inflammation affects the parietal peritoneum, pain becomes well-localized to the right lower quadrant (migratory character). McBurney point, located at one-third the distance between the inguinal ligament and umbilicus, is a sensitive location for tenderness. When the appendix is displaced cephalad, parietal peritoneal inflammation may occur at the right upper quadrant instead, potentially mimicking cholecystitis. Diagnosis is facilitated by MRI or ultrasonography, which may show appendiceal enlargement, appendicolith, appendiceal wall thickening, or periappendiceal fluid. Fluid in the paracolic gutter suggests appendiceal rupture or perforation and is typically accompanied by rising fever and leukocytosis. Immediate surgical exploration and appendectomy is indicated to prevent significant maternal and fetal complications including peritonitis, sepsis, and death. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) presents with vaginal bleeding, severe uterine pain, and tetanic contractions, typically in the third trimester, and results from trauma, smoking, or cocaine use. Braxton Hicks contractions (Choice C) are sporadic, irregular, and usually mild contractions without cervical changes; this patient's constant focal pain with fever, nausea, and vomiting are more concerning for intra-abdominal pathology. Hepatitis (Choice D) presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain with significantly increased transaminases, which are not markedly elevated here. Preterm labor (Choice E) occurs between 20-37 weeks with regular uterine contractions and cervical change, not focal abdominal pain with fever. Educational Objective: Acute appendicitis may occur in pregnant patients and presents with variably located right-sided pain based on appendiceal location or periumbilical abdominal pain, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. Fluid in the paracolic gutter on ultrasonography is suggestive of appendiceal rupture, which is managed with emergent surgical exploration.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Disseminated intravascular coagulation 1 question
Source: 7A #29
A 37-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of abdominal cramping and vaginal bleeding. Two hours later, she becomes obtunded. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a diffuse petechial rash. There is bleeding from the venipuncture and intravenous catheter sites. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL, Leukocyte count 11,000/mm³, Platelet count 80,000/mm³, Prothrombin time 18 sec (INR=1.5), Partial thromboplastin time 40 sec, Plasma fibrinogen 50 mg/dL (N=200-400), Fibrin degradation products 40 μg/mL (N<10). Which of the following should be administered prior to delivery? A) Fresh frozen plasma B) Heparin C) Oxytocin D) Packed red blood cells E) Platelets
Correct Answer: A) Fresh frozen plasma
This patient presents with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a systemic disorder characterized by widespread activation of the clotting cascade resulting in microthrombi formation, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding complications. DIC in pregnancy can be caused by placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage, preeclampsia/eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, amniotic fluid embolism, and trauma. This patient's presentation is consistent with placental abruption given the sudden onset of abdominal cramping and vaginal bleeding at 36 weeks. Laboratory findings confirm DIC: prolonged PT (INR=1.5) and aPTT (40 sec) reflecting consumption of clotting factors, thrombocytopenia (80,000/mm³), low fibrinogen (50 mg/dL), elevated fibrin degradation products (40 μg/mL), and anemia (Hgb 10 g/dL). The clinical presentation includes petechial rash, bleeding from venipuncture sites, and altered mental status indicating severe coagulopathy and shock. Treatment of DIC involves: (1) correcting the underlying cause, (2) correcting coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma (FFP), cryoprecipitate, or prothrombin complex concentrates, and (3) correcting thrombocytopenia if platelets are <50,000/mm³ and the patient is actively bleeding. FFP contains clotting factors, fibrinogen, antithrombin III, and plasma proteins necessary to restore hemostasis. Choice B (Heparin) is incorrect because anticoagulation would worsen the patient's coagulopathy and bleeding. Choice C (Oxytocin) is incorrect because while it induces uterine contractions, it can precipitate catastrophic hemorrhage in a coagulopathic patient. Coagulopathy must be corrected first with FFP before addressing labor induction. Choice D (Packed red blood cells) is incorrect because while the patient is anemic, transfusion is typically reserved for hemoglobin <7 g/dL or higher thresholds with end-organ perfusion deficits. More importantly, correcting coagulopathy takes priority over transfusion to prevent further bleeding. Choice E (Platelets) is incorrect because platelet transfusion is indicated when platelet count is <10,000/mm³ without bleeding or <50,000/mm³ with active bleeding or surgery. While this patient has active bleeding, FFP to correct the underlying coagulopathy is the priority intervention. Educational Objective: DIC in pregnancy requires immediate recognition and treatment. The primary intervention is correction of coagulopathy with FFP or cryoprecipitate, followed by identification and treatment of the underlying cause (in this case, likely placental abruption requiring emergent delivery).
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Vulvar Dysplasia and Cancer 1 question
Source: 7A #42
A previously healthy 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of vulvar itching and discomfort despite treatment with over-the-counter antifungal creams. She is sexually active with one male partner. Physical examination shows several 1-cm, small, firm left inguinal lymph nodes. Pelvic examination shows mild edema and excoriations over the labia majora and minora. There is a 1-cm, tender, raised lesion with an ulcerated center and erythematous edges at the base of the left labium majus. The cervix, vaginal mucosa, uterus, and adnexa are normal. There is a white discharge with no odor in the vaginal canal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Condylomata acuminata B) Herpes simplex C) Primary syphilis D) Vulvar carcinoma E) Vulvar dystrophy F) Vulvar vestibulitis
Correct Answer: D) Vulvar carcinoma
Vulvar carcinoma most commonly presents in older patients (age 55-85 years) with a lesion on the labia majora that may be asymptomatic or present with pruritus or bleeding. The lesion may be a nodule, papule, or plaque with varying degrees of ulceration. Physical examination may show inguinal lymphadenopathy if metastasis has occurred, as seen in this patient. The most frequent underlying histopathology is squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors include HPV infection, cigarette smoking, immunosuppression, chronic inflammation (e.g., lichen sclerosus), and history of cervical cancer. Diagnosis is made with biopsy of the lesion. Further evaluation should include cervical cancer screening and abdominopelvic imaging to determine disease extent. Treatment includes surgical excision and chemoradiation. Condylomata acuminata (Choice A) are soft, fleshy, verrucous growths associated with HPV subtypes 6 and 11. They do not typically cause inguinal lymphadenopathy or ulcerated lesions. Herpes simplex (Choice B) presents with painful vesicles that progress to shallow, painful ulcers with erythematous borders. A single, pruritic, raised lesion would be unlikely. Primary syphilis (Choice C) presents with a single, nonpainful chancre. While it may be associated with inguinal lymphadenopathy, the classic lesion is generally nonpruritic. Vulvar dystrophy (Choice E) refers to chronic inflammatory changes caused by lichen sclerosus, dermatitis, or chronic irritation. A single, ulcerated lesion with associated inguinal lymphadenopathy is more suggestive of vulvar carcinoma. Vulvar vestibulitis (Choice F) presents with erythema, inflammation, and hypersensitivity of the vestibule leading to dyspareunia with entry. It would not cause a pruritic, raised lesion on the labia, and this patient has no history of dyspareunia.
▶ Human Development Puberty 1 question
Source: 7A #43
An 11-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her mother is concerned that her daughter is maturing too early. She reports that her daughter has had breast development and pubic hair growth over the last 6 months, and also had the onset of her first menstrual period 2 weeks ago. The mother adds that none of her daughter's friends have begun their menses. The patient is at the 75th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight and BMI. Breast and pubic hair development is sexual maturity rating stage 4. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Precocious puberty B) Premature adrenarche C) Premature menarche D) Premature thelarche E) Normal development
Correct Answer: E) Normal development
Puberty in girls follows a predictable sequence: thelarche (breast development), followed by pubarche (pubic hair growth) and a growth spurt, and finally by menarche (onset of menstruation). This patient is 11 years old and has experienced the normal sequence of pubertal development with appropriate timing. Puberty is considered delayed if breast development does not occur by age 12-13 years, and precocious if it occurs before age 8 years. This patient's development is entirely within normal limits. Precocious puberty (Choice A) is defined as the onset of pubertal development and secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls. It can be central (caused by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with increased FSH and LH, either idiopathic or from CNS abnormalities like brain tumors) or peripheral (caused by excess sex hormone release from gonads or adrenal glands, or ectopic hCG production from germ cell tumors, with decreased FSH and LH). This patient's development at age 11 does not meet criteria. Premature adrenarche (Choice B) includes pubarche and development of secondary sexual characteristics such as axillary hair prior to age 8 years. This patient developed pubic and axillary hair over the last 6 months at age 11, which is not premature. Premature menarche (Choice C) is uncommon and refers to the development of menses without appropriate secondary sexual characteristics. It can be secondary to ovarian cysts or precocious puberty. However, this patient's menstruation followed the appropriate sequence of pubertal events with prior thelarche and pubarche. Premature thelarche (Choice D) typically occurs before age 8 years and may be the first sign of precocious puberty. This patient's thelarche at age 11 is not premature. Educational Objective: Normal puberty follows a predictable sequence of thelarche, pubarche with growth spurt, and menarche occurring after age 8 years. Precocious puberty is defined as pubertal development prior to age 8 years and can be classified as central or peripheral based on hormonal patterns.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection 1 question
Source: 7A #45
A 1900-g (4-lb 4-oz) newborn has generalized lymphadenopathy on examination. She was delivered at term to a 25-year-old primigravid woman. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. The head circumference is below the 5th percentile for gestational age. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 40/min. Funduscopic examination shows chorioretinitis. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Serum studies show AST activity of 247 U/L and ALT activity of 196 U/L. A CT scan of the head shows scattered intracerebral calcifications. Which of the following intrauterine organisms is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Cytomegalovirus B) Hepatitis B virus C) Parvovirus B19 D) Rubella virus E) Treponema pallidum
Correct Answer: A) Cytomegalovirus
Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is the most likely diagnosis based on the clinical presentation. Although CMV is asymptomatic at birth in approximately 90% of newborns, symptomatic cases present with the classic triad of findings seen here: microcephaly (head circumference below 5th percentile), intracerebral calcifications (most often periventricular), and chorioretinitis. Additional features consistent with symptomatic neonatal CMV include hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis (elevated AST and ALT), jaundice, thrombocytopenia, petechiae, lymphadenopathy, seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss. Intrauterine growth restriction is common, and fetal hydrops is a potential complication. The risk for symptomatic infection is higher with primary maternal infection than recurrent infection. Diagnosis is confirmed via PCR testing or culture of urine or saliva. Treatment involves 6 months of oral valganciclovir with close interdisciplinary follow-up. Congenital CMV is the most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss and can present later in childhood in up to 10% of children who were asymptomatic at birth. Hepatitis B virus (Choice B) is transmitted during labor and birth via contact with maternal blood and secretions. Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth but develop insidious-onset chronic liver disease. Symptomatic newborns present with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive, but central nervous system involvement and microcephaly are not consistent with hepatitis B. Parvovirus B19 (Choice C) causes fetal anemia presenting as fetal tachycardia, hydrops fetalis, high-output cardiac failure, and potentially death. However, children who do not develop hydrops fetalis do not suffer long-term infectious sequelae. Central nervous system involvement and microcephaly are more consistent with CMV. Rubella virus (Choice D) classically presents with the triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease, often with a bluish-red rash. Intracerebral calcifications are not a feature of congenital rubella. Treponema pallidum (Choice E) causes congenital syphilis via transplacental transmission in the second and third trimesters. Manifestations include syphilitic rhinitis, rhagades, dental malformations (notched teeth, irregularly shaped molars), and hepatomegaly with or without splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. The presentation timing after birth is variable and does not include the characteristic intracerebral calcifications and chorioretinitis seen with CMV.
▶ Behavioral Health Postpartum Depression With Psychotic Features 1 question
Source: 4A #5
Five weeks after the uncomplicated delivery of her newborn, a 25-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician with concerns about insomnia, restlessness, extreme fatigue, irritability, and depression. She has not been eating well. She finds the baby's crying increasingly annoying and has been letting him cry alone in the crib for long periods of time. She is having difficulty with her memory and ability to concentrate. While her husband has been supportive, she has had difficulty involving him in the care of the baby. She is afraid that she may hurt her child and says that maybe she "would be better off dead." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Reassure the patient that her postpartum "blues" are normal B) Measure serum estradiol concentration C) Prescribe immediate antidepressant therapy D) Refer the patient to a family therapist E) Arrange for an immediate psychiatric evaluation
Correct Answer: E) Arrange for an immediate psychiatric evaluation
This patient presents with major depressive disorder, postpartum onset, with severe symptoms including depressed mood, insomnia, fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, appetite disturbance, anhedonia, and critically, both passive suicidal ideation ("would be better off dead") and homicidal ideation (fear of hurting her child). The presentation occurs 5 weeks postpartum, within the 12-month window for postpartum-onset major depressive disorder. The most appropriate initial management is immediate psychiatric evaluation to assess safety and determine need for psychiatric hospitalization. Choice A is incorrect because postpartum blues is a transient, self-limited condition resolving within 2 weeks and does not include suicidal or homicidal ideation; this patient has major depressive disorder requiring urgent intervention. Choice B is incorrect because measuring estradiol would not change management, as postpartum estrogen replacement remains experimental, and safety concerns must be addressed first. Choice C is incorrect because antidepressants take several weeks to achieve therapeutic effect and do not address the immediate safety risk of suicide and infanticide. Choice D is incorrect because family therapy does not address acute safety concerns and interpersonal dynamics appear minimal in this presentation. Major depressive disorder, postpartum onset, carries severe consequences including impaired bonding, child neglect, developmental delays, suicide, and infanticide, necessitating immediate psychiatric evaluation and potential hospitalization in high-risk situations like this case.
▶ Cardiovascular System Deep Venous Thrombosis 1 question
Source: 4A #10
A moderately obese 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of pain and tenderness in her left thigh for 2 days. She delivered a healthy newborn at term 6 days ago. Examination shows tenderness and swelling over the left thigh and calf. There is pain in the left calf with dorsiflexion of the left foot. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis? A) Doppler flow study B) Duplex venous ultrasonography C) Impedance plethysmography D) Fibrinogen leg scan E) Ventilation-perfusion lung scans
Correct Answer: B) Duplex venous ultrasonography
This patient presents with clinical symptoms concerning for deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the postpartum period. The clinical presentation includes unilateral lower extremity pain, swelling, tenderness on palpation, and pain with passive dorsiflexion of the foot (Homan's sign), all classic findings for DVT. Pregnancy and the postpartum period represent hypercoagulable states due to overexpression of coagulation factors I, II, VII, VIII, IX, and X, while anticoagulant protein S is under-expressed. Additionally, hormonal changes and compression by the gravid uterus lead to venous stasis and pooling of blood in the lower extremities and pelvis, increasing DVT risk throughout pregnancy and postpartum. Duplex venous ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis. It combines Doppler flow imaging with B-mode ultrasonography to provide detailed visualization of venous structures, offering rapid, safe, and sensitive diagnosis of DVT. A patient's pretest probability for DVT and pulmonary embolism can be estimated using Wells criteria to guide further workup. Incorrect choices: Doppler flow study (Choice A) uses ultrasonography to visualize blood movement through the Doppler effect but lacks the detailed structural imaging provided by duplex ultrasonography. Impedance plethysmography (Choice C) measures venous emptying delay after pneumatic cuff release and is less sensitive than duplex ultrasonography, making it non-preferred for DVT diagnosis. Fibrinogen leg scan (Choice D) uses radiolabeled fibrinogen incorporated into thrombi visualized by nuclear scintigraphy but exposes patients to radiation and is not preferred over ultrasonography. Ventilation-perfusion lung scan (Choice E) is the preferred method for diagnosing pulmonary embolism in pregnant patients due to lower fetal radiation risk compared to helical CT, but it is not useful for diagnosing DVT. Educational Objective: Deep venous thrombosis is common during pregnancy and in the postpartum period, which represent hypercoagulable states. Duplex venous ultrasonography is a rapid, safe, and sensitive method for the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Sickle cell disease 1 question
Source: 4A #11
A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. She has sickle cell disease and is concerned about the risk for transmitting this disease to her fetus. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation. Her husband's hemoglobin electrophoresis shows: Hemoglobin A 42% (N=95%-98%), Hemoglobin A2 3% (N=2%-3%), Hemoglobin F 2% (N=0.8%-2%), Hemoglobin S 53% (N=0%). This patient should be counseled that the probability her fetus will have sickle cell disease is closest to which of the following? A) 25% B) 40% C) 50% D) 100% E) No risk
Correct Answer: C) 50%
The probability that this patient's fetus will have sickle cell disease is 50%. Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive condition inherited in a mendelian fashion. Hemoglobin S results from a point mutation in the beta-globin chain whereby valine is substituted for glutamic acid at position six. The resulting combination of two alpha-globin proteins and two sickle cell globin proteins is called HbS and results in a hemoglobin molecule that is poorly soluble when deoxygenated. Under decreased oxygen tension, HbS polymerizes into long hemoglobin structures that distort the erythrocyte into the classic sickle shape. These erythrocytes become lodged in capillaries leading to vascular occlusion and painful sickle cell crises. The patient has two sickle cell beta-globin mutations and thus has sickle cell disease. Her husband's hemoglobin electrophoresis shows elevated HbS (53%), low HbA2 (3%), low HbF (2%), and low HbA (42%), indicating he has sickle cell trait (one abnormal sickle cell beta-globin gene and one normal beta-globin gene). The patient will pass one sickle cell beta-globin to the fetus, and the father has a 50% chance of passing his sickle cell beta-globin mutation. Thus, there is a 50% chance the child will inherit two sickle cell beta-globin genes and have sickle cell disease. Choice A (25%) would be correct if both parents were sickle cell carriers. Choice B (40%) is incorrect because for monoallelic autosomal genes inherited in traditional mendelian fashion, possible probabilities are only 0%, 25%, 50%, or 100%. Choice D (100%) would describe the risk if both parents had sickle cell disease, which would show absent HbA, low HbA2, higher HbF, and very high HbS on the father's electrophoresis. Choice E (No risk) would only occur if neither parent carried a sickle cell mutation or if only one parent was a carrier. Educational Objective: Sickle cell disease is a mutation in both beta-globin genes resulting in abnormal hemoglobin prone to sickling under low oxygen tension. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. When one parent has sickle cell disease and one is a carrier, the probability their child will have sickle cell disease is 50%.
▶ Renal Urinary System Urethral Diverticulum 1 question
Source: 4A #13
A 57-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because of loss of urine for 2 weeks. She now wears an absorbent pad constantly and frequently soaks the pad. All of her children were delivered vaginally with no complications. Three years ago, she received radiation therapy for cervical cancer and has been cancer free since then. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Genitourinary examination shows thin, atrophic, moist vaginal mucosa; there is a pool of fluid in the vaginal canal. Her postvoid residual volume is less than 10 ml. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Overactive bladder B) Overflow incontinence C) Stress incontinence D) Urinary retention E) Urinary tract infection F) Vesicovaginal fistula
Correct Answer: F) Vesicovaginal fistula
Vesicovaginal fistulas can be a consequence of gynecologic surgery, pelvic pathology, or radiation therapy. This patient's history of radiation therapy for cervical cancer 3 years ago is a significant risk factor. A vesicovaginal fistula occurs when a tract opens between the bladder and the vaginal canal, resulting in painless, usually asymptomatic urinary leakage from the vagina. The key clinical finding is a pool of urine in the vaginal canal on genitourinary examination, which this patient demonstrates. The site of fistulization may be too small or difficult to visualize directly. The normal postvoid residual volume (<10 ml) rules out urinary retention and overflow incontinence. The negative urinalysis rules out urinary tract infection. Stress incontinence would be triggered by increases in intra-abdominal pressure and is associated with pelvic floor weakness or prolapse, not radiation therapy. Overactive bladder presents with urge incontinence and frequency/urgency symptoms. Confirmatory testing for vesicovaginal fistula involves infusing dyed sterile fluid into the bladder and evaluating the vagina for transmitted dye. Treatment involves surgical repair.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Cervicitis and Endocervicitis 1 question
Source: 4A #16
A 27-year-old woman who is a long-distance runner comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of postcoital spotting lasting 1 to 2 days. Menses have occurred at regular intervals since menarche at the age of 14 years. She underwent a bilateral tubal ligation 9 months ago. She is sexually active with a new partner. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Blood dyscrasia B) Broad-ligament leiomyomata uteri C) Cervicitis D) Exercise-related menstrual irregularity E) Ovarian cancer F) Polycystic ovarian syndrome G) Pregnancy H) Premature ovarian failure
Correct Answer: C) Cervicitis
Acute cervicitis, or inflammation of the cervix, is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections, specifically Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It can also be caused by herpes simplex virus, bacterial vaginosis, or Trichomonas vaginalis. Cervicitis typically presents with postcoital spotting, purulent vaginal discharge, and dyspareunia, although it may be asymptomatic. Physical examination reveals mucopurulent cervical discharge and punctate hemorrhages of the ectocervix that are friable. Laboratory studies include nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae, as well as testing for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis. Treatment involves antibiotics tailored to the underlying pathogen; C. trachomatis cervicitis requires azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone to cover potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection. Potential complications include pelvic inflammatory disease and endometritis. Choice A (Blood dyscrasia) may increase abnormal bleeding risk but is less likely than infectious cervicitis in a patient with a new sexual partner and no bleeding history. Choice B (Broad-ligament leiomyomata uteri) is an extrauterine fibroid usually asymptomatic and located along the broad ligament; it would not cause postcoital spotting. Choice D (Exercise-related menstrual irregularity) refers to hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis alterations in patients with extensive exercise and low body weight, typically presenting with amenorrhea from anovulation, not postcoital spotting. Choice E (Ovarian cancer) classically presents indolently in older postmenopausal females with abdominal distention and weight loss, not postcoital spotting. Choice F (Polycystic ovarian syndrome) presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses from anovulation secondary to increased androgens, not postcoital spotting. Choice G (Pregnancy) is unlikely given the patient's tubal ligation and continued regular menstrual cycles. Choice H (Premature ovarian failure) is primary hypogonadism in women under 40 characterized by lack of ovarian estrogen production and infertility; it presents with menopausal symptoms like hot flashes and night sweats, not postcoital spotting.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Down Syndrome 1 question
Source: 4A #20
A 17-year-old primigravid patient comes to the physician because she has had decreased fetal movement over the past 2 days. She does not recall the date of her last menstrual period and has had only one previous prenatal visit. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 32-week gestation. Ultrasonography shows a biparietal diameter consistent with a 31-week gestation. There is a duodenal bubble and flaccid tone of the fetus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) B) Down syndrome C) Fetal growth restriction D) Gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome) E) Placental insufficiency
Correct Answer: B) Down syndrome
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common viable chromosomal trisomy, typically caused by meiotic nondisjunction, though it can also result from unbalanced Robertsonian translocation or postfertilization mitotic errors. The clinical presentation includes hypotonia (flaccid tone), downturned palpebral fissures, prominent epicanthal folds, flat facies, single palmar creases, and intellectual disability. Critically, Down syndrome is associated with multiple congenital malformations including duodenal atresia (presenting as a duodenal bubble on ultrasound), atrioventricular septal defects, and Hirschsprung disease. It also increases risk for acute lymphoblastic leukemia and Alzheimer-type dementia. Prenatal diagnosis is typically made via routine ultrasonography showing increased nuchal thickness or second trimester quadruple screening revealing increased β-hCG and inhibin A with decreased α-fetoprotein and estriol. Choice A (Hirschsprung disease) presents with failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension but would not cause duodenal atresia or hypotonia as primary findings. Choice C (Fetal growth restriction) presents with decreased muscle mass and minimal subcutaneous fat but does not cause duodenal atresia or hypotonia. Choice D (Turner syndrome, 45,X) presents with primary amenorrhea, absent secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma, webbed neck, coarctation of the aorta, and bicuspid aortic valve, but is not associated with duodenal atresia or hypotonia. Choice E (Placental insufficiency) causes late decelerations and fetal distress but does not cause duodenal atresia or hypotonia. Educational Objective: Down syndrome is the most common viable chromosomal trisomy presenting with hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and intellectual disability. It significantly increases risk for congenital cardiac and gastrointestinal malformations (particularly duodenal atresia), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and Alzheimer-type dementia. Second trimester quadruple screening shows increased β-hCG and inhibin A with decreased α-fetoprotein and estriol.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Congenital Varicella Zoster Virus Infection 1 question
Source: 4A #24
An 18-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks' gestation delivers a newborn 2 days after developing chickenpox. The pregnancy had been otherwise uncomplicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate care for the newborn? A) Observation for signs of infection B) Acyclovir therapy C) Immune globulin therapy D) Interferon therapy E) Varicella-zoster immune globulin therapy
Correct Answer: E) Varicella-zoster immune globulin therapy
Primary infection with varicella zoster virus (VZV) manifests as chickenpox. Maternal varicella carries a risk for vertical transmission both in utero and perinatally. Infections in early pregnancy can lead to congenital varicella syndrome, characterized by severe birth defects including microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, cerebral cortical atrophy, intellectual disability, seizures, limb hypoplasia, cicatrizing skin lesions, and ocular defects such as microphthalmia, cataracts, or chorioretinitis. Infections in the perinatal period can lead to neonatal varicella, which presents with fever, generalized vesicular rash, and in severe cases, organ involvement including meningoencephalitis, pneumonia, and hepatitis. Newborns of mothers affected by varicella should be given postexposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immune globulin therapy, which reduces severity and can prevent neonatal acquisition of disease, preventing serious or fatal complications. Observation alone (Choice A) is inappropriate as treatment with varicella-zoster immune globulin can reduce severity and prevent disease. Acyclovir therapy (Choice B) is indicated once neonatal varicella symptoms clinically manifest and is not part of routine postexposure prophylaxis. Immune globulin therapy (Choice C) is an acceptable alternative only if varicella-zoster immune globulin is unavailable. Interferon therapy (Choice D) is useful for hepatitis B and C treatment, not commonly used for varicella, and has potentially serious side effects including neutropenia and flu-like illness. Educational Objective: Perinatal vertical transmission of varicella zoster virus can lead to neonatal varicella presenting with fever, generalized vesicular rash, and in severe cases organ involvement including meningoencephalitis, pneumonia, and hepatitis. Exposed newborns should receive postexposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immune globulin.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Anemia of pregnancy 1 question
Source: 4A #26
A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 7 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. She has no history of serious illness, and pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She began taking a prenatal vitamin 3 weeks ago. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dl, Hematocrit 30%, Mean corpuscular volume 72 µm³, Serum Ferritin 110 ng/ml, Iron 130 µg/dl. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) α-Globin DNA testing B) Hemoglobin electrophoresis C) Hemoglobin solubility testing D) Measurement of serum folic acid concentration E) Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration
Correct Answer: B) Hemoglobin electrophoresis
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the most appropriate next step for this patient with microcytic anemia (MCV 72 µm³) and normal iron studies in early pregnancy. While mild hemoglobin decreases are common in pregnancy due to physiologic plasma volume expansion, a hemoglobin concentration less than 10.5 g/dl is abnormal and requires evaluation. Microcytosis can result from iron deficiency, sideroblastic anemia, anemia of chronic disease, and thalassemia. Iron deficiency is ruled out by normal ferritin and serum iron concentrations. Anemia of chronic disease typically presents with normal to high ferritin and low iron. Sideroblastic anemia is rare and would show increased iron, basophilic stippling, and ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain. Hemoglobin electrophoresis can distinguish between α-thalassemia and β-thalassemia variants, which has important implications for both mother and fetus. α-Globin DNA testing (Choice A) is reserved for confirming α-thalassemia trait after hemoglobin electrophoresis, as these patients may have normal electrophoresis results. Hemoglobin solubility testing (Choice C) identifies only HbS in sickle cell disease/trait and would not provide information about other hemoglobin variants. Measurement of serum folic acid concentration (Choice D) is indicated for macrocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia; all pregnant patients should already be taking folate supplements. Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (Choice E) is appropriate for macrocytic anemia and would assess for deficiency seen in gastric bypass, Crohn disease, or pernicious anemia, not the microcytic presentation here. Educational Objective: Decreased hemoglobin in pregnancy is common due to physiologic plasma volume expansion, but concentrations below 10.5 g/dl with microcytosis require further evaluation. After ruling out iron deficiency with normal iron studies, hemoglobin electrophoresis should be performed to assess for thalassemia.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Placenta previa 1 question
Source: 4A #27
A 42-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has tested positive for the factor V Leiden mutation. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated, and she delivered at term by cesarean section for breech presentation. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and has continued to smoke during pregnancy. She does not drink alcohol. She maintains a vegan diet and owns and manages a vegetarian restaurant. She lives at home with her partner and son. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Ultrasonography shows a fetus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation with normal amniotic fluid volume. The placenta is anterior, and the distal portion covers the internal cervical os. Which of the following is the greatest predisposing factor for this patient's findings on ultrasonography? A) Maternal age B) Nutritional status C) Previous cesarean delivery D) Smoking history E) Thrombophilia
Correct Answer: C) Previous cesarean delivery
Placenta previa refers to abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. It is typically detected on routine prenatal ultrasonography, as in this patient. The most common presenting symptom is third trimester painless vaginal bleeding. Risk factors for placenta previa include causes of uterine scarring, such as multiparity, previous cesarean delivery, and prior dilation and curettage. The condition often self-resolves as gestation progresses and the placenta migrates away from the os. If placenta previa persists into the third trimester and at the time of labor, cesarean delivery is indicated to prevent significant hemorrhage, maternal/fetal complications, and potential fetal demise. Maternal age (Choice A) may contribute to risk of placenta previa, fetal trisomy, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and preeclampsia, but previous cesarean delivery is the greatest predisposing risk factor for placenta previa in this patient. Nutritional status (Choice B) increases the risk of fetal malformations, including neural tube defects, but does not significantly alter the risk of placenta previa. Smoking history (Choice D) increases the risk of placenta previa, but not to as great an extent as prior cesarean delivery. Thrombophilia (Choice E), such as in antiphospholipid syndrome, is an important cause of placental ischemic injury, fetal hypoxia, and miscarriage, but is not a risk factor for placenta previa.
▶ Social Sciences Informed consent to treatment 1 question
Source: 4A #31
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 4, at 40 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of bright red vaginal bleeding for 1 hour. Contractions have occurred every 2 to 3 minutes for 5 hours. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Ultrasonography at 22 weeks' gestation showed no evidence of placenta previa. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender abdomen with a firm uterus. The fetal heart rate is 140/min. On speculum examination, there is copious bright red bleeding from the external cervical os. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80% effaced. The physician informs the patient and her husband that emergency cesarean delivery is recommended. The patient and her husband state that, because of their religious beliefs, the elders of their church must agree to a surgical delivery before they can give their consent. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action? A) Ask the patient to convene a meeting of the church elders to discuss cesarean delivery B) Transfer the patient to another physician C) Appoint a guardian ad litem for the fetus to consent to cesarean delivery D) Obtain approval from the hospital administrator to perform emergency cesarean delivery E) Obtain approval from the pediatric staff to perform emergency cesarean delivery
Correct Answer: A) Ask the patient to convene a meeting of the church elders to discuss cesarean delivery
According to the ethical tenet of autonomy, this patient has the right to convene a meeting of the church elders to discuss cesarean delivery and potentially decline the surgery. Patients are assumed to possess decisional capacity unless they demonstrate otherwise. This patient should be assumed to have decisional capacity since she has no cognitive or psychiatric reasons to suggest the absence of capacity. Her husband's agreement supports that the patient is making a decision that is typical for her and does not reflect an absence of decisional capacity. Patients who possess decisional capacity have the ethical right to decline procedures, even if the procedures are emergent and/or involve a fetus. In patients who lack decisional capacity or are unable to communicate a decision about an emergent procedure, the ethical principle of beneficence should prevail, and the physician should save the patient's life.
